en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Having paid homage to Gaṇādhyakṣa, who is Nṛsiṃha united with Kamalā,
[I offer this] which increases the radiance of the intellect and destroys all evil.
To Śambhu, the father, who fulfills all desires and is the source of prosperity; to Satī, Durgā, the very embodiment of fortune; and to the sages beginning with Pāṇini.

For the sake of those with immature intellects, the scholar named Gopāladeva [composed this work] concerning the supreme guru known as Bālabhaṭāṭa, also called Pāyaguṇḍa (or, according to another reading, the supreme one whose secondary name is Pāyaguṇḍa).
The wise younger brother of Kṛṣṇadeva, known in the world by the name Manudvapa,
following the principles of the ancients as well as those of the moderns in their essence,
expands this "Luminosity" (Kānti) for his small *Bhūṣaṇa*.

In order to pacify the obstacles to the undertaking of this work, to instruct the disciples, and for the incidental auspiciousness of the commentator and the listeners, he composes an auspicious invocation consisting of a salutation to the appropriate deity: "Śrī Lakṣmī... and "...rūpam. [The suffix] *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), and not the possessive suffix *in*. For while the suffix *matup* is established by the rule "tadasyāsti" (Pāṇini 5.2.94), the suffix [in question] is added after words such as *rasa* by the rule "rasādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 5.2.95).

Because of the rule *pinaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.95), which prescribes the suffix *matup*, there is a *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) that excludes any other suffix expressing the sense of "possessing" (*tvarthīya*) after words such as *rasa*. For this very reason, there is no need to suspect the redundancy of postulating two distinct grammatical operations (*vṛtti*), since the desired result is already established by the *bahuvrīhi* compound alone. (Note: The portion of the text beginning with "For this very reason" (*ata eva*) and ending with "such is the intention" (*iti bhāvaḥ*) is not found.)

The sense is that, according to his view, even if one assumes two types of *vṛtti* (compound formation)—on the grounds that in common usage there is sometimes disregard for brevity (*lāghava*) and because of the use of the expression *asu-b-vat* in the Bhāṣya—there is no harm. In fact, this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *rasādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.95), which states: "the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* will also be applied after these [words]. By this, the non-difference (*abheda*) between Viṣṇu and Śiva is indicated. Regarding the phrase "of the nature of *sphoṭa*": its true nature is clear elsewhere; it will be analyzed further ahead in the discussion on *sphoṭa*.

"—*vivartate*—" By this, it is stated that the world is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the form of Brahman. For the meaning of the word *vivarta* is an unreal transformation into something else. We shall establish in the section on *sphoṭa* that, in reality, even that [transformation] is indeed something else. "—*śeṣa*—" The meaning is: for the sake of attaining that which is the "remainder," namely, the "entirety" (*aśeṣa*) of objects. "—*dvaita*—" [The compound refers to: duality... [etc.]

(Vi: ‘It is not seen’—it is not perceived. The meaning is that duality (*dvaita*) and the doctrine of duality (*dvaitavāda*) are indeed the thickest darkness (*ghvāntatama*), and the removal of that is the fruit of this [knowledge]; by the word “etc. (*ādi*), liberation and bliss are included. And the state of duality being “thick darkness” is because it is characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding “*pum-bhāve*”: the meaning is the Goddess of Speech (*Vāgdevatā*) who possesses the nature (*bhāva*) of the Person (*pums*). By this, her form as the Puruṣa is also indicated. (Note: *rūpam api* is found in manuscript *ka*; "for other possessive suffixes are seen after words such as *rasa*, etc."—Mahābhāṣya, p. ...).
590 (Dvikha): It is said by Sarasvatī—by means of arguments and logical reasonings.

—0(bhū.sā.dhā.ni. 1)—0 —0 —0 "Phaṇī" (the Serpent) [refers to Patañjali]. His preeminence is due to his being the author of this very treatise (*prakṛta-śāstra*) and his status as the most excellent among sages (*muni*). —2 "By us" (asmābhiḥ)—2 means by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. By this, it is shown that Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita is the author of the root text (*mūla*). For this very reason, he says: —2 "Extracted from the *Śabdakaustubha*"—2. —2 "The fruit" (phala)—2. And its status as a fruit (1. ...).

The result (*phala*) is to be understood as that which possesses a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) determined by a subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) when that root is mentioned in grammatical coordination with an agentive suffix (*kartṛpratyaya*), while also being produced by the meaning of that same verbal root. Furthermore, this "being produced" (*janyatā*) should be understood as being common to both superimposed (*āropita*) and non-superimposed (*anāropita*) states, such as objecthood (*viṣayatva*) and so forth. The inclusion of both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is for the purpose of excluding [the status of] separation (*vibhāga*) and conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as results in cases such as the meaning of the verb *patati* ("falls"), where the falling consists of a conjunction produced by a prior separation. (Note: The portion of the text reading "...vāraṇā nāvalokyate" appears to be a scribal error or corruption and is not included in the translation.)

Since [the term] exists even when uttered in conjunction with the causal condition (*karmapratyaya*), and since the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not denote that which is delimited by it, he says: "But the operation... (verse 2). Here, the verbal root has a distinct power (*śakti*) with respect to both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). Nor should it be argued that there can be no mutual coreferential connection (*anvaya*) because they are presented by a single word; for we accept such connection due to the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), just as in the case of the agenthood and singularity presented by a finite verb suffix (*tiṅ*).

Otherwise, just as the verbal root has the capacity for an operation delimited by a result when used in conjunction with an agentive suffix, it would necessarily have the capacity for a result delimited by an operation when used in conjunction with an objective suffix; this would entail the fault of postulating two capacities whose delimitors of capacity are unnecessarily complex. (1L)

In discourse—[it is argued that] there is no [fault], because the weight of authoritative tradition (*prāmāṇika-gaurava*) is not a defect; therefore, the postulation of two powers (*śakti*) is indeed superior. Otherwise, since it is a general rule (*autsargikatva*) that between two things presented separately there occurs a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in the form of the relation between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), it would follow that even between the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) there would be such a connection, just as there is between the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-artha*) and the oneness of the agent (*kartṛ-ekatva*). Furthermore, it would entail the postulation of two separate causal capacities (*kāraṇatā*) for the cognition of each respective qualifier, based on the presence of the verbal root (*dhātu*) co-occurring with an agent-suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*) and so forth.

"—0ka —0 'As far as accomplished' (ka. vā. pa. III. kriyā. saṃ. kā. 1). 'Yāvat' means 'all'. 'Siddham' (accomplished) refers to cases such as *apākṣīt* (he cooked [in the past]). 'Asiddham' (unaccomplished) refers to cases such as *pacati* (he cooks) and *pakṣyati* (he will cook). Action (*kriyā*) is that which is expressed as being in a state of being accomplished (*sādhyatva*). In expressions such as 'the jar is being made' (*ghaṭaḥ kriyate*), the jar's state of being accomplished is understood precisely through the mediation of the action. The jar..."

This is because the state of being a probandum (*sādhyatva*) is not perceived from this much alone. Regarding the term “*āśritā*” (dependent): this is intended to demonstrate the etymological derivation (*yoga*), meaning that which is being produced—that is, which arises sequentially through its parts. Furthermore, although the whole (*samudāya*) does not directly constitute the object of the action (*kriyā*), it possesses the status of being an object of the action by way of its parts; for the word *kriyā* ends in the suffix *śa*, derived from the root *kṛ* according to the rule *kṛñaḥ śa ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.100), which denotes the object (*karman*).

And thus, the intended meaning is that "action-ness" (*kriyātva*) culminates in being that which is intended to be produced by means of the successive production of its constituent parts. This is the sense. [The sequence is: *pacati*—*pāka*—*iti*. In expressions such as *pacati*, there is no observation of an expectancy for another action; likewise, in expressions such as *pāka*, there is no observation of an expectancy for another action. This is the connection [of the words], though presented out of order. And so it is. (2V1.1)

And thus: the action conveyed by the word *pacati* (‘cooks’), which does not require another action to complete its sense, possesses that specific form which serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) for such an action; or rather, it possesses that specific generic quality (*vaijātya*) residing in the action which serves as the delimitor of its capacity to not require another action. This constitutes the consistency of the definition.

Nor should it be argued that, if an action were presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*) through its generic nature as an "enabler" (*nirūpakatva*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of non-connection due to a lack of expectancy (*anākāṅkṣatā*) in cases such as "If one should bow to Kṛṣṇa, he would attain happiness," because expectancy arises by virtue of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *cet*. The same should be inferred for words such as *yat* and so forth, just like the co-occurrence of the suffix *ktvā* and others which is prescribed when there is a connection between verbal roots. And [this applies to] the state of having expectancy for another action... [4. Vi.]

And "expectancy for another action" (*kriyāntarākāṅkṣatva*) means the incapacity to produce verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) without the presentation of an action as an action (*kriyātvena*). By this, there is no loss [of the definition] in cases such as "see, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*) or "he is cooking" (*pacati bhavati*), regarding the running action and the action of becoming, which possess the states of being a goal (*sādhyatva*) and being an existent entity (*asattvabhūtatva*). However, some, setting aside the inclusion of an action by way of its being an action, maintain that what must be refined as that [definition] is simply a specific generic property (*vaijātya*) that serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the non-arising of expectancy for another action.

In examples such as *āsa* ("was"), in order to exclude both the state of being a goal (*sādhyatva*) and the state of being a past event (*bhūtatva*), the term "internal" (*antara*) is used, which signifies a different kind of meaning; that is, an expectancy for a different kind of existence (*vijātīyāstitvākāṅkṣā*). Furthermore, in order to avoid the defect of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *pacati*, *bhavati*, and *asti*, the expectancy must be defined in the same manner as previously stated. However, in the case of "Look at the deer" (*paśya mṛge*), there is no fault even according to the literal sense.

The point is this: if "the state of not being a substance" (asattvabhūtatva) is defined as "the state of being connected with gender, number, and case-role," then that definition would be contradicted; for in the two aforementioned verbal forms (*nirukta-kriye*), one observes respectively the connection with the status of object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*), and in examples such as *hataśāyikāḥ śayyante* ("those who were killed are lying down"), one observes the connection with number. If, however, it is defined as "the state of not being connected with a case-role other than agent or object," then there is indeed excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Some, however, having accepted this complexity out of necessity, say the same thing in different words: "the state of not being connected with a case-role that is not a locus of the action. As it has been said:
"Action is not logically possible through gender, action, substratum, or grammatical factors;
its nature is non-substantiality—this alone should be understood. (Vākyapadīya).

In this context, the word *kāraka* refers to "capacity" (*śakti*). Among the *kārakas* that serve as the substrata of action, only the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) [are primary]; the meaning is that [the comparison] is with *kārakas* other than those, such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth. Others maintain that "being non-substantial" (*asattvabhūtatva*) consists precisely in the lack of connection with gender and number. In reality, however, "non-substantiality" is simply the incomparability of the action. For this very reason, in examples such as "he reads as if he were weeping," there is no simile; it does not apply to the agents, because they are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) in relation to the action. Rather, words such as *iva* are suggestors of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). For this very reason—[referring to the rule] "san" (Pāṇini 3.2.127)—[the suffix is applied].

3-1-7) [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.7]: *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ samānakartṛkādicchāyāṃ vā*. Regarding this sūtra, the author of the Bhāṣya states: "Indeed, there is no comparison with that which ends in a finite verb (*tiṅanta*)" (Mahābhāṣya, Vol. II, p. 27). On this point, Kaiyaṭa says that the word *iva* is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). However, the status of being the object of comparison (*upameyatva*) certainly belongs to the action, since such a perception occurs in examples such as "he studies like a Brāhmaṇa."

For this very reason, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra "luṅ for the non-recent past" (*anadyatane luṅ*, Pāṇini 3.3.15; MaBh II, p. 210), having raised the objection as to how the suffix *luṭ* can occur in examples such as "When will she go, who walks with her feet thus?"—which refer to a future action of the recent past—the [proponent] offers the resolution that "she goes as if she were going. However, having refuted this by stating, "Indeed, there is no comparison with a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*)," he provides the following solution: "The non-recent past is like the recent past."

If it is argued that in passages such as, "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey], so does he, by means of the Śyena sacrifice, swooping down, seize his hateful rival whom he seeks to harm," there certainly exists a relationship of similarity (*upamānopameyabhāva*) between the act of seizing performed by the hawk and the act of seizing performed by the sacrificer—this is not so. For, since the word *yathā* denotes a specific qualifying attribute that serves to differentiate, after the cognition arises—"The seizing by the hawk, which possesses the manner (*prakāra*) of [seizing] a bird, is similar in manner to the seizing by the sacrificer of his enemy"—[the comparison is established].

By taking that very property which constitutes the mode of differentiation (*prakāra*), or by taking the act of grasping (*ādāna-kriyā*) prompted by it, the comparison is understood through *abhidhāna-mūla-vyañjanā* (suggestion rooted in denotation) as "the sacrificer, who is distinct from the hawk, is the object of comparison. Thus, both [the hawk and the sacrificer] possess verbal status (*śābdatva*) alone. However, if the cognition of the simile were to occur first through the two actions themselves, a contradiction with the aforementioned Bhāṣya would arise. Nor can it be argued that for the two agents (*kartṛ*) as well, that [simile] is impossible even in the second stage of cognition because they are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). For that very reason, it is not the case that it cannot occur even when those two are cognized in the second instance.

Understand that this is because there is no obstacle whatsoever to the cognition of the suffix *thāl* as expressing similarity (*vaiyañjanika-bodha*). However, for those who claim that *thāl* has the meaning of similarity (*sādṛśya*), the cognition "Hara is like Hari" would not arise even from the sentence "That which is similar to Hari, that is similar to Hara," nor would it arise from "As is Hari, so is Hara. Otherwise, similarity would not be established in cases such as "in every way" (*sarvathā*). For me, however, [the rule] "The suffix *thāl* is used in the sense of a mode (*prakāra*)" (Pāṇini 5.3.23) applies.

In the rule *Pāṇini 5.3.23*, because of the inclusion of the term "vacana" (word), the suffix *thāl* denotes a manner (*prakāra*). Thus, in the cognition "Hari possesses that same manner as Hari," the subsequent understanding occurs according to the method described above. For this very reason, even the *alaṅkārikas* (rhetoricians) cite examples such as "He smears [the limbs] as it were" (*limpatīva*) as instances of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). This is the general direction [of the argument]. (Daṇḍin’s *Kāvyādarśa*, second chapter, verse 226: "The darkness smears the limbs as it were; the sky rains collyrium as it were.
—2— "This very thing" means the aforementioned state of being an abstract entity (*asattvabhūtatva*).

"—by *tiṅ* words"—this means by words in which action (*kriyā*) is predominant. Consequently, there is no failure to include under this category those forms treated as *ākhyāta*—such as *edhitavyam* and others ending in *kṛtya* suffixes expressing a state (*bhāva*)—on the strength of the Nirukta definition accepted by the author of the Bhāṣya: "The *ākhyāta* is that in which action is predominant" (Nirukta 1.1.1). Alternatively, the phrase "by *tiṅ* words" simply means "by words ending in *tiṅ*."

Even for words conventionally treated as verbal roots, such as *edhitavyam* ("it is to be increased"), we observe a requirement for another action such as "to exist" (*asti*) or "to be" (*bhavati*); therefore, they do not possess the status of being a process (*sādhyatva*) or a state of existence (*sattvabhūtatva*). For this very reason, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of case-factors (*kāraka*) with their meaning. The conventional designation of them as "primarily denoting action" (*kriyāpradhāna*), however, is due to the fact that they serve solely as qualifiers of an action. In reality (*vastutas*), "being a process" (*sādhyatva*) is simply the state of being brought about (*niṣpādyatva*), understood from the verbal root precisely in that form. And it is precisely this [state] that serves as the basis for the connection of case-factors.

In cases such as *hiruk* and others, because they signify exclusion (*varjana*) and are not themselves verbal suffixes (*pratyaya*), there is no syntactic connection with a *kāraka*. However, in cases such as *edhitavyam*, because it is understood as having the nature of a verbal root (*dhātutva*), there is a connection with a *kāraka*. Even in cases such as *pacatikalpam*, the action is perceived precisely as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*). Thus, the distinctness (*vaijātya*) mentioned in the root-text as the cause for the connection with a *kāraka* is not tenable; for there is no evidence for accepting a distinctness that consists of the cumbersome expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as previously defined.

Furthermore, in cases such as "one should bow to Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ namet*), by the force of the particle *ca*, there would be no possibility of that [infinitive] connecting with the case-role (*kāraka*). Also, there would be a fault in examples such as "it is to be prospered" (*edhitavyam*) and "he cooks somewhat" (*pacatikalpam*). However, in instances like "Devadatta cooks somewhat" (*pacatikalpaṃ devadattaḥ*), the understanding [of Devadatta] should be grasped as being in a state of qualification toward the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). As for the cognition of non-difference (*abheda*), however, because the suffix is merely indicative (*dyotaka*) and the action is primary, the cognition of the word ending in the suffix [as a whole] is sublated.

Regarding the phrase "of the name and the object," its meaning is "of the object which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the cognition produced by the name. Now, one might object: if the verbal root (*dhātu*) in general denotes action (*vyāpāra*) in general, then the cognition of every single action would follow from the mere verbal root alone. To this, he says: "And this... [referring to the following]. "In that respective form" (*tattadrūpeṇa*). Here...

The statement of Hari, "Non-difference is mentally constructed" (*Vākyapadīya*, Tṛtīyakāṇḍa, Kriyāsamuddeśa 4), is also an authoritative proof. This is because the difference among the constituent parts, such as blowing and so forth, is perceived within the aggregate [of those parts]. Furthermore, that discourse on non-difference would be of no consequence if the operation were not perceived through the verbal root in its respective forms, such as "blowing" (*phūtkāra*) and so on. By this, the view that "the nature of being an action" (*kriyātva*) is the delimiting factor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is refuted. [Regarding the phrase] "in each respective verbal root": it is thereby stated that "the state of having cooked" (*pācitva*) and so forth alone is the delimiting factor of the denotable capacity.

By this, the view that "the state of being a *dhātu* (verbal root) is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)" is also refuted. With the intention that "polysemy (*nānārthatva*) consists in having multiple delimiters of denotative capacity while [otherwise] having a single delimiter of denotative capacity," he raises an objection: "And not... (2). With the intention that "it is polysemy when there is a single delimiter of denotative capacity despite there being a common [anugata] delimiter of denotative capacity," he provides the resolution: "...is not seen" (2). He resolves it with: "In the case of 'tat' and so forth" (2).

The word "that" (*tad*) and so forth has its denotative power (*śakti*) grasped as signifying that which is delimited by the property of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), etc., as characterized by being the object of a [unifying] cognition (*buddhi*). Because the delimiting factor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedakatā*) exists as being delimited by the property consisting in being the object of a unifying cognition—which serves as the common denominator for pot-ness, cloth-ness, and so on—there is unity of the denotative power. This is just like the unity of the denotative capacity delimited by the common property of "pot-ness" with respect to various individual pots.

[The word "pot" does] not appear as having the individual pot as its object; however, this is the distinction: in that case, because one experiences a cognition qualified by "potness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, those [universals] such as "potness" possess the status of being objects of the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) by way of being the delimitors of the subjecthood (*dharmitāvacchedakatva*), and they also possess the status of qualifiers (*prakāratva*) by way of being objects within the cognition that is the locus of the power. But as for "being present in the intellect" (*buddhisthatva*), since it does not manifest in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it possesses the status of an object by way of being the delimitor of the delimitor of subjecthood (*dharmitāvacchedakatāvacchedakatva*).

[The delimitor] is not observed; it is neither the object of the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*), nor does it possess such a mode of presentation (*prakāratva*). Thus, being an object of cognition (*buddhiviṣayatva*) is merely an adventitious indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). But then, how is there sometimes a cognition [of an object] as "being present in the mind" (*buddhisthatvena*)? Because that very "being present in the mind" is itself indicated as an adventitious indicator by way of its own "being present in the mind. For this very reason, from words such as *tad* ("that"), there is sometimes the cognition "the jar," and sometimes "the possessor of the universal" (*jātimān*).

"Sometimes... the pot possessing the universal [of potness] is not perceived. This means that sometimes there is the cognition "the pot possessing the universal," and sometimes there is the cognition "the pot residing in the mind. Nor should it be suspected that this leads to the collapse of the theory of multiple meanings (nānārtha), because even the delimiters of the referents of the word *hari*—such as Indra-ness and so forth—which are intended to have multiple meanings, would be subsumed under the common factor of "residing in the mind."

From that point onward, according to the method described, a single entity is experienced as being understood in various forms from all nouns; this is not the case with words such as *hari* due to the specific nature of their verbal power (*śabdaśakti*). Therefore, it is clear that from those [words], there is never an understanding following the sequence "the genus-possessor *hari*" and so forth—as stated in the *Śaktivāda* composed by Bhaṭṭācārya (Ka. Śaktivādaḥ – Viśeṣakāṇḍam, p. 91).

In reality, because there is an absence of specific cognition regarding those properties such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), it is impossible to grasp the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) for them in their respective forms; consequently, since such a comprehension is impossible, the potency of words like *tat* does not reside in that which is delimited by "pot-ness" as characterized by being an object of cognition. Rather, the potency of *tat* and so forth resides in the object of cognition simply by virtue of its being an object of cognition. Furthermore, everything is indeed comprehended solely through its status as an object of cognition. For this very reason, [the rule] "tasyāpatyam" (Pāṇini 4.1.92).

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *tasyāpatyam* (Pāṇini 4.1.92), at Mahābhāṣya Vol. II, p. 370, a doubt is raised: "In the case of a reference by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), there is no cognition of a specific [referent] because it is a general reference; consequently, the suffix would arise from that very word *tat* alone. Having raised this objection, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached as follows: since the word *apatya* (offspring) requires a specific related entity [as its qualifier], even when it is stated "the offspring of that" (*tasyāpatyam*), the requirement for specification is not satisfied. Therefore, because it is impossible for *tat* and the like to function as qualifiers for the offspring, the suffix arises from a word that denotes a specific instance of that [offspring].

For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *tasminniti* (Pāṇini 1.1.66), it is stated: "This is an indication by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and a pronoun denotes a universal (*sāmānya*). From both parts of the *Bhāṣya*, it is understood that the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*) is precisely the universal characterized by being the object of a comprehensive cognition; however, in your statement, the contradiction with this *Bhāṣya* is quite evident. Furthermore, you have undertaken such great effort to exclude polysemy in words like *tad* and so forth, yet that too has already been excluded by my own method, which is more concise; so, enough!

Now, one might ask: "What is the determining factor (*vinigamaka*) for the claim that 'being present in the intellect' (*buddhisthatva*) is the common property (*anugamaka*) of *phūtkāratva* (the nature of blowing) and the rest? To this he says: "Because of the unity of the action" (*kriyaikatve*). Since it would otherwise be impossible to account for the linguistic usage of "a single action" (*ekākriyā*) with respect to various operations delimited by *phūtkāratva* and so on, one must accept that "being present in the intellect" is the common property of *phūtkāratva* and the rest. And that very same property is also the common property of the objects of the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*). For there is no evidence (*aprāmāṇikatva*) for a lack of commonality in the object-referentiality when the objects themselves are common.

Otherwise, because the objecthoods (*viṣayatā*) of [objects] such as a pot would not be uniform, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an infinite number of powers (*śakti*). In reality, since in cases such as "the wood cooks" (*kāṣṭaṃ pacati*) or "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*), there is a cognition of merely those respective specific operations, it is precisely intended that [the root *pac*] has multiple meanings (*nānārthatva*), just like words such as *hari*; thus, this effort [to establish a single power] is in vain—this is how it should be understood. Regarding the phrase "by those which have become subordinate" (*guṇabhūtaiḥ*): (Vākyapadīya III, Kriyā).

4) Of those [actions] arising in succession—meaning those produced sequentially and possessing the aforementioned functions—the aggregate (*samūha*) is joined with its own parts, which are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to such an aggregate and appear in their respective forms. Now, one might object that an aggregate of parts that perish in each moment is impossible; therefore, he says: "by the intellect" (*buddhyā*). The meaning is that, being of a nature fabricated as non-different by the unifying intellect (*saṃkalanātmikā ekatva-buddhi*), it is conventionally designated as "action."

In this context, it should be understood that sequence (*paurvāparya*) is based on the parts (*avayava*), while unity (*ekatva*) is based on the whole (*samudāya*). Even though the meaning of the roots *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyati*—namely, existence (*sattā*)—is one, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) upon it of the sequence belonging to multiple points of time that underlie it; thus, its possession of sequence is established, and consequently its status as action (*kriyātva*) is proven.

Alternatively, the roots *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyati* have as their meaning the operation directed toward existence (*sattā*). And existence is that nature which is perceived by the cognition "it is" (*sad*), which runs through all things from the six modifications of being onwards. The operation directed toward that object is expressed by the terms "self-sustenance" (*ātmabharaṇa*) and "maintenance of one's own form" (*svasvarūpadhāraṇa*). Here, "self" (*ātman*) and "own form" (*svarūpa*) are indeed existence itself; and in this context, it consists of a gross form.

For at the time of death, there is the perception of an activity conducive to abandoning that [body], whereas here, by contrast, there is the perception of an activity conducive to maintaining it; and this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sūtra* "bhūvādī" (Pāṇini 1.3.1). (Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. ...).

116) However, in cases such as "the jar does not come into being" (*aghaṭo bhavati*) where the verbal root *bhū* and others have the sense of origination (*utpatti*), the meaning is an operation conducive to origination; and this operation, ultimately, is nothing other than the substratum itself. This is clear from the root text of the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-kārikā*, specifically in verses 14 (*sādhyatvenābhidhīyamāne*) and 12 (*astyādāvapi*). Furthermore, this will be demonstrated in that very same place.

Now, since the nature of *āśrayatva* (substratum-hood)—which consists of a specific relation of identity (*svarūpasambandha*)—is manifold because it takes the form of various substrata, such as that which is the locus of the fruit (*phala*) or the locus of the operation (*vyāpāra*), [the author] says: "it has the form of those respective powers. This means it has the form of indivisible properties (*akhaṇḍadharma*) such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and instrumentality (*karaṇatva*). Furthermore, even though the relata that define the substratum differ, that power is one and the same; therefore, the statement by Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra *gatyarthaloṭi* (Pāṇini 8.1.51) should be disregarded, as it contradicts the sūtra *saptamīpañcamyau kārakamadhye* (Pāṇini 2.3.7) and its Bhāṣya.
Therefore, it should be understood that although she is divided by those various differences, she is nevertheless followed through as the agent.

"What is the proof?"—to this, it should be supplemented that "there is no cognition [of it as] a means of knowledge. He states [the view] according to the Mīmāṃsaka doctrine: "by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Their position is that there is a primary denotative power (śakti) regarding number and so forth, while there is secondary indication regarding the substratum. He states [the view] according to the doctrine of Arthāpatti (Presumption): "by way of implication (ākṣepāt). The sense is that without an agent, activity and so forth would be impossible. He states [the view] according to the Naiyāyika doctrine: "or from a word ending in the nominative case"—meaning that the Sūtra itself is the proof.

—2evaḥ—2 (Mahābhāṣya, Tṛtīyakhaṇḍa, p. 333: "Because *tiṅ* and *kṛt* suffixes denote a single substance"). Or, even regarding a well-known meaning: "A single substance is denoted by two *tiṅ* suffixes," and so forth; the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "In the case of a *loṭ* suffix with a sense of motion" (Pāṇini 8.1.51) is also authoritative evidence. If it is objected: "Even if this results in obtaining [the suffix as] referring to the substratum (*dharmiparatva*), it does not result in obtaining [the suffix as] referring to the power (*śaktiparatva*)," we say no—because of the non-difference between power and the possessor of power (*śakti-śaktimatoḥ abhedāt*). That very [power] is the meaning of the suffix.

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa states in his commentary on the sūtra *sārvadhātuke yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.67): "The suffix [yak] denotes the power itself as having attained non-difference from the power that possesses it, by means of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) and others which signify the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth. (Mahābhāṣya, Vol. II, p. 91).

Now, since in the view of the Grammarian who maintains the theory of *sphoṭa*, it is only the substitutes (*ādeśas*) that possess denotative power, how can there be meaning for the verbal suffixes (*lakāras*)? To this he says: "in the form of being a signifier" (*bodhakatārūpām*). That they possess that nature will be explained later. "By virtue of being their substituends" (*tatsthānitvena*) means by virtue of being the substituends of *ti* and so forth. "Residing in the visarga, etc. (*visargādiniṣṭhā*) means the meaning resides even in that which ends in or begins with them. He raises an objection from the perspective of the Naiyāyika:

—2 *na ca* —2. When used in conjunction with an agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an operation distinct from the result; the meaning of the finite verb suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is volition (*kṛti*); and the substratum (*āśraya*) is obtained from the word ending in the nominative case. When used in conjunction with an objective suffix (*karmapratyaya*), the operation is the meaning of the verbal root; the result is the meaning of the finite verb suffix; and the substratum is obtained from the word ending in the nominative case. However, in the case of forms such as *caitreṇa*, it is their view that [the substratum] is obtained as the meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārthatayā*). —2 *ayogāt* —2. The sense is that volition (*kṛti*) is also a specific type of operation. He raises an objection according to the view of Miśra:

"—2abheti-2||" In this view, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the mere result (*phalamātra*), and the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*). And it is precisely because [the agent] is the substratum (*āśraya*) of that [operation] that Devadatta and others possess the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*). "—2kṛtāmapīti-2 ||" Even in that case, the intention is that the word "agent" (*kartrādi*) would consequently come to mean "non-agent" (*akartṛtva*) and so forth.

Now, one might object that the grammatical rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) is the authority for [the suffixes] having the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). To this, he says: "In the case of the agent" (*kartari*). Because of the governing context of the meaning (*arthādhikāra*), it must be stated that even in the preceding rule *kartari kṛt*, the word *kartṛ* refers to the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*). Regarding the phrase "acquisition and preservation" (*yogakṣema*): acquisition (*yoga*) is the obtaining of what has not been obtained; preservation (*kṣema*) is the protection of what has been obtained.

Now, one might object: "Since the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression ‘The village is Devadatta’ requires that [the word] be accepted as denoting the agent, [this view must be correct]. Anticipating this unease, he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*). Having refuted the position of the logicians and others who maintain that [the verbal root] has effort (*yatna*) as its meaning, [he proceeds]. (The portion from "principally" (*prādhānyena*) up to "by that" (*tayā*) is not found in the manuscript.)

He refutes the view of the Mīmāṃsakas with the words: "of the Mīmāṃsakas and others," and "of the *bhāvanā* alone. This [latter] alone is correct. For, having accepted that the *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), if the agent were merely implied by that action, then—since there is a rule that case-factors (*kāraka*) must be connected to an action—other factors would also necessarily be implied. Consequently, the third case endings and so forth, which signify instruments and other such factors, would result in being redundant.

In my view, however, the agent is connected only with the *bhāvanā* (the efficient force of action) and not with any other *kāraka*, according to the maxim "of subordinate elements" (*guṇānām*). Therefore, there is no implication (*ākṣepa*) of [other] causal factors. [Otherwise], the use of the instrumental case and so forth to denote that [agent] would be redundant. Furthermore, if the agent were obtained through implication, the connection of singularity and so on as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) with respect to it would not occur, because it would not be directly expressed by the word (*aśābdatvāt*).

Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) which states, "The *la*-suffixes [denote] the object" (Pāṇini 3.4.69). As for the argument that because the denotation [of the suffix] is invariably connected with the agent, it implies only the agent and not the instrument and so forth, and thus the suffixes denoting them are not redundant—that is not correct. For in cases such as *tiṣṭhati* ("he stands"), even in the absence of an instrument and so forth, since there exists a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) such as the ground, it would follow that this locus is implied; consequently, the locative case and others used to denote it would become redundant. Moreover, in examples such as *ātmanā*, the instrument is indeed possible.

Furthermore, even if it is argued that [the number] is obtained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by way of its connection with the number of the agent—the meaning of the suffix *-ti*—this would contradict the maxim that "that which is connected to the primary meaning is the verbal meaning" (*śābdī*). For this very reason, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "Devadatta cooks" is established. Otherwise, according to your own view—that the agent is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)—coreferentiality would not be possible.

[The opponent argues: "Because the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes the agent (*kartṛ-kāraka*) as a mere power (*śakti-mātra*) extracted [from its substrate], just like the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), since a substance possessing that power is not denoted according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.9, Mīmāṃsā-śāstra-bhāṣya, p. 229). This too is incorrect; for there is no evidence for resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) while abandoning the power established by the Sūtras, Bhāṣya, and other authorities in the sense of the agent. Furthermore, even if only the power is denoted, since there is non-difference between the power and the possessor of the power (*śaktimat*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible without recourse to figurative indication.

By this, the argument that—given the resulting lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding whether the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is what is expressed—the fact that the word for the agent (*kartṛpada*) refers to *kṛti* (the effort to act) according to the stated method serves as the deciding factor—is refuted. This is because it contradicts the Bhāṣya statement, “A substance is denoted by both [the suffixes] tiṅ and sup” (Mahābhāṣya, Trilakṣaṇī-khaṇḍa, p. 333), and because that [rule] is not universally applicable, as evidenced by the rule: “When there is a loṭ [imperative] with a verb meaning ‘to go,’ the lṛṭ [future] does not occur, provided the case-role (*kāraka*) is not entirely different” (Pāṇini 3.3.156).

Even though the word *kartṛ* (agent) has that [individual] sense in rules prescribing the third case, such as "kartṛkaraṇayoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.18), there is no evidence for the word *kartṛ* having that same sense in rules such as "kartari kṛt" (Pāṇini 3.4.67). Furthermore, by the authority of the Bhāṣya—such as "the form (*ākṛti*) is not the meaning of the word, nor is the substance (*dravya*) the meaning of the word," and "of those [words] having the same form, one remains when there is a single case-ending" (1.2.64)—it is established that the qualified entity alone is the denotation. This is the direction [of the argument]. As for the phrase "like *kṛt*-suffixes, etc."—
The sense is: just as in the case of *kṛt* suffixes and the like, an expectation (*ākṣepa*) is projected by the agent, so too should it be here.

He raises an objection: "If that were so... The underlying sense is that [the individual] is not the meaning of the suffix because it has already been implied (*ākṣiptatvāt*). Regarding the phrase "of the individual implied" (*ākṣiptavyakteḥ*): the sense is that, since it was established by them in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.9; Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, p. 229) that "the expressive power resides in the genus alone," they accept that the cognition of the individual occurs only through implication. He raises another objection: "In the case of 'he cooks' (*pacati*)," and "even of the agent."

Because the word *pacati* is explained by such expressions as *pākaṃ karoti* ("he performs cooking") and *pācaka* ("a cooker"). Regarding the phrase "the portion consisting of conjunction" (*samuccayāṃśa*): in examples such as *dhavakhadirau* ("the dhava and khadira trees"), the portion consisting of the meaning of the word *ca* (conjunction)—meaning "the dhava and the khadira"—is illustrated by the expansion [of the compound] as *dhavaśca khadiraśca*. It should be understood that this follows that specific method of explanation and not the established philosophical position (*siddhānta*). This is because, according to that [established] position, since *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) is what will be maintained as the defining characteristic of a compound (*vṛtti*), the meaning of the word *ca* is absent [in the compound].

"Because of their equality"—this is the explanation. The meaning is that it is possible to say that the agent is the explanation of the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*) and that the *bhāvanā* is the explanation of the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*), as both are equally [capable of being so]. [Objection: But if this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*apatti*) of the destruction of the capacity of explanation to convey word-meanings in all cases; with this unease, he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*). Otherwise, even when someone else is cooking, the usage "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*) would result. "And that" (*tac ca*)—the meaning is that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consisting in having the same case-ending (*samānavibhaktikatva*) is the proof for the fact that the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) denotes the agent.

The meaning of "in such cases as [the verse beginning with] 'ityādau'" is that there is an absence of the aforementioned grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the noun and the verbal root, as well as between "king" and "servant. The meaning of "by means of Soma" (*somena*) is that there is an absence of coreferentiality in the form of having identical case endings. Therefore, opponents must admit that there is no direct syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between two nominal meanings that lack coreferentiality except through a relation other than difference; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

"—2By indication—2. This is an elliptical expression for "indication," "implication," and so forth. Thus, the meaning of the objection is this: since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible by taking the agent implied by the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), this [argument] does not prove that the suffix denotes the agent. "—2In the case of *piṅgākṣī* etc.—2. In the analysis "she whose eyes are tawny" (*piṅge akṣiṇī yasyāḥ*), because a compound is prescribed in the sense of the genitive by the rule "several words [form a compound] when another word-meaning is to be expressed" (*anekam anyapadārthe*, Pāṇini 2.2.24), the resulting meaning would be merely "connection with tawny eyes."

Therefore, because of the requirement for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "cow" and so forth, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) situated in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*—that the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi* compound is a related entity (*sambandhin*) implied by the relation—is inconsistent. The sense is that grammatical coreferentiality is established only by taking the related entity obtained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) from the word expressing the relation; thus, [the relation] exists only in the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*).

Regarding the term *anyapadārtha*—wherein "pada" refers to a word ending in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), and within that word, the meaning of the suffix is predominant—the phrase "in the meaning of another word" (*anyapadārthe*) signifies the object that is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the cognition produced by the word; thus, its meaning is "that which is distinct from the meanings of the constituent members" (*vartipadārthabhine*). The sense is that the predominance of the meaning of the relationship (*sambandha*) [of the compound] is obtained through grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*), as is the case with the *bahuvrīhi*.

"—because the substance has not been mentioned. And this is the reason for the consequence of [the word's] annihilation. "—of the formless (ārūpya)—" because, according to that view, the meaning of a word is the universal (jāti) alone. "—in the case of a substance already denoted, such as a cow—" by means of the implication (ākṣepa) of the related [quality], according to the aforementioned method. "—it has been explained in detail"—if the verbal suffix (tiṅ) were the meaning of the productive operation (bhāvanā), then since the agent would not be expressed by the suffix, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the instrumental case for the agent in the sentence "pacati caitreṇa" ("Caitra cooks").

Nor should it be argued that, in order to avoid contradiction with the traditional rule *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), the statement *laḥ karmaṇi* is interpreted as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with *dvye-kayoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.22), such that its meaning becomes "the *l*-suffix occurs when there is singularity residing in the agent"; and that, by implication, the rule *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1) also means "when singularity residing in the agent is not already expressed," thereby preventing the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) because singularity has already been denoted.

Because the designation of "singular" (*ekavacana*) and so forth resides in the substitute (*ādeśa*), and since that [designation] is absent in the *lakāra*, the aforementioned syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is impossible. Furthermore, in cases such as *pacan devadattaḥ*, there would result the undesirable consequence of number being expressed by the suffix *śatṛ* and others as well. Even if there were syntactic unity with the rule *tiptasjhi* (Pāṇini 3.4.78), there is no word therein that conveys the meaning of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth. If it is argued that the third case ending is thus excluded through the aforementioned method by virtue of the three rules forming a single syntactic unit, even so, the third case ending would undesirably apply in instances such as *kartā devadattaḥ*.

Nor should it be argued that the meaning of *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1) is "when the agent and so forth have not been expressed," and that since the expression of the agent and so forth occurs through the power of the *kṛt* suffix (*kṛti*) or by implication (*ākṣepa*) when a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is present, there is no room for the aforementioned fault. For this is untenable, as it contradicts the experience that [the agent] is "verbally expressed" (*śābdāyām*). Furthermore, if the agent were merely implied (*ākṣipta*) rather than verbally expressed (*śābda*), its connection with verbal number would be impossible. Moreover, all forms of implication (*ākṣepa*) will be refuted later on. Nor should it be argued that by the rule *anabhihite*, what is intended is the non-expression of the *kṛt* function.

In the rule *kartari kṛti* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), although the word *kartṛ* (agent) refers to the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix, there is no evidence that the word *kartṛ* in the rule *kartṛkaraṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.18) has that same referent; furthermore, it would be impossible for it to connect with the rule *kṛt-anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1). Therefore, it should also be understood that if the *bhāvanā* were the meaning of the *tiṅ* suffix, the aforementioned undesirable consequence of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) would indeed be firmly established. This is the statement regarding its denotative function (*vācakatva*). In the original text, in the phrase *phale*, the meaning of the locative case is "being characterized by" (*nirūpitatva*). He states this as follows:

"—2 *phalaṃ prati* -2. And this [is understood] when there is co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a verbal suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ-pratyaya*). For, in cases of co-utterance with a verbal suffix denoting the object (*karma-pratyaya*), such as in the word "uncooked" (*apakva*), it will be explained later that the fruit alone possesses primacy with respect to the operation (*vyāpāra*). It should be understood that for this very purpose, a separate potency (*śakti*) was stated for the fruit and the operation, and not for an operation delimited by a fruit; this was established previously. "—2 *kartari* -2. By a change of number (*vacanavyatyaya*), the term "qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa*) is supplied [to the word *kartari*]. The same applies further on as well.

"—because they are introduced by a common cognition. By this, the economy [of the system] resulting from not having to refer to other words is indicated. It should also be understood that, through the syntactic unity of the individual words (*padaikavākyatā*) in the rules "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), "tiptasjhi" (Pāṇini 3.4.78), and "dviekayoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.22), those suffixes are prescribed for the agent and so forth as qualified by singularity and the like. (Note: The portion from "tadārabhya" up to "kartrādau" is not seen in the manuscript.)

"And likewise"—this means that wherever there is the presentation of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth by way of the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*), there is the cognition of number as a qualifier (*prakāratā*) with respect to that agent and so forth.

"2—In other cases, it is characterized by not being a qualifier—2. Thus, the meaning is that one must state that, with respect to the aforementioned cognition, the cause is the mental presentation (upasthiti) produced by a word ending in the nominative case that does not function as a qualifier of anything else. In examples such as "The moon is like [Devadatta]," the moon is a qualifier of similarity—which is the meaning of the word *iva*—as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā* is a qualifier of the referent of the word "Devadatta"; therefore, the number denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha-saṅkhyā*) does not apply to them. Rather, it applies only to the face and Devadatta themselves; this is the intended sense.

We shall explain the true nature of this matter in the section on the meaning of particles (*nipāta*). This [point]—namely, the economy resulting from not introducing the aforementioned qualifiers—is as follows: in reality, the *lakāra*s denote the object (*karman*) and so forth, and in their place, the case-endings (*vibhakti*) such as the nominative (*su*) and others denote singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth; thus, there is a syntactic connection through *vākyaikavākyatā* (unity of sentence) with rules such as "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69). This is the form [of the analysis] according to the *Rūpamālā*.

For in that [context], there is no word such as "in the two" (referring to the second case), "agent," or "object," etc., for which number could serve as a qualifier. Furthermore, there is no evidence for repetition [of the rule]. Therefore, the number is construed with the meaning of the verbal root itself. When it is stated that "the suffixes *tiP* and so on denote singularity and so forth," since there arises an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to "of what [is there singularity]?", it is appropriate that the number be construed with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) which is present [in the cognition].

Since the connection [of the suffix] with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*)—namely, the singularity and so forth residing therein—is already established, the non-repetition of the form is thereby accomplished. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* statement, "When the object is one, the second case ending," because the very meaning of the nominal stem, by virtue of possessing the capacity for the state of being an object (*karmatva*), is what is understood by the word "object" (*karman*).

Furthermore, with respect to the case-ending denoting the object of an injunction (*vidheya-vibhakti*), because the object is subordinate (*guṇatva*) and because of the maxim that "subordinates exist for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*), it is impossible for number such as singularity to apply to the object and so forth. Therefore, by superimposing the number belonging to the means (*sādhana*) expressed by the suffix whose base is the verbal root onto the action itself, there is no sublation of numbers such as duality and so on.

Nor should it be argued: "How can an action, which is not a substance (*asattvabhūta*), possess number, given the statement by Hari in the section on number (*saṅkhyāprakaraṇa*): 'Not every object that possesses number and is a substance is denoted [by a word]; for in the world, the distinction between difference and non-difference is based upon number' (Vākyapadīya III. Saṃskāra-saṃdeśa 1)"?

Just as in the Nyāya system, regarding a quality (*guṇa*), the linguistic usage of "duality" and so forth with respect to a quality is due to the superimposition (*āropa*) of numbers such as duality upon the very number belonging to the substance (*dravya*) [in which that quality inheres]. This is because qualities are not admitted to possess further qualities; for if superimposition were not admitted, the explanation would be untenable. Likewise, this is possible in the case of action (*kriyā*) as well. The conventional usage of action as being "unfit for number," however, should be understood as being either because it is not a substratum of non-superimposed number, or because it is not a substratum of any number whatsoever. For this very reason, [the rule] *ṅyāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.1)...

4-1-1) In the *Bhāṣya* on the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* sūtra (Mahābhāṣya, Second Part, p. 278), even though that [specific] sūtra is not present there, having raised the objection that case endings (*svādi*) might arise after finite verb forms (*tiṅanta*) such as *pacati* and *paśyet*, it is stated that this is not the case because [the number] "oneness" and so forth have already been expressed [by the verb]. However, if number were to be construed with the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, then even if that number residing in the agent has been expressed, the undesirable consequence (of further case endings arising) would be unavoidable, because the number residing in the action (*kriyā*) remains unexpressed. This is due to the restrictive rule that nominal suffixes (*sup*) denote the number residing in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of their own base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*). Likewise, [regarding the sūtra] *rūpap*... (sūtra).

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra (Pāṇini 5.3.66), having raised the objection that forms such as *pacatirūpam* and *pacatorūpam*—derived from verbal bases (*tiṅanta*) ending in primary suffixes (*rūpabādi*)—should not arise because they lack number and gender, it is stated: "A verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning, and action does not possess duality and so forth, since no distinction [from the singular] is perceived from the verbal ending (*tiṅanta*). Nor does the neuter gender possess duality and so forth, since no distinction is perceived from the verbal ending; rather, the neuter gender is due to its own inherent nature. Having raised this objection, it was said: "That [gender] depends upon the grammatical factor (*sādhana*)."

"Dependent upon its means" (*tatsādhanāpekṣam*)—this means dependent upon the superimposition of number residing in the means (*sādhana*). By this, it is clearly stated that the action (*kriyā*) is by nature one, while duality and so forth are merely superimposed. Furthermore, regarding the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), since the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the single [cause], the cognition produced by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the cause for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the entire meaning of the verbal suffix; thus, there is only one [such relation].

However, it should be understood that according to the view that number is a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇatāvāda*), there is the acceptance of multiple cause-and-effect relationships, which results in prolixity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, that [number] is also manifested by the suffix (*pratyaya*), because it is a qualifier. This is because the rule—that meanings functioning as qualifiers are exclusively manifested by the suffix—will be stated later. Regarding the statement "the *laṭ* suffix occurs in the sense of the present," since the suffix is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), time is indeed the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself.

And thus, the meaning is that *laṭ* [the suffix for the present tense] occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) whose function consists in the occurrence of a present action; and its status as a qualifier is due precisely to its being a dyotya (an indicator). Furthermore, it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate a separate denotative power (*śakti*) for each of the various *laṭ* suffixes and so forth that originate from a single verbal root.

In this regard, it should be understood that when the desired result has been produced and the entire operation that brings it about has ceased, the action (*kriyā*) is "past" (*bhūtatva*); when such an entire operation, delimited by such a result, is yet to come into being, it is "future" (*bhaviṣyatva*); and as long as the completion of the activity that brings about the desired result has not occurred, it is "present" (*vartamānatva*). Furthermore, the word "of the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) refers specifically to the operation (*vyāpāra*) alone; the connection with time (*kāla*) is connected to that very [operation].

"—*kartṛkarmaṇoreva*—" [means] because they are conveyed by a single suffix; this is the intended meaning. "—*pakṣyatītyanāpatteśca*"—and because [the form] *pakṣyati* would not result [under such a rule]. One should also understand that "*pūrvavat pacatītyāpatteśca*" (and because *pacati* as before would result) is to be understood [as a point]; however, it is not seen [in the manuscript]. "—*tyanāpatteḥ*"—the meaning is "because the fruit (*phala*) is yet to come into being. "—*na ca*"—the reading is *na caivam*. "—*prayogāpattiḥ*"—because the operation (*vyāpāra*) consisting of effort is necessarily present in the current time.

It should be understood that this undesirable consequence does not apply when the fruit is connected with time, because the fruit in the form of the locus lacks the status of being present. — "Elsewhere" means even in cases such as "the cook" (pācaka). — "The primary element is the action" (bhāvapradhāna).

As for the claim that there is no contradiction with the *Nirukta* (1.1) stating "the root-meaning (*bhāva*) is primary"—which, through the etymological derivation *bhāvayati*, takes the word *bhāva* to mean the form of activity (*kṛti*), and thus conveys the sense that among the factors such as tense, number, and person belonging to verbal forms other than those ending in *-ti*, the root-meaning is predominant—that is not correct.

As stated by Hari: "Action is the differentiator of tense, while number is the differentiator of everything" (Vākyapadīya III, Kālasamuddeśa, v. 2), and because of the rule that number and tense are restrictors [of the action], their status as qualifiers is established even without an explicit statement. Otherwise, the aforementioned definition in the Nirukta would result in being redundant. Furthermore, it will be explained later that the word *ākhyāta* refers to a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). By this, the meaning of the Nirukta—"the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) is that which has a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), and with respect to the meaning of the root, it is primarily concerned with existence (*bhāva*)"—is accounted for.

The argument that "the status of number and time as qualifiers is already established because they are delimiters" is refuted; for since it has been established elsewhere that between the meanings of a base and a suffix, the meaning of the suffix is predominant, the aforementioned statement [of the Nirukta] remains purposeless even if the predominance of the *bhāva* (action/state) as the meaning of the *tiṅ*-suffix were established. Nor should it be argued: "In view of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the action—namely, the *kṛti* (effort)—is predominant as the meaning of the suffix, and since by the word *bhāva* one refers to *kṛti* itself, there is no contradiction with this *Bhāṣya* or the *Nirukta*. [This is because the *Bhāṣya* and *Nirukta* intend to establish the predominance of the *bhāva* over the agent, not merely its synonymy with *kṛti*.]

Furthermore, since the rule would be established simply by stating that "a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has the meaning of the suffix as its primary referent," it would result in the inconsistency of [Yāska’s] statement that "it has the action (*bhāva*) as its primary referent. Moreover, there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) to verbal forms expressing action (*bhāvākhyāta*), because in those cases, no *kṛt* (nominalizing suffix) other than the root-meaning exists to serve as the meaning of the suffix. In my view, however, based on the etymological analysis "of the meanings of the base and the suffix," the agent and so forth would attain primacy; therefore, the purpose of the Nirukta statement—which teaches that the action expressed by the base is primary—is to provide an exception to that [general rule]. (Note: The portion of the text beginning with "In my view, however" (*mama tu*) and ending with "the fruit as well" (*phalam api*) is not visible in the source material provided.)

Thus, according to the method to be explained, because even a nominal stem (*nāmapada*) is followed by a case-ending (*subanta*), the statement "they have substance as their primary meaning" (*asatvapradhānāni*) serves to indicate that the substance denoted by the base (*prakṛti*) is the primary meaning, thereby setting aside the rule that the meaning of the suffix is primary. By this, the view that—in the phrase "they have substance as their primary meaning"—the word *pradhāna* refers to the denotative [word], and therefore, by association with that, the word *pradhāna* in the phrase "that which has being as its primary meaning" (*bhāvapradhānam*) also refers to the denotative, is refuted; for in that very context, that word does not have that referent. In that case, it is the power (*śakti*) of that [word] [which is intended]; such is the direction of the argument.

In the expression "action is predominant" (*kriyāpradhānam*), the word "action" (*kriyā*) refers to the result as well, in accordance with forms such as *pacyate* ("it is cooked"). Furthermore, the predominance of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*) is relative to the tense, the agent or object (*kāraka*), and the number expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Therefore, there is no deviation [from this rule] in cases such as *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("see, the deer runs") or *pacati bhavati* ("he is cooking"), even though in these instances the action of seeing (*dṛśi*) functions as a qualifier for the act of running.

"—2ākhyātamiti—2. By the word *ākhyāta* (verb), that which is invariably dependent on a generator [of action] and ends in an inflection (*vibhakti*) is understood; for such is seen in rules such as "ākhyātamākhyātene"tyādau (Pāṇini 2.1.72: "A verb [is compounded] with a verb [in the sense of continuity of action]"). However, the occasional use of the term *ākhyāta* for a *kṛt*-suffix ending like *tiṅ* should be understood as a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). In cases such as 'pācaka' (cook), although the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) requires a generator, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), which is the meaning of the suffix ending, does not require it.

Furthermore, in examples such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), it is quite evident that the action—which serves as the qualificand of the meaning of the nominal ending—is what is required by that [ending]. By this, the view that "the verbal root alone is expressed by the word *ākhyāta*, based on the etymology: 'that by which the primary meaning is narrated (*ākhyāyate*)'" is refuted; for there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to forms like *śiśye* (perfect tense), and under-extension (*avyāpti*) to the verbal root which is the base of a *kṛt*-suffix. As for the statement in the *Nirukta* (A. 1, Pāda 1, Khanda 1, p. 4) that "all nouns are born from verbs," the word *ākhyāta* there refers to the *uṇādi* suffixes... [sūtra]... "all nouns are derived from roots."

(3-3-1) Thus, according to the statement in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*—“A noun is derived from a verbal root” (*ma.bhā.dvi.kha.pṛ.204*)—it refers to a verbal root that has an inflected suffix as its constituent part. Likewise, in the passage “Nouns have substance as their primary meaning” (*ni.a.1.pā.1.khaṃ.1*), the word "noun" (*nāma*) denotes that which requires an action by virtue of being produced [from a root]; and that [noun] is precisely that which ends in an inflection. This is because it is stated in the *Nirukta-bhāṣya*: “Between the base and the suffix, the name ending in an inflection is the primary element among the meanings of nouns, such as substance and so forth” (*niruktam*).

And because of the statement in the *Nirukta*: "They serve as qualifiers with respect to the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*). That [category] too should be understood as excluding indeclinables (*avyaya*), since the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "noun, verb, prefix, and particle" (*nāmākhyātopasarganipātāḥ*) mentions prefixes and particles separately; the details of this are found elsewhere.

"—it is determined. And thus, by the force of the *Nirukta-bhāṣya* and other authorities, the meaning is that there is an abandonment of the general rule (*utsarga*). Furthermore, more will be said on this point later.

Having stated the contradiction with verbal testimony (*vacanavirodha*), he also states the contradiction with reasoning (*yuktivirodha*)—namely, "Moreover" (*api ca*). He points out the fault in supplying the word "that" (*tam*) by saying, "Established by the Bhāṣya" (*bhāṣyasiddha*). The meaning is that there would be no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the worldly [usage] established by the Bhāṣya. The point is that the rule "a sentence consists of a single finite verb" (*ekatiṅ vākyam*) pertains only to technical grammatical operations such as the placement of the *nighāta* accent. He demonstrates precisely how this syntactic unity is broken, starting with "That which ends in the nominative case," etc., up to "because of the consequence of the accusative case. (Note: The portion of the text beginning from "consequence of the accusative case" (*dvitīyāpatteḥ*) on the previous page and ending at "in the discussion of compounds" (*samāsavāde*) on the subsequent page is not visible.)

But [one might object]: in your view, since the running deer itself is construed as the object (*karman*) in relation to the action of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*) by way of the relation of objecthood, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of using the accusative case ending. Nor can it be argued that the syntactic connection is not understood because of the following grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*): "For a verbal cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of the verbal root and whose qualifier is the meaning of a noun, with the relation of objecthood (*karmatā-saṃsarga*), the cause is the presentation of objecthood produced by a case-ending following a noun"—a rule intended to prevent such usage as *taṇḍulaḥ pacati* ("The rice cooks"). [Response: This is not so. For even if the running deer were construed as the object of the action of seeing, the accusative ending would not follow, because the objecthood of the deer is not presented by a case-ending following a noun. Furthermore, the aforementioned rule does not apply here, because the objecthood of the deer is not presented by a case-ending following a noun; rather, it is presented by the word *viśiṣṭamṛga* itself, which is a compound (*samāsa*). Since the objecthood is not presented by a case-ending, the accusative case is not required. Thus, there is no fault. Moreover, the rule cited above is not universally accepted as a necessary condition for verbal cognition, as it would otherwise exclude valid usages such as *caitreṇa pacyate taṇḍulaḥ* ("Rice is cooked by Caitra"), where the objecthood is presented by the noun *taṇḍula* without a case-ending. Therefore, the objection is untenable.

If it is argued: "Even if one does not accept that the meaning of a mere noun (*nāmārtha*)—as defined by the aforementioned grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*)—can be construed as the object (*karmatā*) within the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), there is no deficiency in accepting its construction as the object within the meaning of the verbal root by virtue of being the subject matter of that rule, since the meaning of the specific sentence (*vākyārtha*) lacks the status of a mere noun-meaning; for this very reason, in cases such as *śrutvā mamaitanmāhātmyam* ('having heard this majesty of mine'), the construction of the sentence-meaning—which consists of an origination qualified by auspiciousness—with the act of hearing (*śravaṇakriyā*) through the relation of objecthood is logically consistent even without a second-case ending," we reply: No.

According to the aforementioned reasoning, even in cases such as "the white rice cooks" (*śubhraḥ taṇḍulaḥ pacati*), there would arise the undesirable consequence of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) because the sentence-meaning—consisting of the rice qualified by whiteness—would be understood as the object (*karman*) through its connection with the action. Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*); for it would contradict the *Bhāṣya* located in the section on *Karmadhāraya*, which, in the context of the second view, establishes that the status of being the object belongs to the qualified entity itself in order to form a compound in examples such as "make a beautiful mat" (*bhīṣmāṃ kaṭaṃ kuru*).

For in that case, even though the qualified [entity] is the object (*karman*), it is impossible to establish the objecthood residing in the qualified without a second-case ending for each of the two [constituents]; thus, it is taught that grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) belongs only to the qualifier and the qualified when they both end in the second case. This will be further analyzed in the *Samāsavāda*. Therefore, the occurrence of the second case after *mṛga* is unavoidable. However, in that case, the formation of the aforementioned sentence would be unestablished, because the suffix *śatṛ* and others would apply due to coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a non-nominative form.

Nor should it be argued that, since forms such as *apacad devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooked") and *dhāvan mṛgas tiṣṭhati* ("the running deer stands") are observed with the suffix *śatṛ* (and others), why is the suffix *śatṛ* not applied here even though the deer (*mṛga*) ends in the nominative case?

By dividing the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāv aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe* (Pāṇini 3.2.124) into two parts and carrying forward the word *vā* (optionally) from the first part, the substitution of *śatṛ* is prescribed optionally when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word in the nominative case; thus, forms such as *dhāvati mṛgaḥ* ("the deer runs") are justified. Furthermore, the subsequent rule *aprathamā* (Pāṇini 3.2.125) serves to make the application obligatory. Consequently, [in your view], the fault would certainly remain, as is clear from the Bhāṣya.

Nor does the case ending *dvitīyā* (accusative) arise [for the word ‘mṛga’] because the sentence-meaning "the deer possessing an effort conducive to running" is the object [of the verb], since a sentence having this meaning is not a name (*nāman*). Nor is there a contradiction with grammatical usage (*vyutpatti*), because it has been stated that the scope of grammatical usage consists in being the object of a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of a name. One should not suspect [the following objection]: "Having heard this from me, he runs"—[this would imply a problem]—because the deer qualified by the action of running is not distinct from the deer itself.

This is based on the maxim: "A qualified entity does not exceed [the nature of] the pure substance. As for the argument that even if the qualified entity is not distinct [from the substance], there is no fault because there is a difference between the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) of the qualified and that of the bare [substance], that is incorrect. For even if such a cognition were possible—given that the two are not distinct and thus the derived meaning (*vyutpatti*) involving qualifierhood is not the object of the rule—it would still be impossible to prevent the occurrence of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*). Precisely for this reason, when one intends to express the objecthood (*karmatva*) of a jar qualified by blueness, as in "He sees the blue jar," the accusative occurs with respect to both the qualifier and the qualificand. If, however, the qualified entity were indeed distinct [from the substance], the accusative would not occur in this very instance.

Nor should it be argued that, because both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*)—namely, the running (*dhāvana*) and the deer (*mṛga*)—are objects of the act of seeing (*darśana-karman*), the accusative case would apply to the word expressing the qualifier, the deer, even though the word expressing the qualified, "running" (*dhāvati*), is unfit for the accusative despite the fact that running itself is an object. This is because, although the running is an object, the word expressing the qualifier, the deer, is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and thus would incur the application of the accusative.

In my view, because the deer is a qualifier of the act of running (*dhāvana*), the internal grammatical operation (*antaraṅga-saṃskāra*)—namely, the nominative case (*prathamā*)—is not set aside. (That is, the nominative is not set aside. For you, however, since the deer is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the running and the eyes are its direct qualifiers, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is unavoidable. This is because the principle that "the operation of the principal [element] is stronger than even the internal one" is accepted in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26; MaBh II, p. 60). In my system, however, in examples such as *aśrutvā mamaitat*, the second case does not apply due to the fact that it is an archaic usage (*ārṣatva*).

As for the claim that, following sentences such as "See, the deer is running," one supplies a word (e.g., *karma*) that brings about the presentation of the object (*karmatva*), and that in all cases where the sentence-meaning functions as an object, there is a relational cognition (*anvayabodha*); this is because there is no obstacle to the cognition of the objecthood—whose meaning is "of the deer possessing an effort conducive to running"—being construed as the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and to the cognition of that objecthood being construed with the act of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*) through the relation of being its determiner (*nirūpakatā*).

Nor should it be argued that in expressions such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the objecthood (*karmatva*) expressed by the second case suffix would have to connect with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) by way of being the intended object (*uddeśyatā*); for even when the required meaning is presented by the very word *iti* which has been supplied (*adhyāhṛta*), and such a sentence serves as the indicator of the speaker's intention (*tātparyagrāhaka*), there is no violation of the established linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) regarding what follows a word.
