If it is argued that such a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) is accepted only when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is employed—since that convention is restricted when used in conjunction with the word *iti*—and that the meaning of the accusative case is "object" (*karman*), whereby the connection between the meaning of the noun and the meaning of the verbal root becomes possible through the medium of the case-meaning, both of these points must be considered.

If that were the case, then in all instances such as "The rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*) and "The white rice cooks" (*śubhraḥ taṇḍulaḥ pacati*), by supplying a word [such as *kartṛ*] and thereby resulting in a direct syntactic connection (*sākṣād-anvaya*) between the meaning of the noun and the meaning of the verbal root, these would result in being grammatically correct (*sādhutva*). Furthermore, in the first example, since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is not presented by the word *iti* as possessing an emergent power (*udbhūta-śakti*) delimited by its capacity to be connected with the action, its connection with that action would be impossible. Otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence of a cognition such as "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭa-karmaka*) even from sentences like "Bring the pot-object" (*ghaṭa-karmatvam ānaya*).

Because the first case-ending (*prathamā*) is a kāraka-case-ending, it is restricted to syntactic connection with a verb; furthermore, since the meaning "of the deer" would be a genitive of agency, its connection as an object (*karma*) is impossible. Moreover, this contradicts the aforementioned rule of word-formation (*vyutpatti*). Some maintain that [the second alternative] is incorrect because there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) for a second case-ending after the word *iti* when it functions as an object. As for the claim that the root *dṛś* itself has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "seeing the deer who is the agent of running," and that the aforementioned sentence merely serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*), that too is not correct. This is because there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*) to determine whether the secondary signification belongs to the root *dṛś* or to another word.
Nor should it be argued that, because the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) is simpler, it is the denotative function (*lakṣaṇā*) belonging solely to the root *dṛś* (to see).

Even so, in cases such as "Look, the deer is running," there would be an infinite regress due to a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether the denotative function belongs to the root *dṛś* or to the suffix *ti*. This is because in both cases, identity remains the very same possible relation. Some maintain that the rule "there is no denotative function in a case-ending" (*na vibhaktau lakṣaṇā*) refers specifically to nominal case-endings (*sub-vibhakti*). Furthermore, some hold that there is a denotative function of the verbal root *dṛś* in the sense of "seeing [an object] characterized by a deer as its agent and superior running as its object," while the sentence "the deer is running" serves merely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*).

"Therefore, there is no failure of explanation in cases such as ‘I know Sītā, the daughter of Janaka,’ and so forth”—this too is not correct. For although in expressions like *citragu* (“one who has brindled cows”), where the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) is constituted by the primary meaning, it is established that words such as *citra* serve to indicate the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*), in your own view, this does not apply to a secondary signification involving a reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). Nor can it be argued that in examples such as *prāptodako grāmaḥ* (“the village reached by water”), it is established that the word *prāpta* serves as the indicator of intention when there is a secondary signification through such a reversal.

In this regard, the most recent scholars have stated that the words *prāpta* and so forth function as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) only within a definition constructed from the meanings of the constituent parts, such as "the action of water which is non-different from the agent of attainment" (*prāptikartṛ-abhinnodakakarma*). In that context, although the property of being the determiner of the objecthood (*karmatānirūpakatva*) is sublated with respect to the water, it should be understood that the term culminates in its qualification, namely, the "attainment" (*prāpti*). [This is supported by the rule: "And an imitation [is treated as the original] provided it is not followed by the word *iti*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.62).

According to the rule (Pāṇini 1.4.62), since there exists the possibility of an imitation even when not followed by the suffix *anit*, [the expression] "Sītā was born of Janaka" is justified as an imitation of knowledge—just as in examples such as "I know Narada"—and because there is no purpose for resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, the Maithilas (Gokulanātha Upādhyāya, *Pañcavāda-ratna*, verse 16) argue that in the view which maintains the primacy of the action (*kriyā-prādhānya-vāda*), in sentences such as "I salute the feet of that person who is going" (*prayāti puruṣas tasya pādayor abhivādaye*), there would be an impossibility of the resulting cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*) if the pronoun *tat* were to refer to the primary element—the action of going—since pronouns refer to the primary element. They claim that in their own view, however, because it refers to the primary element—the person (*puruṣa*)—there is no such impossibility. This too [is incorrect], because the reference of pronouns to the primary element is merely a general rule (*autsargikatva*). For this very reason:

In such instances as "These ten are the king's elephants; these very ones are his horses," "Caitra has gone to the village; what does Maitra do there now? and "O Caitra, this is my pregnant wife; give her the blanket," it is not untenable that the word *tat* (that) refers respectively to the king, the village, and the brother. Furthermore, since the action presented by a finite verb (*tiṅanta*)—being of a non-substantial nature (*asattvabhūta*)—lacks the fitness to be referred to by a pronoun, the pronoun refers instead to the agent who functions as its qualifier.

This is because of the rule that pronouns refer to the principal [element] only when both the qualifier and the qualified are equally capable of being referred to by a pronoun. Furthermore, in the final established doctrine (*paramasiddhānta*), since there is no difference between the action and the agent of the action, there is no impossibility [of the agent being the object of the pronoun], as the action possesses the nature of being the agent through identity (*tādātmya*).

Furthermore, you yourself accept that in such instances as ‘caitreṇa supyate’ (Caitra sleeps), ‘śrṛṇu devadatto gāyati’ (Listen, Devadatta is singing), and ‘brāhmo vivāha āhūya yat kanyā dīyate svayam’ (The Brāhma marriage is that in which the girl is given away by herself after being invited), there arises a cognition where the action (*kriyā*) is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*). — *The passage beginning with “adhyāhāre” and ending with “iti vivektavyam” on page 41 exists in the Vaḍodarā manuscript.*

The portion of the text concerning this subject is mentioned in the footnote on pages 41 and 42 of the London manuscript. He also states the contradiction with logical reasoning—namely, [the verse beginning with] "utkaṭa": even that which is uttered as a sentence where one action is the qualifier (*prakāraka*) and another action is the qualificand (*viśeṣyaka*), such as "he is cooking" (*pacati bhavati*), is indeed ungrammatical. As for the argument that it is grammatical because it was employed by the Author of the Bhāṣya in the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28) due to the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the mention of *atiṅ*, that too is not correct;
for if grammaticality were established by an indicative power, then sentences such as "he is going" (*gacchati bhavati*) would also result in being grammatical.

Nor can correctness be established merely by usage in the *Bhāṣya*; for in the *Bhāṣya* passage, "Roots such as *pac* [denote] actions; [roots such as] *bhū* are the agents of action," the use of plural forms and other such words does not preclude the correctness of expressions like *gacchati* (he goes) or *bhavati* (it exists).

Furthermore, it should not be argued that if this were the case, then expressions such as *candanaṃ saṃyunakti sukhayati* (the sandalwood unites [with the body] and thus causes pleasure) in the sense of "causes pleasure through contact with sandalwood," or *naśyati gacchati* (it perishes and goes) in the sense of "goes toward destruction," would also result in being correct.

In the *Bhāṣya*, by employing the word *śabda* (word), by not employing the word *kartṛ* (agent) as the first member of a compound, and by the usage "paśya mṛgo dhāvati" (see, the deer runs), it is understood that there is no fault because the action’s connection with another action is shown to be grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) when the action is related to a factor other than the agent or object capacities (*kartṛ-karma-śakti*) defined by a verbal root meaning distinct from "to be" (*bhū*). Thus it has been said:
"An action is not joined with gender, another action, or factors (*kāraka*) that do not serve as its substratum."

"Let this very non-existence of its [the sentence's] being a substance be determined. (Vākyapadīya). As for the cases "he cooks" (*pacati*) and "it is" (*bhūyate*), since they possess a real denotation, they are indeed accepted [as sentences]; this is the summary. Furthermore, where a sentence-meaning is produced by one finite verb (*tiṅanta*), and a further sentence-meaning is produced by a second finite verb acting in conjunction, there the status of having a second case ending (*dvitīyāntatva*) and so forth is not the governing factor. For this very reason, the usage "nīlo ghaṭaḥ paśya" ("look at the blue pot") is not employed.

In that case, first of all, because there is no generation of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning by means of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), there is a requirement for [the object] to be in the accusative case (*dvitīyāntatva*). However, in examples such as "He sees the deer running" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), since the comprehension of the meaning is first generated by one finite verb and then the comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) is generated by another finite verb, there is no requirement for the accusative case; thus, there is no fault. But even that is not correct.

For in cases such as "O Lakṣmaṇa, see the most virtuous crane at Pampā," which you consider grammatically correct when the intention is to express the objecthood as residing in the qualified whole (*viśiṣṭagata-karmatva*), it would result in being ungrammatical.

Nor should it be argued that even in that case there is no violation of the stated rule, because there exists a cognition of the connection with a second action preceded by a cognition of the connection with a single action through the ellipsis of the word "exists" (*asti*).

If that were the case, then even sentences such as "Look at the blue pot" would result in grammatical correctness by supplying that [verb] as well; furthermore, it is difficult to maintain that a single utterance is both correct and incorrect depending on the distinction between different positions. As for the objection that in examples such as "Bring the horse that is going," the status of being the object of the act of bringing is contradicted with respect to the act of coming—that too must be resolved either by metaphorically attributing the objecthood residing in the horse to the act of going or by treating the possessor of the action as non-different from the action itself.

This very same principle applies even in cases such as "O Māra, look, the deer is running. Some, however, have cited these two aforementioned examples as instances of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*) by supplying the word "him" (*tam*) and so forth. Others, on the other hand, maintain that according to the maxim—"An injunction and a prohibition transfer to the qualifier when there is an obstruction regarding the qualified"—just as in the case of "the crested one [the peacock] was destroyed," even though the actions constituting the qualified objects—namely going and running—cannot be the objects of the actions of bringing and killing, the connection with those actions still occurs for the horse and the deer, who are the agents and thus qualifiers of those actions.

Nor should it be argued that this results in the occurrence of a second accusative case; for the accusative case applies only when there is a syntactic connection with the status of being the object of the verbal expression. It is for this very reason that the statement of the Bhāṣyakāra—“The mat is also the object, and Bhīṣma and the others are also objects,” made with the intention of each [element] being an object of the action according to the principle of *aruṇaikahāyanī* (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.6)—is consistent. Otherwise, even if the qualified whole were the object, once the production of the accusative case for each individual element is established by taking the implied individual object-hood, the aforementioned statement of the Bhāṣyakāra would be inconsistent.

In the sentence "māraya mṛgo dhāvati" ("Kill! The deer is running"), the root *mṛ* has the sense of an activity conducive to confinement (*avarodhana*), and since this is not contradicted by the act of running, its application is justified. Some also say that the killing in the form of the separation of life from the deer is understood through implication (*ārthika*). Therefore, as stated in the Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini 2.3.1 (*anabhihite*), when there is the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of a verbal root meaning "to know" with another, a natural understanding arises—provided there is no contradiction—in which one action is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the objecthood (*karmatā*) related to it serves as the relation (*saṃsarga*) for another action which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

However, when used in conjunction with a verbal root having a different meaning, [the usage] is barred due to contradiction. If there are usages that can be justified through superimposition (*āropa*) or non-difference (*abheda*), such as "O Lakṣmaṇa, look at him" (*paśya lakṣmaṇa*), then they must be explained as cases of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*). If, however, there is a persistent insistence on their existence, then one should understand that they are to be justified by supplying the word "exists" (*asti*) for the generation of the nominative case according to the method stated above. Regarding the supply (*adhyāhāra*)—the commentary text from the London manuscript on the phrase *utkaṭā* is written two pages further below.

He also states the contradiction with reason (*yuktivirodha*) regarding the [proposed] ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), beginning with the words "intense" (*utkaṭa*). One should understand that while an ellipsis might allow for a resolution in cases such as "Look, the deer runs" or "Look, the deer sings," in instances like "Listen, Devadatta is singing," you have no recourse at all.

If it is objected: "In cases such as *māra mā ghoṣat*, since the root *mṛ* has the meaning of an operation conducive to the separation of life-force (*prāṇaviyoga*), and since the result consisting of the separation of life-force is precluded in the act of running, how can the internal supply (*adhyāhāra*) [of an object] be justified?"—we reply that, due to the lack of any other recourse, it is supplied and construed with the agent, namely the deer (*mṛga*). If it is further objected: "Even so, there would still be the undesirable consequence of a second-case ending (*dvitīyā*)," we say no. This is because the status of being an object (*karmatā*) in the deer is not expressed by the word (*aśābda*). The verbal expression of its connection, however, occurs only with that action; the semantic connection, on the other hand, occurs with the agent, the deer.

The technical term *śāstra* (the grammatical rule), however, operates only with respect to that which is connected with the status of being the object (*karmatva*) of the verbal action. For this very reason, the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*—"The mat is also the object; Bhīṣma and the others are also objects"—is consistent when intended to show the connection of each [word] individually with the action, according to the principle of "the red one-year-old cow" (*aruṇaikahāyanī*, Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.6). Furthermore, because the word denoting the action whose locus is that [object] is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*), the accusative case ending does not occur. Thus, the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) stated in the *Bhāṣya* is established.

Alternatively, since verbal roots have multiple meanings, there is no fault because the root *mṛdh* signifies an activity conducive to crushing, and crushing serves as the limit (*avadhi*) for the action [of seeing]. In the case of the word *mṛga*, however, what is understood immediately following is "killing," which consists in the separation from life. [The phrase] "and because of the consequence of non-correspondence" means that the action of running, which is intended to be presented as the object of the act of seeing, is not referred to by the pronoun *tam*, which refers back to the primary subject in the masculine gender. Even if one supplies the word *tam* [as an ellipsis], the same applies, because the pronoun would still refer back to the non-primary element.

To exclude the agent’s connection with the result, he says: “having the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) as its qualifier” and “delimited by the nature of productive activity (*bhāvanātva*); this refers to objects such as "the cook" (*pācaka*). The phrase “the productive activity which is the meaning of the verbal root” (*dhātvarthabhāvanā*) is supplied here; it is drawn over from the requirement for a cognition qualified by productive activity. He states the purpose of that: “see,” etc.; [this is indicated by] the word “direction” (*dig*). What is the primary element? It is action (*kriyā*).

The passage from "starting with what? up to "when action is predominant" is not seen [in the current edition]. To the question, "Is it that substance is predominant?", the answer "the Brahmin family delights" shows that action is predominant; furthermore, the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "hrasvo napuṃsake" (Pāṇini 1.2.47) [Mahābhāṣya, Pradīpa-khaṇḍa, p. 53] should also be understood as supporting the predominance of action.

"—the softening (*viklitti*) that is conducive to that [action]. For this very reason, the Dīkṣitas hold that in "Hari is served" (*hariḥ sevyate*) as well, it is exactly the same. In reality, however, the understanding in sentences such as "The rice is being cooked" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacyate*) has the result as its primary object (*viśeṣya*), namely: "The softening residing in a single grain of rice, which is produced by the present productive activity (*bhāvanā*) residing in a single [grain of] rice. This is because even you must necessarily admit that the result functions as the primary object in cases such as "The rice is cooked" (*pakvastandula*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the well-established rule that, in every instance, the meaning of the suffix directly relates to a qualifier of the meaning of the base (prakṛti). Furthermore, this relation [of being a qualifier] should be understood as being by way of the predicate (viśeṣyatā) in cases such as *pacyate* ("is cooked"), and by way of the attribute (viśeṣaṇatā) in cases such as *pakva* ("cooked"). For this very reason, the form *putrīyati* is not used in the sense "a son is desired," because the meanings are different; rather, it is used only in the sense "one desires a son."

Regarding the statement "putrīya," the suffix [denoting the object] does not apply after the *kyac*-derived form because it is intransitive; this was stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on *Pāṇini* 3.1.8 (*supa ātmanaḥ*), at volume two, page 36. Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency in explaining the difference in meaning between the two cases, since in both instances the cognition would be that of an activity conducive to the desire for a son as the object. Furthermore, the activity conducive to the desire is simply the contact between the self and the mind, and so forth.

In this view, it is quite clear that there is a difference in meaning: in one case the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the qualificand, while in the other the result (*phala*) is. Kaiyaṭa also says (Mahābhāṣya, Vol. 2, p. 37): "When the result of the action is primary, then the expression is simply a sentence, such as *iṣṭaḥ putraḥ* ('the son is desired') or *iṣyate putraḥ* ('the son is being desired'), but not a form ending in *kyac*. For this very reason, we have stated that the verbal root has a twofold power (*śakti*): with respect to the operation delimited by the result, and with respect to the result delimited by the operation. This is the general direction.

"By means of the agent and so forth, which are the meanings of the verbal suffixes, [there is the connection] of that meaning"—thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: since the agent and so forth are objects of cognition as qualifiers of the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), how can Caitra and others be construed as qualifiers [of the agent], according to the maxim "a word-meaning [is construed] with a word-meaning"? If this is asked, the answer is no; for the general form of the meaning, namely "agency" (kartṛtva), invariably requires a specific instance due to the force of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā). Consequently, even though it is itself a qualifier, the agent is construed as a qualifier of that [general agency] by means of that [specific instance]. This is just as, for example, in sentences such as "Caitra went to the village," the case-factor (kāraka) is construed as a qualifier of the action, which itself is a qualifier, solely by virtue of a fixed expectancy.

[Objection: But surely, even though the operation consisting of destruction in the form of *dhvaṃsa* (annihilation) is something produced (*janya*), since it is imperishable and thus eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of using the expression "the jar perishes" [even when the jar has already been destroyed]. To this he says: "The jar perishes. The point is that although that [destruction] is eternal, because the operation conducive to it is non-eternal, the use of that expression does not occur at all times.

[Objection: Surely, since the operation that produces destruction does not exist in the jar and so forth, it would follow that the jar and so forth are agents [of that destruction]. Furthermore, because the jar is the locus of the result in the form of destruction, it possesses the status of an object (*karman*), which would entail that [the verb] is transitive; and thus, the dative case would result for "jar. To this, he says: "qualified by being the counter-correlative" (*pratiyogitvaviśiṣṭa*). The meaning is "qualified by being the counter-correlative" through the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And the point is that this [qualification] exists only in the jar.

Although, like antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) also resides only in the constituent parts such as the potsherds and not in the jar itself, the point is that the operation consisting of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva-vyāpāra*) certainly exists in the jar and so forth. —2 For this very reason—2; "precisely because of the acceptance of the operation. —2 "Upon its cessation"—2; the meaning is that the qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) occurs precisely when there is the absence of the qualifier, namely the operation in the form of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). In some cases, the verbal root *naś* (to perish) also possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) for an operation conducive to intervention (*vyavadhāna*).

As in examples such as "the lost [horse] is found unslain" (*ahataṃ naṣṭaṃ labhyate*), if one were to accept the primary denotative power (*śakti*) in both cases, it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); therefore, the power resides only in the operation conducive to destruction (*nāśānukūla-vyāpāra*). Destruction (*nāśa*) is concealment (*dhvaṃsa*), and that is a state of disappearance (*tirobhāvāvasthā*). Antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is likewise the subsistence of the effect in its causal form, because of the acceptance of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). This will be explained further below. Consequently, in the aforementioned usage, even if one does not accept the stated meaning, there is no fault in the verbal root *naś*. — 2. Regarding "knowledge, desire, etc. — 2.

In this context, the relation that delimits the status of being an object (*kalatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is objective determination (*viṣayatā*), not inherence (*samavāya*). For if it were inherence, then because the fruit and the operation would reside in one and the same locus, the [object] would lack the status of an object (*akarmatva*); consequently, the usage "Devadatta knows the jar" (*devadatto ghaṭaṃ jānāti*) would be untenable.

[Objection: Granted that in persons such as ourselves there exists an operation conducive to cognition and the like, consisting of the contact between the self and the mind; nevertheless, since the cognition and so forth of God are eternal, such an operation is absent in God. Consequently, the usage "God cognizes" would be untenable. To this, he says: "Ultimately, it is simply the state of being the substratum. The meaning of the root *iṣ* is an operation conducive to desire; and some hold that this [operation] is cognition itself. That is not correct, because since God’s desire, like His cognition, is eternal, the usage "God desires" would likewise be untenable.

Even in the case of the past and the future, [the status of being] possessed of a result arises from its presence in the intellect (*buddhyupāroha*). Although the nature of action (*kriyātva*), consisting of a collection of operations (*vyāpārasamudāyatva*), cannot exist in the locus [of the action], nevertheless, it should be understood here too through superimposition (*āropa*), according to the manner that will be explained in such expressions as "the action of kings of the past" and so forth. Alternatively, following the aforementioned method, the nature of action should be understood by superimposing the distinction of time belonging to the substratum onto the operation in the form of the locus (*āśrayatā*). ||2||

(Regarding *bhū.sā.dhā.ni.3*)—the phrase "the consequence of the cognition of both" means that since the object (*karman*) has already been expressed [by the verbal suffix], one should also note that in cases such as *odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), the occurrence of the accusative case would not be possible. Nor is it the case that the cognition of both [agent and object] cannot arise from a single word due to contradiction; rather, it states that they occur alternately:
"only the agent," etc., and "the *taṅ*-suffixes, etc."

The term *taṅ* (the ātmanepada endings) is to be understood as that which is prescribed by the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.13). Consequently, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to cases such as *edhate* ("he prospers") or *niviśate* ("he enters"). Although [the agent] is understood even in the absence of the *śatṛ* suffix and others—as in *gacchet* ("he should go")—and although [the agent] is understood even in the absence of *tiṅ* endings—as in *abodhi* ("he was awakened")—nevertheless, since the *ciṇ* suffix and others do not indicate the object in *abodhi*, this general rule (*utsarga*) serves to remove the inconsistency (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) [where the presence of the object does not entail the presence of the *taṅ* ending]. There is no fault here, because the statement in the root-text is accepted as applying even to the case of *vyatireka-vyabhicāra* (inconsistency in the absence of the object).

One raises the objection that even for [roots] such as *yak* and *ciṇ*, there is sometimes no indication of the locus of the result—this is expressed by "But if this were so" (*nanvevam iti*). [The response is] "favorable to cooking" (*pākānukūla iti*). When...

Even for transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*), when there is a desire to express an excellence of ease (*saukaryātiśaya*) by abandoning the focus on the agent’s operation (*kartṛvyāpāra*), they become intransitive (*akarmaka*) by focusing instead on an operation that resides in the same locus as the result (*phalasamānādhikaraṇavyāpāra*), with the intention of attributing the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) to the object itself. In that case, for roots such as *pac* (to cook) which have operations residing in the object (*karmasthakriya*), when the agent expressed by the suffix is [the object], the object undergoes the behavior of the agent (*karmavadbhāva*), resulting in forms such as *pacyate odanaḥ svayameva* ("the rice cooks by itself"). It should be understood that the status of being intransitive arises simply from the intention to attribute the status of agent to the object, based solely on its being focused on the result (*phalaparatva*).

The word "himself" (*svayam eva*), however, serves to indicate the intention of excluding any other agent. Furthermore, the meaning of *pacyate* is "it becomes softened" (*viklidyate*). In the case of roots whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛstha-kriya*), such as *paśyati*, the meaning is "it becomes an object of cognition. Because there is an absence of the state of having an action residing in the object (*karmastha-kriyatva*), the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply, and thus [the suffix] *niC* and so forth do not occur. Nor should it be argued that if one root, having abandoned its own primary meaning, functions with another meaning, the eternity of the relationship between word and meaning (*śabdārtha-sambandha-nityatā*) would be lost; for [in such cases] it is actually a different root. The indication of meanings such as "√*ḍupacaṣ* in the sense of cooking" is an indication made by way of a technical convention (*tantra*). As it has been said:
"Verbal roots such as *pac* [and others] function by their very nature toward both a single part and the aggregate of actions, relying upon an identical form.

(*Svabhāvataḥ pravartante tulyarūpasamanvitāḥ*—*Sādhanasamuccaya*, *Tattvabodhinī*, *Kāśikā-bhāṣya-sāra-saṃgraha*, verse 58; *Vākya-padīya-sāra-saṃgraha* 58). In the case of a verbal suffix (*lakāra*) whose meaning is *bhāva* (the action itself), the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) alone is the qualificand (*viśeṣyā*). The *tiṅ*-suffix is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*) and indicates time (*kāla*). Considering that action is capable of being numbered, the singular number is used as the default rule (*autsargika*).

Since number is understood from the word itself as inhering in the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), there can be no superimposition (*āropa*) of it upon that [intransitive action] which lacks them. For this very reason, the second and third persons [of the verb] do not occur either, because of the absence of *yuṣmad* and so forth which would be coreferential with the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). This is what some say. That is incorrect; for action is inherently singular. Therefore, since there is an absence of number in indeclinables (*avyaya*), the possibility of a grammatical number [ending] was raised as an objection, and the *Bhāṣya* stated that the singular ending applies by default (*autsargika*). It was not stated in that way after raising an objection that it would not arise even from roots expressing pure being (*bhāvārtha*).

[Objection: But then, even the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*) would not occur in the case of a [verbal] action (*bhāva*), because that too is restricted by the rule "in the remainder" (*śeṣe*). [Response: No; for there is no fault, since it has been stated that the first person is the general rule (*utsarga*) by omitting the word "in the remainder" (*śeṣe*) from this context. Therefore, in the sūtra—namely, *śeṣe prathamaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.108)—the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a portion of both "remainder" and "non-remainder. This is explained in detail elsewhere. ||3||
(Bhū.Sā.Dhā.Ni-4) ||-2Bodha-2|| Because the object itself possesses agency, as it is the substratum of the activity.

"—*sāmānyaviśeṣajñāna*—" || —0kha—0 "That collection of rays... and so forth (*Śiśupālavadha*, first canto, third verse) refers to what was stated in the preceding verse. "—*sakarmaka*—" || By this, there is the exclusion of *yaṅ* and other suffixes occurring in usages such as "the rice cooks by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*) or "he lies down" (*śayyate*), which are associated with intransitive roots under the view that the rule is extended (*śāstrātideśapakṣa*). Furthermore, the inclusion of qualifiers such as "common to the state of being" (*bhāvasādhāraṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding the *ciṇ* prescribed by the rule "after the roots *dīp*, *jan*, etc. (*sū. 3-1-61*) when used in proximity to the *luṅ* [aorist] in the sense of the agent (*abodhi*); otherwise, it would apply to "he was enlightened" (*abodhi* [as agent]) as well. ||4||

(From *Bhūṣaṇasāradīpanibandhana*, verse 5) — [This is] against the Prābhākara school and others. In their view, the fruit (*phala*) alone is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). However, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is not the denotation of anything; for the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) does not have that as its object. Only in the case of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is it denoted by the verb ending (*ākhyāta*). The statement "the verb is primarily concerned with action" (*kriyāpradhānamākhyātam*) refers exclusively to the optative (*liṅ*), because it is only there that action is understood as the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

Even the analysis (*vivaraṇa*) of the word *pacati* as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) is merely an analysis of the activity (*kṛti*) that constitutes the relation between the meaning of the verbal root—which is not explicitly denoted by the word—and the object of action (*karman*), which is also not explicitly denoted by the word. Since, in the cognition produced by the sentence "Caitra cooks" (*pacati caitraḥ*), the meaning of the verbal root—namely, cooking—is a qualifier of Caitra by way of the relation of being conducive to an activity (*svānukūlakṛtisambandhena*), even this analysis does not prove that [the activity] is the denotation of the verbal suffix. The causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is such that the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case is the cause of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in which the meaning of the verbal root is the qualificandum (*prakāra*).

Even for the factors of action (*kāraka*s), their connection is only with the fruit within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*); this must be inferred according to the specific case. Furthermore, the meaning of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) consists of number and time. The term "Prābhākara and others" refers to those who are included by the word "others," namely the Bhāṭṭas, who maintain that all finite verbs denote *bhāvanā* (productive activity) by virtue of being finite verbs. For they hold that the accomplished state (*siddha-bhāva*)—such as the form of a sacrifice or an offering—is expressed by the verbal root, whereas the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) residing therein is expressed by the finite verb; thus, the meaning of the finite verb is *bhāvanā*. As they say:
"—Even though this [injunction] is not perceived apart from the meaning of the verbal root... (*Tantravārttika*, Adhyāya 2, Pāda 1, Sūtra 1).

"Nevertheless, it is denoted solely in its universal form. This very [view] is the refutation [of the opponent's position], because from the cognition "he cooks" (pacati) there arises the understanding "he exerts effort toward cooking" (pāke yatate), and thus effort is not the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha). Furthermore, in cases such as "the chariot goes" (ratho gacchati), the bhāvanā consists simply of the nature of being a substratum (āśrayatā). And since even the Grammarians (śābdika) accept that this [substratum-nature] appears as something to be accomplished (sādhyatārūpatvena), as will be explained later regarding instances like "the mountains exist" (parvatāḥ santi), they say that this very thing is called the "non-chariot bhāvanā" (arathabhāvanā). To refute them, he says:

"Activity (*vyāpāra*) is *bhāvanā*, etc."—the sense is that because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) lacks the nature of being already established (*siddha-rūpa*), activity itself is *bhāvanā*. Although there is a distinction in that *bhāvanā* necessarily possesses an object (*sakarmika*) while action (*kriyā*) may also be objectless (*akarmika*), nevertheless, due to the specific quality of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there is no difference between *bhāvanā* and action. "Of those without effort" (*ayatnānām*) means those distinct from [volitional] effort (*yatna*). Since in other systems (*tantrāntara*) the word "speech" (*bhāṣa*) is well-known as referring specifically to effort, the term "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is used for the sake of including things such as blowing (*phūtkāra*).
He raises an objection according to the Nyāya perspective:

"And it is not thus"—after the word "āpatya" (consequent upon), the phrase "having accepted that the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is *kṛti* (activity)" is to be supplied as the remainder. By this, there is no contradiction with the view of the Naiyāyikas. For this very reason, he will say later: "according to the method of the Naiyāyikas. Alternatively, by omitting the word "view" (*mata*) and using the word "method" (*rīti*), it is implied that this objection is raised precisely while accepting only that much difference. Or rather, it should be understood that this is according to the opinion of a certain school of Logicians (*Tārkikaikadeśin*) who hold that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an effort conducive to the result (*phalānukūla-yatna*). [Regarding the example: "The chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*).

The point is that since there is a sublation [of the meaning] in the case of an insentient chariot with respect to an effort conducive to going, and because it is accepted that knowledge, desire, and effort occur sequentially—as in "he knows" and so on—and because effort lacks the capacity to produce knowledge, the term [denotes] a favorable operation by way of secondary signification (lakṣaṇā).

"—of the *śakyatāvacchedakatva* (the property of being the delimitor of denotability) as well—" — the sense is this: in this view, since the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has the agent (*kartṛ*) as its denotation, the agency consisting of an operation (*vyāpāra*) is the *śakyatāvacchedaka*. But for you, in cases such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), that [agency] is merely the *lakṣyatāvacchedaka* (the delimitor of what is indicated). "—heavy [properties]" — the sense is this: there is a rule stating that "when a light [property] is possible as a delimitor, it does not occur in a heavy one," and this rule concerns only things like the *kāraṇatāvacchedaka* (delimitor of causality), not this [present case]. "—by the root *kṛ*" — by the verbal root *kṛñ*.

—Because [the definition] is unestablished. Thus, in the *Bhūvādi* sūtra (Pāṇini 1.3.1), in the *Nyāsa* commentary on the statement from the *Mahābhāṣya* (Dvitīyakhaṇḍa, p. 144–146): "A verbal root (*dhātu*) is that which expresses action (*kriyāvacanaḥ*)," it is stated: "Since these [roots] stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb *karoti*: 'What does he do?'—'He cooks' (*pacati*); 'What will he do?'—'He will cook' (*pakṣyati*); 'What did he do?'—'He cooked' (*apākṣīt*). Having raised the doubt, "How is it known that *pac* and the other roots express action?", it was said: "Because of their coreferentiality, as in: 'What does he do?'—'He cooks'."
And thus, from this very commentary, it is clearly established that the root *kṛ* denotes action in general (*vyāpārasāmānya*).

Furthermore, according to the view that the agent is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), one would have to accept a multiplicity of cause-and-effect relations: namely, that for a cognition having the substratum (the agent) as its qualifier, the cause is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case; for a cognition having the number of that [agent] as its qualifier, the cause is the knowledge of the substratum of that meaning; and for a cognition having the time of that [meaning] as its qualifier, the cause is the mental presence generated by the verbal root. This is not tenable.

However, according to the theory that the meaning of the verbal suffix is the action (kṛti), it must be stated that the cause for a cognition whose qualifier is a meaning of the verbal suffix distinct from being a means to a desired end (*kāleṣṭasādhanatva*) residing in time is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case; thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) because number and the agent are one and the same [in this view].

Because it is impossible for one who does not know that [the suffix] is a verbal suffix (ākhyāta) to grasp such a causal relationship [between the suffix and its meaning]. Furthermore, there would result an infinite number of cause-and-effect relationships: in some cases, the cognition produced by the verbal suffix would be the cause for the understanding of an effort (*kṛti*); in some cases, the cognition produced by the verbal suffix would be the cause for the understanding of a substratum (*āśraya*); and in yet other cases, the cognition produced by the suffix itself would be the cause for that very same [understanding]. Thus, an infinite number of such causal relations would follow.

As for the claim that in expressions such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the substratum (*āśrayatva*), that too is incorrect; for there is no relation between the action (*kṛti*) residing in the chariot and the substratumhood defined by the act of going. Furthermore, a mediated relation (*paramparāsambandha*) does not serve as a determinant for indication, nor is there any experience of a cognition preceded by knowledge of such a relation. Moreover, indication in the case of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) would be inappropriate, as it would render the specification of meaning redundant and lead to the redundancy of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) concerning the transposition of case-endings. Thus it is said: "There is no indication in a case-ending" (*na vibhaktau lakṣaṇā*).

As for the claim that "there is no indication [of gender] in a case-ending (*sup*) because it is a grammatical marker (*lakṣaṇa*)," that is not correct; for there is no evidence for such a restriction, and the aforementioned restrictive rule applies equally to both *sup* and *tiṅ* endings. This is the general direction of the argument. Having thus refuted the view of the Naiyāyikas, he now refutes the "Mixed" (*miśra*) view—which is common to certain followers of that school—on the grounds that the agent (*kartṛ*) is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*). He introduces this with "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*): "In the non-expression of the *bhāvanā*," that is, in the non-expression of the operation (*vyāpāra*) by the verbal root (*dhātu*), since according to their view, the meaning of the root is merely the result (*phala*), while the *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

And likewise, in cases such as *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati* ("he brings about a pot"), just as the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) arises because the pot is the locus of the fruit—which is the production (*utpatti*) resulting from the operation denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—so too in cases such as *ghaṭo bhavati* ("the pot comes into being"), there would be the undesirable consequence of the second case ending, since the pot possesses the fruit of the verbal root's meaning, which is production resulting from the operation denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). In my view, however, the second case ending does not occur because it is sublated by the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*), which takes precedence on the grounds that [the pot] is the locus of the operation that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root. This very principle is the universal rule regarding transitive verbs. [This refers to] "the non-uniform nature of agency."

In our view, the meaning is simply "the state of being the locus of the primary operation denoted by the verbal root in question. [The phrase] "because it would over-extend to all mere instruments" means that otherwise, if one intended to express that even firewood, a pot, and so forth are loci of the operation for the sake of highlighting an excellence of ease, there would be the undesirable consequence (anāpatti) of such usages as "the firewood cooks" or "the pot cooks."

[Objection: But surely, that [agency] consists in being the locus of the verbal root's operation upon the meaning of the sentence. And in cases such as "the pot becomes" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), because the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) sublates it by virtue of its being that locus, the accusative case does not occur. Nor should it be argued—following the Mīmāṃsakas—that the verbal root does not express the action (*bhāvanā*) because there is no analysis (*vivaraṇa*) of "becomes" (*bhavati*) etc. by means of the verb "to do" (*karoti*); for how could agency [be established] by virtue of being that locus? (Note: The portion of the text starting from "by virtue of being that locus" (*tadāśrayatvena*) up to "is established" (*siddham*) is not visible.)

Even so, since the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) here has as its sole purport the substratum (*āśrayamātra*), it must be stated that agency (*kartṛtva*) belongs to the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, which possesses the property of being coreferential with the result (*phala-sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Even so, since the verbal suffix here has as its sole purport the substratum, and the verbal root alone expresses the operation (*vyāpāra*) that is coreferential with the result, the status of being an intransitive verb (*akarmakatva*) is established. Because [the agent] is the substratum of that [operation], there is no second case ending (*dvitīyā*). And in cases such as *āṭaṃ bādhayati* ("he causes the vowel *āṭ* to be lengthened"), the second case ending occurs because [the object] is the substratum of the result of the meaning of the verbal root, which is qualified by the operation expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇij-artha*).

Nor should it be argued that, by the force of the rule *na caiva hetumati ca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.26), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would apply because [the agent] is the substratum of the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), since this [agenthood] is more remote [than the primary agenthood]; for the intention [of the sūtra] is that [agenthood] consists precisely in being the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix when it is not coreferential with its own result, provided there is co-occurrence with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). If this is said, we reply: no.

Regarding the definition "the state of being the substratum of the operation denoted by the verbal suffix" (*ākhyātārthavyāpārāśrayatvam*), when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is present, is it intended that the operation residing in the instigator (*prayojaka*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix, or rather the operation residing in the one being instigated (*prayojya*)? It cannot be the first [option], because in examples such as *pācayati devadatto viṣṇumitreṇa* ("Devadatta causes Viṣṇumitra to cook"), Viṣṇumitra—the one being instigated—would fail to be an agent, and consequently the instrumental case would not apply to him. Furthermore, since his agency has already been expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is no evidence for it being expressed again by the verbal suffix.

Nor should it be argued that the suffix *ṇic* is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), because a fault will be stated later regarding the consequence that the indicated meaning would then become a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). [This fault applies] in cases such as "he brings about a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati*). In [the case of] the jar...

Furthermore, by excluding agency (*kartṛtā*) merely on that basis, the qualification "not having the same locus as the fruit" (*phalāsamānādhikaraṇa*) would result in being redundant. Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable: although the stated qualification prevents the fault in cases such as "he brings about a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati*), in cases like "the teacher causes the two students to cook" (*guruḥ śiṣyābhyāṃ pācayati*), there would be the undesirable consequence that the dual ending in "śiṣyābhyām" would not occur. This is because of the rule that number must necessarily conjoin with only that which is conjoined with the operation expressed by the verb (*ākhyāta*) that denotes its own [number]. Likewise, the singular ending in "pācayati" would also not occur.

By not mentioning the teacher (*guru*), there would be the occurrence of the first case-ending (*prathamā*) [instead of the third] there; and from the word *śiṣya*, there would also be the occurrence of the first case-ending. Furthermore, there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) in providing a qualifier. In my view, however, because the two *ṇic* suffixes are denotative, and because the state of being the locus of the activity expressed by the primary root-meaning ending in *ṇic* exists in the instigator (*prayojaka*), he possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛ*). And since that [agent] is denoted by the personal ending (*tip*), the third case does not occur for the instigator. [Regarding the] one to be prompted (*prayojya*)... (L.)

[The third case ending] for the *prayojya* (the one being caused to act) is not seen [in the examples provided]; however, due to the distinction between verbal roots (*dhātu*), there is agency (*kartṛtva*) because he is the locus of the operation that is primary to the meaning of the root *pac* which serves as the base (*prakṛti*) of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). And since that agency is not expressed by the personal ending (*tip*), the third case ending occurs. This is exactly the same in cases such as *ghaṭaṃ bāvayati* ("he causes the pot to cook"). The difference is that because the root *bhū* has a supreme object (*paramakarmaka*), the second case ending applies to it according to the rule *gati-buddhi-* (Pāṇini 1.4.52).

Nor should it be argued that because the causative suffix (*ṇic*) indicates instigation (*preraṇā*), that which is indicated becomes a qualifier; and thus, since the agent (*kartṛ*) is the substratum of the activity consisting of instigation—which is the primary meaning of the causative verbal root—the instigator possesses the status of an agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*).

According to the authority of the Bhāṣya, the suffix *ṇic* is denotative (*vācaka*), and therefore its meaning is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Otherwise, since the agenthood of that substratum would not be established, the suffixes *la* and so on could not occur after a causative (*ṇyanta*) verb in reference to the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). If one does not accept the rule that "that which is indicated (*dyotya*) is necessarily a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)," but instead accepts that it can be the primary qualificand even while being indicated, then in examples such as *gamito grāmaṃ devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta was caused to go to the village by Yajñadatta"), the operation of the instigator would be denoted by the root *gam*, and because it would be the primary meaning of "motion" (*gatyartha*), the suffix *kta* would undesirably apply to the instigating agent.

In cases such as *pācayati devadattaḥ caitreṇa* ("Devadatta causes Caitra to cook"), since the instigator (*prayojya*) does not serve as the locus of the primary operation, it would follow that he cannot be designated as the agent (*kartṛ*); this is sufficient [to show the flaw]. Regarding the phrase "in its non-denotability" (*avācyatve*), this means "in its non-denotability by the verbal root" (*dhātvavācyatve*). Regarding the phrase "its own meaning" (*svārtha*), the intended sense is that the operation is not denoted by the verbal root. [The author] states [the following] because there is no decisive evidence [for choosing one over the other] (*vinigamanāvirahāt*). [Note: The commentary beginning with "vinigamanā" and ending with "vikṣepādi" on the next page is not visible. Regarding the phrase "operation which is its own meaning" (*svārthavyāpāra*).

Nor should it be argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as "Devadatta lives" or "he dances," because these denote results consisting of the maintenance of life or the movement of limbs which are non-co-referential with the operation (*vyāpāra*). This is not so, because of the qualification "provided it does not denote the locus of the result. Since those [verbs] do denote the loci of the results—namely, life and the limbs—and because the result is qualified by the absence of non-intentionality (*avivakṣāvirahaviśiṣṭatvena*), there is no over-extension even to those [verbs] where the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitakarma*). [The phrase "because they denote the loci of the results consisting of life and limbs" is not seen in the manuscript.]

Although there is a lack of universal applicability (*ananugama*) in the case of the entry for *svādayati*, nevertheless, one may adopt any single transitive verb as the term "itself" (*sva-śabda*) and thereby establish the conventional usage of "transitivity"; thus, there is no fault. In reality, however, to exclude this [undesirable application], it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to provide the qualification "provided that it does not denote the locus of the result. Furthermore, qualifying the result by the condition "being distinguished by the absence of non-intentionality" (*avivakṣā-viraha-viśiṣṭatva*) is also defective due to its complexity.

Even if one holds the view that there is identity of the word despite a difference in meaning, even when the qualification [of "not denoting a result"] is added, there would still be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as *ghaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a pot"), because even during a state where the object is intended to be expressed, the word lacks the quality of not denoting a result—provided it is qualified by the absence of non-intentionality—as recognized through re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Furthermore, according to the view that "there is a difference in words due to a difference in meaning," it is asserted that the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself is distinct; in that case, the addition of the qualification is entirely redundant, since the root is already intransitive (*akarmaka*) precisely by virtue of its occurrence with a different meaning.

By this, the view that in cases where the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita-karma*), the verbal roots (*dhātu*) must necessarily be distinct from those whose objects are intended, is refuted. This is because, in the verse cited by the learned authorities beginning with "dhatorarthāntare vṛtteḥ," the separate mention of the term "from non-intention" (*avivakṣātaḥ*) would otherwise be redundant; for the status of being intransitive (*akarmakatva*) is already established by the phrase "dhatorarthāntare vṛtteḥ" alone.

If it is asked, "Since this definition is defective, what then is its [correct] definition?", the answer is no; for understand that a different [definition] will be stated later in the verse beginning with "anyādṛśasya" and continuing with "phalavyāpārayoreka" (Vaiśeṣikasūtra-kārikā 13).

Regarding the phrase "being one among many" (*anyatamatvam*): the meaning is that *sakarmakatva* (transitivity) must be defined as "being different from what is different from those [verbs]," having taken those specific individual transitive roots (*dhātu*) as the basis by way of their respective individual identities. Regarding the phrase "of one and the same": for example, the root *sthā* is seen to be intransitive in the sense of "stability" (*sthairye*) but transitive in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsāyām*). In this view, since transitivity would result in both senses, it should be understood that transitivity and intransitivity must be defined precisely by including the specific difference in meaning.

"—it would follow that [a root] would be either intransitive or transitive. Regarding the phrase "the denotation of the operation" (*vyāpārasya vācyatve*): since it is impossible for the definitions of transitivity and intransitivity stated [previously] to be constituted by the "own meaning" (*svārtha*) [of the root], they must instead consist in "denoting a fruit whose locus is distinct from the operation" and "denoting a fruit co-located with the operation," respectively. Consequently, by taking any operation whatsoever, every fruit denoted by a verbal root exists [in all cases], and thus the consequence follows that all roots would be of both types [transitive and intransitive]. This is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "or else" (*evamathavā*) which is about to be stated: even if one assumes that the fruit (*phala*) is not denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), since [the two types of roots] are possible only as those denoting an operation (*vyāpāra*) that is either coreferential with the fruit (not involving its own object, etc. or denoting an operation that is non-coreferential with the fruit, the root-meaning operation has been explained in the aforementioned manner by taking some fruit or other. Now, the author explains the source text (*mūla*) as being intended solely to refute the view that [roots] denote mere operation—hence the words "or else" (*athavā*)—and "that," namely, "denotability" (*vācyatve*); and "merely operation" (*vyāpāra eva*).

The sense is that his view is that the action, which is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), connects with the result through its relation to the possessor of the activity (*vṛttimat*). Regarding the phrase "the consequence of [the root's] being [limited to] cessation": the sense is that the result is not the meaning of the verbal root. Regarding the term "figurative" (*bhākta*): the meaning is that it is "figurative" (*gauṇa*) because it is produced by "figurative usage" (*bhakti*), that is, by indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In the Nyāya school’s view, when a verbal root whose meaning involves an object (*saviṣaya*) is used in conjunction [with a noun], the meaning of the accusative case is "object-ness" (*viṣayatva*). The sense is that being "figuratively transitive" (*gauṇasakarmakatva*) is precisely this state of having an object as its meaning. Regarding the phrase "mere effort" (*yatnamātra*): the ellipsis is "in the capacity of being the place of the operation" (*vyāpārasthānīyatvena*). ||5||

( *Bhūṣaṇasāradīpikā* 6) — "Another argument" means: in comparison with the argument consisting in the abolition of the distinction between transitive (*sakarmaka*) and intransitive (*akarmaka*) verbs, it is another argument. — "Otherwise"—that is, if [the root] were to denote only the result (*phala*)—then that would not be the case. This is because the rule for the *ya*-class suffixes (*yagādi*) applies to those whose action resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*). If the very same action that exists in the state of the object is [also] present in the state of the agent, then only then do the *ya*-class suffixes occur. And the act of creation (*kṛti*) does not reside in objects such as jars; this is the intended meaning. — "Because seeing does not subsist in the jar," etc.

This is based on the misconception that [the relation] is inherence (*samavāya*). In reality, since cognition exists in both [the self and the object] by virtue of being the object of cognition (*viṣayatā*) and inherence, we shall explain later that such a usage does not occur because, as an action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyaka*), it would result in the application of the *karmavat* rule. || 6 ||
(From the *Bhūṣaṇasāradīpikā*, 7) — "It will be stated that [the object] is to be produced" — ||2||
"That which is non-existent [before] and comes into being, or that which exists and is manifested through birth—that is the *nirvartya* (to be produced).
But the *vikārya* (to be modified) is established as twofold:
some, such as wood and the like, arise from the destruction of their original nature (*prakṛti*), becoming ashes. (Vākyapadīya III.7.49)
"Sometimes another quality [is produced], as in the case of transformations such as gold [into ornaments] (Vākyapadīya III.1.50).
That which cannot be established through either perception or inference based on specific qualities produced by action is called 'attainable' (prāpya)" (Vākyapadīya III.1.51).

These are the definitions of that [action] as stated in the *Vākyapadīya*. The meaning is that examples such as "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), "he presses Soma" (*somaṃ sunoti*), and "he sees a form" (*rūpaṃ paśyati*) will also be explained. Regarding the phrase "produced by action" (*kriyākṛta*): we shall explain in detail in the *Sunnirṇaya* how a specific change indeed occurs in rice and the like through cooking and so forth, whereas no such change occurs in a village and the like through the act of going.

"—Even in the case of being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇatva*)"—this is the intended meaning: the meaning of the verbal root *gam* is an operation indicated by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), while the meaning of the verbal root *tyaj* is an operation indicated by disjunction (*vibhāga*), and so forth. By the phrase "they say" (*vadanti*), the author indicates his own dissatisfaction (*asvarasa*) with the view that there is no fault because the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with each respective verbal root acts as the regulator for the cognition of those specific results (note: the portion from 'bodhe' up to 'rūpaphala' is not seen in the manuscript). The phrase "without any dispute" (*nirvivādameva*) [refers to this].

The point is that while in transitive contexts such as ‘he cooks rice’ (*odanaṃ pacati*), it is possible for the fruit (*phala*) to be the meaning of the accusative case, in intransitive contexts such as ‘it exists’ (*bhavati*), since there is no occurrence of a fruit in the form of existence (*sattā*) and so forth, it must be expressed by the verbal root itself. For this very reason—namely, because it possesses both meanings—it is said that “the root *pac* has two meanings. In reality, however, the meaning of *pac* is both the softening (*vikledanā*) and the production (*nirvartanā*). This is because the meaning of ‘he cooks’ (*pacati*) is: “while softening the rice-grains, he brings about the production of the cooked rice.
Thus, it should be understood that this Bhāṣya passage is intended to show that [the root] culminates in the production of the rice, which is subordinate to the softening. (7)

(From the *Bhūṣaṇasāradhara*, 8) — "Because it would contradict the rule [of logic]" — this means that, according to the maxim that "the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is primary," the sense is that the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is indeed the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Regarding the phrase "for it is observed upon its appearance": since that efficient force is observed—that is, cognized—upon the appearance—that is, the hearing—of that suffix, the sense is that it is therefore the meaning of the suffix. And this maxim was stated by Jaimini: "But it is perceived as having the nature of a word, for it is observed upon its appearance; its cognition... (Jaiminisūtra 1.1.2).

Of that—[it is] indeed perceived, yet it is not seen—as stated in the sūtra: "Because [it is so] for others" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 4.1.15). And its meaning is as follows: just as in the case of words, that which is denoted by the word is perceived as being one; for when there is the occurrence of the singular number (*ekavacana*), that [oneness] is seen, just as there is the cognition of the subsidiary nature (*aṅgatva*) of other particulars such as "animal-ness" (*paśutva*).

In such cases as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), if the animal qualified by singularity is the object to be enjoined, then since singularity is also conveyed by the word in the form of the singular suffix, and since that [singularity], through the medium of the animal, serves as an auxiliary to the sacrifice—just like the "animal-ness" (*paśutva*) and so forth—it follows that it is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice; this is the ultimate truth, which we shall explain in the determination of the intentionality of number (*saṃkhyāvivakṣānirṇaya*). Some also maintain that its predominance is seen in the sense of what is adventitious (*āgantuka*). (Note: Regarding the phrase *tatprādhānyamāgame*, the reading *tat* is not found.)

In this view, the reading following "hi" is without the word "tat. Regarding the phrase "and because of contradiction": the intention is that since the word *kartṛ* in the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) refers to the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), it is precisely by that [word] that the suffixes *ghañ* and others are prescribed for the action (*vyāpāra*).

"And thus, 'connected with its own' (svayukta)"—here "its own" (sva) refers to the verbal root (dhātu). The meaning is: that which is expressed by whatever [verbal suffix] is connected with it. The inclusion of the qualifier "connected with its own" is for the purpose of preventing the root *bhū* from being considered transitive (*sakarmaka*) by taking any arbitrary meaning of a verbal suffix as its object, on the grounds that it would then express a result residing in a different substratum. The followers of Bhaṭṭa maintain that in all cases both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are denoted by the verbal root; however, that operation is established in a completed state (*siddhāvasthāpanna*), which is another matter. Intending to refer to the mere result, he says: "one who considers himself a Mīmāṃsaka. This is the intention.

He states the very reason: “of the mere fruit” and “because of being the locus. The meaning is that since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the meaning of the verbal root *gam* (to go), and since movement is uncontradicted in relation to the village. “[Thus] there is no [undesired] consequence”—this is because the fruit in the form of cooking, which is the meaning of the verbal root *pac*, is present; the same applies to what follows. “Of *ghañ* and so forth” means in cases such as *pāka* (cooking). “Because of being expressive” [is the meaning].

Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the agent [the suffixes] kṛt": this is because the intention is that since the word *kartṛ* (agent) in the sūtra refers to the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), it is by this very rule that the suffixes *ghañ* and others are prescribed for the action (*vyāpāra*). Regarding the phrase "because it would result in the futility of the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*")...

In the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), you have accepted that the term *kartari* (which is being carried over from the previous rule) refers to the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), and thus its meaning is "in the action which delimits that [agency]. Since that very meaning must be accepted as a governing topic (*adhikāra*) in accordance with the context of meaning, the sense of "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is obtained; therefore, the intention is that the rule *bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.18) would be redundant. [This applies to] *laḥ karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.69).

In this regard, one should understand that the portion of the rule prescribing *tiṅ* suffixes, namely "in the sense of the action" (*bhāve*, Pāṇini 3.3.18), is likewise redundant according to the reasoning already stated. Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*. The meaning is as follows: for you who maintain that the root denotes the result (*phala*), since the meanings of roots such as *ghañ* and others denote a completed state of being distinct from the action (*bhāva*) of the root which has reached a state of being in progress, there would be a contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* statement: "The *ghañ* [suffix occurs] when the meaning of the root is in a completed state."

For this very reason, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra *akartari ca kārake* (Pāṇini 3.3.19), [Patañjali] asks: "What is the purpose of the mention of *kāraka*? He replies to this question by stating that, because its meaning has not been previously specified, [the suffix] should not apply in its own sense (*svārthe*), and since the "own sense" is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it would already be established by the preceding sūtra *bhāve* (3.3.18) when applied to the meaning of the root. Consequently, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), it will apply only to a *kāraka*. Having thus established its redundancy, he then says: "In that case, [let it apply] when [the action] is in a state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanne*)."

Having stated that the term *kāraka* must be employed so that [the designation of *karman*] does not apply to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—since in the rule "in the sense of becoming" (*bhāve*), that which is indicated is established in its accomplished state (*siddhāvasthāpanna*), and thus the [designation of *karman*] is not established by that [accomplished state] alone—and having thereby obtained [the exclusion of the root-meaning] through the prohibition "not when there is an agent" (*akartari*, Pāṇini 3.3.19), he raises the following objection: the operation (*vyāpāra*) expressed belongs to the verbal root alone, and not to the suffix.

"—2 atheti—2 || —2 sakalavyāpāreti—2 || The meaning is that there is the possibility of obtaining even that operation which is intended as the *bhāvanā* (productive activity). —2 tadapi—2 refers to the *vivaraṇa* (explanation) as well. —2 mīmāṃsakoktam—2 refers to the objection [stated by the Mīmāṃsakas]. The meaning is that it takes the form of a contradiction with the logical principles: "the meaning of the suffix is primary" (*pratyayārthaḥ pradhānam*) and "for when that [suffix] is present" (*tadāgame hi*). —0 ka 0—2 aruṇādhikaraṇarītyeti—2 ||"

The meaning is that, according to the method of that [Pūrva Mīmāṃsā] section, all the case-factors (*kāraka*) presented in the sentence—"He buys Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, yellow-eyed cow"—are first construed with the action alone; subsequently, there arises a mental cognition (*mānasa-bodha*) through the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*). For this very reason, the Bhāṣya on the rule *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1), which states, "the object is the pot, and Bhīṣma and others are also the object," becomes consistent. This is according to our own method, which will be explained below.

The meaning is that, according to our own system which will be explained later, only those things connected with an action possess the status of being *kārakas*. "Incompatibility of connection" means incompatibility of mutual connection. "Primacy" means primacy as determined by the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). "As stated" means in the manner beginning with "by way of being the qualificand. "And not merely a relation" [is the meaning].

In such injunctions as "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," it is heaven itself—introduced by the word *svargakāma* (desirous of heaven)—that is connected as the object to be accomplished (*bhavya*) within the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verbal suffix; however, the sacrifice, which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), is not so connected, even though it is introduced by the same word. This is because the sacrifice, being of the nature of a non-substantial entity (*asatvarūpa*) and not being a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), cannot be the intended object. Nor should one raise the objection that the sacrifice alone is more appropriately the object to be accomplished, on the grounds that the uniformity of the word-form (*samānaśruti*) consisting of the verbal suffix is stronger than syntactic expectancy (*vākya*) consisting of the introduction of different words.

Having established this general relationship—that *bhāvanā* is connected with the sacrifice—the Bhaṭṭapāda has settled the final position (*siddhānta*) in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* (Mīmāṃsā-darśana, A. 2, Pā. 1, A. 1, pp. 383–384, together with the Śābara-bhāṣya and Tantravārtika), stating that the purpose of the co-occurring word (*samānapada-śruti*) is fulfilled by this alone. Furthermore, the literal meaning of the aforementioned verse is that it expresses merely the relationship between the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) and the *bhāvanā*, which exist respectively in the states of the accomplished (*siddha*) and the to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*). By the word "merely" (*mātra*), specific [relationships] are excluded.

By "direct statement" (*śruti*)—that is, by the direct statement within the same word (*samānapada-śruti*)—there is a general relation. Regarding the introduction—that is, the cognition—of one aspect of that [relation], namely a specific relation such as instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and so forth, this direct statement within the same word lacks the capacity for operation. This is because at that time there is an absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). If it is asked why there is an absence of expectancy: it is because, in accordance with the requirement that the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) must incite what has not yet been set in motion, the [productive urge] expects an instrument only when it is already connected to a result.

For this very reason, the direct (śrauta) meaning of the word *pacati* is simply "the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) connected with cooking"; the subsequent mental cognition that "the productive operation is conducive to cooking" follows later. For this same reason, in cases such as *dadhnā juhoti* ("he offers oblation with curds"), the meaning is that "one should effect a refinement of the curds by means of the productive operation connected with the oblation. And for this reason, even in cases such as *jyotiṣṭomena yajeta* ("one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"), the direct meaning is simply "the productive operation connected with the sacrifice non-different from the Jyotiṣṭoma"; the subsequent cognition, however, is of the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the oblation, the sacrifice, and so forth.

According to the maxim, "that which is not accomplished [by itself] cannot be an instrument," one adopts a *bhāvanā* (efficient force) whose objects to be accomplished are the *homa* (oblation) and *yāga* (sacrifice), since these are already established [as instruments]. Regarding this, he states "2ajeti-2" in response to the latter view. As for the former view, the fault—that the *ajā* (goat), being the primary element, would result in becoming the meaning of the suffix—is so obvious that it is not even mentioned. [This is because] the phrase "2prādhānyāpatteriti-2" implies that in cases such as *ajā*, there is an actual experience (*anubhavikatva*) of a cognition where the goat is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and femininity is the qualifier (*prakāra*).

In fact, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *striyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.3) (*Mahābhāṣya*, Vol. II, p. 300), regarding the view that feminity (*strītva*) is the meaning of the suffix, it is argued that—given the principle that "the meaning of the base and the suffix [are related]"—since the primary element, feminity, denotes a non-substance (*asatvabhūta*), and because there is a rule that number must necessarily connect with the meaning of the base which qualifies its own denotatum, dual endings and so forth would not arise due to the lack of connection with duality and other numbers. Anticipating this objection, [the author] accepts that even the primary feminity is non-different from the substance that is the meaning of the base.

It is [the gender] that is inherent (*samāhita*), but not by resorting to its being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). And thus, even though femininity (*strītva*) is predominant, since it is possible [for it to be expressed], there is a deviation from the rule of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) which states "of the meanings of the base and the suffix. However, in the view that femininity is manifested by the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), its being a qualifier of that [meaning] is something else, due to the rule that things manifested [by a suffix] are necessarily qualifiers. For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras also said only "because the meaning is established by other means of knowledge" (Sūtra 1.2.56), and not...

This is also because [the reason] is inconclusive (*vyabhicāritva*). Therefore, it is not logical that [the agent] possesses the status of a primary element (*utsarga*) by virtue of being inconclusive. If it is asked, "How then is the agent and so forth, which are the meanings of the suffix in expressions such as *pacati*, subordinate?"—it is replied as follows:

Regarding the principle that "between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the meaning of the suffix is predominant," this is correct only when the suffix possesses denotative power (*vācakatā*). This is because, in the case of the dual compound *prakṛtipratyayau*, it is only grammatically valid if the portion *prakṛti* is connected by the same relation—namely, the relation of being denoted—to the word heard at the end of the compound which expresses the object [of the rule], as the portion *pratyaya* is also connected to that same word by that very same relation.

Furthermore, since it will be stated that when a suffix makes known the predominance of a meaning indicated by it, that indicated meaning must necessarily be a qualifier—a point established in the Bhāṣya—it is impossible for such an argument (nyāya) to apply here. Likewise, in the case of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), because the agent and other factors are accepted as being the meaning of the root, and because the verbal suffixes indicate them, it is proper that the agent and so forth—the meanings indicated—should be qualifiers; thus, they do not fall within the scope of that rule. The sūtra "kartari laḥ" (P. 3.4.67), for instance, means simply "after a root whose object is the agent."
