This is because, for you as well, such a connection [of the suffix] with the *bhāva* (action/state) is necessarily required by the rule beginning with *bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.18); for since the *bhāva* is obtained from the verbal root (*dhātu*), no other alternative is possible. For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *snukramoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.36), the meaning of the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.13) is explained as "from a verbal root that occurs in the sense of *bhāva* or *karman*."

And the meaning of the rule "from that root" (*tasya ca dhātoḥ*) is "from a root whose domain consists of the state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Kaiyaṭa says: "The status of being its domain belongs to the root either because it denotes an action qualified by the agent, the object, and so forth, or because the object and so forth are denoted by suffixes whose base is that [root] itself. Among these, the former applies to instances involving *lakāras* whose domain is that [object or state], because of another traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating: "A finite verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning."

The portion ending with "having *śatṛ* and others as their objects" [refers to] the statement, "Nouns (*nāman*) have substance (*asatva*) as their primary meaning. [Thus,] the meaning is precisely "the *la*-suffixes [denote the agent]" (Mahābhāṣya, Vol. II, p. 263–264). For this very reason, the fact stated in the Bhāṣya—that rules such as "for two and one" (Pāṇini 1.4.22), which concern *tiṅ*-suffixes, also function as restrictive rules—becomes consistent [with the following]: "Because *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes are prescribed without distinction, and because usage is observed [otherwise], this statement is for the purpose of restriction" (Mahābhāṣya, Vol. I, p. 237).

Furthermore, a restrictive rule (niyama) occurs only when there is a possibility of multiple purposes [for a grammatical operation]. If number and so forth were denoted by the verbal root itself, then, according to the maxim "suffixes whose meaning has not been specifically assigned denote their own inherent meaning," the suffixes *vib* and others would be established for all meanings by the general rule alone; thus, the status of a restrictive rule would be appropriate only in cases such as the imperative (*yujyādau*), where understanding of all meanings would arise from the mere root. However, the claim that "understanding arises from the recollection of what was elided" is not correct, because understanding would fail to occur for one who is unaware of the elision.

Regarding the rule *sārvadhātuke yaki* (Pāṇini 3.1.67), the meaning of the phrase "the meanings of sārvadhātuka suffixes are [the agent] and so forth" (*kartṛādayaḥ*) is simply that they are "illuminated by those [suffixes]. Similarly, in the view that these are the meanings of the *vikaraṇa* suffixes, the meaning is that they are "also illuminated by the *vikaraṇas*."

Nor can it be argued that the doubt expressed in the Bhāṣya—"On the view that [the suffixes] express the vikaraṇas, there would be no vikaraṇa because the meaning is already denoted"—is untenable, as this would indicate a collective inclusion (samuccaya) since we see [suffixes expressing vikaraṇas] in forms such as *vyatilunīte* and *gārgyāyaṇī*; for the maxim *uktārthānām aprayogaḥ* ("there is no employment of what has already been expressed") applies to expressive elements (*vācaka*). Therefore, one must say that by relying on the denotative nature of the *lakāra*, the expression of the doubt based precisely on the maxim *uktārthānām* is appropriate.

The underlying concern of the objection is that since the *liṅ* and *loṭ* [suffixes] are indicated even by the mere *lakāra* when they are devoid of *vikaraṇas* (conjugational markers) and belong to the *ad-ādi* class, the purpose would be fulfilled by that alone; consequently, it follows that the *vikaraṇas* should not arise. Furthermore, the maxim "of things whose meaning has already been expressed" (*uktārthānām*) applies even in the case of indicators (*dyotaka*), as is clear from other sources and will be stated further on.

In cases such as *vyatilunīte* and *gārgyāyaṇī*, however, the reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), the feminine gender, and so forth are understood through the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) alone and the suffix *eṣ* alone respectively, because those two [suffixes] exist elsewhere as well; therefore, there is a combination of them. The underlying intention is that, due to the very nature of word-potency (*śabdaśakti*), in some instances the indicator is accompanied by a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), while in others it is even the bare primary suffix (*sārvadhātuka*). Consequently, it is established that the meaning of a verbal root consists solely of the state of being (*bhāva*), the agent (*bhāvaka*), time (*kāla*), the grammatical relation (*kāraka*), and number (*saṃkhyā*).

For this very reason, there is no inconsistency even with the rule "the five [categories] are the meaning of a name" (Pañjikā). Therefore, it should be understood that there is no occasion for the grammatical analysis (*vyutpatti*)—which concerns the expressive word—to apply to the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). Since comprehension follows grammatical analysis, and not grammatical analysis following comprehension, he says: "But rather... because of conformity to grammatical analysis."

The meaning is that this follows from the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) such that, in cases like *aupagava*, "the cognition produced by the suffix following [a base], in its capacity as the object of awareness (*viṣayatā*), is the cause of a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the base, [occurring] through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*)."

The phrase "having as its qualifier the delimitor of possibility" (*śakyatāvacchedakaprakāraka*) means that in instances of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), such as "There is a crocodile in the Gaṅgā," the theorists of poetics (*alaṅkārikas*) accept that for the sake of conveying the intended purpose (*prayojana*)—such as coolness and purity—one superimposes the nature of a current upon the bank and cognizes the bank precisely as a current. Furthermore, in cases such as "He trembles at the glittering [moon]," according to their view, there is no fault because they admit the presence of the poetic figure of commixture (*saṅkara*) consisting of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) and metaphorical identification (*pariṇāma*), since these arise from a specific defect.

—2 Not [the view] of the Naiyāyikas and others—2. Regarding the scope of *lakṣaṇā* (indication): if one accepts a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), (V1. the word "prakāraka" is absent)—0ka-0 "The face trembles at the sight of the face; the circle of the breasts fears the breasts. (Seen in the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, in the *Bhūmikā*; Madhusūdana Śāstrī, p. 126).

In passages such as "The eye fears the middle [of the body], and the lower lip trembles before the eye," although Rāhu and the moon are understood by way of their being "tresses" (*kaca*) and "faces" (*mukha*), there is no cognition of them by way of their being the *lakṣyatāvacchedaka* (the delimitor of the indicatedness), namely "Rāhu-ness" and so on; for otherwise, the capacity to cause terror would be inexplicable. Therefore, the point is that one must accept that the cognition occurs precisely in the mode of the *lakṣyatāvacchedaka*.

In reality, however, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) with respect to that which is delimited by it," there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the cognition of [Rāhu] as delimited by Rāhu-hood (*rāhutva*), because [the word] shines forth as such. The phrase "even for those who are proficient in the opposite way" means "for those who are unskilled in the correct usage. Being "proficient in the correct usage" (*sadvyutpannatva*) consists in possessing knowledge regarding the division of bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) as stated in the grammatical treatises (*vyākaraṇaśāstra*), as well as the division of their respective meanings and the comprehension of their mutual relations (*anvaya*). The meaning is: "for those other than such [persons]."

Alternatively, the meaning is: "for those who have acquired proficiency through the linguistic usage of elders in which the relationship between the prompted (prayojya) and the prompter (prayojaka) is inverted. For instance, [one might understand] the second-case-ending and so forth, whose denotata are "objectness" (karmatva) and the like, by means of the very words "objectness" and so on.

When a certain instigating elder who is proficient in grammar utters the sentence "The pot—[objecthood]—bringing—[action]," and having heard it, a certain prompted elder, following the investigation of the meaning according to the rules of grammar, understands the sense to be "the pot's objecthood" and brings the pot; then, for the child observing that bringing of the pot by the elder, [the thought arises]: "Surely, in this matter..."

The meaning is that the apprehension of capacity (*śaktigraha*) occurs through the thought "this sentence is capable [of conveying this meaning]," and there is also the apprehension of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣāgraha*). In this same manner, the word "also" (*api*) is employed to indicate that even the acquisition of proficiency (*vyutpatti*)—beginning with the production of words such as *diś*—occurs only for those who possess proficiency in verbal expression (*vyākaraṇa-vyutpatti*). Regarding the phrase "that [sentence] is devoid of expectancy" (*tannirākāṅkṣam*): the meaning is that it is devoid of expectancy toward the cognition "the objectness (*karmatā*) residing in the pot. Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the state of a word being such that, due to the absence of another word, there is a lack of experience of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*). In the case of a cognition of identity (*abheda*), expectancy consists simply in having the same case-ending (*samānavibhaktikatva*).

In cases such as "Bring the blue pot," since the connection [of the action] with "Bring the pot" is observed even in the absence of the word "blue," whereas in cases such as "The pot is the objecthood" (ghaṭaḥ karmatvam), despite the presence of the expectancy for non-difference, there is no cognition of non-difference due to the absence of semantic competency (yogyatā).

In reality, the cognition of semantic competency—defined as the absence of the property of being a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absolute non-existence residing in the related term, with respect to a property that subsists in the relation which is the intended object—is not a cause of comprehension; nor is the ascertainment of semantic inappropriateness, defined as the state of being such a delimiting factor for counter-correlativity, an obstacle to comprehension, because comprehension is observed even from inappropriate sentences such as "The son of a barren woman goes" and "He sprinkles with fire."
Otherwise, how could the derision expressed by listeners—“How can you speak of sprinkling with non-fluid fire for one who utters such a sentence?”—be logically consistent?

Nor should it be said that after hearing a sentence characterized by semantic incompatibility (*ayogyatā*), there is merely the mental presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) for the listener, but no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

Otherwise, this would lead to the same undesirable consequence in all cases. Nor should it be argued that, in such instances as "sprinkle with fire," verbal comprehension would likewise result in purposeful action; for, just as the cognition of a contradiction (bādhajñāna), so too the certainty of semantic inappropriateness (ayogyatāniścaya) gives rise to a doubt regarding the validity of the cognition already produced. It is only a cognition unassailed by such [doubt] that generates purposeful action. Consequently, even though a cognition arises from expressions such as "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*), there is no possibility of that effect [action] occurring, because the cognition of that [meaning] is rendered invalid by the certainty of its inappropriateness.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), however, fitness (*yogyatā*) is the possession of the capacity to produce the effect as co-uttered [in the sentence]. And that [fitness] is manifested in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). For this very reason, in cases such as "bring water with a jar" (*ghaṭena jalam āhara*), there arises a cognition having "being other than perforated" as its qualifier, because only that which is not perforated possesses the capacity for carrying water. For this very reason, the scriptural status (*śrautatva*) of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is established.

For instance, in cases such as "the sacrificial post is made of khadira wood" and "one binds the animal to a post made of khadira," even though the [wood] is taken up for another purpose because it possesses the capacity for the action of binding—which consists of a specific conjunction resulting in the effect of lack of independence—there is no loss of the scriptural meaning. Likewise, in verbal cognition, the knowledge of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) alone is the cause, not the knowledge of compatibility (*yogyatā*) as established by the Naiyāyikas and others. Similarly, the causality of the knowledge of proximity (*āsatti*) and the knowledge of intention (*tātparya*) will also be refuted later. Thus says the statement.

This is an ancient grammatical sūtra. In that context as well, the phrase "even of the kṛt [suffixes]" means "even of those that are kṛt. Thus, the sense is that the explanation "pakvam" (cooked) is indeed correct. There is also an alternative reading: "and because the root *kṛ* is perceived through its explanation. In that case, the meaning is that the root *kṛ* is explained by the verbal root *pac*, as in "pakvam. The phrase "in common to both" means that "bhāvanā" (the efficient force) is common to both the *tiṅ* (finite verb) and the *kṛt* (nominal suffix). The phrase "the verbal root alone" refers to this.

The point is this: in a verbal cognition where the operation (*vyāpāra*)—related by the relation of "conduciveness" (*anukūlatva*) to a specific type of result (*phala-prakāraka*)—is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), you must accept that the causal status (*hetutā*) belongs to the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) of both the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), as well as to the verbal root and the *kṛt*-suffix. For me, however, it belongs to the verbal root alone; thus there is parsimony (*lāghava*). Regarding the phrase "and the consequence of [the *bhāvanā*] being the primary element": the meaning is that even for the effort (*kṛti*) and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), primacy would follow [from your view], which is not seen [to be the case] according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would contradict the settled tenet (*apasiddhānta*). ||8||

( *Bhūṣaṇasāradhāmanī* - 9) "Another proof" (*sādhakāntaram*) means: the very cognition of *bhāvanā* in the case of suffixes marked with *kṛt* is the proof for its being denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*). For if that were so, the cognition of *bhāvanā* in *kṛt*-suffixes and the production of suffixes such as *anīyar* in the sense of the object (*karman*) would be established. Your view, however, holds that since *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*), there would be no occasion for the cognition of *bhāvanā* in *kṛt*-suffixes due to the absence of a denoter there, and there would likewise be no occasion for the production of suffixes such as *anīyar* in the sense of the object; such is the intended meaning. — "Without [the suffix] *asat*" (referring to *kṛt* suffixes). — 2.
