The underlying intention is that the agent, the object, and so forth are defined by the action; thus he says "without" [the action]. "The Bhaṭṭa method": for it is their method that the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is implied by the agent and the rest. "In the event of such a consequence": in the event of the consequence that the productive activity would be implied [rather than expressed].

"—the state of being denoted by the *kṛt* suffix. The word "action" (*kṛti*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "—there would be no compound. The sense is that since the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is not denoted by the verbal root, the nails and so forth lack the status of being the agent or the instrument with respect to the action denoted by the base of the *kṛt* suffix. "—directly. This is because the root *kṛñ* has the meaning of "activity" (*vyāpāra*). "—through a mediated relation. This means [a relation] consisting in being produced by a productive operation whose agent is oneself, and so forth. "—in one and the same [instance]."

The sense is that there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) because, in the case of implied cultivation (*ākṣiptabhāvanā*), there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the two word-meanings "nail" and "split. [This avoids] the consequence of the compound being "semantically incompetent" (*asamartha*). The sense is that, according to the method you have stated, there is semantic competency because the two—negation (*abhāva*) and the sun (*sūrya*)—are connected with the action of seeing (*dṛśikriyā*) by way of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) and the object (*karmatva*) respectively. The sense is that [in the phrase] "all is done" (*kṛtaḥ sarvaḥ*), there is a connection between "all" (*sarva*) and "clay" (*mṛttikā*) with the action denoted by the verbal root *kṛ* by way of being the object (*karmatva*) and the instrument (*karaṇatva*) respectively.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by Viṣṇumitra": this has been established above. This [instrumental case ending] is not the instrumental of the instrument (*karaṇa*), because it would result in the impossibility of the causative suffix *ṇic* occurring here under the rule "hetumati ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.26). This is because the designation *hetu* (cause/instigator) is prescribed only for the instigator of the agent by the rule "tatprayojako hetuśca" (Pāṇini 1.4.54). Moreover, due to the restriction in the rule "gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha... (Pāṇini 1.4.52), the instigated agent, Viṣṇumitra, does not attain the status of an object (*karman*).

"—and because there would be no occurrence [of the definition] due to the state of being an object of motion (*gamyakarmatva*)—[it is said: by the force of the rule *'kartur īpsitatamam'* (Pāṇini 1.4.49), [the object] is precisely that which is intended to be connected with the action residing in the agent."

Because of the prescription of the technical designation *karman* (object). [The term *karman* applies] only to that which is the substratum of the result produced by an action denoted by a verb meaning "motion," and which is itself defined by that action denoted by a verb meaning "motion. By this—namely, by pointing out the flaw in the form of the non-occurrence of the accusative and dative cases in the aforementioned instance, even though the instrumental case is justified in the sentence "Devadatta causes Viṣṇumitra to cook"—[the definition is established]. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in that usage": the meaning is that since it is necessary that the status of being an agent (*kartṛ*) belongs to the substratum of the operation which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in whichever usage that may be.

Otherwise, there would be no established rule that in some instances wood and the like possess agency while in others they do not; rather, the implication is that agency would result for everything in every case. Thus ends the direction. Furthermore, the fact that *bhāvanā* is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is obtained from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "kārake" (Pāṇini 1.4.23).

For in that regard—when Devadatta is said to "cook" while performing the actions of placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, adding rice, and bringing fuel, at that time the root *pac* (to cook) applies to those actions such as placing on the fire. When pieces of wood are said to "cook" while performing the action of burning, at that time the root *pac* applies to them.

It has been stated that when a cooking pot is said to "cook" (*sthālī pacati*), it performs the action of taking up [the grain]—expressed as "it cooks one *droṇa*" or "it cooks one *āḍhaka*"—as well as the action of bringing [the process] to completion and the act of sustaining [the contents]; thus, in that case, the verbal root *pac* (to cook) is operative. This refers to the aforementioned meaning: that the verbal root denotes the activity (*vyāpāra*). And this—namely, the similarity—is what is ultimately established.

And likewise: according to the method stated by you, if one does not accept that a verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses action (*kriyā*), then it would lack the defined status of being a root; consequently, the grammatical operations prescribed under the governing rule "after a root" (*dhātoḥ*, Pāṇini 3.1.91) would not apply—this is the intended meaning. ||9||

Regarding the phrase "in the statement of merely that much": this means in the statement of merely being recited in the *bhvādi* class. Nor should it be argued that the word *vā* ("or") is redundant, since the intended meaning would be established by the words "beginning with *bhū*" (*bhvādayaḥ*) alone. This is because the Vārttika—"The [word] 'vā' is employed in the rule 'Roots beginning with *bhū* are *dhātus*' for the sake of auspiciousness" (*bhūvādīnām... vakāro 'yaṃ maṅgalārthaḥ prayujyate*)—justifies the word *vā* in the Sūtra as having the purpose of ensuring auspiciousness. Even though [the meaning] is already established by its being recited in the class, [the author] abandons the position that it serves the purpose of auspiciousness precisely due to a lack of satisfaction with that [explanation].

The two concise alternatives stated in the *Vārttika*—"those which express the meaning of *bhū*, thus they are called *bhv-ādayaḥ*" (the form *bhvarthāḥ* is not observed), or "or they are remembered as *vādayaḥ*"—have the following meaning: the intended sense (*tātparya*) is that those which express the meaning of *bhū*, i.e., the root *bhū*, are *bhv-ādayaḥ*. However, the literal meaning (*śabdārtha*) is as follows: *bhū* is the act of becoming (*bhavanam*), which is general action (*kriyāsāmānya*). The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) according to the rule for the *saṃpadādi* group. Thus, *bhū* is the act of becoming. Those which express this *bhū* are *vādayaḥ*; here, the suffix *iñ* is added to the root *vad* according to the *Śaiṇādika* rules.

[In this case] the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) is not observed; that is to say, a suffix (*pratyaya*) denotes general action (*kriyāsāmānya*). However, those [words] denoting specific actions possess the status of a verbal root because the general is permeated within the particulars. Now, an objection is raised: there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *hiruk*, *pṛthak*, and *śiśye*. To this, he says: "Or else, they denote the state of being (*bhvarthāḥ*). That is, "the roots beginning with *bhū* are traditionally remembered as denoting action" (*kriyārthāḥ*). This too is merely a statement of the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*). But the literal meaning (*śabdārtha*) is as follows: "being" (*bhū*) is the state of becoming, which is general action; or, "those beginning with *vā*" means those whose first is *vā*, i.e., the verbal root *vā*. Thus, they are called *vādayaḥ*.

Regarding the compound *vādayuñca vādayaśca* (both *vādi* and *vāday*), there is a *tatpuruṣa* and a *bahuvrīhi*. By the rule "of those whose vowels differ" (*svarabhinnānām*), which prescribes a single remainder (*ekaśiṣṭa*) in a *bahuvrīhi*, the word *vādi* forms a compound with *bhuva* as *vādayo bhuvaḥ*. The genitive case in *bhuvaḥ* expresses the relationship of denoted and denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*). Thus, the established meaning is: "those beginning with *vādi* are verbal roots when they have an action as their object. Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of a definitive determination": the meaning is that it is impossible to determine that only a root is recited in the list [of roots] and not an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Regarding the phrase "there would be usage": [this refers to the possibility of such usage occurring].

In reality, since it would not be a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*), the occurrence of case-endings (*sub*) would be impossible; this is clear elsewhere, because according to the literal reading, the production of *tiṅ* endings is untenable due to the absence of number, grammatical relation (*kāraka*), and so forth. [Regarding the phrase] "as a regulator": the intention is that the designation "verbal root" (*dhātu-saṃjñā*) applies to meanings such as "motion" or "smelling," and not to the meaning of "optionality. 10.

(From *Bhūṣaṇasāradīpanibandha* 11) — [Objection: "Let it be so. [Response: Regarding the status of *staṃbhu* and other roots that are well-known only in common usage (*loka*) among those listed in the *sūtra*s, their being verbal roots (*dhātutva*) should be understood through the addition of the marker *u* in the list of *staṃbhu* etc., and by the *gaṇasūtra* in the *curādigaṇa*: "This illustration is manifold" (*bahulam etan nidarśanam*). Otherwise, if taken literally, there would be the consequence of inconsistency (*asaṅgati*). [The phrase] "in production (*utpatti*), in making known (*jñapti*), or in grasping (*graha*)"—the fact that this constitutes a fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) should be understood as a form of logical reasoning (*tarka*).

For instance, if a pot were produced by a pot, it would have to be distinct from that pot. This should be understood to apply to production as well; however, the mutual dependence regarding persistence is not mentioned here because there is no purpose for doing so.

"—and not being any one of them. The meaning is that, having taken all those intended to be designated by the technical term *dhātu* (verbal root) as individual instances (*tattadvayaktitvena*), [the property of being a verbal root] consists precisely in the nature of being a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the respective differentiators (*bhedakara*). "—the various results (*phalāṃśān*). It was not suspected that [being a verbal root] consists in "having the sense of an action such as existence (*sattā*) while being enumerated in the list [of roots]. For otherwise, those very same items would fail to be verbal roots when they have other meanings; therefore, only the results are taken up by way of being any one of them. "—by the word 'action' (*kriyāśabdena*)."...

In the rule *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), as well as in the phrase *kriyāyāḥ pariniṣpattiḥ* and others, the word *kriyā* refers exclusively to the result (*phala*), because [the grammatical tradition] does not perceive [the term] as denoting anything other than that. Thus, [the root] *kṛp* means "capacity," preceded by the prefix *vi-*; hence, "he discriminates" (*vikalpayati*). 11.

(From *Bhūṣaṇasāradīpikā* 12) —2 "Of this very [word]" —2. This means: of that which possesses the status of being listed in the *gaṇapāṭha* while simultaneously denoting an action. —2 "Of those not denoting that" —2. Of those distinct from what denotes an action. —2 "In such cases as *asa bhuvi*" —2. This is the underlying point: when the root *bhū* signifies both "abiding" (*sthiti*) and "origination" (*utpatti*), the scriptural indications (*liṅga*) found in rules such as "in the sense of the place where grains grow" (*dhānyānāṃ bhavane*, Pāṇini 5.2.1), "born there" (*tatra jātaḥ*, 4.3.25), and "occurring there" (*tatra bhavaḥ*, 4.3.53) serve as evidence.

And thus, when there is a connection with a verbal root meaning "to abide" (sthiti) or a verbal root meaning "to arise" (utpatti), the establishment of *bhāvanā* occurs; this same establishment also occurs when there is a connection with the root *bhū*, which has the same meaning as those. Accordingly, [the meanings are] an activity conducive to arising (*utpatty-anukūla-vyāpāra*) and an activity conducive to abiding (*sthityanukūla-vyāpāra*).

Existence (*sattā*) and the operation conducive to it are also the meanings of verbs such as *asti* (is). In this context, the "operation" is ultimately nothing other than the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatā*), which is expressed as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*). In the system of Patañjali, since all entities undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*) through successive states, there is no impairment of their having parts occurring in temporal sequence, because the various instances of being a substratum—defined by those respective transformations—are manifold. Alternatively, it may be due to the superimposition of temporal priority and posteriority residing in time upon existence itself. Thus, its status as an action (*kriyātva*) is established.

In this regard, it has been established below that when one asks "What does he do? with reference to someone whose destruction is imminent, the answer "He exists" conveys either existence (*sattā*) or an activity conducive to that [existence]. Similarly, in the answer "He exists" to the question "Has he gone or not?", an activity conducive to staying (*sthiti*) is understood.

In cases such as "The red horse [goes]," however, an activity conducive to origination (*utpatti-anukūla-vyāpāra*) is perceived. The phrase "with great effort" is stated so that, in instances such as "This stands," the *bhāvanā* (productive urge) underlying the state of remaining may be clearly understood as being of the nature of effort (*prayatna*). The expression "of that very [thing]" means "of that very *bhāvanā*."

"Elsewhere"—this means that what is distinct from the locus of the operation lacks the status of being a qualifier defined by the result, because it is only the substratum of the operation that serves as the qualifier of the result; this is the sense. Since the word *śeṣa* (remainder) here has the sense of "qualifier," he says: "because of its being coreferential with the result."

[Objection: Is it not the case that in expressions such as "the jar exists" (*ghaṭo 'sti*), since the jar is perceived as being in the process of being accomplished (*sādhyamānatva*), an unestablished jar cannot possess agency; and once it is fully produced, its state of not being in the process of accomplishment is possible? [Response: No—for the state of being in the process of accomplishment is possible because the jar established by the cognizer (*boddha*) takes on identity with the external jar that is being accomplished, and thus both states are possible. [Regarding the word] "exists" (*asti*): it has the sense of existence (*sattā*), or it has the sense of the activity (*vyāpāra*) that follows from that [existence]. 12.

In the verse "phalavyāpārayoḥ" (Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā, Bhūmikā-khaṇḍa 13), the word *dhātoḥ* (of the verbal root) connects with what precedes it—this is the extent of the meaning. Herein lies the essential point: the intended sense of the root text is that a verbal root is intransitive (*akarmaka*) precisely when it denotes an absence of a result that resides in a different locus from its own operation (*vyāpāra*). And this absence [of such a result] occurs sometimes due to the non-existence of a difference in locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). This difference in locus consists of two forms: [the result] not residing in the locus of the operation, and having a locus other than that [locus of the operation]. In the first case, inexpressions such as *abhāvad uttiṣṭhati* ("he rises from non-existence"), there is intransitivity.

Furthermore, if one adopts the definition of "intransitivity" (*akarmakatva*) as consisting in having different substrates (*bhinna-adhikaraṇa-vṛttitva*) as stated in the root-text, then since the result in the form of conjunction with an upper region (*ūrdhva-deśa-saṃyoga*) exists in the upper region as well, the action would lack intransitivity. Consequently, being subject to the definition of "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) stated in the root-text, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of an accusative suffix (*karma-pratyaya*). In that regard, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because the result itself is primary, [the action] is characterized by the completion of time (*bhūta-kāla*) therein.

Furthermore, [the definition] is not futile because if the result—namely, the conjunction with a higher location—were already present, the usage "he has stood up" (*utthita*) would be impossible. For me, however, since the aforementioned result does not reside in the locus of the operation (*vyāpāra*), there is an absence of the qualified [result] due to the absence of its qualifier [the operation]. Thus, to indicate the intransitivity, the *kta* suffix occurs only when the agent is the substratum of the operation; consequently, even though that [result] is currently present, it is logically consistent because the operation conducive to it has passed.

In the case of the verbal root *gam* (to go), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because of the presence of "heterogeneity" (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), which consists in the result not residing in the locus of the operation. It should be noted that in some cases, such as in the verb *as-* (to be) in expressions like *asti*, there is an absence of the factor of the result, according to the view that *as-* signifies mere existence (*sattā*).

"—2 Because of inclusion—2. The meaning is that the action whose nature is the self (ātman) is included within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because it has become that [very thing]. Now, since it is impossible for the aforementioned meanings of "origination" and "subsistence" to apply to expressions such as "the self exists" (*ātmā asti*) or "the direction exists" (*digasti*), he says: "—2 In its own support—2. In the verse, this meaning is obtained because the root *bhṛ* signifies "supporting" (*dhāraṇa*). "Supporting itself" (*svadhāraṇa*) means supporting its own nature; the result is the connection with a subsequent moment.

And the operation (*vyāpāra*), as in the case of "the rice is cooked by itself" (*pacyate taṇḍulaḥ svayameva*) and so forth, is expressed as the very substratum (*āśrayatā*) being the object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*) according to the aforementioned method. Thus, the meaning is that the self (*ātman*) and so forth perform the maintenance of their own nature. [This is because] there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). (Note: *sāmānādhiṃ* ... *dhikaraṇavyāpāra* does not exist. Therefore, there is a connection that supports the subject at hand.

Now, an objection is raised: since in such cases as "the self knows itself," a single self serves as the locus for both the result and the operation, it follows that the verb would be intransitive (akarmaka) because its operation is coreferential with its result; to this, he says:

—2 "With respect to itself"—2. In reality, *sakarmakatva* (transitivity) consists in having a meaning that is connected with an object designated as such by the technical terminology (*saṃjñā*) of the grammatical treatises (*śāstra*). This is because the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *sakarmaka* yields exactly that. That which is different from this is *akarmakatva* (intransitivity). For this very reason, in cases where the locus (*ādhāra*) receives the designation of "object" (*karman*) according to the rule *adhiśīṅsthāsāṃ karma* (Pāṇini 1.4.46), the suffix *kta* is successfully formed in the sense of the object in examples such as *adhyāsitā bhūmayaḥ* ("the lands were occupied").
However, if the definition of *akarmakatva* followed the method stated in the root-text [of the *Dīpikā*], that would not be possible.

Nor is there any fault in the case of verbs such as *jīvati* ("he lives"), which signify activities conducive to the maintenance of life (*prāṇadhāraṇa*). This is because it must be stated that the meaning of the verbal root is connected with an object in the form of "life" (*prāṇa*) and so forth. [This objection is] refuted by the very term "connected" (*anvaya*), which denotes a relation distinct from the cognition of the verbal root itself; for in this case, the object in the form of "life" is understood from the verbal root alone. It has been established below that adding qualifiers to the definition stated in the Sūtra in order to avoid this fault is beset by the defect of prolixity (*gaurava*).

In all instances such as "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), the word *karman* occurring in the term *akarmaka* refers exclusively to those [actions] distinct from time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), path (*adhvan*), and location (*deśa*). [This applies to the rule] "gatibuddhi... [and so forth].

In the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra *gati-buddhi-* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), it is stated: "Since [the rule] is established by the restriction regarding the class of transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*) within the category of similar items (*sajātīyapakṣa*), the mention of 'intransitive' (*akarmaka*) [in the sūtra *gatibuddhipratyavasāna-*] is for the sake of its own force (*sāmarthya*). Or rather: "By that object (*karman*) through which [verbs] become transitive and intransitive, [the rule applies] to those that are intransitive; and no verb becomes intransitive by means of this [specific] object. This is clear. Consequently, in forms such as *māsam āsyate* (or *māsayati*), the derivation of the *l*-suffixes (*lādi*) in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) is established.

However, because the word denoting the object (*karman*) in a transitive verb (*sakarmaka-pada*) refers to the object of that transitive action, forms such as *dāsyate* ("he will be given") and *māsam āsyate* ("he remains for a month") are also accounted for. For this very reason, since the accusative case is already established by the rule *kālādhvanaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.5), the formulation of the *Vārttika*—"time, state, and the distance to be traversed are [treated as] objects"—which prescribes the technical designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) here for the purpose of applying the *l*-suffixes and others to the object, becomes logically consistent. Alternatively, by accepting the operation of the root *ās* ("to sit") in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāpti*)—the act of occupying space—and thereby establishing its status as an "object" according to the rule *kartuḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.49), one may justify the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of the *Vārttika*. This is the general direction of the argument. 13.

(From *Bhūṣaṇasāradīpikā* 14) — "Expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix" — this contradiction was stated with the sense that "expressed by a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix" kept in mind. — "Because of contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*" — the intention is that there is a contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* because the term "like a substance" (*dravyavat*) excludes the state of being a non-substance (*asattvabhūtatva*). — "Because both parts exist" — the intention is that even in that case, by taking the force of the suffix (*pratyayaśakti*), there would result the cognition of an action situated in its accomplished state (*siddhāvasthāpanna*).

In reality, since the agent and other factors are expressed within the suffix (*pratyaya*), it should be understood that there is no fault even according to the literal reading [of the rule], because [the action] resides in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Regarding "in due order": the meaning is that in the word *paśya* (see), there is the nature of the goal (*sādhya-rūpatā*), whereas in *dhāvati* (he runs), there is the nature of the means (*sādhana-rūpatā*). Regarding "being connected" (*anvayitva*): the meaning is that because the action of running (*dhāvana-kriyā*) is connected as the object (*karman*) [of the seeing], it possesses the status of a means (*sādhanatva*). Regarding "by the base" (*prakṛtyā*): this means by the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself. Regarding "expressed" (*upāttā*): the word "action" (*kriyā*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

"In being expressed as such" means "in being expressed as something to be accomplished. "By the genitive of the object" [is said] because the status of being an object is impossible without connection to an action that has reached the state of being something to be accomplished; the sense is that the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is defined only with respect to an action situated in such a state. "Because of connection with the action" [is said]; this is the ablative used after the elision of a word ending in *-lyap*, meaning "taking into account the connection with the action. "Only with connection to a *kṛt*-formed word" [is meant].

The meaning is that, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the genitive case is prescribed by that [rule] only for the object (*karman*) as determined by the action denoted by the base of a *kṛt*-suffix. One should also understand that if proximity were not accepted, the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.65) would result in being redundant, as per the prohibition "na lokā" (Pāṇini 2.3.69). It should be understood that in cases such as *edodanapāka* ("the cooking of rice"), a compound is not applicable here because of a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*).

Nor can there be a compound with a genitive of residue (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), because in cases such as *nalapāka* ("rice cooked by Nala") or *odanapāka* ("cooking of rice"), there would be no resulting cognition characterized by the relation of agenthood or objecthood. Furthermore, this would lead to the undesired consequence of accepting the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65)—which is not favored by the Mīmāṃsakas—as applicable there; he states that this is accepted as desired in that context. In this manner, the expression *stokaṃ pākaḥ* ("a slight cooking") is justified.

In expressions such as *stokaṃ pacati* ("he cooks slightly"), because the fruit (*phala*) also has the status of an object (*karman*) by virtue of being based on a part [of the action] through the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs precisely for qualifiers such as *stoka*, since they are non-different from it. This is the meaning even in cases such as *stokaṃ pākaḥ*. However, it should be understood that according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*) who maintain that "the status of being an object belongs to adverbial qualifiers" (*kriyāviśeṣaṇānāṃ karmatvam*) is a rule based on explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanikatva*), there would result the undesirable consequence of a second case ending after the word *jyotiṣṭoma* even in sentences such as *jyotiṣṭomena yajeta*. 14.

Nor should it be suspected that in examples such as "stokaṃ pākaḥ" ("a slight cooking"), the genitive case prescribed by the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.65) ought to occur, on the grounds that *stoka* possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) as defined with respect to the action denoted by the base of the *kṛt*-affix.

Because, by association with the agent (*kartṛ*), only that object (*karman*) which is construed as distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is understood; and because in the original [text] it is stated that "action (*kriyā*) is that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhyatvena*). For this very reason, the formation of suffixes such as *tumun*—prescribed when another action is the purpose of the action denoted by the verb—is established in cases such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ* ("cooking for the sake of eating"), since the word *kriyā* applies specifically to an operation (*vyāpāra*) characterized by being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*).

Nor should it be argued that the suffix *tumun* is unjustified by taking the meaning of the verbal root—which constitutes only a part of the "word-meaning" (*padārtha*)—as the governing factor (*upapada*), according to the maxim "that which is a part [is not the whole]. This is because the stated maxim applies to cases other than those involving actions; for we observe that in examples such as *bhoktuṃ gataḥ* ("he went to eat"), *devadattena gato grāmaḥ* ("the village was gone to by Devadatta"), and *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"), the various *kārakas* (case-relations) are construed with the subordinate action. In reality, however, forms such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ* ("cooking to eat") and *bhoktuṃ gata* ("gone to eat") are simply ungrammatical.

(The word *tumun* is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]). By the statement "when there is an action for the sake of another action," through proximity (*pratyāsatti*), one obtains the fact that the two actions belong to the same class; consequently, only an action for the sake of another action—which is subordinate to the meaning of the suffix attached to its own base and exists merely in a state to be accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanna*)—is grasped. [Objection:

But if this is so, according to the reasoning stated, then even the suffix *kṛtvasuc* would not occur in examples such as *pañcakṛtvaḥ pākaḥ* ("cooking five times"), because in the rule prescribing that suffix as well, such an action could not possibly be grasped. [Reply: This is not so.

In a rule where there is the mention of a word denoting an action (*kriyāvācaka-śabda*), only that specific action mentioned therein is understood. However, in a case where there is the mention of the meaning in the form of an action (*kriyārūpārtha*), even that which has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) and so forth is included; thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, it should be understood that in the rule for the suffix *tumun*, there is a mention of the word as a co-occurring item (*upapada*), whereas in other cases there is not. Nor does it follow that in examples such as *pākaḥ* ("cooking"), there would be the undesirable consequence of the action being understood twice; for the intended meaning is that a single word-meaning is presented through both its states as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and as something already established (*siddha*). Nor should it be asked how a single word-meaning can be presented by these two contradictory [states].

Just as there is no contradiction in the simultaneous presentation of both "teacher-hood" and "maternal uncle-hood" for one and the same person due to the difference in their relations to the relatum (*nirūpaka*), so too, it is accepted that there is no contradiction when those two [masculinity and femininity] are presented as residing in a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*) through the difference in their relations to the *kāraka*, gender, and so forth, and through the difference in the expressive words (*bodhaka*). This is because they are perceived as being endowed with all genders and numbers. This is also to be understood from the phrase "because of being the means of knowledge" (*mānatvāt*).

The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself possesses the status of a qualifier by virtue of being the object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), and it possesses the status of a qualificand by virtue of being already established (*siddhatva*). The fact that these two reside in one and the same locus is precisely what constitutes the obstacle to their being apprehended as distinct. Thus, it is established that the "being" (*bhāva*) denoted by the suffix *ghañ* is the primary element.

For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), it is stated: "That state denoted by the suffix *ghañ* is external to the meaning of the verbal root" (*anyaḥ sa bhāvo bāhyaḥ prakṛtyarthāt*). Thus, in the example *stokaḥ pākaḥ* ("a slight cooking"), the nominative case is used because the action denoted by *ghañ* functions as a qualifier of the verbal root's meaning, and not the accusative. This is because that [action] lacks the status of an object (*karman*), and consequently, its qualifier also lacks that status.

Nor is that [result] established through the connection with the *bhāvanā* of the root-meaning; for some maintain that even if the nominative case were somehow impossible—as in the case of "one sacrifices with the Jyotiṣṭoma"—neuter gender would be unavoidable according to the rule "the neuter is used for general [terms]" (*sāmānyenapuṃsakam*). This refers to the second [alternative]. The phrase "and neuter gender" is to be supplied as the remainder. With the intention that the forms beginning with *ghañ* might serve merely for the grammatical correctness of usage, he raises an objection:

"—and not so," it says. "The locative *tātpuruṣa* compound is to be established in the sequence. This is the direction [of the analysis]. Herein is the essential point: when words such as *stoka-* (little) function as qualifiers of the verbal root's meaning—the activity (*vyāpāra*)—there is the nominative case and the neuter gender; however, when they function as qualifiers of the *bhāva* (the abstract action) which is the meaning of the suffix, there is the nominative case and the masculine gender.

In the domain of the *tumun* suffix and others, it is the very state of being that has reached the condition of being accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanna-bhāva*) which is denoted by the verbal root; and by the *tumun* suffix and others as well, exactly that same [state] is denoted. Thus, these suffixes possess merely the character of restating the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthānuvādakatā*). Therefore, they differ from words such as *pāka* (cooking) and the like; we shall explain this in the section on "The Determination of the Meaning of Nominal Stems" (*prātipadikārthanirṇaya*). || 15 ||

(bhū.sā.dhā.ni -16) — "Only when there is a restriction" (*niyama eva*) means: only when there is a restriction (*niyame sati*). (*"That very [thing]"*—*sa eva iti*—and *"that very [thing]"*—*tadeva iti*—are neuter in the sense of a general category; the meaning is that the restriction regarding the connection of the factors of action (*kāraka*) with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is precisely this. The reading *sa eva* is indeed easy to understand. "*Only in a single sentence*" (*samānavākye eva*) means: only in a single syntactical unit (*ekavākye*). The definition of a worldly sentence (*laukika-vākya-lakṣaṇa*), as stated by the author of the Vārttika (*vārttikakṛt*) in the Mahābhāṣya (Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 336, sū. 2.1.1), is: "A sentence is a verbal form (*ākhyāta*) together with its qualifiers (*saviśeṣaṇa*)."

Here, by the word *ākhyāta* (verb), the expression of action (*kriyā*) is understood. This very point was also stated by Amara: "A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of verbal and nominal forms (*tiṅ-subanta-caya*), or it is an action associated with its factors (*kāraka*). (Amara-koṣa, Prathama-kāṇḍa, Śabdādi-varga, verse 2). Regarding this, the word "or" (*vā*) should be understood in the sense of "if"; that is, if the action associated with the factors is to be expressed. Thus, the resulting meaning is: a sentence is a collection of nominal forms that expresses an action associated with its factors.

"Su and tiṅ" form *suptiṅ*. That which is characterized by *su* (nominal suffixes) and *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes) is *suptiṅ*. Through the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of these two, there is a compound with the word "end" (*anta*). By this, there is the acquisition of three definitions: a collection of words ending in *su*, a collection of words ending in *tiṅ*, and a collection of words ending in both *su* and *tiṅ*. Regarding these, the example for the first is "caitreṇa śayitavyam" (It must be slept by Caitra); for the second, "pacati bhavati" (He cooks [and] exists); and for the third, "caitraḥ pacati" (Caitra cooks). By the qualifier "expressing action" (*kriyāvat*), the exclusion of meaningless aggregates (such as those formed by the suffix *yaṅ*) is achieved.

Even a mere collection of nominal and verbal suffixes, such as *pacati* and the like, is a word because it conveys a qualified action with respect to its agent and so forth. This very point was stated by Hari:
"That which has expectant parts yet does not require another word for its completion [is a sentence], even when there is a distinction [between its parts]. (Vākyapadīya, Kāṇḍa II, verse 4).

Regarding the statement, "A sentence is held to be that which has action as its primary element, possesses qualities, and has a single purpose," the term *vākya* here means "a single sentence. This is in accordance with Jaimini’s Sūtra (2.1.46): "Because of the unity of meaning, there is one sentence, provided that if it were divided, there would be mutual expectancy. In this context, the claim that "sentence" (*vākya*) refers to that which conveys the meaning of a sentence is incorrect; for according to the rule "the substitution of *ku* [for *v*] does not occur when *vacas* is a technical grammatical term," the word *vākya* is not employed in the sense of "meaning" (*artha*), as that would preclude the application of the *ku*-substitution.

Furthermore, according to the manner stated above, both definitions [of *samānavākya*] are afflicted by the fallacies of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Consequently, since this vocative lacks the status of being an adverbial adjunct to a verb, it does not constitute a sentence at all. Therefore, where could there be "sentence-unity" (*samānavākyatva*), which is synonymous with "single-sentence-unity" (*ekavākyatva*)? Thus, the rule "in a non-uniform sentence" (*asamānavākya*, Mahābhāṣya, Tṛtīyakhaṇḍa, p. 324)—which prescribes the absence of accentuation (*nighāta*) for a vocative following a word—would not apply here.

Therefore, since the vocative case functions as the subject of the restatement (*anuvādya*), and since that which is restated must be connected with what is enjoined (*vidheya*), and since the status of being enjoined resides in the action (*kriyā*), it is logical that its connection must be with that very action; this will be clarified further on.

"—that [the vocative] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the action. The meaning is that it possesses the nature of a qualifier by way of being a differentiator (*vyāvartakatva*), because the action of going toward Devadatta who is being addressed is distinguished from other actions by Devadatta who is being addressed. "Devadatta, go! is not cited as an example because it lacks the status of being after a word (*padāt paratva*). He states the necessity of the definition of a worldly sentence as "a verb (*ākhyāta*) together with its qualifiers" by saying "he cooks."

He states the very method of the Sūtra: "—*tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*—" (Sūtra 7.1.88)—thus [he says]. The point is that otherwise, since there would be no single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) between two *tiṅ*-ending words, there would be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and consequently, the prohibition by the word *atiṅ* would result in being redundant. However, the Author of the Bhāṣya has clearly stated that there is indeed single-sentence status, because he provides the meaning of "pacati bhavati" and so forth as "pāko bhavati" and so forth. If it is objected: "But if, according to the stated method, single-sentence status is accepted in cases such as 'pacati bhavati', then the mention of *atiṅ* is necessary to prevent the application of the rule for the elision of a finite verb (*nidhāta*). Therefore, its rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) in the Bhāṣya is inconsistent," we say: No.

Even though there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) in common worldly usage, because the technical definition provided in the grammatical treatise—that "a sentence consists of a single finite verb" (*ekatiṅ vākyam*)—is not applicable here, that [definition] would be rendered useless; such is the [author's] instruction. As stated by Hari: "In the science [of grammar], a sentence is defined as having one finite verb (*ekatiṅ*). For that [definition], the mention of 'not having a finite verb' (*atiṅ*) is unnecessary, since no division of sentences exists [in such cases]. This applies even when there are many finite verbs.

Since [sentences] that require mutual expectancy constitute a single sentence (*ekavākya*), the prohibition of *nighāta* by the rule *atiṅ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28) becomes meaningful. Therefore it is said: "In this way, even that which ends in a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is stated to be a qualifier of another finite verb. Even according to the Vārttika view, he states what is desired: "In reality, as it were—having a single finite verb as its qualificand," meaning having the meaning of a single finite verb as its qualificand. And thus, in the case of "He bathes first, then he goes," the *nighāta* prescribed by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28) is established.

"—repeated birth—repeated origination. Regarding that which is to be indicated [by the suffix], this is the meaning. From a numeral word denoting the number five, when it occurs in the sense of counting things characterized by origination, the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is added; however, the suffix is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), while the object characterized by origination is the action itself. Thus, in examples such as "he eats five times" (*pañcakṛtvo bhuṅkte*), the word "five" refers to the number five as characterized by the objects of origination, and its connection is with the action alone, according to this grammatical treatise.

And [the suffix *suc*] expresses the production of the number five in the act of eating (*bhuji-kriyā*). However, when there is multiplicity of agents, as in "they eat five times" (*pañcakṛtvo bhuñjate*), the plural number is used even though [the suffix *suc*] is present. In cases such as "ten repeated twice," the suffix *suc* likewise serves to count the occurrences of the act of repetition. Where no action is explicitly heard, it should be understood that an action is to be supplied (*adhyāhāra*). By the statement "only those connected with an action [are kārakas]," it is stated that being a *kāraka* consists in being connected with an action.

In reality, the status of being a *kāraka* consists precisely in being a producer of action (*kriyājanakatva*), because it is explained in the *Bhāṣya* by means of the verb *karoti*, which has the sense of "producing," as that which brings about designations such as agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*). We shall explain this in the *Subarthanirṇaya*. Regarding the phrase "because it has been so stated": the intended meaning is as follows. When the thing compared (*upameya*) is an action (*kriyā*), the suffix *vati* occurs after a word denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) ending in the third case, in the sense of "equal to" (*tulyam*). This is the meaning of the first rule: *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced vatiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.115).

Nor should it be argued that [the suffix *vat*] would not apply in cases such as "he studies like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇavad adhīte*), because similarity defined by the Brāhmaṇa is absent in the act of studying;

for the words "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth are used metaphorically (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote the study performed by that [Brāhmaṇa]. Furthermore, excellence (*sauṣṭava*) and the like constitute the common property (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*). Consequently, the understanding in cases such as "the Kṣatriya studies like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇavad adhīte kṣatriyaḥ*) is that the study performed by the Kṣatriya is similar to the study performed by the Brāhmaṇa. Thus, it is quite clear that its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) exists only when there is a connection with an action (*kriyānvaya*).

In expressions such as "the face is beautiful like a lotus," a verb must be supplied (*kriyādhyāhāra*) for the sake of grammatical justification through the suffix *-vat*. By the word "lotus" (*aravinda*), the "becoming a lotus" (*aravindabhavana*) is indicated by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, beauty (*saundarya*) is indeed presented as the common property (*sādhāraṇadharmā*). Thus, the cognition is: "The becoming of the beautiful face is similar to the becoming of a lotus. Subsequently, however, the similarity characterized by the quality of beauty between the lotus and the face is understood through suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

For this very reason, in expressions such as *brāhmaṇena tulyam asya rūpam* ("his form is equal to that of a Brahmin"), the suffix *-vat* is not used, because there is no connection with an action (*kriyā*). Since this [suffix] is already established by the rule *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.1.116), however, the rule *tena tulyam* (Pāṇini 5.1.115) is for the purpose of expressing equality in terms of substance, quality, and so forth. Furthermore, the rule *tadarham* (Pāṇini 5.1.117) is for the purpose of expressing "worthiness"; the details of this are explained elsewhere. Regarding the phrase "because of the prescription": in examples such as *vasan dadarśa* ("while dwelling, he saw")—as in: "The Lord of Śrī, whose abode is the glorious house of Vasudeva, went to rule the world."
While dwelling there, Hari beheld the sage Hiraṇyagarbha descending from the sky to the earth. (Śiśupālavadha, First Canto, Verse 2). [Note:
Regarding the point that "even when the meaning of the subsequent member [of the compound] is predominant," this will be analyzed in the determination of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).

"—because of the cognition of a negation."—The meaning is that otherwise, the second person [imperative] would not be applicable. "Such an application" refers to the formulation: "A pot is not produced. The meaning is that at the time of that application, there is the existence of the absence of production. 16.

(From *Bhūṣaṇasāradīpikā* 17) — "Let it be determined by the action alone. (*Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntabhūṣaṇakārikā* 17). The word "alone" (*eva*) in the root [verse] has the sense of exclusion (*avacchedārtha*). Even though the eighth case (*aṣṭhaka*) is grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) only when there is a connection with the action according to the stated method, why is there a restriction that the connection occurs only through the denotative function (*bāvanā*)? [As in the example: "The accomplishment of the action... (*kriyāyāḥ pariniṣpattiḥ...*) and so forth. ("The accomplishment of the action is that which follows immediately from whose operation...")

"When that [instrumentality] is intended to be expressed, then it is traditionally understood as such. (Vākyapadīya, Tṛtīyakāṇḍa, Sāra-saṃgraha, verse 90). Since it is possible to understand the word *kriyā*—which is well-known for denoting the "fruit" (*phala*)—in the sense of "action" in expressions such as *kriyām abhyeti*, he says: "The meaning is this"—namely, that it is etymological (*yaugika*). The meaning is: "that which is performed is *kriyā*. Regarding the term "of the technical name" (*saṃjñāśabdasya*): it refers to the technical name *kriyā* which has the sense of "becoming" (*bhāva*). Regarding "independent" (*anapekṣā*): the meaning is independent of its etymological derivation (*yoga*). Regarding "the *Rathantara* [sāman] on the higher [verse]" (*rathantaram uttareti*): [this is an example].

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "One sings the Rathantara on the two subsequent verses. This refers not to a distinction among specific verses, but to the distinction of the Rathantara Sāman. "Abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ" is the source-verse (yoni) of the Rathantara Sāman; following that, there exists in the Veda the verse to be recited, beginning with "Tvāmiddhi havāmahe," and so forth.

In this regard, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *rathantara* sāman—which is to be understood from the injunction "one sings the *rathantara* on the two *uttara* [verses]"—is not to be sung upon the verses mentioned in this statement; rather, it is to be sung only upon the verse that will be specified in the section known as the *uttara-grantha*, because in that *uttara-grantha* (Mīmāṃsādarśana 9.2.23), the original source-verses (*yoni-ṛc*) for all the *sāmans* are specifically distinguished.

"In some cases," as in "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) and so forth, such [words] serve as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) within the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). Regarding the phrase "of the qualities" (*guṇānām*): according to the Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.22, "And because qualities are for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them], owing to their equality," being for the sake of another (*parārthatva*) is the reason for [the lack of connection] regarding the qualities, while equality (*samatva*) is the reason for [the lack of connection] regarding the connection itself. Thus, the meaning is that because qualities are for the sake of another, there is no mutual connection between them, owing to their equality. Regarding the phrase "by that which has its function already determined" (*klptakāryya*): [this refers to the fact that the relationship between the word and its meaning is already established].

The meaning of "established causal relation" (*klptakāryakāraṇabhāva*) is that the cognition produced by the word *kṛt* (the verbal root *kṛ*) is the cause for a cognition in which the meaning of the verbal root is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and [the object] is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). [The phrase] "because it is not seen" means that [such a rule] does not exist; rather, it exists because we do observe the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in the form of "what does he do? (*kiṃ karoti?*). [The phrase] "without that" means "without action" (*kriyā*). The expression "they say" (*āhuḥ*) indicates a lack of conviction (*asvarasa*). The seed of this [doubt] is that even a sentence such as *aidhitavyam* ("it must be kindled"), which lacks an action presented by a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), is indeed accepted by you. As it was stated by "Hari": *... [text fragment]* ... *tasmād asty eva kriyā sarvatra vākye.* (Therefore, action certainly exists in every sentence.)

Regarding the statement, "They consider even that sentence to be one whose action is internalized" (*Vākyapadīya* II.326), the meaning is that even this [expression] *piṇḍīm* ("the ball of rice") is considered a sentence because its action is internalized. This is an illustration; it also applies to sentences consisting of words expressing a single action, such as those containing a subject (*viśeṣya*) and so forth.

As it has been said: "Where a verb (*ākhyāta-śabda*) is understood as necessarily accompanied by its factors (*sadhana*), that too is called a single sentence whose meaning is a composite whole" (*Vākyapadīya* II.326).

By this, it is indicated that the Mīmāṃsaka position—that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in a word within a sentence consisting of a single word as being related to others—is accepted, and not in a sentence composed of multiple words; furthermore, the "others" are to be inferred through the force of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

[Objection: "In that case, the combined usage of sentences such as 'Enter the house' (*gṛhaṃ praviśa*) and 'Eat the piṇḍī' (*piṇḍīṃ bhakṣaya*) would not be possible. [Response: This is not so; for since these are distinct words, their usage is possible in common parlance even without regard for brevity. Regarding this, the ancients held that just as the word "Bhīma" (an avayava of Bhīmasena) causes the recollection of the qualified word "Bhīmasena," so too a single part of a sentence such as "enter" (*praviśa*) causes the recollection of the full sentence "enter the house" (*praviśa gṛham*); that itself is the *adhyāhāra* (supplying the ellipsis), and from that, comprehension arises. However, that is incorrect.

Because there is no cognition of the meaning through recollection; because, due to the absence of conveying a meaning through its own operation (*vṛtti*), it lacks the status of a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatva*), which would result in the impossibility of the application of case-endings (*sub*); and because of the authority of the commentary on the sūtra *aṇudit* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), which states, "A word that is uttered is expressive" (*uccaritaḥ śabdaḥ pratyāyakaḥ*)—as evidenced by the Mahābhāṣya: "That which is being uttered is the conveyor of meaning" (*uccāryamāṇaḥ saṃpratyāyako bhavati*, MaBh Pra-kha-pṛ. 327)—and because there is no comprehension [of meaning] from [the mere form] itself. By this, the view that there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a factor of action (*kāraka*) based on a verb such as "enter" (*praviśa*) and so forth is also refuted.

Furthermore, is there an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), an implication (*ākṣepa*), or an inference (*anumāna*)? Even so, does the word imply or infer another word, or does it do so through its meaning? It cannot be the first, because it is impossible for a word—while occupied with conveying its own meaning—to imply or infer another word. Nor can it be the latter, because a meaning has no connection with another word. By this, the view that a word implies a meaning is also refuted, since a word already employed has no connection with the meaning of another word.

For even if some kind of indirect connection exists, it lacks the capacity to function as the motivator for an inference. Furthermore, because there is no lack of logical consistency—as in the case of "Fat Devadatta [must eat during the day]"—there can be no implication (*ākṣepa*). Moreover, implication cannot be considered a means of valid cognition distinct from inference. If it is argued that the meaning is inferred from the meaning, then the resulting cognition would not be verbal (*śābda*).

Therefore, at the time of grasping the power (*śakti*) of a specific word or sentence for its respective meaning, there is also the grasping of the power of its constituent parts, which are produced along with it; thus, the cognition of the qualified meaning arises. This very principle is called the "maxim of the part of a sentence" (*vākyaikadeśanyāya*). For this reason alone, the consistency of the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra "igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam" (Pāṇini 1.1.45) is established:

"For we see people employing parts of sentences within sentences, and parts of words within words" (*Mahābhāṣya*, Prauḍhamanoramā-khaṇḍana, p. 252). It is precisely for this reason that the mental cognition (*mānasaṃ jñānaṃ*) occurs immediately after the utterance [of the word]; such is the direction of the argument. || 17 ||

Regarding the statement "There is no pot on the ground," since the cognition is that "the pot possesses the absence of being located upon the ground as defined by the ground," there is no need to supply an implied verb (*kriyādhyāhāra*). Furthermore, refuting the Naiyāyika claim that the verbal form in the Vedāntin-stated proposition "The mountain ought to possess fire, like a kitchen" is redundant, he says in the *Mūla*: "If [it were so] even in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*)," and "like a kitchen. (Vaiśeṣikasiddhāntabhūṣaṇakārikā 18). "Like a kitchen" (*mahānasavat*).

In this case, according to their view, the similarity—which is the meaning of the suffix *vat*—is construed with the mountain. However, that is incorrect, because the rule *tena tulyam* (Pāṇini 5.1.115) prescribes the suffix *vat* only when the similarity is produced by an action (*kriyā*) that has been expressed. For this very reason, the Vedāntins maintain that the words "it ought to be" (*bhavitum arhati*) must be supplied as an ellipsis. In reality, however, there is no fault; for the suffix *vat* is prescribed even in the absence of a connection with an action by the rule *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.1.116), and since such [similarity] exists in the present context, one should take note of this. (1) L. *taditi*)

"—Even in the face of contradiction with the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*). This means that even when there is a contradiction with the grammatical rule *saptamy adhī* (Pāṇini 2.3.36), which prescribes the locative case under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "kārakas," by means of the rule *tena tulyam* (Pāṇini 5.1.115). "—*caturthyāḥ spṛhī*. In this view, it should be understood that the justification for the dative case occurs either through the supplying of a word (*padādhyāhāra*) or through the supplying of a meaning (*arthādhyāhāra*).

In my view, however, it should be understood that by the force of the rule *spṛherīpsita* (Pāṇini 1.4.36), [the object] is understood through the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the verb *spṛhayati*. In reality, even here, its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is established either through the use of that verb by the force of the aforementioned rule, or—by the maxim of the "single part of a sentence" (*vākyaikadeśanyāya*)—even without its use, in accordance with the method already stated. This is because, regarding the domain of the rule *kriyārthopapada* (Pāṇini 2.3.14), it is stated that in examples such as *phalebhyo yāti*, where the suffix *tumun* is not employed, the sense of the root is present as the underlying element (*sthānin*).

Even in cases such as "lyablope" (*lyablope karmaṇyadhikaraṇe ca*, Vārttika-pāṭha, Saṃvat 1474–75), the grammatical correctness of the *padyamī* suffix is established only when there is the usage of a portion of a sentence devoid of the *lyap*-affix. This is because of the statement "lyablope. In that context, the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word's constituent part is accepted with respect to its respective qualified meaning according to the aforementioned method. || 18 ||

(bhū.sā.dhā.ni -19) He states the meaning of the word *vi*—namely, "not separately" (*na vivicya*)—which means "not by way of distinction" (*bhedena*). The ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*) is to be supplied as "by way of being the qualificand" (*viśeṣyatayā*). That is to say, it is [an action] devoid of being grasped as separate from the agent. And thus, the full meaning is that the primary object [the action] is connected with the case-factors (*kāraka*s) even by an action that is not yet conjoined with the agent—as in the example "one who has previously made a mat" (*kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*). In this instance, the suffix *kta* in *kṛta* is not used in the sense of the object (*karmani*).

Furthermore, since there is no possibility of a second accusative case following the word *kaṭa*, the status of being intransitive (*akarmaka*) is accepted by means of merely superimposing an artificial absence of an object onto the portion [of the action] denoted by the verbal root (*kalāṃśa*). Thus, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). Alternatively, because the specific object is not intended to be construed with its particular form at the outset, the verb is considered intransitive, and the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the abstract state. Although a general object exists in the form of "object-ness" (*karmatva*), it is simply not intended to be expressed because it is an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyakatva*). Consequently, in the compound *kṛtapūrva*, the suffix *ini* is added to the word *kṛtapūrva* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

When there is a desire to restrict the meaning of the verbal root—which is a part of the *ktvā* suffix occurring after that [causative]—to a sense connected with the object [of the causative], its connection with the object such as "the hand" (*kara*) is precluded. This is as in the view of the moderns regarding the second sentence of the rule *ṇeraṇau* (Pāṇini 1.3.67), in the general example cited in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "The elephant causes men to mount the high ground" (*sthalam ārohayati manuṣyān hastī*). As stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The elephant-keepers mount the elephant; the elephant, being caused to mount, causes the men to mount the high ground. Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*). (Ma.Bhā.Pra.Kha., p. [number]).

177) Just as in the case of "men mount the elephant" (*manuṣyā hastinam ārohanti*), although in the state without the causative suffix (*aṇ-antāvasthā*) there is no connection with the object in the form of the ground (*sthala-rūpa-karman*) within the meaning of the verbal root, in the causative state (*ṇyanta*) there is a clear connection with the object such as the ground, because one intends to express the meaning of the verbal root as being connected to that very object; and this is clearly explained in the *Śekhara* on that rule (specifically in the section on *kāraka* in the *Laghuśabdenduśekhara*, in the commentary on the rule *gati-buddhi-* [Pāṇini 1.4.52], which deals with the present subject), so too is it in the present case.

This is because of the Bhāṣya on the rule *kṛta-* [Pāṇini 2.3.65], which states: "What is the purpose? It is so that [the genitive] may apply when those two are the agent and the object; it should not apply when those two are the agent and the object of something else. This is also evident from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). (Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 525) Furthermore, if one does not accept the intention to express the object (*karman*) after the formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), then the aforementioned Bhāṣya would be inconsistent. This is also supported by another Bhāṣya passage on the sūtra *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). (Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. [same])

526) Therefore, one should not accept the view of a certain [scholar] who, by refuting the application of the objecthood (*karmatva*) of the mat (*kaṭa*) to the meaning of the suffix *kṛt* ending in *avaktṛ*, introduces an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) elsewhere; for such a restriction—which pertains to the scope of these two specific usages—is not accepted anywhere else, on account of the authority of the aforementioned Bhāṣya. In this context, however, the genitive case prescribed by "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.65) does not apply.

In this context, by the force of the word *kṛti*, the meaning is that the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies only to the agent and the object as defined by the action denoted by the base of a *kṛt*-affix, which is presented through the cooperation of the knowledge of the power of that *kṛt*-affix. Otherwise, since the genitive would be established by implication only in connection with *kṛt* affixes—due to the prohibition "not in common usage" (*na loke*, Pāṇini 2.3.69) regarding connection with verbal suffixes (*viṅ*)—the [present] rule would clearly be redundant. This is made explicit in the *Mahābhāṣya* on that very point (Mbh Pra-kha p. 525).

In this case, however, by the very power of the *taddhita* suffix [in *pūrva*], which is assisted by the knowledge of the power of the verbal root *kṛ*, the primary suffix, and the preceding word, there arises the cognition of the agents of the prior action as mutually qualified; thus, the knowledge of the power of the *kṛdanta* suffix is also an auxiliary factor therein. This is because, elsewhere, since there is no usage of the root *kṛ* with the suffix *kta* in the sense of abstract action (*bhāva*), there is no evidence for grasping a separate power for that suffix alone.

Since the state of forming a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) exists for both [the compound and its constituent parts] when four words are involved, there is no lack of grammatical correctness (*asādhutva*) here. Furthermore, there is no fault in examples such as *taṇḍulānāṃ pācakatara* ("one who cooks rice better"). Because the word *pācaka* and others occur in independent usage, the apprehension of their *kṛt*-suffix-based meaning also exists; thus, the presentation of the meaning from the entire complex form occurs precisely through the cooperation of the knowledge of the suffix-meaning, owing to the ease with which the genitive case is applied. By this, [the objection that the form is incorrect] because it ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix, according to the rule *na loke* (Pāṇini 8.2.82), is refuted.

By the prohibition [in Pāṇini 2.3.69], it is refuted that the mention of *kṛt* in the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ" (2.3.65) is redundant, since the absence of the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) from the word *kaṭa* in the aforementioned example is already established. For, according to the reasoning stated above, even here, the prohibition does not apply because the sixth case is not intended for the agent or object that are construed with the action presented through the cooperation of the knowledge of the word-meaning of the *niṣṭhā*-ending term. Furthermore, one should not raise the objection: "How can there be a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) here, given the lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*)?"

At the time of the derivation of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) from the word *kṛtapūrva*, which contains a noun ending in the abstract suffix *-tā* (*bhāvaktanta*), there is no connection with the mat (*kaṭa*) and so forth due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). However, after the secondary suffix has been produced, the word "mat" and so on connects with the agent—the meaning of the secondary suffix—through a relationship mediated by the action; this is another point. For this very reason, the prohibition—"there is no connection with a qualifier for that which has already undergone composition" (*vṛttasya viśeṣaṇayogo neti*)—does not apply, because that prohibition is applicable only to the portion of the qualifier belonging to a part of the compound (*vṛttaikadeśa*).

For this very reason, in expressions such as *rājapuruṣa* ("the king's man"), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—such as the king—does not admit connection with another qualifier; however, for the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), such as the man, such connection certainly occurs. As for the rule "there is no compound formation (*vṛtti*) of those that have qualifiers," there is no possibility of its application at all, because prior to the formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita-vṛtti*), there is an absence of having qualifiers. Furthermore, according to the view that the capacity (*sāmarthya*) is characterized by constant one-meaningness (*nityaikārthībhāva*), both of these statements [of Pāṇini] are rejected in the Bhāṣya. By this, the objection—"How can there be a compound formation (*vṛtti*) given the aforementioned prohibition?"—is refuted.

In this manner, there is no non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding the object (*karman*) in such a sentence; thus, forms such as *kṛtaḥ kaṭam* do not occur. By this, the argument that "due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would not arise" is refuted. This same principle should be observed here and also in the case of *adhīti vyākaraṇe*. However, in the latter instance, the locative case (*saptamī*) supersedes the accusative (*dvitīyā*) by virtue of the Vārttika: "An addition [to the rule] is made for the object of a word ending in *kta* when it relates to the sphere of *in*."

The meaning [of the rule] is that when there is a connection with a *kta*-suffix ending in its basic form (*prakṛtibhūta*), the seventh case (*saptamī*) is used provided that the object (*karman*) is not already expressed by another means and remains to be denoted. Regarding the word *adhītī*, since it ends in a *kta* suffix denoting the object, the seventh case would not otherwise apply; therefore, the entire aforementioned method must be applied there as well—this is the path of all grammarians (*śābdika*). To this very effect, Gokulanātha Upādhyāya states in his *Padavākyaratnākara* (verse 165): "Or the seventh case may occur in the sense of the object when [the suffix] *ini* follows words such as *iṣṭa*. This is the explanation of the seventh case as a *kāraka*. (Page 830).

Others, however, have declared that the locative case (*saptamī*) is always used here. Thus, the teachers (*upādhyāyāḥ*) agreed regarding the locative as a residual kāraka (*kārakaśeṣe*); yet, their statement of an alternative view is without authority, as it is not supported by the *Bhāṣya* or other [authoritative texts] and is merely a different position. The Bhaṭṭācāryas remain indifferent on this point. Furthermore, the author of the *Śabdaśaktiprakāśikā* (pp. 294–390, section on Kārakas) also validates this very usage through a different rule found in another grammatical system; thus, everything is well-said.

This being the case, let the wise discern that the labor of some, undertaken for the sake of establishing the grammatical usage "he has studied grammar" (*adhītī vyākaraṇam*) by means of a word ending in the second case, is indeed fruitless.

"—the [action] becomes subordinate by means of the suffix *in* and so forth. Although there is a disparity between the two cases—since in the example "he went to the village" (*grāmaṃ gataḥ*), the action of going, which has become subordinate to the meaning of the *kta* suffix, is construed as the qualificand with respect to another factor such as the village;

whereas in the illustrated case "one who previously made a mat" (*kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*), the action of making, which has become a qualifier of the expressed meaning, is construed as a qualifier of the agentive factor denoted by the suffix *in*—nevertheless, there is no fault, because the intent is merely to demonstrate that an action which has attained the status of a qualifier of the agent may be construed elsewhere with another kāraka. This is the general direction. || 19 ||
(From *Bhūṣaṇasāradīpikā* 20):

"The inclusion of even an action established in a completed state [is justified] precisely by the indication in the rule *dvirvacane'ci*; however, the mention of the word *kriyā* in the sūtra *saṃkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttau* (Pāṇini 5.4.17) is for the sake of subsequent rules. Some, however, maintain that forms such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ* are indeed incorrect, because of the mention of *atiṅ* in the sūtra *upapadamatiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19).

Having stated that the prohibition of compounding in the case of *kārakaḥ gataḥ*—where there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a word denoting action (*kriyāvācin*) within the scope of the suffix *ṇvul*—is the intended result, [the author] notes that this is not so, because it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "This does not denote an action; what then? It denotes a substance" (Ma.Bhā.Pra.Kha.Pṛ. 439).

"—that which has become a subordinate factor. This means the action expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) when it is in a state of being yet to be accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanna*). As stated in the *Hari-kārikā* (Vākyapadīya III, Kriyāsaṃuddeśa 52):

"The verbal root is the denoter of that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), as well as of [words ending in] *la*, *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal*-affixes, and likewise of indeclinables (*avyaya-kṛt*), participles in *-niṣṭhā*, and [words such as] *agha*. Since, according to this statement of Hari, the verbal root denotes an action situated in a state of being yet to be accomplished.

"—*sādhyamātrasvabhāveti*—the meaning is: having the nature of being yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), without having attained the state of being already established (*siddha*). The word *mātra* (only) excludes the fact that this [action] has instead attained a distinction as an action situated in the state of being established (*siddhāvasthāpanna*). "—*atiprasaṅga iti*—" the meaning is: just as suffixes such as *ktvā* are grammatically correct when construed with an action denoted by a *kṛt*-affix base which is not yet established (*asatvabhūta*)—as in the case of "cooking after eating" (*bhuktvā pākaḥ*)—so too would there be the undesired consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) of suffixes expressing the sense of *kṛtvasuc* (frequency) being correct when construed with such [established] actions, leading to ungrammatical usages such as *dvipākaḥ* or *tripākaḥ*. However, in cases like "cooking" (*pākaḥ*), the action has indeed attained that [established] state; thus, those instances are excluded. He will explain this later.

"—and it is not so. This must be stated; "not" means indeed not. The phrase "so they say" (*āhuḥ*) indicates the emergence of a lack of satisfaction (*asvarasa*). The reason for this has already been explained above. || 20 ||
(Bhūṣaṇasāradīpikā - 21) In order to further refute, by means of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*) maxim, the Mīmāṃsaka position that *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the *tiṅ* suffix, he says:

"But [in] the Siddhānta..."—the meaning is "in the form of a sentence. He states that if the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not express *bhāvanā* and the verb (*ākhyāta*), ending in a *tiṅ* suffix, does not express the agent (*kartṛ*), then the word would be grammatically incorrect (*asādhutva*).

"—is not to be divided. (Vai.si.bhū.kā. 21). The tradition is on that very point: "The state of being a *śakti* (expressive power) exists only in [the case of] grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Just as the property of "stickness" (*daṇḍatva*), which is the delimitor of the causality residing in a stick, is not distinct from the causality itself, so too the property delimiting grammatical correctness is not distinct from grammatical correctness; rather, it is grammatical correctness itself—this is the meaning. And thus, the implication is that this [grammatical correctness] is also dependent upon the traditional grammar (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*). "It must indeed be so."

The meaning is this: with respect to a particular substratum (*viśeṣya*) endowed with a particular qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), that word which has been declared correct by any one of the authors of the Sūtras, Vārttikas, or Bhāṣyas through a particular sequence of sounds (*ānupūrvī*) is correct in that context, but incorrect elsewhere. For this very reason, the word *aśva*—which has a dental *s* in its middle—is not correct when it refers to a horse; likewise, if a verbal root (*dhātu*) does not denote productive activity (*bhāvanā*), it would indeed be incorrect, because grammar teaches correctness only in that specific manner.

Nor should it be said that this grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is without foundation; for its source is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating: "The *Brāhmaṇa* must, without any [other] motive, study and understand the Veda along with its six ancillaries" (Mbhā. Paspaśāhnika, p. 16). Furthermore, there is the Parāśara Upapurāṇa: "The great treatise of Pāṇini, which defines the correctness of words—this entire work is beneficial; nothing within it is to be rejected."

If it is objected: "Since the injunction of *bhāvanā* by means of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has been described by Teacher Jaimini, how can it be incorrect in that sense?"—we say no. For the treatise [of grammar] was composed solely for the purpose of investigating the meaning of sentences; thus, those [teachers] have no intention of investigating word-meanings here. Furthermore, grammar functions as a means of determining correctness, like a dictionary (*kośa*). As they say: "The apprehension of [word-]power... and so forth.

"—'Not untruth'—[this refers to] the Vedic injunction and so forth studied within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of a sacrifice (*kratu*). The Mīmāṃsaka raises an objection: 'But in your view'—the meaning is: in the view that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes the agent. By 'Vedic text' (*śruti*) is meant by the verbal suffix; by 'context' (*prakaraṇa*) is meant the context of the sacrifice. If [the prohibition] pertains to the sacrifice, then speaking untruth causes a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in the sacrifice; if it pertains to the person, then there is sin (*pratyavāya*) for the person. Thus, there is a difference in the result."

The grammarian offers a resolution: "But the meaning of the *tiṅ* [suffix]..."—thus he states the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)—"let it be so. "While yawning"—meaning one whose mouth is opened by a yawn—"according to the rule for mantras. The sense is this: just as this injunction, because it occurs in the context of mantras intended for the sacrifice and because the agent is denoted by the suffix *-śānac*, pertains to the person associated with the sacrifice, so too does the prohibitory injunction.
