—The Determination of the Meaning of the Tense-Suffixes (Lakāra). Śrīḥ! Having defined the meaning of the finite verb (ākhyāta), the author of the *Mūla* now defines the specific meanings of the tense-suffixes (*lakāra*) which stand in its place, by means of the verse beginning with "in the present" (*vartamāne*, Vai.Si.Kā. 22). On this point, some maintain: "Time is the very movement of the sun, whose magnitude is well-known; because it serves as the cause for delimiting other actions such as going, it is called 'time' (*kāla*). Nor should it be argued that if action itself were time, then just as one says 'the jar is now,' one would have to say 'the jar is action' (*kriyā*)."
This is because its locus-hood, delimited by temporal relation, is accepted as having precisely that form—namely, being time itself.

That [position] is incorrect; for since an action lasts for three moments (*trikṣaṇāvasthāyitva*), the conventional usage of "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) would not be possible. Furthermore, if one were to accept that even the measure of the sun's motion is itself another action and so forth, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.

Others, however, assert that time is eternal, all-pervading, partless, and distinct [from space]; yet this too is not tenable. For even if time were a cause in its capacity as an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to various effects, it would be impossible for it to serve as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) suitable for conventional usage such as "the jar is now," unless it were delimited by an adjunct (*upādhi*). Since an unlimited solar motion cannot function as such an adjunct, and since accepting another delimiter for that [solar motion] would lead to an infinite regress, the flaw in their position remains firm.

Furthermore, since non-duality (*advaita*) is established elsewhere in our final doctrine (*siddhānta*), its permanence is impossible. Others, however, hold that time is the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of a stream of moments (*kṣaṇa*). The conventional designations such as *lava*, *pala*, and so on, up to the *dviparārdha*, are derived from specific accumulations of those very moments. These [moments] are Buddhist [in view], possessing successive parts in the form of multiple moments. The aggregations of moments are of the nature of an uninterrupted flow of moments.

The solar motion, delimited by a collection of certain moments as determined by various water-clocks and the like, serves as the indicator of its specific divisions from a *nimeṣa* up to a *parārdha*. This is because, for people such as ourselves, individual moments cannot serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for days and so forth, since they are beyond the senses and thus not inferable.

However, yogis who perceive what is beyond the senses, having understood that days and so forth are delimited by the solar motion as defined by a collection of those respective moments, determine the number of water-clock measures, shadows, and the like as the regulators of those times, and then proceed to regulate them accordingly; thus it is said.

Since, according to the method stated above, the extremely subtle present time in the form of a *kṣaṇa* cannot be ascertained through perception, he states that it is to be known through inference: "the state of having begun but not yet being completed. The essence (*tattva*) of this is: being a locus that is neither the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the first action included within the collection of actions constituting a single result, nor the locus of the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of the final action. Furthermore, the nature of being "first" and "final" is to be understood in this very same manner.

Starting from "anusandheye" on page 121 up to the penultimate "ādhe" (four pages), these appear as if omitted. This definition [applies] to time as belonging to action alone; having accepted this, however, the properties of time residing in action—such as its being the measure (*kartamānatva*) and so forth—are conditioned by their respective states (*bhāva*).

The nature of a jar or other object, perceived through its state of being present and so forth, is superimposed upon its own substratum, time; therein, the apprehension of "presentness" or "pastness" occurs when the efficient causes are present. That form which is determined by the intellect as being "future" becomes possible at the time of the stainless mirror-like reflection, because of the identification of the original object (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*). Having superimposed that "futurity" residing in the reflection onto time—due to the determination of their identity—that futurity is then conventionally designated in relation to the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) and the states (*bhāva*) thereof.

However, according to the view that a momentary flow (*kṣaṇadhārā*) constitutes time, "presentness" should be understood as being the locus of an action that has begun but not yet been completed. On this position, the phrase "the present action" means "an action existing at that [present] time. Now, one might object: in cases concerning an action beginning (*ādikarma*), such as *aprākṛtaṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta has begun to weave") or *prākārṣīt kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta has started making a mat"), since the aggregate of operations (*vyāpārasamudāya*) does not exist within the past time, there would be no occurrence of past suffixes and there would instead be the undesired occurrence of present suffixes. This is not so—

This is because the pastness belonging to the parts is superimposed upon the whole, and thus the term is employed [in that way]. For this very reason, when one desiring to go to a village reachable by traveling over many days has traveled some distance on the first day, even though the action of going delimited by its result is not yet completed on that day, the expression "this has been gone today" (*idam adya gatam*) is used by taking the pastness of the whole based on the pastness of some portion of the act of going. This is made clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Mahābhāṣya* under Sūtra 3.2.102 (*niṣṭhā*). (Note: The reference *ma.bhā.dvi.kha.pṛ.* likely refers to the second volume of the Madras edition of the Mahābhāṣya.)

170) Thus it should be understood. From the *Vākyapadīya* statement, "But time [is] for the differentiation of action" (*Vāk. Pa.* III, verse 2), one also obtains that time is the delimiter of action, and thereby the distinction between the two [time and action] is obtained. —2 *madhye* —2. By this it is indicated that when all activities are past, there is the state of being past (*bhūtatva*), and when all are yet to be, there is the state of being future (*bhaviṣyatva*). —2 *tad asti* —2. The state of being present (*vartamānatva*) exists.

Now, one might object: "Action is a continuum of operations; for just as in the case of 'cooking' (*pacati*) and the like, because the distinctness of individual parts such as blowing and so forth is not perceived, their aggregate constitutes an action, so too in cases such as 'the self exists' (*ātmā asti*), since the action consisting of persistence (*sthiti*) is of a single uniform nature, there is an absence of distinction among its parts, and thus the definition [of action] beginning with 'that which has begun' (*prārabdha*) is impossible. To this, he says: "The self exists" (*ātmā asti*).

Others, however, [raise the objection]: since the activity conducive to the maintenance of the self (*ātmadhāraṇā*) has already begun in such cases as "the self exists" (*ātmā asti*), the state of being present—which consists in an action that has begun but not yet been completed—is not possible; how then is this consistent? To this they say: "They say 'the self exists'. But others [raise another objection]: since the activities of mountains and the like consist in their persistence or existence (*sthitisattārūpa*), and because their distinctions are difficult to perceive due to the similarity of their constituent parts, there is an absence of temporal differentiation; how then is this consistent? To this they say: "They say 'the self exists'. [This applies] even to those [activities] belonging to that very moment—for indeed, of them...

Because they are experienced as having parts distinct from the action itself, and because their difference is determined by their dissimilar continuum—just as actions such as cooking, which consist of parts with dissimilar natures like placing the pot on the fire and so forth, are well-known to possess temporal distinctions—the stability of mountains and the like is differentiated by those [actions] associated with them. Thus, royal activities are employed as the differentiators of the stability of mountains and the like.

The intended meaning is that, by way of the principle that "there is a distinction [of action] due to the distinction [of its substratum] even in the case of specific actions such as those of a mountain because of their association with it," the state of being "present" (vartamānatva) consists simply in this much. —2 Because of non-eternality—2: Because of being distinct through differences such as origination and so forth. —2 Of that which is qualified by it—2: Of the operation residing in the self and so forth. —2 The locus of the root *sthā* (to stand)—2: And this is with reference to the fact that action possesses temporality.

For this very reason, Kaiyata (on *Mahābhāṣya*, Prauḍhamanoramā, Vol. II, p. 284, on Pāṇini 3.2.123: *vartamāne laṭ*) says, taking up this portion of the commentary: "The meaning is that the state (*sthiti*) of various kings differs according to the distinctions of time such as the past and so forth; and since this [state] is the differentiator of the state of mountains and so forth, its nature as action and its connection with the three times are logically established."

In reality, even according to the view that "time is a stream of moments," it should be understood that the *bhāṣya* is easily reconciled by taking the verbal action (*kriyāpada*) as referring to the time that delimits it, and thereby attributing the existence of that time—whether in the persistence of a mountain or in its own being—to the substrate. "But the self" (*ātmā tu*) means "but the essential nature" (*svarūpaṃ tu*). [As stated: "Everything is divided by another" (*vākyapadīya*, Kālasamuddeśa, verse 80). "It does not waver" (*na vikampate*) means "it is not divided. "By the form of another" (*pararūpeṇa*) means "by the form of another's action. "By that [action]" (*taccchedena*).

The meaning is that knowledge (jñāna), which exists all around, was covered by dense darkness. Regarding the phrase "of the *laṭ* and so forth": the indicative function (*dyotakatva*) of the *laṭ* and other such suffixes consists precisely in their serving as indicators of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) when a word uttered in proximity [to them] brings about the cognition of a meaning, whether through primary denotation (*śakti*) or secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). It should be understood that this alone is what constitutes their "conveying of power" (*śaktyādāyakatva*). And this is logical, because it avoids the burden of postulating a separate power for the *laṭ* and so forth. This has been established below. He states another position: "of the connection... (*anvaya...*).

—2Otherwise—2|| If the present tense and so forth were not denotable by *laṭ* and other suffixes, then even the natural sense of the rule "In the present tense, *laṭ*" (Pāṇini 3.2.123) would be consistent with this view. —2Another alternative—2|| Since both alternatives are understood from the Bhāṣya, this is clear in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*.

—2 "Present and non-present" (adyatanā'nadyatana)—2. That which occurs today is "present" (*adyatana*). Here, through the conceptualization of a distinction between the whole and its parts, there is an indication of a single time itself by means of words expressing the locus and the located. As it was stated by *Hari*: (Note: The four pages beginning from the final sentence on page 117, starting with "anusandheya," up to this point "ādhe," have been omitted.)

"Laypeople indeed point to another time even for [what they call] 'time' itself" (Vākyapadīya III, Sambandhasamuddeśa, verse 85). Thus, because the definitions of the past (*bhūta*) and so forth are constructed around the aforementioned time, terms such as *anadyatana* (non-current) function as qualifiers of the past and so on. Furthermore, since both "remoteness from the speaker's perception" (*parokṣatva*) and "non-currentness" (*anadyatanatva*) manifest in the cognition produced by words such as *apapāca* ("he cooked [yesterday]"), there is no doubt regarding their referents.

The commentators on the *Vṛtti* maintain that the "present day" (*adyatana*) consists of the latter half of the past night together with the first half of the coming night; they define "presentness" (*adyatanatva*) as being this very day, and "non-presentness" (*anadyatanatva*) as being different from that. However, the teacher Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on Sūtra 3.2.110 (*luṅ*), states: "The present day is that which is conjoined with the last watch (*yāma*) of the past night and the first watch of the coming night.
(Mahābhāṣya, Vol. II, p. 275).

He states the functions of each one in sequence—[beginning with] "by that"—and [the phrase] "I perceive"—"in such an object. The meaning is this: that which is the objectivity determined by such a determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*), and the fact that the knowledge which is of the nature of that determinative cognition has that [object] as its object—that is what resides in the thing (*artha*). [This occurs] through the mediacy (*pārokṣyeṇa*) of all the actions consisting of a collection of operations—[as opposed to] "immediately" (*aparokṣe*).

He raises the objection that the term *parokṣye* lacks any restrictive function—“*na ca*” (and not), where “*na dṛśyate*” (it is not seen). The reading is *atyantāparadṛṣṭa*. The meaning is: "not seen at all by another through a means of valid cognition consisting of perception."

"—consisting of parts arranged in a temporal sequence"—is stated in order to demonstrate the impossibility of the absence of a unified mass (*piṇḍībhāva*). [The phrase *bhāvāsambhavāt* is not seen. "[Of that which has become a unified mass]"—the sense is that because the parts are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), a unified mass itself is impossible. "[Because of the possibility of being an object]"—for this very reason, Kaiyaṭa stated in the commentary on the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.1) [in the *Mahābhāṣyapradīpa*, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. ...].

115) "Even though the aggregate [of moments] is not perceptible, because each individual moment consisting of action is perceptible, one employs the expression 'he cooks' by mentally synthesizing those moments. —2*Otherwise*—2 means: in the case where the action is not an object of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) in its constituent parts. —2*Of that*—2 refers to the action of running. —2*Being the object of seeing*—2 means: being an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Now, [it may be argued: is it not the case that "action" (*kriyā*) is a collection (*samūha*)—the constituent parts of which have become subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) because they are being designated as things to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*)—and which is apprehended by a single cognition whose object is the production of a single result from the operations of the agent? In that case, since a conglomeration of the parts is impossible, the collection itself would be imperceptible. Furthermore, just as pouring water and so forth are the parts of the action "he cooks," those [parts] too must likewise possess their own further parts; thus, they too would be of the nature of collections.

However, that final constituent which consists of a single moment is pure and cannot be designated by the term "element" (*dhātu*); rather, because that which is so designated possesses a sequential nature, it can only be designated as having the nature of a collection. And thus, action, being of the nature of both existence and non-existence, is not graspable by the senses whose objects are existent things. As it has been said: "The natures of those [moments], which are existent and non-existent in succession, do not belong to a collection; therefore, they do not enter into a relationship with the eyes and other senses whose objects are existent things. (Vākyapadīya III, Kriyāsamuddeśa, verse 6)

In reality, even the parts consisting of moments are indeed imperceptible; for even when one who is extremely close to it splits a lotus petal, there is no cognition of the hundred distinct actions occurring in his own fingers and the various resulting distinctions in conjunctions, just as [one does not perceive] the minuteness of a thing. (The phrase "vastu-saukṣmyavat" occurs here; the word "vastu" does not appear in V1.)

Since it is necessary that even being delimited by subtle time acts as an obstacle to perception, the direct perception of action is impossible. (In the text, the phrase "pratyakṣā ----- kriyāyāḥ" is not seen. The inclusion of the word "atyanta" (extreme/absolute) in the expression "atyantāparokṣa" (absolutely imperceptible) is intended to demonstrate that action is remote both in its individual parts and in its aggregate. Therefore, every action is indeed to be inferred through time.

In expressions such as "see, the deer runs," the verb *dṛś* (to see) refers to cognition in general, whereas the verb *dhāvati* (runs) refers to the result consisting of conjunction with a subsequent location. This is similar to the usage of the verb *niṣpad* (or *saṃpad*) in the sentence "If it rains, the rice will flourish," where it refers to the conjunction of the rice seeds with water.

Otherwise, even though the constituent part (*avayava*)—that is, the state of being a constituent part (*avayavatva*)—is perceptible in the present context, because it is not denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*), the usage "paśya mṛga" (look at the deer) would be untenable. Precisely because the constituent part is not denotable by the verbal root, it is stated in the *bhūvādi* sūtra (Pāṇini 1.3.1): "When there is the usage 'he cooks' (*pacati*) in a single moment, even then there is a superimposition (*āropaṇa*) of the form of a collection (*samūha*) upon that [moment]."

Furthermore, Kaiyata’s statement in the *Mahābhāṣyapradīpa* (*Pra-kha-pṛ.* 115)—“And because of the very nature of the expressive power of words, a single moment is certainly not what is denoted by a verbal root”—is consistent [with this view].

Moreover, just as in cases such as *aprakṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* (“the mat was not made”), where the suffix *kta* and others are justified by taking the completion of the whole to be based on the completion of the parts when the parts are perceptible, so too, when the parts are perceptible, one may take the perceptibility of the whole to serve as the exclusionary factor for the term *parokṣe* (“in the case of the imperceptible”). Thus, the rule *vartamāne laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.123) [remains applicable].
Because this would result in an inconsistency between the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he states another view (*matāntara*).

"—*vyāpārāviṣṭānām iti*—" means "of those engaged in activity. However, the aforementioned Kaiyaṭa refers to the domain of the usage of *yogins*. Thus, this is the meaning of the Sūtra: *liṭ* occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) that expresses an action which is either a past non-current action, or an action involving a remote instrument (*sādhana*) engaged in activity. "—*ayam iti*—" [refers to] the agent (*kartṛ*), who is the referent (*padārtha*) of the instrument conducive to the action; even though this agent is perceptible (*pratyakṣatve*), because he is engaged in activity, there is indeed a remoteness (*pārokṣya*) regarding such an instrument as it is occupied with its operation. Therefore, the employment of *liṭ* is appropriate.

However, this [explanation] is unsatisfactory because, without the perception of the action (*kriyā*), it is impossible to perceive that which is qualified by it [the action]. Furthermore, since the action itself is remote (*pārōkṣya*), the suffix *liṭ* is more appropriate on account of parsimony (*lāghava*); for, when the term "root-meaning" (*dhātvartha*)—which is the subject under discussion in Pāṇini’s rule 3.1.91—is taken as a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the relation is "being its own denotation" (*svavācyatva*), whereas if the "means" (*sādhana*) were indicated, the relation would be "being the means denoted by it" (*svavācyasādhanatva*), which involves greater complexity (*gaurava*).

In ultimate reality, however, because the result of the action—such as softening—is directly perceived, there is no cognition of the action itself as being directly perceived; rather, its indirectness follows from that [result's] indirectness. Thus, the meaning is that the suffix *liṭ* occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) denoting an action whose result occurred in the past, is not of the current day, and is beyond the range of direct perception (*parokṣa*). This is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "The *liṭ* suffix is used for what is beyond the range of direct perception" (*Pāṇini* 3.2.115). One should understand it thus.

"—by means of distraction and so forth—" —the "and so forth" includes mental distraction and the like. "—by the absence of non-recent pastness and pastness"—(V1 *anadyatana* is not seen). The meaning is that those two [tenses] are absent in the activity of composing an extensive work consisting of verbal arrangements that produce a determination of the meaning of a treatise achievable through extensive mental application (*manaḥ-praṇidhāna*). In reality, the use of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is justified by the superimposition (*āropa*) of pastness, non-recent pastness, and indirectness (*parokṣatva*).

The result of the superimposition (*āropa*), however, is the communication [to the reader] of the extreme ease [of the work], its rapid completion, and so forth—[in the manuscript V1, the reading *granthavivekaphalakamamum* appears as an error for *granthavivekaphalakaṃ amum*]. The fruit of that [superimposition] is the delight of those students who, desiring to know this treatise which results in the discernment of meaning, are filled with longing. The superimposition of being beyond direct perception (*parokṣatva*) has precisely this same result. Thus... (L.)

Thus—it is not seen. [This is said] because of the teaching that "I shall do it in a subtle time," wherein even at the time of the action itself, it is impossible to perceive directly. And this is logical: for in the usage of the *Bhāṣya*—"When will she go, who thus sets her feet? (*Mahābhāṣya*, Vol. 2, p. 210)—the *luṭ* suffix is employed merely by superimposing non-recentness (*anadyatanatva*) upon what is recent (*adyatana*). The result of that superimposition, however, is the communication of an extremely delayed departure.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), however, there is no superimposition of indirectness (*parokṣatva*) in cases such as "having pervaded," because at the time of the actual usage, the indirectness of that which is yet to be [perceived] is real. In some instances, when one does not personally perceive [an action] oneself due to the mind being occupied elsewhere by one’s own activity, the optative (*liṅ*) indeed occurs when there is subsequent knowledge through the words of a friend or the like, and that [action] is inferred from its effect. For example:

"I am indeed considered by many before the world" (*Śiśupālavadha*, Canto 11, verse 37). But in this case [of the present discussion], it should be understood that the two aforementioned [conditions] are impossible.

"—*bhāvinī* (future) in the root [sūtra]"—the word *iva* is used as an illustration for *paraśvaḥ* (tomorrow) and so forth. This is expressed as: "*bhāvinī* in the sense of what is not of today. It should be understood that when there is a desire to express merely the state of being future (*bhaviṣyatva*), the *lṛṭ* suffix is applied; subsequently, when it is construed with the word *śvaḥ*, even in cases such as *śvo drakṣyāmaḥ* ("we shall see tomorrow"), the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) already produced is not set aside. And as for "thatness" (*tattva*): it refers to the prior absence of the present (*vartamāna-prāgabhāva*), specifically the prior absence of the subsequent time belonging to the present moment.

The counter-correlate of that is the subsequent time (*uttarasamaya*). The meaning is that "future-ness" (*bhaviṣyatva*) consists in having that [subsequent time] as its point of origination. [This refers to] "in the general category of the future."

[Objection: But surely, when it has rained, one uses expressions such as "if it has rained" (*devaśced vṛṣṭaḥ*) and "the rice has ripened" (*saṃpannāḥ śālayaḥ*); that is incorrect, because since the ripening is yet to be, the form "it will ripen" (*saṃpatsyate*) would be appropriate. [Response: No—this usage is justified by accepting that the root *sam-pad* functions [in this sense] precisely upon the contact of the water with the rice seed. Alternatively, the meaning of *sam-pad* is simply the production of the fruit. [Objection: But since that [production] is yet to be, how can there be a past-tense usage? [Response: No—

[The effect, which consists of the production of this or that [result], is superimposed upon the conjunction of the water, the soil, and the rice seed—] because that [conjunction] has already passed away, the past tense suffix (*kta*) is used; or rather, the pastness residing in the production of the cloud, which serves as the cause, is superimposed upon the rain and the ripening of the rice, and thus the *kta* suffix is applied to the past. By this, the usage in such a manner even after the time of the cloud's production is justified. The result of this superimposition, however, is the cognition of the necessity of the event, achieved by way of demonstrating the absence of dependence on any other causes.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the act of cooking (*bujikriyā*) would likewise never occur; for even when rice grains have already arisen, there is still a waiting for their manifestation in the form of cooked rice, just as there is a dependence on threshing and other processes. Similarly, even though the water exists in the well, one employs the expression "the well will exist" by superimposing the future status pertaining to the acquisition of that water onto the existence of the well itself. Likewise, one says "the well existed. This point is clearly explained in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtras beginning with "luṅ" (Pāṇini 3.2.110). (Mañjūṣā, Vol. II, p. 175).

"—*etayoḥ*—" means "of *leṭ* and *loṭ*. "—*tannirṇayenaiva*—" means "by the determination of the meaning of *liṅ* alone. (1) (Bhū.Sā.Dh.Ni. 22) "—*haya-*" (Vai.Mi.Sva. 22). The word "yesterday" (*hyas*) is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the previous day and so forth. Thus he says: "—*anadyataneti*—" For even when referring to the past that is not of today (*anadyatana*), if there is merely the intention to express "pastness" (*bhūtatvamātra*), as in "he cooked yesterday" (*hyo 'pākṣīt*), etc., only *luṅ* is used.

If it is asked how there is the connection of the word *hyas* (yesterday), [the answer is as follows]: according to the view that the formation of words (*pada-saṃskāra*) occurs first, by the speaker’s intention to express merely the state of being past (*bhūtatva-mātra*), the *luṅ* suffix is used; subsequently, when there is a connection with the word *hyas*, the cognition of "non-recent past" (*anadyatanatva*) arises. Regarding the term "instigation" (*pravartana*): the phrase "in the object desired by the master" is to be supplied as the remainder. This very thing is called an "order" (*ājñā*). Furthermore, even instruction in the form of instigating one who has not yet acted toward a means for attaining what he desires—when that means is unknown—is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*).

As in "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," and so forth; or as in the speech of a trustworthy person, "Go by this [path]," which constitutes an injunction (*niyoga*). The meaning is: the instigation toward what one desires, such as the performance of a *śrāddha* feast or other necessary acts. 2. Permission for acting at will (*kāmacārānujñā*): This is the non-restraint of one who is to be prompted from acting at will regarding what they themselves desire. And "acting at will" (*kāmacāra*) is the statement of permission that prompts the benefit of the one being prompted—once they have already begun to act—by preventing their cessation.

The form "begin what has been commenced" (*prārabdhaṃ kuru*), as well as the statement "act in such a way that it is beneficial" (*tathā kuruṣva yathā hitam*), is also indeed an *anujñā* (permission). "—and this" (etacca)—the sense is that the remaining portion [of the meaning] cannot be obtained through the connection with other words and so forth. "On account of parsimony" (lāghavāt)—the meaning is that because the property of being an instigation (pravartanatva) is an indivisible adjunct (akhaṇḍopādhi), there is parsimony regarding the delimitor of what is to be expressed (vācyatāvacchedaka).

"—For the purpose of explaining *nyāya* (the method of reasoning)" means for the purpose of knowing the different types of instigation (*pravartanā*). "—For the sake of elaboration" means for the sake of clarifying the intellect of the student. "—Of the four"—refers to those [means] accompanied by a request. And "the nature of being an instigation" is defined as that which generates activity. This refers to the knowledge that generates activity, namely the knowledge whose qualifier is the state of being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), in the form: "This is a means to my desired end. The meaning is that the delimitor of the objecthood (*viṣayatāvacchedaka*) of that [knowledge] is the state of being a means to what is desired.

Regarding the phrase "and that [is] activity": the word "desired" (*iṣṭa*) refers in some cases to what is directly desired, and thus it is intended as such; it does not, however, intend the absence of desire in general. For the sake of encompassing all [motivations], the knowledge that something is a means to a result characterized by being an object of desire is the motivator. And it is precisely in that form that the potency of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*) resides. Furthermore, since "being a means" (*sādhanatva*) is an indivisible category (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), and because it is accepted that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is simply that which has been established elsewhere, there is no need to postulate a new entity such as the "unseen potency" (*apūrva*).

In such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," the fruit of the meaning of the root *yaj*—consisting of the renunciation of a substance for the sake of a deity—is the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), which takes the form of the effort (*kṛti*) and so forth that constitutes the meaning of the root *yaj*. And within that productive activity, there occurs the connection of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), which is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*). Thus, [the meaning of the optative] is the state of being a means to a desired end residing in the productive activity.

Since it has not been stated that the *bhāvanā* possesses the quality of making what is undesirable desirable, even though the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is mentioned, the instrumental case ending remains unaccounted for in words such as "Jyotiṣṭoma" (the word "ādi" does not appear in the manuscript), because the instrumentality residing in the sacrifice—defined as the capacity to bring about the object of the *bhāvanā* as determined by the *bhāvanā*—has not been stated. Furthermore, the name "Jyotiṣṭoma" and so forth also refers to the sacrifice itself.

The conventional usage [of the term "sacrifice"] for the entire collection of rites beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and ending with the *udavasānīyā*, which are constituted by the sacrifice, is secondary (*gauṇa*). It should be understood that the conventional usage of its being the instrument (*karaṇa*) for attaining heaven (*svarga*) is likewise [secondary].

[Objection: But how can the cognition that something is a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) be the motivator [of action]? [Reply: It is not so; for it cannot be said that one does not act toward what is a means to the undesired (*aniṣṭasādhana*) and so forth because God acts as an obstacle to such activity, or because of aversion (*dveṣa*) toward the means to the undesired. This is a faulty reading. For it is precisely by taking aversion to be the obstacle to activity that one does not act toward what is a means to the undesired or toward what is indifferent (*udāsīna*). If you say, "Because of the maxim 'action is painful' (*kaṣṭaṃ karma*)," we reply: no.

For otherwise, activity would result even during the state of intermediate effort, whether in the absence of aversion or in the presence of aversion and ignorance. For this very reason, even when there is knowledge that [an action] is a means to a desired end, one who feels aversion toward the intermediate effort does not engage in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and the like. Nor should it be argued that this is an acceptable consequence because of the presence of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*); for that [desire to act] is also absent when there is no knowledge of its being a means to a desired end, since the knowledge of that [means-to-an-end] is the cause of that [desire].

In the case of study forced by compulsion, however, the desired result is simply the absence of the beating inflicted by the teacher and others due to the absence of study. In the case of the obligatory daily *sandhyā-vandana* and similar rites, the desired result is simply the absence of sin (*pratyavāya*). This is what constitutes the nature of "instigation" as defined here. [The phrase] "from worldly experience alone" means that it is through inference alone—namely, "Sacrifice is achievable by my effort, because it possesses a property incompatible with being unachievable by my effort (like a jar)"—that one proceeds. Otherwise, a person who possesses only internal desire would not engage in such acts as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

Thus [it would be] a corruption of the language. For, since a person who is himself incapable would otherwise be driven toward an action achievable only through the effort of another person, it is necessary that the knowledge that "this is to be accomplished by an effort qualified by my own part" (*madaṃśaviśiṣṭakṛtisādhyatājñāna*) be the motivator. And such a knowledge cannot be obtained from a Vedic injunction. In my view, however, the desire for the fruit is the cause of the desire for the means through the relation of "co-inherence-based co-referentiality" (*samavāyaghaṭitasāmānādhikaraṇya*). (Note: *asāmānādhikaraṇya* in the manuscript appears to be a scribal error.)

By taking the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end belonging to another person, one avoids the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the theory]; yet, if the knowledge of being a means to a desired end is held to be the cause by including the element "mine" (*mad-aṃśa*), there is neither a result nor a means of valid cognition (*māna*). This is because the desire for the result, the inquiry into the means, and the knowledge of the means are admitted to be simultaneous due to the stability of the desire; thus, there is no loss of the fact that the desire for the means precedes the desire for the result. (The word *nañ* is not seen in V1. In reality, the knowledge that something is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is not the motivator (*pravartaka*).

Nor should it be suspected that this leads to the undesirable consequence of activity occurring even in cases such as the fetching of the moon's orb; for, since such things are not desired, they are causes of futile exertion and thus give rise to aversion. Furthermore, it is the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) alone that is the cause of activity, according to the established doctrine that the cognition of something being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is the cause of that desire. Moreover, since both the desire to act and the resulting activity are observed to arise from the cognition "cooking is a means to be accomplished by my effort"—just as they are from the cognition of its being achievable through effort—it would follow that such a cognition too must be the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*).

[Objection: "But even so, there would still be the undesirable consequence of engaging in such acts as eating food mixed with honey and poison, because there exists a cognition that the portion consisting of the food is a means to a desired end, namely satisfaction. [Reply: This is not so; for this refutes the view of those who maintain that the motivator [of action] is the cognition that [an act] is not connected with a powerful undesired result (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). [The compound] *balavadaniṣṭa* means a powerful undesired result; *tadananubandhi* means not being connected with that, i.e., not being its producer. [The phrase] *dveṣābhāvena* [means] by the absence of aversion.

Even when there is knowledge that [an action] is a means to a desired end, activity must be prevented during a state of aversion; therefore, the absence of aversion necessarily functions as a cause for activity. Furthermore, since aversion (or, according to V1, the object of aversion, such as death in the case of a powerful aversion toward it) acts as an inhibitor by being the counter-positive of the absence that constitutes the cause, activity is prevented in the aforementioned instance due to the powerful aversion toward death—which is to be accomplished by that action—when compared to the desired fruit of satisfaction.

"A living man shall see auspicious things"—this is from the words of Kālidāsa, who is an authoritative source (*pramāṇabhūta*) (the original source for this should be sought). Furthermore, it should be understood that even though there is a great deal of suffering, because it is slight in some respect, and even though there is a small amount [of happiness], because it is powerful in some respect, it is difficult to describe [the former] as possessing superior strength (*anugatabalavatva*). (V1: *balavatvena*) 02-0.

He says "of the theist who is lustful" because an atheist lacks even the knowledge that [sexual intercourse] is a means to hell; he says "by intense desire" as the reason for the absence of aversion. Some, however, argue that since knowledge persists for three moments, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because, once the knowledge that it is a means to hell has perished, the knowledge that it is not connected with a powerful undesirable consequence is present; for a delay of a single moment is difficult to discern.

Others, however, say that there is no deviation [in the rule], because when there is an intense desire (*rāga-autkaṇṭhya*), the very knowledge that the cognition of the means to hell produced previously is not sublated by a grasp of its invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-graha*) acts as the inhibitor; thus, activity occurs easily. Still others, however, maintain that since the motivator of action is the knowledge of the absence of being unaccompanied by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavad-an-iṣṭa-ananubandhitva-abhāva-jñāna*) qualified by the absence of intense desire, and since intense desire serves as an "excitant" (*uttejaka*)—just as the desire-to-know (*siṣādhayiṣā*) is for the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) consisting in the absence of proof—[there is no fault].

They say that [in such cases] there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*). However, in instances such as "One should not eat *kalañja*," the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is also the state of being a means to an undesirable result (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*), because the negative particle (*nañ*) serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*) precisely in that regard. Consequently, even though eating *kalañja* is a means to a desired end in the form of satisfaction (*tṛpti*), there is no inclination toward it; nor is there a cognition of the mere absence of being a means to a desired end, because that would be contradicted by the actual existence of its being a means to a desired end in the form of satisfaction.

"—it is not desired by men" (*Mandana Miśra, Vidhiviveka*, p. 246). [The meaning is: other than being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭābhyupāyatva*) or a producer of what is desired (*iṣṭajanakatva*), there is no other motivator (*pravartaka*) for actions—that is, nothing that is the object of the knowledge which generates the inclination to act. In reality, being a means to the desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is neither the "impulsion" (*pravartanā*)—meaning even if there is no actual activity—nor is it the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*). This is because, just like the knowledge that something can be accomplished through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*), the knowledge that something is a means to the desired is also rendered superfluous (*anyathāsiddha*) by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).
For the very desire that "may this means for achieving such-and-such a fruit, which is to be accomplished by my effort, come to pass" is itself the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).

Nor should it be argued that the knowledge of the means-to-a-desired-end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*)—which serves as the door to the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*)—is not "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*) by the unseen potency (*apūrva*), just as the sacrifice is [not otherwise established] by the *apūrva*. For, while the causality of those "doors" (the means) may be established by other means of knowledge—as is the case with the sacrifice and the animal—and thus an *apūrva* or similar entity might be postulated because their [direct] causality would otherwise be inexplicable, there is no evidence for the "otherwise-establishment" of the "doorkeeper" (the primary act, such as the sacrifice) by means of such a postulated *apūrva*. Indeed, even if such "otherwise-establishment" were to occur, there would be no sublation (*bādhaka*) against it.

Furthermore, because there is the natural worldly usage—"What is this? It is a means to achieve what is desired, it is achievable through volitional effort, and it contains no pain; therefore, you should do it"—it is impossible to claim that those [words] have the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*), as that would result in redundancy.

Nor should it be said that this is a mere tautology according to the maxim *dvirbaddhaṃ subaddhaṃ bhavati* (what is bound twice is well-bound), for [the repetition] is for the sake of accomplishing the desired goal in every respect; otherwise, there would be the consequence of the word *tasmāt* ("therefore") having no syntactic connection. Furthermore, from the common usage "I am impelled by the king with the command 'Do!'," it follows that the instigation (*pravartanā*) resides in the person who impels. And since that [instigation] is the denotable meaning (*śakya*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, this is in accord with the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra *vidhinimantraṇāmantraṇādhīṣṭasaṃpraśnaprārthaneṣu liṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.161).

Neither the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) nor the cognition thereof is what is intended by the communication of [the Vedic injunction’s] being based on that [desire], even though it is indeed based on that. Furthermore, since you do not accept that [the injunction] has that [status] as its capacity (*śakyatva*), and because—given the experience of activity arising not only from the cognition of being a means to a desired end but also from the cognition of having a desired object to be accomplished (*sādhyeṣṭakatva*)—there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) to prefer one over the other, both would have to be accepted as capacities, which would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Therefore, *pravartanā* is not the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*); rather, *pravartanā* is an activity conducive to engagement, residing in the instigator (*pravartaka*), and consisting in the employment of words containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. And the state of being an instigator (*pravartakatva*) consists in being the utterer of the optative suffix and so forth while possessing independence (*svātantrya*). The phrase "while possessing independence" is included to exclude the conventional designation of "instigator" for a foot soldier who, though he utters the optative suffix and so forth, is prompted by a king. [As it is said: "I do not act because I am prompted by the foot soldier, but because I am prompted by the king. (L.)

This is because of common usage [expressed as "aha"]. In the Veda, however, the capacity to impel—which consists in being constituted by *pravartanā*—resides solely in the word itself, because there is no person [to issue the command]. If it is asked: "In that case, how is the understanding of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) produced regarding the sacrifice and so forth, which are the objects of the instigation? The answer is: through the instigation (*pravartanā*), which is qualified by the absence of obstacles due to the authority of the source (*āptokti*), there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of being a means to a desired end with respect to its own object; thus, that [fact] is understood. From that, activity (*pravṛtti*) arises.

Nor should it be argued that, because for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), when engaging in the teaching of Brahman out of a desire to help another, the cognition of the means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatājñāna) is not the motivator—and thus there is a deviation (vyabhicāra)—it is impossible for [the cognition of the means to a desired end] to imply [the cognition of obligation].

Because of the ease with which an implication (*ākṣepa*) arises through the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.26)—as explained in the commentary on that sūtra (Mahābhāṣya, Vol. II, p. 61)—which establishes a necessity that any activity other than [the primary one] must be prompted by it; and because of the statement "by way of an implication" (*ākṣepe āpatyoktyā*), there is neither such an implication nor an activity arising from the sentence "Eat, for you hate [your] enemy," since [in this case] one is not prompted by the enemy.

Regarding the statement, "Eat poison, but do not eat in his house," once uttered, [the injunction] is qualified by the absence of an obstacle in order to prevent that [eating]. In this case, there is no fault, because the obstacle—namely, the aversion prompted by the certainty that [eating in his house] is a means to an undesirable end—is present. This is because the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) lies precisely in making known that eating in that house is an absolute means to an undesirable end (*atyantāniṣṭasādhanatva*). Even from a sentence spoken by an angry or jealous person, such as "Eat clay" or "Eat milk-rice," the understanding of that [undesirability] indeed arises.

But there is no such activity [of speech], because that which is spoken by a person characterized by defects lacks the capacity to imply [truth]; for [authoritativeness] belongs only to one who is free from defects. And authoritativeness (*āptatva*) consists in being free from defects and, with respect to the action [prescribed], being devoid of any effort conducive to the obstruction of what is desired or the production of what is undesired. For this very reason, even robbers who have plundered all one's possessions remain authoritative when they provide directions regarding the path.

And the implication of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) occurs sometimes by way of being a means to a desired end in general, and sometimes specifically—as in the case of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and other rites accomplished through great wealth and effort—by way of its specific nature as leading to heaven (*svarga*). This implication is seen in commands such as "cook" (*paceti*). Here, the future act of cooking, though not yet present, is made the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of its nature as cooking and is understood through the aforementioned reason. Furthermore, the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding sacrifices and the like is derived from scriptural instruction (*upadeśa*); whereas the first instructor’s knowledge of it arises from yoga.

Even in the absence of a word, in the context of one's own activity, there occurs the apprehension of the form "this [act] is a means to the desired," directed toward a future cooking that has been presented by the recollection of the word "cooking" (*pāka*)—that is, the state of being the object of linguistic usage regarding the act of cooking (*paci*) arises from that [recollection]. Even for the mute and others, the recollection of words experienced in a previous birth must be postulated; for this is necessary even in the case of a child’s initial inclination toward suckling at the breast, in order to account for the knowledge that it is a means to the desired.

The necessity of performing obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) injunctions, such as "one should eat daily" (*aharahaḥ*), is also understood through the impulsion (*preraṇā*); [therefore,] in their absence, the attainment of demerit (*pratyavāya*) is established. In cases such as "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," since there is no desired object other than heaven, the status of being a means to the desired object—namely, heaven—is implied by the instigation (*pravartanā*).

And the very setting in motion (*pravartanā*) [of the agent] is *preraṇā* (instigation). Its nature (*tattva*)—as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the meaning of verbal roots such as those denoting "to impel" (*prer*)—is established as an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*). It is in that very form that it is the denoted object (*vācyatā*), and because it consists of the word itself, it is called *śābdībhāvanā* (verbal productive energy). Furthermore, because it exists in that [word] by virtue of its being instigation (*preraṇātva*), there is also the conventional usage of calling it "residing in the word" (*śabdaniṣṭhā*). And in common worldly usage, it resides in the person (*puruṣaniṣṭhatva*) by virtue of being the user of such a word. By way of being the delimitor... (L. 010)

It should be understood that although [the injunction] is designated by words functioning through the application of gender, number, and so forth as its delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*), it possesses an object by virtue of being an instigation (*preraṇā*). Even in cases such as "One should not eat *kalañja*," the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is that the eating of *kalañja*, which is superimposed [as the object], is the object of the instigation. Its absence is the object of the instigation—this is the actual meaning (*tattvārtha*), but it is not the literal verbal meaning (*śābda*). This is because, according to the *Nañvāda*, there is no status as a case-meaning (*vibhaktyarthatva*) for the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) through its primary denotative function (*vācyavṛtti*). This will be explained in the *Nañvāda*.

And by that [prohibition], the fact that the counter-positive is a means to an undesirable end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*) is made known. This is because of the following pervasion (*vyāpti*): when the absence of something is understood as being the object of an injunction, then that [thing] is established as a means to an undesirable end that exceeds the desired [end] associated with its counter-positive. Furthermore, the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) regarding the eating of that [forbidden thing] serve as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) in establishing it as such.

—03— What is the meaning of "not being a means to a desired end" (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*)? Does it mean the absence of being a means to *any* desired end, or does it mean being a producer of an undesired result? In the first case, there is a contradiction regarding the eating of *kalañja* and similar acts, because they are indeed means to a desired end in the form of satiety.

For, since the [prohibition] is established by the second [interpretation], namely, through connection with the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) or through connection with the performance of a portion of that injunctive meaning—as in "One should not kill a Brāhmaṇa" (*na brāhmaṇaṃ hanyāt*), where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the meaning of the verb *han*—there would result an inconsistency with Śaṅkara’s commentary on the *Brahma-sūtra* (1.1.4, p. 149). By this, the view that in the presence of a negative particle, the meaning is the state of being a means to a desired end consisting in the absence of sin (*pratyavāyābhāva*)—or, as some say, the cognition of pleasure—is refuted, because it contradicts the aforementioned commentary. Therefore, the incitement (*pravartanā*) expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others is indicated (*lakṣya*), but not denoted (*vācya*).

Regarding the passage beginning with *pacet*—the additional reading (*ava*) states that the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) is the absence [of non-performance] as manifested by the negative particle (*nañ*).

In cases such as "one who is feverish (*jvaritaḥ*) should not eat," the meaning of the injunction consists in the fact that the non-increase of suffering is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Thus, the view that by performing what is prohibited one incurs sin (*pratyavāya*) or an increase in suffering as a matter of course is refuted, because it contradicts the aforementioned Bhāṣya. Furthermore, this instigation (*pravartanā*) is indicated (*dyotya*) by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like, but it is not their denoted meaning (*vācya*), since instigation is understood even in the absence of the optative suffix in expressions such as *pacet*.

Because it is observed that the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consists in instigation (*pravartanā*) when the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is internalized—and thus there is no need to postulate an *apūrva*—and because, under the view that "the five [factors] constitute the meaning of the root," it is observed that even in the case of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, they function solely as that which is indicated (*dyotya*), and therefore must be uniform with that [instigation]. For this very reason, in expressions such as "I would invite you" (*nimantrayeyaṃ bhavantam*), the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is established even though the invitation (*nimantraṇa*) is already expressed by the verbal root; for you, however, since those whose meaning has already been expressed are not employed, that [establishment of the suffix] would not be possible.

For me, however, since the rule of "conjunction of illuminators" (*dyotakasamuccaya*) is observed elsewhere, the aforementioned principle applies only to denoters (*vācaka*); therefore, it does not apply to the present case. Furthermore, if that [number] were the expressed meaning (*vācya*), then because it alone would be the substantive (*viśeṣya*), and because it possesses eternal oneness, the use of dual endings and so forth would be impossible; for there is a rule that number must invariably connect with the substantive produced by the cognition following the suffix that denotes its own [number].

Nor should it be argued that the occurrence of dual endings and so forth is justified by superimposing the number residing in the agent onto the instigation directed toward that [agent], just as it is superimposed onto the activity of the root-meaning (*dātvartha*) which resides in that [agent].

Even so, the indication [of the instigator's activity] is preferable to [the indication of] the affliction [of the object]. Among the operations of the instigator and the instigated presented by the verbal root, the operation of the instigator—consisting of the act of impelling—is a qualifier by virtue of being the object [of that impulsion], whereas the other operations of the instigated are the qualificands by virtue of being the objects [of those operations]. Thus, in cases such as *pacet* ("one should cook"), the cognition arises in the form: "an action conducive to cooking, which is the object of an impulsion having a single agent," and so forth.

It is not correct to say that even though [the optative suffix] is an indicator (*dyotaka*), the instigation (*pravartanā*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). For it is more logical that the indicated meaning itself should be the qualifier. Furthermore, if that [instigation] were the qualificand, then since the instigator—such as Devadatta—would not be the agent because he does not bring about the meaning of the verbal root which constitutes the object to be accomplished (*pradeya*), the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth would be impossible in reference to the agent. Moreover, such an instigation appears only as belonging to the present time, due to the inherent nature of the expressive power of words (*śabdaśakti*).

Precisely because of that [fact], the meaning of the other verbal root (the action of cooking) residing in the person to be impelled (*prayojya*) must belong to the future time alone. By this, the objection that "in the present state of the cooking to be impelled by the instigation (*pravartanā*), there would have to be the form *pacet*" is refuted. However, the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*) does not occur in the case of the optative suffix of injunction (*vidhi-liṅ*) and so on; for, since one's own instigation is not the cause of one's own activity, knowledge of that [instigation] is of no use [for initiating action]. Intending exactly this, the experts in the system (*tāntrikāḥ*) say: "The first person is an obstacle to the power of injunction."

In this way, it should be understood that the word *yacchabda*—as well as the word *yadadi* (which does not exist here)—is also an obstacle to that [intended meaning], as in the example: *yo brāhmaṇāya*.

The meaning understood from the passage is as follows: "One should undergo a hundredfold torment by Yama for such a threatening act committed against a Brāhmaṇa, which is caused by the agent who performs that threatening act. Since the authority of this Vedic statement lies solely in its function as a deterrent—once one has grasped the relationship of means and end between the two actions (*kriyayoḥ*) by understanding that the threatening act is the cause and the torment is the effect—and once it is recognized that the purpose of the text is the cessation of threatening, the injunction "Therefore, one must not threaten" is inferred. Threatening (*avagoraṇa*) refers to the attempt to kill.

—2Regarding "not existing" (avidyamāne): the meaning is the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of that destruction of an action conducive to the production of a jar which belongs to the present time. (In the manuscript, the phrase "the state of being the counter-positive" is not seen. And in cases such as "the jar existed," the meaning is the state of being the counter-positive of that destruction of an action conducive to the production of a jar which belongs to the present time. He says "even though [the jar] exists" to show that this applies only to such an action, and not to the jar itself. —2Thus ends the section. —2.

Now, [the objection]: "It is untenable that 'it was' refers to something yet to come (*bhāvī*), because there is a contradiction between the states of being past (*bhūtatva*) and being future (*bhaviṣyatva*). Nor can it be argued that, by the rule *dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.1), the suffix in the word *āsīt* follows the primary force of the verb *bhāvī*, such that the suffix denotes the past alone and not the future."

For if this were the case, since the meanings of the verbal roots would be identical, the meanings of the suffixes would likewise be identical; consequently, the words *āsīt* (was) and *bhāvi* (will be) would become synonyms, making their simultaneous usage untenable. Furthermore, that which is intended to be expressed—the fact that what is yet to be (*bhāvin*) possesses the temporal character of the past—is not understood [in that way]. Rather, by the maxim "what is doubly bound," this thing to be done (*kartavya*) would be perceived as having simply been so (*tādāsīd eva*). If it is argued that this is not so, because the sense is that "that task which was treated as future for all this time has now come to be" (*yatkṛtyam iyantaṃ kālaṃ bhāvitvena vyavahṛtaṃ tadāsīd ity arthāt*), [we reply: no.

From the statement "the son of one who has performed the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice will be born," there arises the understanding: "the son of one who is about to be designated as a 'performer of the Jyotiṣṭoma' will be born. Thus, this is the employment of a single part of a sentence (*vākyaikadeśaprayoga*) with respect to such a sentence-meaning. For this very reason, everything is to be explained in this manner. It is in this direction that the author of the Bhāṣya has rejected the rule *dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.1). This is the general principle.

He summarizes the very meaning already stated: "This is here"—referring to these two [cases], namely the past and the future. Regarding the past, it is by the rule *bhūte ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.140). Regarding the future, it is by the rule *liṅ nimitte* (Pāṇini 3.3.139), because the word *bhaviṣyati* ("in the future") is understood as a carry-over from the preceding rule *bhaviṣyati maryādā* (Pāṇini 3.3.136). For example: "If there were good rain... (*suvṛṣṭiśced*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that *kriyātipatti* consists in the non-occurrence of an action? And thus, in that context, the non-accomplishment of the two actions—namely, "the state of having abundant rain" and "the state of having plenty of food"—is taught as being necessarily due to the deficiency of their means (*sādhana*). Consequently, their future occurrence is impossible. For when a capable means is present, that which is possible is said to be "future.
But here, due to the absence of the means, even the possibility [of occurrence] does not arise. [Response: If this is argued, it is not so.

Because of the absence of the means (*sādhana*), "future-ness" is superimposed even upon an object that will not come to be—namely, its "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*)—so as to serve as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for the negation; thus, there is no fault. One who, failing to conceive of a good rain—which is the cause for the occurrence of an abundant harvest—as being future, speaks in this manner. For it is in this way that the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*) is understood. By this, the claim that a superimposed object cannot be the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is refuted, since such a thing is accepted here precisely because there is no other way [to account for the meaning]. [The phrase] "caused by the absence of operation" (*vyāpārābhāvaprayojya*) should be understood to mean that the absence of operation is itself caused by the absence of the means (*sādhana*).

"—2 'Even in other meanings'—2 refers to the fact that other meanings have been mentioned previously, and their inclusion therein has already been stated. He states another alternative: —2 'well-known'—2. —2 'Of these'—2 refers to the *lakāras*. 'The sequence of the *anubandhas* itself' means the very sequence of *a*, *i*, *u*, and so on. —2 'Precisely for this reason'—2 because the sequence of the *anubandhas* determines the sequence of the *lakāras*. 2" (23) (Bhūṣaṇasāradhātunirṇaya - 23) —0 Thus ends [the section] in the *Laghubhūṣaṇakānti*.

—The Determination of the Meaning of Sub-affixes.

Homage to Śrī! Now, regarding the *kāraka* (grammatical participant): since a collection of words ending in *su*-affixes and *tiṅ*-affixes constitutes a sentence, and because of the predominance [of the latter], after the meaning of the *tiṅ*-ending has been thoroughly explained in detail, the determination of the meaning of the *su*-ending follows by way of context and on its appropriate occasion. Since it is the primary element, the author first explains the meaning of the *su*-affix in the root text with the verse beginning "—2āśraya—" (Vaiśeṣika-siddhānta-kārikā 24), and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that there is a deficiency due to the first case-ending (*prathamā*) not being defined [as a *kāraka*]; for the intention is that it is not defined as a *kāraka* because the meaning of the first case is not a *kāraka*. In reality, however, the first case is indeed a *kāraka*-case ending, as is clear elsewhere. This is according to the *Bhāṣya*: "The meanings of the nominal suffixes (*sup*) are also [their] objects (*karman*) and so forth, as well as number (*saṅkhyā*)," [from the *Mahābhāṣya*, Prauḍhamanoramā-khaṇḍa, p. 239, on the rule *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (Pāṇini 1.4.21)]. This is the meaning of the statement from the *Bhāṣya*.

(An additional reading: *ityarthaḥ*)—For instance, regarding [Pāṇini’s] sūtra 2.3.2, *karmaṇi*: here, for the purpose of including all types of objects (*karman*), the definition of "objecthood" (*karmatva*) to be understood in this rule prescribing the second case is that which consists in being designated as an "object" (*karmasaṃjñaka*) as taught by the science of grammar. Among these, he explains the "objecthood" taught in the sūtra 1.4.49, *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* ("the object is that which is most desired by the agent"), with the words: "In that context, 'by the agent' (*tatra kartuḥ*)."

For in that sūtra, since the word *īpsita* is a verbal noun (*kriyāśabda*), the genitive case in *kartuḥ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). In the term *īpsitam*, the suffix *kta* is applied to the desiderative (*sannanta*) form of the root *āp* in the sense of the present tense, denoting the object (*karman*). The connection between the meaning of the root and [the agent] consists in being the locus of what is produced (*janya-āśrayatā*). And "being desired" (*iṣyamāṇatva*) is simply the state of being the intended goal (*uddeśyatva*); and this is already implied by the desiderative suffix (*san*).

And in the case of [the relation], when there is an expectancy for an instrument (*karaṇa*), because [the object] is proximate, it is precisely the operation—which serves as a qualifier of the agential referent not delimited by a fruit—that connects [with the verb]. And thus, the meaning is: "that which is desired to be related to the agent by means of a fruit produced by an operation residing in the agent" (note: the reading *svaniṣṭha* does not appear in L). That is to say, it is the intended object (*uddeśya*) through its connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), consisting in being the locus of the fruit produced by an operation residing in itself.

The ultimate meaning is that [the object] is the locus of a result that is non-co-referential with the activity [of the agent], which is itself prompted by the activity denoted by the root in its primary sense as residing in the agent—that is, it is the object of the agent’s desire (this is the intended sense).

In expressions such as "he cooks rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the status of being an object (*karmatva*) arises because [the rice] is the locus of the softening; furthermore, the softening itself, which is the result, is also considered an object by virtue of the principle of "designation as if possessing the property" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), since it possesses the aforementioned nature of being a result. For this very reason, the status of being an object also applies in cases of coreferentiality with that [rice], such as in "he cooks slightly" (*stokaṃ pacati*).

Alternatively, the relation [of the object] is being produced (*janyatva*) and being the locus of what is produced (*janyāśrayatā*), which is connected to the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, because the softening (*viklitti*) is intended as the goal by virtue of being produced by an action residing in the agent, it is established as the object (*karman*) even without the application of the principle *vyapadeśivadbhāva*. Or else, the relation is being the locus of what is produced (*janyatvāśrayatva*) and being the locus of what is produced (*janyāśrayatva*); consequently, because it is the locus of being produced by such an action, its status as the intended goal is established even without that [principle].

Although the state of being intended by the agent (*karturuddeśyatva*) resides directly only in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) in the form of the result—since [the object] is the locus of the desire preceded by the desire for the result within the action (as in the rule *dhārayateśca kriyāyāḥ*); nevertheless, because they are the substrata of that [result], rice and other such things are also objects of the desire.

Nor should it be argued that, although the fruit (*phala*) is designated as an object (*karman*) by virtue of its being treated like a named entity (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it would lack the status of a *kāraka* because it lacks the quality of being produced by an action (*kriyājanyatva*). This is because the status of a *kāraka* is established merely by the production of an action preceded by the cognition of the fruit. In examples such as "the chariot goes to the village" (*ratha ugrāmaṃ gacchati*), however, since the chariot is insentient and thus lacks desire, the status of being the intended goal (*uddeśyatva*) relative to it is indeed obstructed with respect to the village; nevertheless, this is rendered unobstructed through superimposition (*āropaṇa*).

In cases such as "one kills oneself by oneself," there is no fault, because one superimposes a distinction upon the Self based on the difference between limiting adjuncts (upādhi) in the form of the body and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Thus, the status of being the object of reference (uddeśyatva)—defined by the aforementioned substratumhood—is attributed to the sentient being delimited by the body, with respect to the sentient being delimited by the internal organ which functions as the agent. Furthermore, the over-extension (ativyāpti) [of the definition] to that which is the locus of the result through relations such as temporal connection (kālika-sambandha) is to be avoided either by incorporating the relation that delimits the resulthood (phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha) into the definition, or by noting that such a thing is not intended as the object of reference in that capacity.

When it is stated that [the *karman*] is that which is produced by the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the root in question, residing in the agent (*kartṛgata*), then in examples such as "he wards off the boy from the fire" (*agnim māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), the fire and so forth do not possess the status of *karman*. Otherwise, the rule "vāraṇārthānām" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.27) would become an exception (*apavāda*) to this very definition. Furthermore, the boy (*māṇavaka*) would also not have the status of *karman*. Moreover, the meaning of the roots *vārayati* and *dhārayati* is an operation conducive to the absence of an operation that is conducive to conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

In expressions such as “he causes the village to go to Caitra” (*caitraṃ grāmaṃ gamayati*), because the village possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*), the inclusion of "being caused" (*prayojyatva*) is necessary. Furthermore, "being caused" should be understood as that which is produced by, or produced by what is produced by, the means [of action]. It should be noted that the phrase "of the meaning of the root in question" (*prakṛtadhātvartha*) is also a qualifier for the result (*phala*), intended to exclude cases such as “he ties the horse to the beans” (*māṣeṣvaśvaṃ badhnāti*), where the beans—being the locus of eating which is caused by the act of tying—are not considered objects.

In the expression "he eats milk-rice" (*payasaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*), because the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the milk alone is intended to be expressed, and its status as the locus of the fruit of the action denoted by the verbal root is not intended to be expressed, it does not possess the status of an object (*karman*). However, if both [instrumentality and objecthood] were intended to be expressed, then objecthood alone would prevail due to its higher rank in the hierarchy of grammatical operations.

Nor is there a failure to apply [the rule] simply because milk lacks the status of being an object (*uddeśyatva*) as determined by the agent; for when one who has not yet eaten proceeds to eat rice-gruel upon obtaining milk, since that action possesses the quality of having milk as its object, the rule applies. Furthermore, the status of being a result (*phalatva*) occurs when there is the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with an agentive suffix.

[The definition of the object (*karman*) is: being the locus of the property that is the qualifier (qualificandhood) residing in the meaning of that verbal root, while simultaneously being the meaning of that same verbal root. In examples such as "Look, the deer is running," the term "of that verbal root" (*taddhātu*) is included to exclude the exclusion of the running itself from being the result. Otherwise, since the status of being an object—which conforms to the primary [action]—is more powerful, the deer would not have the status of an agent; this is what is established by the phrase "produced by the action" (*kriyājanya*). [And it is said: "the locus itself is the [object]."

The meaning is that [the object] is the *uddeśya* (the intended recipient) by virtue of being the locus (*āśraya*) of that [action]. In that context, according to the literal reading, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is a qualifier of the locus—the meaning of the second case—either non-differently (*abhedena*) or through a difference of locus (*āśrayabhedena*). The property of being a locus (*āśrayatva*) is the indivisible delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Consequently, in expressions such as "He worships Hari" (*hariṃ bhajati*), the cognition is: "An activity conducive to that pleasure which is the result residing in a locus non-different from Hari.

It should not be argued that if the state of being the recipient (*yādeyatva*) is accepted as the relation (*saṃsarga*), then there would be the undesirable consequence of such a cognition even from the sentence "The rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*).

Because there is no established linguistic competency (*avyutpatti*) for the direct relation (*sākṣāt bheda-anvaya*) between the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*)—without mediating the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*)—and the meaning of another [stem] (the reading *prātipadikārthadhātvarthayoḥ* is an additional one). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of a cognition where the relation is "objecthood" (*karmatā*). However, some maintain that the denotatum (*śakya*) of the second case is "substratum-hood" (*āśrayatva*), and the property of being a substratum (*āśrayatātva*), which is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), serves as its unifier (*anugamaka*).

In that case, the connection with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—the chariot—is through its being the locus (*āśrayatva*) by way of being the substratum (*ādheyatā*); and its connection with the fruit is by way of being its determiner (*nirūpakatva*). [The word *anvayaḥ* does not appear in L. According to the *Harivṛtti*, the cognition is: "an operation conducive to pleasure which is the determiner of the state of being a locus. That is not correct.

This is because it would result in a violation of the natural force (*svarasa*) of the rule *karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.2). In reality, the meaning of the accusative case in *karmaṇi* is the substratum (*dharmin*) possessing the power of being an object (*karmatva-śakti*), according to the natural force of the rule *karmaṇi*. In this same way, it should be understood that all case-endings (*sarva-vibhakti*) denote a substratum possessing the respective powers of their specific *kārakas*. In that context, regarding the meaning of the accusative as possessing the power of being an object, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is a qualifier by way of non-difference (*abheda*), while the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) through the relation of being the determiner (*nirūpakatva*) of that power.

And thus, in cases such as "hariṃ bhajati" (he worships Hari), the understanding is that there is an operation conducive to pleasure, which is the relatum of a power residing in that which possesses the power of being an object non-different from Hari. And the operation conducive to pleasure is the meaning of the root *bhaj*. However, the claim stated in the original [text] regarding its having the locus as its meaning is not tenable.

In the rule *saptamī pañcamyau kārakamadhye* (Pāṇini 2.3.7), the word *kāraka* refers to "power" (*śakti*), because—as the Bhāṣya states, "power is [the same as] that which possesses power" (*śaktiriti bhāṣyam*)—it is the possessor of power itself that is accepted by the Bhāṣya and other authorities as the referent of the second case and subsequent cases.

Furthermore, according to the primary view accepted in the Bhāṣya—that "the application of words is threefold"—the cognition of a superimposed basis for its own application occurs through technical (saṃjñā) terms; as it is clearly stated by Kaiyaṭa on the *Ṛlk* (Māheśvara Sūtra 2) rule: "Just as with words such as *ḍittha*, the cognition of *ḍittha* arises through the superimposition of *ḍitthatva* (the state of being Ḍittha), preceded by the superimposition of qualities such as [the former] Ḍittha. (Note: The reading "pūrvam" is an additional one.)

And thus, since even technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) in grammar possess the capacity to function as the grounds for the application of various terms such as "object" (*karman*) by virtue of being based on etymological derivation (*nirukta*), it is appropriate that they convey the very thing designated (*uddeśya*) as the substratum of that derivation. Furthermore, if the ground for the application of those respective technical terms were merely the state of being the substratum of the etymological derivation—which serves as the delimiting property of the status of being the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*)—then it would result in the inconsistency of linguistic usage such as "it is an object because it is the substratum of the fruit (*phala*)."
