Nor does the phrase "not being an object" mean that it lacks the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "object" (*karman*); for that would entail the fault of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), and because such usage occurs even by one who is unaware of the technical designations. Furthermore, in the view of the three [grammatical systems], since the words "object" (*karman*) and so forth lack a basis for the application of the term (*padapravṛttinimitta*), the suffixes following those words do not denote the objects themselves. As for the claim that "being a substratum" (*āśrayatva*) is the delimiting property of the denotable meaning (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), that too is incorrect; for it is over-extended (*atiprasakta*), and only a property that is not over-extended can serve as a delimiting property.

Nor should it be argued that "substratum-ness" (āśrayatva) as qualified by being defined in relation to a fruit (phala) is not over-extensive; for there would be the fault of complexity (gaurava) if each such specific form were taken as the delimitor (avacchedaka). Furthermore, in expressions such as "He dwells in Vaikuṇṭha," even the qualified [substratum-ness] is absent; since it occurs in a narrower domain, it is inappropriate for it to be the delimitor of the denotative power (śakti) of the second case-ending. Moreover, if pure substratum-ness were the delimitor of the denotative power, it would result in the undesirable consequence of the word having multiple meanings (anekārthatā). Nor is there denotative power in [the word] as a *kāraka* (case-role) like other words, because of complexity. In my view, however, although the possessor of power (śaktimat) is obtained from the word "Hari," there is no fault, because [the possessor] is not obtained specifically as the "possessor of power."

—(a)—According to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (*Jaiminīya-mīmāṃsā* 1.3.10), it is held that the *śakti* (power/abstract capacity) alone is denoted by the case-ending, and [the specific object] is something else. —(b)—The supreme teachers (the supreme teachers being Nāgeśabhaṭṭa), however, state that the meaning of the accusative (*dvitīyā*) is the possessor of the power of "objectness" (*karmatva*) and so forth, as well as its status as a qualifier and the relation of "action-object" (*kriyākārakabhāva*). In this view, since the relation of the form of the "action-object" (*kriyākarmabhāva*) is the meaning of the accusative, it is the "object" (*karman*). Thus, the cognition is: "Worship having Hari as its object" (*harikarmakaṃ vā bhajanam*).

The same applies hereafter. As it is clearly stated in the *Ga-kalā* and *Mañjūṣā* (Laghu-mañjūṣā, Subanta-vicāra, p. 1208): "All this meaning [of number, gender, etc. is expressed (*dyotya*) by the second case endings and so forth; for the position that 'the fivefold [set] is the meaning of the nominal stem (*pratipadika-artha*)' alone is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). For this very reason, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *kutsite* (Pāṇini 5.3.74), [it is said]: "Having denoted its own primary meaning (*svārtha*), the word [becomes] independent... (P. [text fragment]).

"Indifferent [to its own gender], it expresses the substance as inherent; and in expressing that which is inherent, it employs gender, number, and case-ending. Having denoted those specific qualities while remaining indifferent to them, and having expressed its entire self as the agent (*kartṛtva*), that word ending in a case-ending proceeds once again toward words such as *priya* and *kutsna*. Thus it has been stated. For here, in every instance, it is understood that the word itself, which establishes its own meaning, is the agent of expression.

The view that "the five [categories] constitute the meaning of the nominal stem" (*pañcakaṃ prātipadikārtha*) is precisely what is obtained here. For this very reason, in the rule *krītāt karaṇapūrvād i* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.50), having raised the objection regarding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *gavākrīta*, the Bhāṣya states: "It is not so, because of the intervention by a case-ending" (*vibhaktyā vyavadhānān na*). (Mahābhāṣya, Vol. II, p. 332).

"Because it is separated by a case-ending, [the suffix] will not occur"; otherwise, since only that which ends in a case-ending would denote the instrument, that inconsistency would be obvious. For this very reason, in examples such as *dadhirājāi*, the comprehension of everything from the nominal stem alone is established. (The indicator)

If the meaning [of the root *pac*] is an activity conducive to cessation (*nivṛtti*), then in examples such as "he cooks rice-grains into porridge" (*taṇḌULĀN ODANAṂ PACATI*), both [the rice-grains and the porridge] possess the status of object (*karman*) by this very [rule], because the factor of being prompted (*prayojyatva*) is included. Furthermore, the *L*-suffixes (verbal terminations) apply only to the primary object (*pradhāna-karman*), according to the statement: "When the primary object is to be expressed, the *L*-suffixes are used for roots with two objects; when the non-primary [object] is to be expressed, they are used for roots such as *duh*. (Mahābhāṣya, Prauḍhamanoramā, p. 269).

And the status of being the primary object (*pradhānakarmatva*) consists in being the locus of the fruit that qualifies the operation which is primary when there is co-utterance with a suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛpratyaya*). This is because such primacy exists only in the case of roots ending in the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*). And that [primacy] occurs only in the case of *codana* (to impel). By this, the claim that "the *lādi* suffixes occur in the object consisting of rice" is refuted; for since it is not enumerated among the roots like *duh* in the Bhāṣya, the rule "of *duh* etc., when the non-primary [object]" does not apply here either. However, if the rice is construed only with the cooked rice (*odana*) through its connection to modification (*vikāra*) and preparation (*saṃskāra*), then the genitive case is used: "he cooks rice into cooked rice" (*taṇḍulānām odanam pacati*).

If it is asked, "Why is there no connection with the action (*kriyā*) for the rice grains (*taṇḍula*) here as well?", we say: No—for there is a grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that the meaning of a word ending in a genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) connects only with that noun (*nāman*) with which it is co-occurrent and with which it is semantically compatible. Thus, in cases such as "He leads the goat to the village" (*ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati*), where the roots *nī*, *hṛ*, *kṛṣ*, and *vah* have as their meaning an operation conducive to an operation conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location, these roots possess two objects (*dvikarmaka*) precisely by this [rule], and the lightness of expression resides only in the primary object (*pradhāna-karman*), such as the goat.

In this way, even for *duh* and other such verbs, when they signify an operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to the separation of a liquid substance situated within [the object], as in "he milks the cow for milk" (*gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*), both [the cow and the milk] are objects (*karman*) by this very rule. And the *la*-suffixes (such as *kta*) appear in the primary object (*pradhānakarman*), such as the cow, according to the Nirukta. However, when [the verbs] *duh*, *yāci*, *rudhi*, *pracchi*, *bhikṣi*, *ci*, *brū*, *śās*, and *mṛj*—exactly those mentioned in the Bhāṣya—[signify an operation conducive to the separation of a liquid substance situated within... [the cow and the milk are both objects].

[The word] *drava* [in the commentary] is seen as having been omitted. If [the root *duh*] has as its sole meaning an activity conducive to separation (*vibhāga*), then by the rule "And that which is not [otherwise] mentioned" (*akathitaṃ ca*, Pāṇini 1.4.51), the cow and so forth are designated as the object (*karman*). [The word] *karmaka* [in the commentary] is seen as having been omitted. However, milk and so forth possess the status of object by virtue of being the agent's [desired goal]. The *la*-affixes and others also apply only to the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*) consisting of the cow and so forth, because of the statement: "In the case of roots such as *duh*, [the affixes apply] to the secondary object. And the state of being a secondary object is the state of being an object distinct from the primary object.

In expressions such as *māsam āste* ("he sits for a month"), when the root *ās* (to sit) denotes a repeated activity conducive to a pervasion (*vyāpti*) characterized by the act of sitting, the month and so forth possess the status of an object (*karman*). This is because the agent (*kartṛ*) is the sole locus of the result produced by that activity, according to the rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* (Pāṇini 1.4.49). The same should be understood in the case of *māsam odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice for a month"). However, when the root refers merely to the act of sitting and so forth, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used because [the time] functions as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

If it is argued that since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is defined by its inclusion of being intended (*uddeśyatva*), then in cases such as "he sees thieves" (*corān paśyati*) or "while going to the village, he touches grass" (*grāmaṃ gacchan tṛṇaṃ spṛśati*), there would be no status of being an object; for these [thieves and grass] are not intended, but rather are merely seen undesirably and are thus objects of aversion (*dveṣya*). Furthermore, even the grass is not intended due to indifference (*audāsīnya*). If this is said, we reply: no.

Because it possesses the status of an object (*karman*) by virtue of the rule *tathā yuktaṃ cānīpsitam* (Pāṇini 1.4.50), [the term 'object' applies here]. In this context, "being thus connected" (*tathā-yuktatva*) means being the locus of the result brought about by the operation denoted by the relevant verbal root. "Not being intended" (*anīpsitatva*) means simply not being the primary goal. Furthermore, that [status of being an object] is to be understood as belonging to that which, by virtue of being the locus of the result of the verbal root's meaning, is the object of the agent of that same verbal root's meaning—this is to be grasped through proximity.

Therefore, in cases such as "he wards off the boy from the fire" (*agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), although the fire lacks the status of being an unintended object (*anuddeśyatva*) relative to the warding-off (*vāraṇa*) which is the locus of the primary operation, it still lacks the status of being an unintended object relative to the boy, who is the locus of the operation conducive to conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Consequently, even though the fire is the locus of the conjunction produced by the operation residing in the boy, it does not acquire the status of an *object* (*karman*) by this rule. Now, one might object: "In examples such as 'he eats poison' (*viṣaṃ bhuṅkte*), since the poison is the locus of the result produced by the act of eating, and thus is an intended object for the agent, why is it not grasped [as an object] by the term 'unintended object' (*anuddeśyatva*)? This is not so.

Because that [object] is intended as the goal, its status as an object (*karmatva*) is established by the rule *kartur īpsitatamam* (A 1.4.49). For this very reason, the Bhāṣya—"And therefore, that which is desired as unequally desired is what is to be eaten"—is consistent with the sūtra *tathāyuktam cānīpsitam* (A 1.4.50). By this, it should be understood that the root text is refuted, which claims that being "desired" (*īpsitatva*) or "not desired" (*anīpsitatva*) does not fall within the scope of the definition of an object (*karman*).

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, maintain that "the status of being an object (*karmatva*) pertaining to both types of injunctions consists in the nature of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*). In the case of the [injunction] *vrīhīnavahanti* (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, p. 40, 75, 77), the meaning is that one should effect them (*tān*) by means of threshing. Although rice grains are already established as existing entities, nevertheless, what is intended here as 'being something to be accomplished' is precisely their state of being something to be refined (*saṃskāryatva*), in the sense of being the means for producing a specific transcendental result (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*)."

However, in cases such as "he offers groats" (*saktūn juhoti*), since it is impossible for the groats—which have been reduced to ashes by the act of offering—to possess the status of an object (*sādhya*) as previously described, they say that the accusative case ending is used in the sense of the instrumental according to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85). But that [rule] applies specifically to instances involving the use of an accusative-ending word within a Vedic injunction; this is the general direction. As for the claim that the mere act of knowing (*jñāna*) is the meaning of the verbal root *jñā*;

The view that Devadatta and others possess the status of an agent because [the cognition] has them as its locus by way of being its object—that position is flawed. This is because, in the case of a jar that has perished or one that is yet to come into existence, there is an absence of the object; consequently, since a relation of "objectness" in that form is impossible, the usage "he knows the jar" would be untenable. Thus, it is stated that [the root *jñā*] must necessarily have the meaning of an activity conducive to the aforementioned result—namely, the removal of the veil (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*). This is expressed in the phrase "past and future," etc., where "of that" refers to the result consisting in the removal of the veil.

Otherwise—that is, if the object of knowledge alone were the meaning of the verbal root—it would be as before. The point is this: in reality, if there were no activity conducive to the removal of such an obscuration regarding an existing jar, then just as one has the cognition "I do not know the jar" with respect to an existing jar, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "I do not know [it]" even with respect to a destroyed jar. This is because, due to the absence of the object, a relation of objective character (*viṣayatā*) of that nature would be impossible.

If, however, one accepts that [the destruction of the veil] is itself the fruit, then there is no possibility of such a cognition [of "I know"] with respect to a pot that has already perished and so forth; for even though the substrate—the destruction of the veil delimited by that [pot]—has ceased, the operation conducive to it, which consists of knowledge, is present at the time. Nor does the aforementioned sequence lead to the undesirable consequence of "I know" occurring even when the fruit is non-existent. The phrase "as if" (*yathā*) means "taking the Buddhist position" (*bauddhāśrayatām ādāya*). He states another alternative: "In the theory of the pre-existence of the effect" (*satkāryavāde*). [This refers to] by way of the nature of the cause (*kāraṇībhūtātmanā*).

Arising (*utpatti*) is simply the manifestation in a gross form of that which exists in a subtle form as the essence of its cause. The implication is that if arising were from what is absolutely non-existent (*asat*), then everything could arise from everything. (Note: This does not, however, exclude the impermanent and non-Vedic non-existence of destruction; this is an additional reading.)

[Objection: "But since destruction is a non-entity (*avastu*), how can it have the nature of existence (*sattārūpatā*)? Thus, the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is inconsistent. To this, he says: "In the case of concealment" (*tirobhāve*). (Vākyapadīya III. Jāti-saṃkhyā-kāla, verse 38). The meaning is as follows: Existence, which is of the nature of eternal Brahman, is not rejected. Non-existence (*abhāva*) is not something distinct from existence; rather, it is simply existence itself that has become concealed. When things remain in their causes in the form of potentiality (*śaktirūpa*), that is their "destruction."

That very state of concealment (*tirobhāva*), when perceived as occurring sequentially through contact with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), is expressed by the verb "perishes" (*naśyati*). Furthermore, by the phrase "having acquired sequence" (*labdha-krama*), its nature as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is indicated. Consequently, it should be understood that this precludes the usage of "perishes" (*naśyati*) in reference to what has already perished (*naṣṭe*). Some, however, maintain that the meaning of verbs such as "knows" (*jānāti*) is an operation (*vyāpāra*) consisting of the conjunction of the mind and the eyes conducive to cognition; and that, as in the case of the Naiyāyikas, even past objects like jars possess the status of being the substratum of the result—namely, cognition—by virtue of being its object (*viṣayatā*).

Furthermore, some say that the meaning of the root *jñā* is "an operation conducive to [the object] becoming an object" (*viṣayatvānukūlo vyāpāraḥ*). This is incorrect because of the faults already mentioned: for while it might be justified to say "the mind knows" (*mano jānāti*), it would lead to the absurd conclusion that "the eye knows" (*cakṣur jānāti*), and it would fail to account for the fact that "God knows" (*īśvaro jānāti*). In reality, it is impossible to state that the meaning of the verb *jānāti* is an operation consisting of knowledge itself that is conducive to the removal of obscuration; for if that were the case, the verb *jānāti* would result in being a "transitive action" (*karmasthakriyā*) [where the locus of the action is the object].

To explain: where the result (*phala*), which takes the form of a property common to both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), is expressed by a verbal root (*dhātu*), that [root] is termed "agent-resident" (*kartṛstha-bhāvaka*). For example: "he sees the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ paśyati*) and "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*). In the former case, cognition (*jñāna*) resides in both [the agent and the object] by virtue of being its object (*viṣayatā*) and its locus (*samavāya*); in the latter case, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) resides in both. Indeed, neither the removal of an obstruction nor being an object (*viṣayatā*) resides in both.

However, where the result, in the form of a property residing in the agent, is expressed by the verbal root, that is a verb whose action resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*), as in *bhinatti* ("he splits"). For the result, consisting of being split into two parts, is not perceived in any way as residing in the agent. Therefore it has been said:

"For others, the determination of action is established by words alone" (Vākyapadīya III, Sāṃkhyasamuddeśa, verse 66). Furthermore, since it is stated in the *Dhātvarthanirṇaya* that the meaning of the root *jñā* (to know) is the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanassaṃyoga*) which is conducive to cognition—lest there be a contradiction with what precedes and follows—and because even past and future [objects] possess the status of being the locus of the fruit through the superimposition of the form of cognition, let this matter rest for now. Even if one does not accept a conjunction between two all-pervading entities (*vibhu*), the conjunction is possible because the mind is accepted as being atomic (*aṇu*).
In ultimate reality, however, it has been stated previously that the very locus [of the action] is the operation (*vyāpāra*), in accordance with such expressions as "the Lord knows.

By this, the view that "where a distinction produced by the action is perceived in the object (*karman*), that is an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriya*)" is refuted. For, since distinctions in the form of fatigue and so forth are observed even in the agent (*kartṛ*) of actions such as "cooks" (*pacati*), that too would result in being an action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*). Furthermore, because no distinction produced by the action is perceived in the agent of actions such as "thinks" (*cintayati*) or "sees" (*paśyati*), they would not result in being states residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*). Enough of this.

"—Because it is the substratum of the result."—The meaning is that, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) resides in two things, Caitra is also its substratum, just as a village [is the substratum of one who enters it]. "—Of disjunction (*vibhāga*)."—Since conjunction is preceded by disjunction, disjunction also is produced by that same action; this is the meaning. "—Because the technical name itself is the regulator."—This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be understood that the agent lacks the status of being intended (*uddeśyatva*) because he is not the substratum of the result of the action denoted by the root, which is itself brought about by the operation denoted by that same root. Otherwise—that is, if the technical designation were not restrictive—there would be an undesirable consequence (*āpatti*). [The opponent might argue: "Since [the agent] is the substratum of the operation which is the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), [he should be the object]. [The author replies: "If you say this, it is not so. For in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the agent Caitra appearing in two ways in the cognition: "The operation residing in Caitra, which produces the conjunction residing in both the village and Caitra. [The author concludes: "Or let it be stated [as follows]."

—(a)—Such a cognition [arises]. (It is as if there were "such a cognition" [in the village]) in the village by way of the relation of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*). —(b)— And in that case (the phrase "and in that case" does not seem to connect). There is the presentation of the aforementioned locus by way of being the object (*viṣayatā*); thus, in expressions such as "he goes to the village," the consistency of the causal relationship [between the cause and effect] is established. —2— Regarding the term "co-occurring" (*samabhivyahṛta*): it refers to the relevant meaning (*prakṛtārtha*).

And thus, since the definition of the object (*karman*) is "possessing a fruit of the action denoted by the root in question, which is produced by the action denoted by that same root," there is no fault; for even in the case of the fruit, the action denoted by the root in question is included, whereas separation (*vibhāga*) is not the meaning of the root in question [in the verb *gam*]. Regarding the phrase "the first fault": it means the fault consisting in the agent (*kartṛ*) in examples such as "Caitra goes" (*caitro gacchati*) being reduced to the status of an object (*karman*). Regarding the phrase "the second [fault]": it means the fault consisting in the occurrence of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) for Prayāga in examples such as "from Prayāga to Kāśī" (*prayāgāt kāśīm*). Regarding the phrase "in the same way": [it refers to the same logical structure].

The causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) should be understood as follows: with respect to a cognition whose qualifier is the fruit (*phala*), the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) of an operation (*vyāpāra*) that resides either in the object denoted by the second case-ending or in something other than that, [this presentation] being the objective factor (*viṣayatā*). This same [relation] applies to the conclusion as well—namely, "with respect to the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthāpekṣayā*). Furthermore, in cases such as *taṇḍulaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is cooked"), it should also be understood that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) conveys posteriority (*paratva*) with respect to the rice, which is the correlate of the number inherent in its own meaning.

"And likewise"—thus [it is said]. And likewise, with respect to the village, which is the object denoted by the base (*prakṛti*) of the second case (*dvitīyā*), Caitra is "other" (*para*); because he is the locus of the conjunction produced by the action inherent (*samaveta*) in him, the second case occurs after the word "village. However, the second case does not occur after the word "Caitra," because there is no otherness (*anyatva*) of Caitra with respect to Caitra, who is intended as the meaning of the base. (P. *anyatvābhāvāt*)

(Regarding the objection: "Because it is not expressible by the verbal root"—this refers to the fact that [the property of] being the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthatāvacchedakatva*) is absent. For although the verbal root's denotation might somehow be possible as a *vyāpāra* (activity) delimited by the *phala* (result), there is no delimitor for its power (*śaktatā*) with respect to each individual [element]. Consequently, the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) would follow that one could say "he causes the cow to go" (*gamayati gopaḥ*). (This remains the case) because Kṛṣṇa is the locus of the activity denoted by the simple verbal root (*śuddhadhātvarthavyāpāra*), which is produced by the activity denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇijartha-vyāpāra*) residing in a cow other than Kṛṣṇa. This is the meaning.

"—because it is the locus of the meaning of the verbal root"—this means "by the reasoning already stated. "Precisely by the aforementioned method"—the meaning is that one may say [it is grasped] through the relation of *prakāratā* (modehood), or through the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and so forth. As for what the Naiyāyikas refine [their position]: since there is complexity (*gaurava*) in defining the status of an object (*karmatva*) as "being the locus of a result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root, which is produced by an action consisting in the meaning of the verbal root and inhering in another [substance]," and since both the action and the result are obtained from the verbal root itself, that [status of being an object] is not the meaning of the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*).

Rather, the meaning of the second case is both receptivity (*ādeyatva*) and distinction (*bheda*). In that context, the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatva*) is construed with the fruit, which is the distinction within the meaning of the verbal root.

(The term "of the state of being locatable" [ādheyatvasya] refers to the following: The difference (*bheda*) is related to the verbal root-meaning action (*dhātvartha-vyāpāra*) by way of the relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And with respect to that difference, the accusative case-ending is connected to the village or other object denoted by the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) delimited by a specific individual which is itself connected to the result (*phala*). Thus, in cases such as "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), the cognition is: "one who possesses an action that is coreferential with a difference from the village, and which is conducive to a result located in the village. By this—[the following objection is addressed: regarding the difference... (L.)

If the meaning of the verbal root were to relate to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) by way of a general counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-sāmānya*), then since the difference from Caitra—whose counter-correlativity is delimited by duality—exists in Caitra himself, the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) would arise that "Caitra goes to Caitra. [To avoid this,] it is held that the difference relates to the meaning of the base by way of a counter-correlativity delimited by the delimitor of the relatum (*anvayitāvacchedaka*); thus, there is no such consequence as "Devadatta goes to a substance" (*dravya*).

This is refuted by the fact that there is an absence of a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by substantiality (*dravyatva*) in Devadatta, who is the locus of the operation; for [the opponent] intends to specify a relation whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a particular individual (*vyakti*) connected with the result. That is not so; because, since the aforementioned application would be impossible due to the sublation [of the rule] by the subsequent technical designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) and the resulting lack of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*), the postulation of a power (*śakti*) in the sense of "difference" is redundant.

—02— But surely, it was stated here that such a conceptualization [of the root-meaning as the object] is for the purpose of excluding a cognition of that kind; for such a cognition is desired by those who possess proficiency [in grammar]. Furthermore, that [undesired cognition] is also excluded by postulating that the cause of a cognition whose qualifier is a fruit (phala) connected with the locus of the meaning of the accusative case is the presentation of an operation (vyāpāra) whose counter-correlate is a difference residing in the meaning of the accusative ending. —03— (L. because of this reason).

If it is objected that in the sentence "Caitra and Maitra go to each other," the construction fails because there is no difference between the two actions residing in the referents of the accusative case, we say no. For just as in your view there is a difference between the referents of the word *paraspara* when they function as the referents of the accusative case in the case of Caitra and Maitra, so too in my view there exists a difference between Caitra and Maitra within the referent of the word *paraspara*, which also possesses the two actions. Furthermore, [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-application of the accusative case in expressions such as "he knows the jar."

[This is] the second objection: because the fruit (*phala*) is not the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it does not fall under the definition of "object" (*karman*) as formulated above—which consists in being comprised of the fruit that is the meaning of the verbal root. Nor can the use of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) be justified through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when [Vaikuṇṭha] is the object; for by the rule "the accusative occurs only in the sense of the object," etc., it is understood that even through indication, the word is ungrammatical (*asādhutva*) when applied to any other meaning. For this very reason, it was stated previously that there is the traditional dictum (*udghoṣa*) that "there is no indication in the case of nominal suffixes (*sub-vibhakti*). Furthermore, there would be the fault of non-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "he presides over Vaikuṇṭha" (*vaikuṇṭham adhitiṣṭhati*).

Because Vaikuṇṭha lacks the status of being the locus of the fruit [of the action]. If it is accepted that a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is the determining factor for this purpose, then let that very name be the determining factor in all cases; what is the use of introducing the distinction? By this same line of reasoning, the view that "karmatva" (the state of being an object) consists in being the locus of the fruit of the verbal root's meaning within the scope of the term "vyāpaka" (pervasive) should also be refuted; let it rest.

In the root [text], the phrase “*taccepsitatamaṃ karma*” (that which is most desired to be reached is the *karman*) follows from what precedes it. That which was stated as “*caturdhānyattu kalpitam*” (the other, however, is conceived in four ways) is precisely what is approved by the *Vākyapadīya*. Regarding the phrase “*audāsīnyene*” (by indifference), [it refers to] grass and so forth which are reached through indifference; and that which is not desired by the agent (*kartuḥ anīpsitam*), such as poison or a thief, is designated by another technical term as “*kathitaṃ ca*” (and that which is mentioned [otherwise])—this is explained by the rule *akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51). (2.P.)

In the section on *adhikaraṇa*, he states the very definition of the *nirvartya* (that which is produced), etc., as taught in the *Vākyapadīya*: "‘That which did not exist [before]... (*Vākyapadīya* III, Sādhana-saṃskāra-kārikā 47). And this is according to the method of the logicians (*tārkika*). However, in the view that maintains the existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), since the production of what was non-existent has been refuted, he says: "‘That which exists... (*Vākyapadīya* III, Sādhana-saṃskāra-kārikā 49). Regarding the third type of object (*karman*), namely the *prāpya* (the object reached), which is characterized by these definitions, [he says]: "‘[That which is] brought about by action... (*Vākyapadīya* III, Sādhana-saṃskāra-kārikā 49).

In cases such as "he sees the jar," although the specific change produced by the action of seeing—which consists in the removal of an obscuration—is accessible to the perceiver, there is no fault, because by the phrase "it is not perceived," what is intended is its inaccessibility to a person other than the perceiver.

In reality, since the fruit to be realized—which consists in the destruction of the veil—is common neither to the agent nor to the object, but resides solely in the object, it is impossible for it to be a state residing in the agent; rather, it results in being a state residing in the object. This has already been established as something that must be reflected upon.

[This refers to] the fruits of specific [actions]. By the word "is understood" (*gamyate*), there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*). "Wood" (*kāṣṭham*): the meaning is that by transforming the wood, he produces ash—just as in the expression, "by moistening the rice grains, he brings about boiled rice. This is because the meaning consists of an activity conducive to an activity that is itself conducive to the process of softening (*viklitti*). Since the definition of the aforementioned objecthood (*karmatva*) includes the element of being "instigated" (*prayojyatva*), both [the wood and the ash] possess objecthood with respect to the agent.

However, when there is an absence of the connection with an action (*kriyānvaya*) regarding pieces of wood, the genitive case is used, as in: "He makes ash from pieces of wood" (*kāṣṭhānāṃ bhasma karoti*). The meaning of the case-endings of *upapadas* (governing words) is that which is expressed by particles such as *ca* and so forth (the meaning is: expressed by particles like *ca*, etc.). In examples such as "He studies for a month" (*māsam adhīte*), the sense of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) is the meaning of the accusative case; this and other points should be understood from the *Mañjūṣā*. May there be auspiciousness!
—This is the second [definition].

—2— "The state of being the locus of the meaning of the verbal root (i.e., the operation)" —2—; because there is a fault in the literal reading. Some refine this very independence (*svātantrya*) as follows: namely, in the case of co-occurrence with a suffix denoting an agent (*kartṛ-pratyaya*), it is the state of being the locus of the meaning of that verbal root, which is not the locus of the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) determined by the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of that same verbal root, [the relation being] the relation that delimits the nature of the operation (*vyāpāratāvacchedaka-sambandha*). (P. [Note: The reading 'karma' is inappropriate]) (P.)

That is not the case. By the phrase "in the presence of an agentive suffix" (*kartṛ-pratyaya-samabhivyāhāre*), even in instances such as *pākvastaṇḍulaḥ devadattena* ("the rice has been cooked by Devadatta"), where the result (*phala*) is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), Devadatta’s status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) is established. The inclusion of a specific relation (*saṃbandha-viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to that which is the locus of such an activity (*vyāpāra*) through relations such as temporality (*kālika*) and so forth. In cases such as *rūpavantaṃ gacchati* ("he goes toward the colored object"), the result—consisting of conjunction with a subsequent location—and [the property] color (*rūpa*) and so on, do not possess the nature of being the meaning of such a verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

By [specifying] "the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to that which possesses the form of the substratum (*āśraya*). By this, [it is shown that] in an action to be accomplished by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), all [factors] in their own respective operations...

Because of its independence and because it is not present in all [entities], the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*)—possessed by that independent entity which is the nature of the substratum as defined therein—is understood through the teaching of the technical designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) by the rule *svatantraḥ kartā* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.54). And this power of agency resides in a conscious agent precisely as co-located with the state of being the substratum of both the effort (*kṛti*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). For this very reason, even when there is a result directed toward such tasks as lifting a very heavy load, if the respective operation is not accomplished, the conventional usage of the term "agent" does not apply.

In the case of insentient things such as a chariot, however, [the effort] is co-referential with the operation [of the agent]. That effort, which is the meaning of the verbal root, must be understood as having the action itself as its object, by way of the objective relation known as "being-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhyatva*). Therefore, there is no inconsistency in the common usage: "I have become intoxicated, but it was not done by me. Furthermore, in the case of one who eats sugar situated in the middle of a mixture where the flour is being prepared as a necessary concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*), there is no conventional usage of "agency" (*kartṛtva*) toward that [action of preparing the flour].

By this, the view that "action" (*kṛti*) is some entity distinct from "operation" (*vyāpāra*) is refuted. Alternatively, the direction is that action is simply a specific internal effort (*āntara-ceṣṭā-viśeṣa*). In that case, since the operation is obtained from the verbal root itself, the agent (*kartṛ*)—possessing the capacity for agency—is the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyā*). However, it is not tenable to take [the agent] as signifying merely the substratum (*āśraya-mātra*), because the fault previously stated—that it would lead to the inconsistency of common usage such as "agency consists in being the substratum of the operation"—would apply.

In that context, the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha) is construed non-differently with the meaning of the third case-suffix (tṛtīyārtha), which is the possessor of power (śaktimān). And that [meaning of the base] is construed as being resident in the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) through the relation of being the locus (ādheyatā). Alternatively, it is construed there through the relation of being the determiner (nirūpakatva) of the power residing in itself. Consequently, in cases such as "caitreṇa supyate" ("sleeping by Caitra"), the cognition is either "sleep residing in an agent non-different from Caitra," or "sleep which is the determiner of the power residing in an agent non-different from Caitra."

In the opinion of the supreme teachers (*paramaguru*), however, according to the method stated in the *Prakaraṇa*, the cognition is either "the sleep belonging to the agent Caitra" or "the sleep whose agent is Caitra"; for even the relation between action and agent is the meaning of the third case.

On this point, some say: being the locus of the operation that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root—either directly or indirectly—is what brings about the capacity for agency (*kartṛtā*). Of these, the first [type of agency] is well-known; the second is illustrated by the example "he plows with five ploughs. For here, through the relation of being the prompter of its own locus, the prompter-agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) is the locus of the operation that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root. Otherwise, if the operation of the prompted agent (*prayojya*) were itself the meaning of the verbal root, then those who are the locuses of that [operation]...

Because there would be a plurality [of agents] due to the multiplicity of the substrata (*āśraya*), the consequence of using the plural number would follow. Furthermore, if the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) were also denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*), then the suffix *ṇic* would necessarily arise. If it is argued that this is precisely the meaning of the traditional maxim "those in which the causative sense is internalized" (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), we say no.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of losing the transitive character [of the verb] due to the inclusion of the causative sense (*antarbhāvitaṇyarthatva*); yet, it is accepted that even transitive verbs possess a double object (*dvikarmatā*) when the causative sense is included. This is the function of the verbal root (*dhātu*). However, this applies only in cases where the meaning of the causative is indicated even in the absence of the suffix *ṇic*, as is the case here with the addition of the phrase "with five ploughs. (As illustrated: If, however, a usage devoid of a second object is desired in such a context, then the solution is to be reached by relying on the fact that the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) alone constitutes the meaning of the verbal root. (The term used is: "is to be resolved" (*samādheya*).

In reality, however, independence (*svātantrya*) in the sūtra consists in being the prompter (*prayoktṛ*) of the entire circle of factors (*kāraka-cakra*) belonging to that verbal root-meaning. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra *kārake* (Pāṇini 1.4.23)—in the section concerning the primary factor (*pradhāna*)—that "when there is a conjunction with the primary, the pot is dependent; when there is no intervention [by the primary], it is independent. Furthermore, the statement of the Bhāṣya says: "What, then, is the primary? It is the agent (*kartṛ*), who, among all the factors (*kārakas*, i.e., means of accomplishment) present, becomes the prompter (*pravartayitṛ*)."

This sign of perception (*saṃjñānimitta*) is both superimposed (*āropita*) and non-superimposed (*anāropita*). The former [applies] to a pot and the like; the latter, to a person (*puruṣa*). Therefore, in this view, the fault mentioned in the root text does not apply. Thus, independence (*svātantrya*) also consists in having an activity that is governed by one's own will. And this—[even] when a prompter (*prayojaka*) is present—...

[The prompter] is not the cause of the prompted [agent's] action; for even when that [prompter] is present, activity occurs only when there is a purpose of one's own, and it does not occur when such a purpose is absent. For this very reason, it is stated in the commentary on the *Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.4.54, "The independent is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*), in the Mahābhāṣya (Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 279): "One who acts is independent; one who does not act is not independent. By this, the agency of the prompted person is established. Alternatively, let it be accepted that independence consists solely in the aforementioned state of being a prompter, as a universal principle.
If it is asked how this applies to the prompted person in cases such as "He causes Caitra to cook" (*pācayati caitreṇa*), the answer is: no.

In this regard, although the prompted agent (*prayojya*) is dependent upon the operation of the prompter (*prayojaka*), there is no fault; for by taking up its own operation directed toward another means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), its status as such an instigator remains entirely unimpeded.

Nor should it be argued that since instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth are also dependent on the agent, they would incur the status of being agents themselves due to their independence when taking up their own operations even while in the state of being instruments and the like.

Because it is precisely the independence [of the agent] established by the action expressed by the verbal root that is intended to be signified, there is no expression of the operation residing in the instrument or other factors during their state as instrument and so forth, since that operation is not denoted by the verbal root.

Furthermore, the dependence of the *prayojya* (the one being prompted) upon the prompter (*prayojaka*) consists merely in its following the master’s command, because it acts solely for the sake of accomplishing its own purpose. In contrast, instruments (*karaṇa*) and the like are in every respect dependent on the agent (*kartṛ*), and they do not act even for their own sake; such is the difference. And according to this view, just as before, the science of technical definitions (*saṃjñā-śāstra*)—by means of teaching the technical designation—makes known the possession of the power of agency (*kartṛtva-śaktimatva*) in that independent entity delimited by such prompting; everything else is as previously stated.

However, the definition of *āśrayatva* (the state of being a locus) stated as the root [meaning] is not tenable. This is because such a form of *āśrayatva* is not a technical term (*paribhāṣā*) for the word *svatantra* in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), and in common usage, that [term] is understood only in its aforementioned senses. Consequently, since the one being employed (*prayojya*) lacks independence, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) would not apply; yet, fearing this, if one were to offer a resolution by taking independence to mean "acting according to one's own will," it would result in a contradiction with the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra "The independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*, Pāṇini 1.4.54). Thus, enough of this.

And they say that the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) is based on the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). (The author says: "Expressed by the verbal root" (*dhātuvokta*). The meaning is that when an action is expressed by the verbal root, the status of being the agent is always understood in relation to that *kāraka*. Regarding the phrase "it is consistent": it should be understood that in the case of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*), there is no intention to express independence (*svātantrya*) because such independence is not denoted; therefore, their respective operations are not what is expressed by the verbal root.

In the Śruti passage, "He who consists of mind, whose body is breath, is to be meditated upon," it was established in the preceding Sūtra that it is Brahman alone—characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind—that is intended, and not the individual soul (jīva). Regarding this very point, the author of the Sūtras states another reason: "And because of the designation of [Brahman] as both object and agent" (Brahmasūtra 1.2.4). The meaning of the Sūtra is that if the individual soul were understood by terms such as "consisting of mind," then two contradictory states—being the object of action and being the agent—would be attributed to a single entity.

He states the remainder of that passage concerning the individual soul (*jīva*): "This" (referring to the one previously mentioned), meaning the *jīva* consisting of mind (*manomaya*). "From here"—that is, from this world—"having departed"—that is, having gone—"[I shall] attain"—meaning "I shall reach"—such is the meaning of the remainder of the sentence. Thus, since the status of being the object and the agent as stated in the remainder of this sentence would be contradictory [if applied to the *jīva*], the purport of the Sūtra is that by the word "consisting of mind," Brahman alone must be understood. [The opponent asks: "How can these two be reconciled?"

The meaning is that since the agency (*kartṛtva*) of that [Self] qualified by a particular limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) at one time, while at another time it is otherwise, there is no contradiction according to the stated principle; therefore, the designation [of the Self as both object and agent] is not inconsistent. [Notes on the terms: - *Jñeyatve*: in the state of being an object of knowledge. - *Upāsyatve*: in the state of being an object of meditation. - *Śabdavirodha iti*: "Regarding the contradiction of words. - *Etam iti* (or *etad iti*): through the contradiction arising from the production of the accusative case-ending, that designation of [the Self as] both object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*). - *Bhede*: in the difference between the object of meditation (*upāsya*) and the meditator (*upāsaka*).

—2 *Hetuḥ*—2 means "the cause. —2 *Āśrayamātram*—2. And this is inconsistent, as has been stated immediately below. —2 *Kṛtyāśrayatvam*—2. Since the root *kṛ* denotes "action" (*kṛti*) in the word "agent" (*kartṛ*), the referent of the term "agent" is that which is the substratum of action; because the substratum is already obtained by the base [of the word] itself, the meaning of the third case [suffix] is "action"—this is the sense. —2 *Avyāptam*—2. Because action is precluded in an insentient staff. If it is argued that it exists there as something superimposed, even so—01-0 its... (P.)

This is because, by virtue of its very root-meaning (*dhātu*), it lacks the status of being expressible by the third case (*tṛtīyā*); because the root *kṛñ* does not denote mere action (*kṛti*) alone; and because the theory of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for nominal suffixes has already been refuted. However, in cases where the meaning of the verbal root resides solely in a sentient being, one should understand that the agency (*kartṛtva*) of an insentient object occurs through the superimposition of sentience upon it, or through the superimposition of the action residing in that [sentient being] upon it.

This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "dāmahāyanāntācca" (Pāṇini 4.1.27): [Mahābhāṣya, Vol. II, p. 319] "But surely this [process of departing or coming forth] belongs to that which possesses consciousness, whereas a tethering rope (*dāman*) is insentient. Yet, we observe the metaphorical treatment of insentient things as if they were sentient. He provides examples of [the suffixes] *śuddha* and so on in sequence: "it transcends" (*atyeti*), etc., and "the activity of the substratum" (*āśrayavyāpārau*). By this, it is indicated that in the root text (*mūla*), the word "substratum" (*āśraya*) is indicative of "activity" (*vyāpāra*).

In that context, the referent of the base (prakṛtyartha) is construed non-differently with the locus (āśraya). And the operation (vyāpāra) is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) by way of the relation of "having an immediate subsequent origination as determined by its own inherent generativity" (svaniṣṭhajanakatānirūpitāvyavahitottarotpattikatva). Consequently, in such cases as "Rāma killed [him] with an arrow," the understanding is: Vālī is the locus of that result, which is the separation from life—the killing produced by the operation of Rāma as agent—which has an immediate subsequent origination as determined by the generativity residing in the operation occurring in the locus identical to the arrow.

In reality, the meaning of the instrumental case in the sense of "instrumentality" (*karaṇatva*) is the capacity for instrumentality. In that context, the meaning of the base (the stem) is construed with it through identity (*abheda*). And that [capacity] is construed with the fruit, which is the meaning of the verbal root, through the relation of being immediately preceded by an operation residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhavyāpārāvyavahitottarotpattikatva*). The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), however, is as before. In this view, the distinction is that the operation is not directly denoted by the instrumental suffix, but rather serves merely as a constituent of the relation; the cognition occurs specifically as possessing the capacity for instrumentality.

By the inclusion of the suffix *tamap* in the rule *sādhakatamam* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.42), that which is intended as the immediate cause for the production of the result—namely, that which possesses the capacity for the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being the substratum of such an operation—is understood. However, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), according to the aforementioned method, the understanding is either "the killing by means of an arrow" (*bāṇena vadhaḥ*) or "the killing having an arrow as its instrument" (*bāṇakaraṇakaḥ*), because the relationship between the action and the instrument is the meaning of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*).

This point is also intentional, as is clear from the root text itself in the discussion of examples such as *sthālyā pacyate* ("it is cooked by means of a pot"). Furthermore, in this sūtra (*prakarṣe*), excellence (*prakarṣa*) does not depend on another instrument (*karaṇa*), but rather depends on another factor (*kāraka*) alone; for the suffix *-tamap*, being produced from the word *sādhaka* which denotes a factor (*kāraka*) in general, conveys excellence precisely from that [general category]. For this very reason, [the reading] *aśvena yathā* contains an inconsistency (*ananvaya*).

The word *yathā* [is used] as in the expression, "he goes by means of a lamp" (*dīpikayā*) or "he goes by means of a palanquin" (*śivikayā*). In this regard, some maintain that the instrumental case (*karaṇa*) is construed only with the operation (*vyāpāra*), and not with the portion consisting of the result (*phala*), due to the very nature of the verbal power (*śabdaśakti*). For this very reason, in cases such as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" (*udbhidā yajeta*), it was established as a name (*nāmadheya*) out of fear of the figurative indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). Otherwise, [if it were construed with the result], it would be construed as an instrument (*karaṇa*) toward the operation, [and thus the word *udbhid* would denote a sacrificial material].

The reading of the *Mātṛkā* is incorrect. Since it is possible for the name to be construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the factor of the result (*phalāṃśa*) which is the meaning of the verbal root, there is no occasion at all for resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that in such cases as "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), the figurative indication of possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is a Vedic peculiarity (*chāndasī*). They argue that if the name were construed with the operation (*vyāpāra*), then because the result would be construed as the instrument, and because another instrument cannot be construed when the sacrifice is already occupied by an instrument prescribed in its originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), such indication is necessary.

Others, however, say that even with respect to the result (*phala*), there would necessarily be a requirement for [the auxiliary relationship] because of the occurrence of two sets of contradictory triads (*viruddha-trika-dvaya*): namely, the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) as defined by the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) with respect to a portion of the result, and the state of being an end to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) as defined by its own instrument. Thus, they argue that the [auxiliary relationship] must necessarily exist.

[Objection: "In that case, would not the second [case-ending] and others be rendered without scope? For since [the agent] is everywhere [regarded as] an instrument (*karaṇa*), the third [case-ending] would apply [everywhere]. To this he says: "When intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣita*). The sense is that it has already been stated previously that it is impossible to intend to express all [factors] as instruments simultaneously; therefore, there is no lack of scope for [the other case-endings]. "That which is indescribable" (*tadanirdeśyam*): "that"—namely, the entity such as the instrument—is "indescribable," meaning it is impossible to describe it as "this is precisely the instrument. He states the reason for this: "For not... (*na hi*).

For this very reason, when there is a desire to express the predominance of the instrument (*karaṇa*) over the disregard for the donor and so forth—as in the expression "he cuts with strength" (*balena lunāti*)—it occurs. Furthermore, although the cooking pot (*sthālī*) is an *adhikaraṇa* (locus), because it is made of earthenware and because it is a means for cooking more quickly than other vessels, it also experiences the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) according to the speaker's intention.

"Because the meaning of the scripture [is possible] only if there is an agent" (Brahmasūtra 2.3.33). The meaning of the Sūtra is this: the Self alone is the agent, and not the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as maintained by the Sāṃkhyas; for the purpose of scriptural injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" is possible only with respect to the Self. This occurs in the [relevant] section (adhikaraṇa) of the Uttaramīmāṃsā. The word "stated" (uktā) is to be construed with this. Furthermore, the word "by that very Sūtra" is also to be construed with the word "instrumentality" (karaṇatva).

—0ka—0 || —2Because of the reversal of capacity—2 || (Brahma Sūtra 2.3.38) The meaning of the Sūtra is that if the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) were the agent, it would lack the capacity of being an instrument (*karaṇa*). —2It is not logical—2 || The sense is that since the status of being an instrument, according to the stated method, depends on what is intended [by the speaker], both [agenthood and instrumentality] are possible. —2Of the vital breaths—2 || [This refers to] the senses. —2By means of discernment (*vijñāna*)—2 || By the etymological derivation "that by which one discerns" (*vijñāyate 'nena*), *vijñāna* means the intellect (*buddhi*), that is, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Discernment.

The meaning of the Śruti is that this individual soul (*jīva*), having taken up the power of consciousness (*vijñāna*) which possesses the capacity for grasping [objects], indeed knows. And as it is said, "And like a carpenter, in both ways" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.40). Even though the Self is the agent, there is no constant state of suffering and so forth; for just as a carpenter is pained only when he is engaged in work with his hands and tools, and not otherwise, so too is the Self—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. [This is established] from the rule "from *prakṛti* etc. and "when joined with [the word] *saha*" (Pāṇini 2.3.19).

The meanings of the case endings prescribed by rules such as Pāṇini 2.3.19 and others should be determined from the *Laghumañjūṣā* (in the *Subarthavicāra* section, pp. 1255–57). Thus ends the discussion on the third case.

Regarding "of the seventh [case-ending]" (*saptamyāḥ*): it refers to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and so forth. "The meaning is the substratum" (*āśrayo'rthaḥ*). In reality (*vastutaḥ*), that which possesses the power of being a locus is its referent (*tadartha*). This follows from the rule *adhikaraṇe saptamī* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.36). Furthermore, the state of possessing such power is established by the definition: "the locus is the substratum of the action through the medium of the agent or the object. This is expressed in the rule *adharo'dhikaraṇam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.45).

By the rule (Pāṇini 1.4.45), that which is delimited by such a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is understood; therein, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is construed non-differently with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), which possesses the power [to denote the locus]; that [meaning of the base] is construed as the locus (*ādheyatā*) within the agent or the object; and those two [agent and object] are construed within the action (*kriyā*). Thus, the cognition occurs in the manner: "existence having Caitra as its agent, residing in a substratum non-different from the mat," and so forth. However, in the view of the Guru[s], the cognition is either "that which has the mat as its substratum" (*kaṭādhikaraṇakam*) or "a mat whose substratum is [that existence]" (*adhikaraṇakaṭakam*).

Because the state of being an object (*adhikaraṇa*) is also for the sake of that [action]. However, it is not correct to say that its meaning is the locus (*āśraya*) as stated in the root [sūtra], because that would lead to an inconsistency in usage—such as the term "locus" (*adhikaraṇatva*)—since the status of being a locus arises through the action's locus; this is what we have already explained. The phrase "the designation *ādhāra* (locus) should apply" means that the designation *adhikaraṇa* (locus) should apply. And thus, the intention is that the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) should apply everywhere. The phrase "by those" refers to the designations such as *kartṛ* (agent) and so forth. The phrase "of this" refers to the designation *adhikaraṇa*. The phrase "in the locus of the action" refers to the substratum of the action.
By this, it has been stated that the status of being a *kāraka* consists in being the substratum of an action; however, that [definition] is not tenable, as will be made clear immediately hereafter.

—2 By way of the agent and the object—2. Although time is the direct locus of action as its delimiting factor, [the designation of *adhikaraṇa*] would apply only in cases such as "he cooks during the day" and not to mats and the like; nevertheless, because of the inclusion of the superlative suffix (*tamap*) in the rule "the most effective means" (Pāṇini 1.4.42), it is understood that within the governing context of *kāraka*s, there is no application of excellence (*prakarṣa*). Thus, even that which is the locus of action through a mediated succession is included. However, if the operation residing in time were what is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), then one could also say, "Time cooks."

Nor should it be argued that even if the substratum of the action is included through a mediated succession (*paramparā*), there would be the undesired consequence (*prāpti*) of rice being designated as the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) in expressions such as "he cooks non-rice" (*ataṇḍulaṃ pacati*); for by the principle of "behaving like the principal designator" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the fruit itself is the object (*karman*) because it is the substratum of the fruit, and thus the rice is the substratum of the action through that [fruit]. This is not to be said, because the designation of "object" applies to the rice as well—since it is the substratum of the fruit produced by the operation—and this [designation] sublates [the status of being a locus] by virtue of being a subsequent application of the technical term "object. Furthermore, it is because the object is understood as non-different from the fruit.

Nor should it be argued that in cases such as "Devadatta cooks," "it exists," or "liberation comes to one who desires it," Devadatta and liberation would have the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) when there is an intention to express that the act of cooking and the desire—which are of the nature of an agent and an object—serve as the substrata for the action of coming into being (*bhavana*).

Because [the agent and object] are more remote (*paratva*) and because they are more internal (*antaraṅgatva*), the status of being the agent and the object applies only to those [entities] distinct from the action; furthermore, by the maxim of "the curd for Kauṇḍinya" (*takrakauṇḍinyanyāya*), only the agent and object distinct from the action are grasped. However, in expressions such as "there is a desire for liberation" (*mokṣe icchāsti*), since it is intended that the desire—which is presented by the suffix *tva* and exists in a state of accomplishment—connects with the action of "being" (*asti*) through its role as the agent, it possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*).

If, however, there is a connection with that [locus] by way of the desire which has entered the state of being accomplished (sādhya) as the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), then because it is an object (*karman*), the genitive case would indeed apply to the object, as in "there is a desire for liberation" (*mokṣasyecchāsti*). The venerable teachers (*gurucaraṇāḥ*), however, maintain that the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) connects only with the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth. The cognition is, for example, "the lying down whose locus is the mat and whose agent is Caitra. Its connection with the action (*kriyā*) occurs precisely through that [agent]. Furthermore, the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that "factors of action (*kāraka*) connect with the action" applies even to such indirect connections, by virtue of this very system.

For this very reason, the author of the *Bhāṣya* did not entertain any suspicion of a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) in compounds such as ‘*akṣaśauṇḍaḥ*’ (skilled at dice), under the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.40; Ma.Bhā.Pra.Kha.Pṛ. 383). Consequently, the views of Kaiyaṭa and others—that semantic competency exists there by way of an internalized action—are indeed questionable. They argue that, unlike in the case of ‘*dadhyodanaḥ*’ (curd-rice), where an intermediate action is internalized, no such cognition is experienced here; rather, the cognition experienced is simply "one who is proficient in the desired object. [The phrase] ‘*asākṣāddhārayat*’ means that this [locus-hood] is not like the locus-hood seen in the world, which depends upon substances and so forth.

Regarding the charge of tautology: in cases such as "he sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*) or "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*), the agent and the object, being supported by the mat and so forth, do not themselves accomplish the action; rather, the meaning of the whole is that the locus (the mat, etc. assists the agent and object which are the supports for the action.

—01-0"—2a *Upaśleṣika*, etc.—2|| (L. and A. Through conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*), when there is a relation between the agent and the object, the first [type of] locus (*ādhāra*) occurs, as in: "Devadatta sleeps on a mat," "The jar exists in the potsherds," "He cooks rice in a pot," or "He weaves a cloth in the threads," and so forth. When the relation between the agent and the object is by way of being an object (*viṣayatā*), it is the second [type], as in: "There is a desire for liberation," or "One experiences knowledge in God," and so forth.

The relationship between the agent and the object is one of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*), as in the third [type of locative], for example: "oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*). The other views on this matter should be determined from the *Mañjūṣā* (specifically the *Laghumañjūṣā*, in the discussion on case-endings, p. 1326). It has been explained in detail in the *Dhātvarthavāda* that in words such as *adhītī* ("one who has studied"), the meaning is the same as that of the locative used in the sense of the object.

Furthermore, it is clear elsewhere that for the locative case used as an *upapada* (co-occurring word), the meaning is a relationship characterized by pervasion and so forth, according to the specific context. Thus ends the section on the locative case.
