Śrīḥ) —2The limit (*avadhi*) is the meaning of the fifth case—2|| And the referent of the term "limit" is that which possesses the capacity for being the *apādāna* (ablative). By the rule "That which is fixed (*dhruva*) when there is separation (*apāya*) is the *apādāna*" (Pāṇini 1.4.24), which means "that which is fixed with respect to the action producing separation is the *apādāna*," it is taught that something possesses such a capacity when it is the locus of the separation denoted by the meaning of the root in question, provided that it is not the substratum of the operation (*vyāpāra*) that produces the separation expressed by that same root. This is because [the rule] makes known the possession of such a capacity for that which is the locus of the separation in the sense of the root in question, while not being the substratum of the activity that brings about the separation conveyed by that same root.

He will state this later: "And thus, [in the case of] separation... As for the claim that "it is simply the state of being the locus of such a separation"—that is not so; for if it were so, the conventional usage of the term "ablative" (*apādānatva*) would result in incoherence. Furthermore, being the primary subject of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*) does not consist in its being explicitly expressed by the word; rather, it is merely the state of being intended (*vivakṣitatva*). For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya*—which states that in the example "he pierces with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*), the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇasaṃjñā*) prevails over the designation of "ablative" due to its higher priority—is consistent. (Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, Pradīpa, p. ...)

247) Regarding the case of *śara-niḥsaraṇam* (the exit from an arrow), since both [the source and the destination] exist simultaneously as cause (*nimitta*) and effect (*naimittika*) by virtue of the former reaching the state of a limit (*avadhi-bhāva*) with respect to the latter, and by virtue of the latter being accepted as the instrument of piercing (*vyadhana-karaṇatā*), when there is a simultaneous intention to express both, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) arises. Similarly, in the expression *kāsyapātryām annaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats food from a bronze vessel"), the meaning is that he eats the food situated therein after having taken it out from there; thus, even in that case, when there is an intention to express both [the source and the instrument], the status of the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) should be understood [as prevailing] due to its higher priority (*paratvāt*).

Even though [the application of the fifth case] is preceded by a relationship conceptually constructed within the scope of the designation "saṃjñā," nevertheless—by relying on the fact that roots such as *jugups* have the sense of cessation (*nivṛtti*) preceded by aversion (*jugupsā*) and so forth, and having established the fifth case by the very rule itself—the lack of consistency in the Bhāṣya-stated rejection of the rule beginning with "jugupsā-virāma... is not a fault. Nor is there a lack of consistency in the rejection of the rule "bhītrārthānām" (Pāṇini 1.4.25) and others.

In the Sūtra, mere falling—defined as an activity conducive to conjunction with a lower location—is not considered *apāya* (separation). This is because even when a leaf has not yet left the tree, once it touches the ground, the expression "the leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patati*) is not used; rather, the expression "the leaf of the tree falls" (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*) alone is used. Since separation is not intended to be expressed here—as the tree functions merely as a qualifier of the leaf—the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed. As it has been said: "Without a movement [of the object], there is no separation from a limit (*avadhi*). (Vākyapadīya III, Sāṃkhyasamuddeśa, verse 10).

143) This is illustrated in the *Bhāṣya* (Mahābhāṣya, Prauḍhamanoramā-khaṇḍa, p. 247 [Sūtra 1.4.24]) with the example: "The leaf of the tree falls" (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*). Likewise, in expressions such as "The leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patati*), the meaning of the root *pat-* is "conjunction produced by disjunction. In this context, the sense denoted by the base (*prakṛtyartha*)—namely, the leaf—is construed non-differently (*abhedena*) with that which possesses the capacity for being the *apādāna* (ablative source), which is the meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamy-artha*). The meaning of the fifth case is construed as the locus (*ādheyatayā*) within the disjunction. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "A conjunction produced by a disjunction residing in the *apādāna*, which is non-different from the tree."

According to the manner of the aforementioned ultimate doctrine (*paramasiddhānta*), however, the cognition is that "the falling has the leaf as its agent and the tree as its *apādāna*," or "the falling has the tree as its *apādāna*. This is because the state of being the *apādāna* of the action is also part of its meaning. In the sentence "The leaf falls from the tree to the ground" (*vṛkṣāt bhūmiṃ parṇaṃ patati*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the operation conducive to a conjunction produced by separation (*vibhāga*). The cognition, however, is exactly that [as stated above]. In cases such as "He comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*), the meaning is simply the operation conducive to separation from the village. Thus it should be understood everywhere.

"—Because that action is not perishable"—this means: because it does not serve as the substratum for that action which produces disjunction. "Of the leaf"—the intention is that disjunction resides in two things (*dviṣṭatvāt*). (P. viśleṣa) The sense is that [disjunction] belongs to both.

One might object: "Is it not the case that the designation *kartṛ* (agent) should override [the designation *apādāna*] by virtue of being the substratum for an operation (*vyāpāra*) inherent in the verbal root? This must be addressed as follows: It is stated that while the designation *kartṛ* finds its scope of application in connection with roots such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), it is overridden by this [designation *apādāna*] when connected with a root whose meaning is separation (*viśleṣa*). In reality, *dhruvatva* (fixedness/stationariness) consists precisely in being the substratum of the disjunction that constitutes the meaning of that verbal root, provided that it is not the substratum of an operation conducive to a state of being a limit (*avadhitva*) other than the attainment of the status of a limit itself. The meaning of the Sūtra is that when there is a specific motion (*gati-viśeṣa*) during a departure (*apāya*), that which possesses the aforementioned fixedness is endowed with the functional capacity (*śaktimat*) of being an *apādāna*.

Therefore, in cases such as "he falls from similarity" (*sādṛśyāt patati*) or "he falls from a running horse" (*dhāvataḥ aśvāt patati*), one might raise the objection: "How can the horse possess the status of an *apādāna* (ablative point of departure), given that it is not fixed (*adhruvatva*) because it serves as the locus of fear and so forth? Anticipating this, [the author] states: "Even though something exists, if it is not intended to be expressed, then even what exists is not expressed. This accords with the resolution stated in the Bhāṣya—namely, "The ocean is a small pool" (*samudraḥ kuṇḍikā*) and so forth (Mahābhāṣya, Prauḍhamanoramā-khaṇḍa, p. 249; Sūtra 2.4.24). (Note: The reading *api* is considered an error for *apy-*, which would yield the sense "even though it exists.")

In this context, the doubt arises from the misconception that fear and the like are useful for [establishing] the status of being a limit (*avadhi*). The response is that in cases such as "the leaf falls from the tree," since there is no fear or the like, they are not useful for that purpose; furthermore, even if such [fear] were present in the case at hand, it is not intended to be useful for that purpose, and thus it does not possess utility for the status of being a limit. In examples such as "the leaf falls from the tree," because the operation (*vyāpāra*)—which consists in the attainment of the state of being a limit—is present in the tree as something useful for the status of being a limit, the phrase "distinct from that" (*tadatiriktatva*) serves as a qualifier of the operation.

Furthermore, since such an operation resides in the agent (*kartṛ*), the tree is not its locus; thus there is no fault. However, if the condition stated by the author of the *Mūla*—namely, "being the locus of the separation that is the meaning of that verbal root, while not being the locus of the action that produces the separation denoted by the verbal root in question"—is taken as the delimiting factor for the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), then an inconsistency would arise with the *Bhāṣya*. Specifically, in the example "the horse is frightened" (*trastādaśvaḥ*), the state of instability (*adhrauvya*)—which consists in being the locus of the operation that is the meaning of the root *pat*—is absent [in the horse]; consequently, the statement in the *Bhāṣya* that "the existing instability is not intended to be expressed" would be untenable. Therefore, it should be understood that the previously stated [definition] alone is superior.

"It would not be so"—this is the sense: because disjunction is a single entity, its generative action is understood by the single word "moving away," and since there is no solidity in the two rams understood by the word "mutually" (paraspara), [the action cannot be distinct]. He establishes this with an example: "Just as..."—and likewise here too. This means even in a case of disjunction produced by the actions of both [agents], despite the unity of the disjunction, there is a distinction due to the difference in the actions.

The meaning is as follows: although the nature of the separation (*vibhāga*) is one and the same, because it is understood by the intellect through its various individual instances (*tattadvayaktitva*) as being distinct, even though it is denoted by a single word, there is a difference based on the diversity of the means (*sādhana*) for a single action. Consequently, while one instance possesses the action conducive to that specific separation, the other lacks it; thus, both [the tree and the bird] possess the status of being "fixed" (*dhruva*).

In reality, this is not tenable. Even though there is a difference between the two actions residing in those [two agents], because the root *sṛ* (to move away) is employed to denote that [action] as one in which the distinction has ceased, both [agents] become the substrata of that same action; consequently, due to its priority, the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) would result for both. This very point was stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *ekaśeṣa* (Pāṇini 1.2.64)—"Of similar forms, only one remains when a single case-ending follows" (Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 82)—where it says: "Verbs ending in *tiṅ* do not necessitate the formulation of *ekaśeṣa*, because the action is one."

If it is asked, "In that case, how is the ablative case [the *pañcamī*] justified in examples such as *parasparasmānmeṣāvapasarataḥ* ('two rams move away from each other') according to the author's own view?"—it is not so; for there is no fault, since the state of being the locus of such an action belongs only to those denoted by the word *meṣa* (ram), whereas the state of being the locus of disjunction (*vibhāga*) belongs only to those denoted by the word *paraspara*, provided they are not themselves the loci of that action. For this very reason, in examples such as *devadattayajñadattāvanyonyamāśliṣyataḥ* ('Devadatta and Yajñadatta embrace each other'), the status of those two as objects (*karman*) is established.

Otherwise, due to its priority, it would be the agent itself. In passages such as "the self strikes itself by means of the self," there is a distinction created by the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the internal organ; likewise, in the present case, there is a distinction based on the difference of the limiting adjunct of the form of the word, because it was previously stated that only the object conjoined with the word appears [in cognition]. This method is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "like the object, [the agent] in relation to the object" (Pāṇini 3.1.87). (Mahābhāṣya, Vol. II, p. [page number]).

109) Likewise, according to the view that "in reality" (*vastutas*), it must be established that the two things which constitute the respective referents (*padārtha*) lack any basis for an operation [of separation]. Furthermore, it should be understood that "moving away" (*apasaraṇa*) consists of moving backward preceded by a disjunction (*vibhāga*).

If "action" (*kriyā*) were taken in the sense of "movement" (*spanda*) by the word *itikriyā*, then in cases such as "the cloth falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣād vastraṃ patati*), where there is a separation produced by movement residing in the tree, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) would not be applicable; for since the movement resides in the tree, the cloth would not be the locus of the action that causes the disjunction. However, if "action" is taken in the sense of the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha-kriyā*), then it is established because the cloth is not the locus of the falling action that produces the disjunction. This is the intended meaning. — "It should be stated. — 2. The meaning is as follows: if one were to understand *itikriyā* as referring to physical motion (*spanda*), then in the sentence "the cloth falls from the tree," the fifth case ending would fail to occur. This is because the motion (*spanda*) is located in the tree, and thus the cloth would not be the substratum (*āśraya*) of the action that serves as the cause of the disjunction (*viśleṣa*). On the other hand, if one understands *itikriyā* as the action expressed by the verbal root (the "falling"), then the rule is satisfied, because the cloth is indeed not the substratum of that falling action which generates the disjunction. Therefore, it must be stated [that the term refers to the root-meaning]. — 2. "It should be stated. — 2.

However, the intended meaning is that since the internal component of the operation (*vyāpārāṃśa*) is already obtained by the verbal root itself, the meaning [of the ablative] consists of the locus (*āśraya*) and the separation (*vibhāga*). In that case, the base-meaning (such as "tree") is construed with the locus-component by way of identity; the locus is construed with the separation by way of being the substratum (*ādheyatā*); and that [separation] is construed with the operation—which is the meaning of the verbal root—by way of being its generator (*janakatā*). Alternatively, the meaning of the ablative is merely separation; in that case, the base-meaning is construed with it by way of being the substratum, and the separation is construed with the operation by way of being its generator.

But the [meaning of] *bodha* (understanding) is indeed clear. Regarding the phrase "of the over-extension of usage according to the manner stated for the meaning of the second [case-ending]"—in examples such as "Caitra goes to the village," there is an over-extension of the application of the second case-ending to Caitra because he is the locus of the conjunction produced by the activity; this is prevented just as in the previous case, because the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "agent" (*kartṛ*), based on his being the locus of the activity conveyed by the root *gam*, sublates the designation of "object" (*karman*). Similarly here, if only that much were stated, then in the example "the leaf falls from the tree," the leaf would [erroneously] be designated as the object because it is the locus of the disjunction.

[Objection: It might appear that the suffix *pañcamī* (the ablative case ending) would result in over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) for one who has attained the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being the substratum of the operation denoted by the root *pat* (to fall); however, since the designation of "agent" is sublated by the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*), there is no occurrence of the *pañcamī*, and thus the qualification regarding the positive portion [of the definition] is redundant. [Response: But this is actually incorrect. For there is indeed a cognition such as "having the tree as its ablative" (*vṛkṣāpādānaka*). Furthermore, in cases such as "he separates from the tree" (*vṛkṣādvibhajate*), there would be the undesirable consequence of not cognizing the act of separation (*vibhāga*). If you argue that in this context the ablative alone is the meaning of the *pañcamī*, then why resort to this "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) approach? [That is, why apply one part of the rule and ignore the other?]

In the second [alternative], it should be understood that there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the meaning of the base and the meaning of the case-ending, for which no connection by way of non-difference has been established elsewhere. Nor, even if this were so, would there be the application [of the rule] in the case of "vṛkṣāt syandate" (it flows from the tree), where the sense is "the tree flows. This is because the root *syand* is intransitive; thus, since both the separation and its concomitant activity do not reside in the tree, the tree cannot be the locus of the separation. This is the intended meaning.

If it is argued that there can be no status as an *apādāna* because it is sublated by the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*)—which is higher [in the hierarchy of technical terms] due to its being the locus of activity—that is not so; for that [designation of agent], which has already fulfilled its purpose in connection with the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and so forth, is sublated (by this [designation of *apādāna*]) when used in conjunction with a verbal root whose meaning is "separation" (*vibhāga*). By this [reasoning], since the aforementioned usage is desired, [the objection is refuted]. However, in reality, the desirability of such a usage is not established.

From the usage "he has moved from his seat" (*āsanāccalita*), it is understood that only the root *cal* (to move) signifies an activity conducive to disjunction, and not this [root *spand*]. Therefore, since *spand* denotes mere activity and the tree is its locus by way of the agent, the expression "Devadatta moves in the tree" (*vṛkṣe spandate devadatta*) alone occurs. Thus, it should be understood that there is no harm even if one accepts the aforementioned causal relationship. The phrase "even so" (*evamapi*) means: even if the stated usage is accepted on the basis of accepting the aforementioned causal relationship.

Regarding the phrase "durvāram" (difficult to ward off): the intention is that the root *tyaj* signifies an operation conducive to separation (*vibhāga*). In the sentence "He separates the leaf from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ vibhajate*), what is meant is the destruction of the prior conjunction with the previous location, which is produced by the separation. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The destruction of the conjunction with the previous location, residing in the leaf, is produced by a separation that resides in the locus (*apādāna*) which is non-different from the tree. In this manner, the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is to be understood everywhere.

Now, one might ask: since the root *dyut* does not have the meaning of "an operation conducive to separation," how can the ablative case (*pañcamī*) be used in the word *balāhake*? To this, he says: "having emerged" (*niḥsṛtya*). [This] is to be supplied (*adhyāhāryam*). However, this is improper because, in reality, all forms of such ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) have already been refuted. As for the justification for the ablative in *balāhakāt*, it should be understood by accepting that the root *vidyotate* denotes an act of shining preceded by an emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*), which is an operation conducive to a conjunction produced by a separation.

The verbal cognition [of the sentence] is as follows: [the action of] flashing is that which has Balāhaka as its point of departure (*apādāna*), is produced by a disjunction, consists of an activity conducive to a conjunction, and occurs at a time subsequent to the activity of flashing preceded by movement; it is an act of flashing whose agent is Vidyut.

If it is objected: "Since the entity *balāhaka* consists of a conglomeration (*sannipāta*) of smoke, light, water, and wind, and since disjunction (*vibhāga*) presupposes difference (*bheda*), and since such difference is absent here, how [can there be disjunction]?"—it is not so.

For when one intends to express the difference of the light (*tejas*) which is a constituent part from such a collection, one intends to express disjunction, and thus the status of the limit (*avadhi*) is established. However, when the cloud (*balāhaka*) is intended as the substratum (*ādhāra*) defined by the light in the form of lightning, then the locative case is used: "lightning flashes in the cloud" (*balāhake vidyotate*).

However, when there is a desire to express non-distinction—because lightning and a cloud are both composed of light and because smoke and such things do not obstruct visibility—then the nominative case occurs in the expression "the cloud flashes" (*abalāhako vidyotate*). (Also, it is said: "In [cases] constructed by the intellect. Because qualities are not admitted to exist in a quality, and because a quality in the form of disjunction is impossible in taste, this recourse [to the intellect] is taken. [The rule] "separately from" (*pṛthak-vinā*) [implies] the fifth case (*pañcamī*).

This alone is logical, because a fifth-case ending (*pañcamī*) for an agent (*kāraka*) is impossible without the presence of an action (*kriyā*). The meaning of the fifth case in *rasāt* and so forth is counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*). [In the example] *rasapratiyogikavṛttipṛthaktvam*, others hold that it is of the nature of a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣarūpa*); others, however, maintain that it is simply difference (*bheda*). In this very same way, in all instances of the fifth case used as a nominal suffix (*upapadavibhakti*), the understanding should be determined by taking the fifth case to signify a relation (*saṃbandha*).

"—*dhātvantarārthāṅgam*—" means that in which the meaning of another verbal root (*dhātvantara*) is a constituent part (*aṅga*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound in its own sense (or in the sense of "and," according to Pāṇini 2.2.29). "—*adhyāhṛtya*—" [is also incorrect]. This too is improper because there is no such ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). However, the justification is as follows: when, keeping in mind a physical arrival established by direct perception (*pratyakṣasiddha*), one answers "from Pāṭaliputra" to the question "Where have you come from?", the resolution should be understood according to the principle of supplying an elliptical portion of a sentence (*vākyaikadeśanyāya*), following the method stated for the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

The meaning is this: in all instances where the designation *apādāna* (ablative) applies—specifically in cases governed by rules such as *bhītrārthānām* (Pāṇini 1.4.25)—the cognition is of that which possesses the capacity (*śakti*) for being an *apādāna*. However, in cases where the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is prescribed by rules such as *lyablope karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca* (Vārttika 1474), the cognition is of that which possesses the capacity for being an object (*karman*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus ends the discussion on the fifth case.

—01—The meaning of the dative case is the "intended recipient" (*uddeśya*). —2— And being an intended recipient is the state of being the object of a desire (*icchā-viṣayatva*). He states this very point: —2— "by means of the object" (*karmaṇā*), that is, "by means of that which has become the instrument" (*karaṇabhūtena*). Thus, in examples such as *viprāya gāṃ dadāti* ("he gives a cow to the Brahmin"), [the dative] is connected through the relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a part of the meaning of the verbal root—which consists of an activity conducive to the production of another's ownership (*para-svatva*) qualified by the cessation of one's own ownership (*svatva-nivṛtti*). —02— (P. 4)

In the case of *sva-parasvatve* (one's own property and another's property), there is an analysis (*nirūpitatvena anvaya*) of the meaning of the dative case as being non-different from the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). Consequently, that which is the ownership (*svatva*) characterized by the desire distinct from the Brahmin is the referent of the word *para* (other); for it is precisely that [Brahmin] which characterizes the ownership. In reality, however, according to the aforementioned method, the meaning of the dative case is the state of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*), which possesses the capacity [to characterize].

By the rule *karmaṇā yam abhipraiti sa sampradānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.32), which means that one whom [the agent] intends to connect with the object (*karman*) is the recipient (*sampradāna*), it is taught that that which is the object of the desire—by virtue of being the determiner of the result residing in the object defined by the meaning of that verbal root—possesses the power (*śakti*) of being the recipient.

"—2 *sambandhum* —2 the relation (*sambandha*) is the state of being the qualifier of a fulfillment residing in the object (*karma-niṣṭha-phala-nirūpakatvam*). Consequently, in cases such as *'viprāya gāṃ dadāti'* ('he gives a cow to the Brahmin'), because the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed with identity (*abheda*) with that which is expressed by the dative case, the cognition is either: 'the act of giving is the qualifier of the objective-to-be-attained (*uddeśyatā*) residing in a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) non-different from the Brahmin'; or, the relation is the state of being the qualifier of an objective-to-be-attained that resides in itself (*svavṛtty-uddeśyatā-nirūpakatvam*)."

But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the cognition is either "the giving to the Brahmin" (*viprasaṃpradānaṃ dānam*)—as if it were [expressed as] "the gift, the Brahmin is the recipient" (*dānasaṃpradānaṃ vipraḥ*)—or "the giving whose recipient is the Brahmin" (*viprasaṃpradānakaṃ dānam*); for the state of being the recipient of the action is also the object of that [cognition].

"Regarding the phrase *śeṣatvam* (the state of being a subordinate): it follows, therefore, that the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*) and the status of being the subordinate (*śeṣatva*) consist respectively in the nature of being the beneficiary (*upakāryatva*) and the benefactor (*upakārakatva*). And indeed, a cow is a benefactor to a Brahmin through the provision of milk and so forth; likewise, the handing over of the staff (*daṇḍapradāna*) is a benefactor to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest. (The handing over of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa is like the throwing [of the grass-bundle], Jaiminīya-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra 4.2.6). For it is only one who possesses the staff that is authorized to utter the *praisha* and *anuvacana* (directions and recitations). (P. *preṣānuvacana*) "Precisely for this reason... ||-2||

In examples such as "He leads the goat to the village" (*ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati*), the dative case is not used for the village because the goat does not provide benefit to the village, and furthermore, it is sublated by the designation of the goat as the *karman* (object). By the phrase "residing in the object" (*karmaniṣṭhā*), it is demonstrated that the object is the cause for the dative; thus, it is understood that the dative rule (*caturthī-śruti*) is stronger than the rule for the object (*karman-śruti*). He states this with the words "for this very reason. [Regarding the term] "in the *cātvāla* pit" (*cātvāle*).

"Like the throwing away [of the horn]"—this is an additional reading. In this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the throwing away of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇa*) serves as the illustrative example for a disposal rite (*pratipattikarman*). Regarding the phrase "it is not a disposal": the prima facie view is that the handing over of the staff by the Adhvaryu priest—which the sacrificer will hold until the purchase of the Soma—is a disposal rite, similar to the throwing away [of the horn], because it involves the giving of a staff already used for holding. A disposal rite is an action that effects the non-confusion of what has been used.

"—2 *arthakarma*—2. This means an action whose purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭaprayojanaka*), such as the act of consecration (*saṃskāra*). For instance, the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, leaning upon a staff, will recite the *praiṣa* (directions); thus, the staff is something to be employed. Accordingly, it is heard in scripture: "He recites the *praiṣas* while holding a staff" (*daṇḍī praiṣānanvāha*). Furthermore, in cases such as "one should give a *śrāddha* to the ancestors," although the ownership (*svatva*) defined by the ancestors is sublated, it has been stated more than once that through the various sūtras on technical names (*saṃjñā*), there is the cognition of the presence of the respective case-power (*kārakaśakti*) for those respective meanings.

There is no fault [in the case of ancestral rites], because the meaning of the verbal root *dā*—which consists of a renunciation conducive to the arising of another's ownership (*paraskhatva*) characterized by the cessation of one's own ownership (*svasvatva*)—is present when the ancestors (*pitṛs*) are the intended recipients (*uddeśyatva*). Furthermore, it is the renunciation itself, and not the acceptance (*svīkāra*), that is the cause for the arising of another's ownership; this has been explained in detail elsewhere. For this very reason, in cases where wealth is renounced with reference to a recipient located in a foreign land—in the manner of "one pours water into water"—even without acceptance, [the gift is established].

Even upon the death of the recipient (pātra), it is the established practice that his wealth is divided and taken as paternal inheritance by the intended son and others alone, and not by anyone else. Furthermore, it is clear elsewhere that acceptance (*pratigraha*) indeed produces a superior fruit compared to mere giving. Regarding the expression "giving clothes to the washerman" (*rajakāya vastram*), since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the meaning of the root *dā* here is "bringing under one's control" (*adhīnīkaraṇa*). When there is a desire to express the sense of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*), the genitive case also occurs.

Thus, in the expression "the teacher of a single section" (*khaṇḍaikopādhyāya*), the meaning of the root *dā* (to give) is an activity conducive to a specific conjunction (*saṃyoga*). A *capoṭā* is an open palm. Similarly, in such cases as "one should not give instruction (*mati*) to a Śūdra," the verb *dā* signifies the act of making known. By the word *mati*, the scripture consisting of the Vedas and so forth—which generates knowledge—is denoted. Consequently, the meaning is that one should not cause him to understand that scripture.

In examples such as *patye śete* ("she lies down for her husband"), according to the view of the author of the Bhāṣya—who rejects the Vārttika—the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) arises because the husband is intended by the action [of lying down]. Specifically, by taking the objecthood (*karmatva*) defined by the initiating action—which is produced by perception, prayer, or determination—as belonging to the action of lying down, the husband becomes a recipient because he is desired to be connected with that action of lying down which has become the object (*karman*). This is based on the rule: *karmaṇā yam abhipraiti*. (Note: The phrase *'yam... bhāṣyaprayoga na dṛśyate'* appears to be a marginal or editorial remark stating that this specific usage is not seen in the Bhāṣya.)

By the rule (Pāṇini 1.4.32), the understanding is that the act of lying down has the husband as its recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the wife as its agent (*kartṛ*), and the act itself as its object (*karma*).

According to the view of the *Vārttika*, however, the understanding is simply that "lying down has the husband as its recipient" (*pati-saṃpradānakaṃ śayanam*). [In cases such as "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), it is the reverse, but this is due to non-expression (*anabhidhānāt*)]. Thus they say. Here, the seed of dissatisfaction should be understood as consisting in contradiction with the usage cited in the *Bhāṣya* mentioned above, and also as consisting in contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* cited in the refutation. This [phrase] "and the recipient" (*saṃpradānaṃ ca*) is connected with the word "threefold" (*trividhām*). "Because of not warding off" (*anirākaraṇāt*) is connected with "renunciation" (*tyāga*). In such a meritorious action, that which is desired is the primary [recipient].

[Objection: "Is it not the case that since the sense of 'being for the sake of that' (*tādarthya*) is established everywhere by the dative case itself, the introduction of the dative case for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is redundant? [Response: No;

for the resolution is given that the action of the recipient is indeed for the sake of the action of giving, because all factors of action (*kāraka*) are for the sake of the action. Furthermore, in other contexts, it is explained in detail that the sense of "being for the sake of that," characterized by the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor, is not perceived everywhere [by the dative alone].

"—2 *prerakam* — to the one who impels; *viprāya iti* —2 || The meaning is: because [the teacher] gives, having been prompted (*pravartita*) by the Brahmin with the thought, 'Let this be for me,' (it may also be said that he was 'requested,' *prārthita*). —2 *upādhyāya iti* —2 || The teacher does not request, but rather consents. Herein lies the truth: in all cases of the dative case used for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), there is a cognition [of the object] as possessing the capacity of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva-śaktimatva*). (The term *āveditam* is not present in the manuscript.)"

It has been stated more than once that by means of various technical rules (*saṃjñāsūtra*), there is the cognition of the capacity for various specific *kāraka*-roles in relation to their respective meanings; however, in the case of the dative case prescribed by rules such as *gatyarthakarmaṇi*, there is cognition [of the object] as possessing the capacity for the role of "object" (*karmatva*) and so forth.

In instances where the fourth case is used as a secondary nominal suffix (*upapadavibhakti*), such as in "avaprāya sukam" and "haraye namaḥ," the meaning should be understood as the respective relation [of the object or the agent]. This is clearly stated in the *Mañjūṣā* (in the *Laghumañjūṣā*, under the discussion of *sārthaka* [meaningful elements], page 1281).
Thus ends the section on the fourth case.

—2 "In all these cases"—2 as has been stated here and there. —2 "Having the sense of an object" (karmārthaka)—2 as in examples such as ‘pakva odanaḥ’ (the rice is cooked) and ‘vasiṣṭhena kṛto granthaḥ’ (the work composed by Vasiṣṭha). —2 "And because of [the attainment of] gain" (lābhāt)—2 otherwise, there would be an impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with [words like] ‘village’ and so forth.

And because of [the statement] "and from the Bhāṣya"—thus, the sense is that, in accordance with the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya, words such as "karma" (action) and so forth refer exclusively to the substratum (dharmin).

He introduces the view "or rather, it is the capacity itself" with the words "of the substratum also," and so forth. If the substratum were the denoted object, then "substratum-hood"—defined as existing in all substrata while not occurring in anything other than a substratum—would have to be stated as the delimiting factor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Since this is a determinate property (*sakhaṇḍopādhi*) and is therefore excessively cumbersome, he says: "And that very [capacity]... The word "also" (*api*) includes "substratum-hood."

—0ka—0—the section on *ākṛti* (the class-character). (Mīmāṃsādarśana 1.3.9, p. 229)—The essential point here is this: "Since no cognition of a qualified object arises without first apprehending the qualifier, it follows by logic that for words such as 'cow' (*go*), the denotable meaning is exclusively the property (*dharma*) such as 'cowness' (*gotva*). This is because it has been established therein that the denotable meaning is always the property alone.

And thus, in that case, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is construed with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) by way of its occurrence therein; and that property (*dharma*) is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) through the relation of being the qualifier (*nirūpakatva*). The resulting cognition in examples such as *odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice") is: "an operation conducive to softening, which is the qualifier of the substratum residing in the rice. And on this view, even the grammatical rule "the second case [is used] for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2) and others are justified precisely because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between the power (*śakti*) and the possessor of the power (*śaktimat*).

In words such as *paktā* ("cook") and *pāka* ("cooking"), because there is a cognition of the substratum (*āśraya*) and because one experiences grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Devadatta and others, [it follows that the suffixes] *tṛc* and so forth denote the substratum. Nevertheless, since the substratum is obtained through the base (*prakṛti*) itself in the case of nominal suffixes (*sup*), those suffixes do not have the function of denoting it. Even in Bahuvrīhi compounds where the meaning is not expressed by the genitive case, such as *prāptodaka* ("to whom water has come"), the substratum is obtained either by accepting that the meaning of the respective nominal base is included within the compound or by the force of "unification of meaning" (*aikārthībhāva*). This principle should be understood to apply everywhere in this manner. Furthermore, this very position is the more logical one.

If a substance (*dravya*) were the sole *kāraka*, then because it possesses a single form, the diversity of effects would be untenable. Yet, a diversity of effects is observed in instances such as "see the jar," "bring water with the jar," and "place the water in the jar. Although everything is indeed the substratum of all potentialities (*śakti*), nevertheless, due to the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) regarding a particular [potentiality] at a particular time, those various diverse effects are established. Furthermore, in the Bhāṣya on the *kāraka* section (sūtra...):

(1-4-23) *Mahābhāṣya*, Prauḍhamanoramā, p. 246: Since the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is shown as "it performs [the action]" (*karoti*)—meaning "it brings about the action"—the meaning of the term *kāraka* is precisely the capacity to produce an action. And that [capacity] is the meaning of all case-endings (*vibhakti*). Because the locative case in the rule "in a *kāraka*" (*kārake*) signifies the nominative sense, and because that [rule] is a governing heading (*adhikāra*), it is present in every subsequent rule; thus, through syntactic unity with each respective rule, it refers to that which is delimited by such [properties] as being the locus (*āśrayatva*) and so forth.

This is clear elsewhere [in other works], because by means of the prescription of the technical designation *kāraka*, the capacity to produce an action (*kriyājanakatva-śakti*) is also communicated. In examples such as "He asks the son of the Brāhmaṇa the way" (*brāhmaṇasya putraṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati*), the Brāhmaṇa does not possess the status of a *kāraka*. The phrase "not otherwise" (*ananyathā*) must be understood; for if taken literally, it would be the opposite. The phrase "not otherwise" must be understood; for if taken literally, it would be the opposite. Since the son alone is established as the producer (*janaka*) by virtue of being an invariably antecedent factor (*niyatapūrvavartin*) already established through common experience, the Brāhmaṇa—being merely an indirect appearance (*anyathāsiddha*)—lacks the capacity to be its producer. As it was said by Hari:

"They know the *sādhana* (means of accomplishment) to be the capacity for the production of actions in another substratum, [arising] precisely because of that [capacity] which inheres in its own substratum. (Vākyapadīya III, Sādhana-samuddeśa, verse 1). Here, by the word *sva* (own), the power (*śakti*) residing in the substance (*dravya*) to produce an action is meant; that very thing is called the *sādhana*. The underlying intention is this: since it is logically untenable for an established substance to be a producer of action by its mere nature, its status as such must be predicated only when it is permeated by power. Thus, according to the maxim of "distinguishing between what is already obtained and what is not yet obtained," power alone is the *sādhana*. As it has been said: "When [the operation] is not expressed... (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.1).
In the commentary on the sūtra 2-3-1), [the Mahābhāṣya] states: "What, then, is the correct means of accomplishment? He says: "The *guṇa* [substitution]," (MaBh PraKa p. 485).

Regarding the statement "qualities (*guṇas*) are the means (*sādhana*)," it is *śakti* (capacity) itself that is here designated as a "quality" due to its state of dependence. For this very reason, the formation of an *avyayībhāva* compound with the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is consistent. However, if only substance (*dravya*) were the means—or rather, if it possessed the common property of being the substratum (*sadharmitva*)—then since that [substance] would already be expressed by words such as "lion" (*hari*), the indeclinable (*avyaya*) would not even be employed; how then could there be a compound with it? Furthermore, it is not correct to maintain, as the original author suggests, that the capacity in the form of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) and so forth is what is not denoted by the case-ending.

Because its being a locus (*āśrayatva*) and so forth serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the subject matter of the rules prescribing technical designations such as "object" (*karman*). Furthermore, it is indeed the aforementioned capacity (*śakti*) [that is meant]. This is because, through the prescription of designations such as "object" by means of sūtras like "the agent" (*kartuḥ*, Pāṇini 1.4.49), it is that very capacity—namely, the state of being an object (*karmatva*)—as delimited by such locus-hood, which is understood as the meaning of the case-ending by rules such as "the second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*, 2.3.2).

In this regard, it should be understood that while the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are the generators of an action inherent in their own substratum (*svāśrayasamaveta*), the instrument (*karaṇa*) and other factors are the generators of an action inherent in a different substratum. It has been stated that in some cases, even a substance (*dravya*) permeated by a capacity (*śakti*) is designated as a *kāraka* and so forth, because of the non-difference between the capacity and that which possesses the capacity (*śaktimat*). Consequently, there is no room for the aforementioned fault. For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule "The [suffix] *liṅ* is used for the past when the agent is not witnessed" (*parokṣe liṅ*, Pāṇini 3.2.115), it says: "If that is so, then [the rule applies] when the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are not witnessed... (*ma.bhā.dvi.kha.pṛ.*)... [etc.]

178) Having stated that [the rule] "parokṣe" is non-restrictive because action (*kriyā*) is imperceptible, it was then said: "In that case, [it applies] when the means (*sādhana*) is imperceptible. In that context, if by the word *sādhana* one were to take "capacity" (*śakti*), then once again that would be non-restrictive. Therefore, one must accept the non-difference between the two; enough of this. In the expression "he acts with capacity" (*śaktyā karoti*), even for capacity, there is no connection with another capacity, because—as will be explained—it is designated as a substance (*dravya*) through technical terminology such as being a "characteristic of the object to be expressed" (*vācyopalakṣaṇa*). (Note: 'la' is not present in P.)

In the case of [the rule] *paśau kartari* and so forth, the meaning is established through such modes as "in the locus of power" (*śaktyāśraye*). Furthermore, all *kārakas* (factors of action) bring about the principal action by means of their respective intermediate actions. For this very reason, they are construed (*anvaya*) with the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) alone. Since the cognition that something is a generator of an action gives rise to the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) "What is that action?", it is appropriate that they be construed precisely therein.

Even for a recipient who is not physically present, since that recipient exists within the mind of the agent, they function as a cause precisely by being preceded by [the agent’s] cognition; it is by this much alone that the act of giving is established. Furthermore, in cases such as "he remembers the pot" (*ghaṭaṃ smarati*) or "he makes the mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti*), the mental pot and so forth bring about the completion of the memory and other actions because they exist at a prior time. This is the general direction of the argument. As for the claim that "being a *kāraka* (participant in action)" consists in being connected to an action—in order to exclude the status of being a *kāraka* for things like the Brahmin in sentences such as "he asks the Brahmin's son the way"—that is incorrect.

For [the statement] "the connection of factors of action (*kāraka*) with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)" would result in redundancy and incoherence, since this would imply—by logical necessity—that "those connected with an action are connected with an action. Furthermore, it would result in the incoherence of your own conventional usage, which treats the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as a factor of action and thus as being connected with an action.

Since the connection with the action must necessarily be stated through a traditional succession in accordance with the locus-factor (*adhikaraṇa-kāraka*), the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to [the *brāhmaṇa*] in the case of "he asks the son of the Brāhmaṇa for the way" (the phrase "in this case" being understood as the remainder of the sentence) would be unavoidable. Furthermore, the claim that "being a factor" (*kārakatva*) consists in being connected with the meaning of an affix that is itself connected with an action is also incorrect; for in cases such as "the rice is cooked" (*pakva odanaḥ*), the technical usage of "factorhood" (*kārakatva*) and "objecthood" (*karmatva*) would not apply to the meaning of the affix.

Furthermore, this would result in the undesirable consequence of violating the principle that "the factors of action (kārakas) are connected with the action. By this, the view that "the state of being a kāraka consists in being connected with the meaning of a case-ending that is itself connected with an action" is also refuted. Now, one might object: since the *Bhāṣya* states "it acts" (*karoti*) meaning "it accomplishes an action," the word *kāraka* is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *ṇvul* (denoting the agent). Consequently, while words such as *karaṇa* (instrument) are derived from the same root with the suffix *lyuṭ* (denoting the instrument), the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions like "the *kāraka* is the instrument" (*kārakaṃ karaṇam*) is contradictory; moreover, the expression "the *kāraka* is the agent" (*kārakaṃ kartā*) is redundant. If you raise this objection, we say no.

Since fire and other [factors] possess independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to their own respective operations such as burning, they constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); yet, because wood and other [objects] are observed to function as agents (*kartṛ*) in that context, there is no fault. This is because they possess the status of a *kāraka* by virtue of their momentary independence, and they also possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of producing the principal action through their own respective operations. Even for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*), their status as a *kāraka* is established precisely by taking their independence with respect to their own respective operations. However, due to the lack of formal expression (*anabhidhāna*), constructions such as "the village comes" (*grāma āgacchati*) or "the Brahmin gives" (*vipraḥ dadāti*) do not occur.
It should be understood that "agency" (*kārakatva*) is a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*); it is always present and serves as the basis for those respective designations.
Thus ends the determination of the power of agency (*kārakaśakti*).

"—2. 'Of that [relation], there is merely the relation'—2. By the word *mātra* (merely), the exclusion of the related entities is intended. For this very reason, although the relation was mentioned prior to the verse "Or rather, it is simply power" (*śaktireva vai*), it is defined later, after the definition of *śakti*, by way of transposition. And that relation, whether as the general category of 'relation' or in its specific forms such as 'owner and owned' (*svasvāmibhāva*) and so on, is what is to be expressed; the meaning is that even the relation of 'action and factor' (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is to be expressed by it. In the absence of the intention (*tātparya*) that serves to restrict the specific relation, [one would say] 'the garment of Caitra'."

In expressions such as "(P. 'sa'—it does not exist)," there is the cognition of that [relation] in its general form as a relation (*saṃbandhatva*). For this very reason, the hearer of the sentence has a desire to know the specific [relation] therein. Even though many relations may exist, in cases such as "This garment is not Caitra's," there is the cognition of that [relation] in its specific form as ownership (*svatva*) and so forth, because the intention (*tātparya*) is directed toward that specific relation of ownership and the like. For this same reason, it is said: "There are one hundred and one meanings of the genitive case" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.50), and "The genitive occurs in place of the sixth [case-ending] when used in connection with a word" (sūtra).

(1-1-49) Thus ends the *Bhāṣya* on the *Vārttika* and *Sūtra*. [Question: For what purpose is this stated? [Answer: This undertaking is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). There are one hundred and one meanings of the genitive case, or as many as there are; all of them would apply when the genitive case is uttered. [This] is consistent. Otherwise, since relation is a single entity by virtue of being a relation, that [distinction] would be inconsistent. As in examples such as "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*). [Objection: In the case of *mātuḥ*, [the genitive] is not observed; for there is no perception of a relation as a *kriyā-kāraka-bhāva* (action-agent relationship). Indeed, if that were perceived as *karman* (objecthood) and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) and others. [Response of the Siddhāntin: Even in the case of the genitive used in the sense of the *śeṣa* (remainder), what is intended as the relation—whether as the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) rooted in the *kriyā-kāraka-bhāva*, or as the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*), or simply as the state of being a cause (*nimittatva*)—is indeed that very relation. As it was stated by Bhartṛhari: "A relation other than the *kārakas* is preceded by the *kriyā-kāraka-bhāva*."

"He is designated [as a *kāraka*] in relation to an action, whether that action is explicitly stated or unstated. (Vākyapadīya III. Sādhana-samuddeśa, verse 156). Here, by the word *kāraka*, the powers (*śakti*) such as instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and so forth are expressed. This is the intended meaning: in the case of an unstated action... (P. 02-0a)

The passage from "immediately after [the word] ‘action’ (*kriyā*)... up to "...is not heard" (*aśrūyamāṇā*) is to be repeated twice (this sentence alone). In examples such as "the king's servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), [it is understood that] "the king gave [something] to the servant"; thus, the king and the servant previously existed in the roles of agent (*kartṛ*) and recipient (*saṃpradāna*) through the act of giving. Since a mutual relationship between things is impossible at present without an action based on that [prior state], such an action as giving, even if unexpressed, [is inferred].

Since the relation characterized as a grammatical effect (*kārya*) cannot otherwise be established, it is inferred that [the relation] is present; thus, through that [relation], there is *samanvaya* (syntactic connection). For action (*kriyā*) establishes the relation, much like a series of steps on a staircase. And in this way, even the two related entities possess the status of a "factor" (*kāraka*), consisting in being the cause for the inferred action. Similarly, in cases where the action is not directly heard (*aśruta-kriyā-viṣaya*), such as "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*), the aforementioned relation is based on the objecthood (*karmatva*) of the action. For this very reason, one does not say "the trees of the mountain" (*parvatasya vṛkṣāḥ*), because a relation based on the locus-and-located relationship (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) between the tree and the mountain is impossible.

If it is argued that conjunction itself is [the cause] in that manner, we say no—because conjunction lacks the status of being rooted in that [inherence], whereas on the contrary, it is precisely that [inherence] which is the root of conjunction. In fact, conjunction does not even possess the nature of a relation; this has been explained in detail elsewhere.

In the expression "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣa*), the meaning of the genitive case is the relation of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), which consists of ownership (*svāmitva*) and being owned (*svatva*). As for the claim that either ownership or being owned individually constitutes the meaning of the genitive, that is incorrect;

for since each of those resides in only one of the two relata, they cannot logically be a relation. A relation must reside in both relata, be distinct from the relata themselves, and be that which necessarily determines the cognition of the qualified entity.

Nor should it be argued that ownership and the like are also present in one [of the two] as its locus, while in the other they exist as its qualifier (*nirūpaka*), and thus the relation is established as residing in both; for since being a qualifier (*nirūpakatva*) is not a determinant of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*), there would be no resulting cognition of the relation as existing in both. Furthermore, that relation appears precisely as a relational object (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*). For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe" (Pāṇini 2.3.50), it is stated: [Ma.Bhā.Pra.Kha.Pṛ. 519].

If it is argued that "the sixth case [is used] for the remainder" (Pāṇini 2.3.50), then there would be a contradiction regarding the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). In the expression "the king's servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), it has been stated that the king is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the servant is the qualificand. Otherwise, one would have to describe the relationship either as being the qualificand or as being the qualifier.

If it is asked: "Since a relation resides in two things, why is there this restriction that the genitive case occurs only after the qualifier such as 'king' and not after the [qualified] person? It could apply to the person as well," Hari says on this point: "Although this [relation] resides in both, it is distinguished as residing in the subordinate members because they exist for the sake of another."

"In that case, even when [the relation] is being expressed, it is figuratively attributed (upacaryate) to the principal [substantive]. This is the intended meaning: since a distinction must exist, and because a qualifier cannot function as such without a connection to that which is intended to be qualified, the connection is distinguished within that qualifier—meaning it is perceived as being prominent—and thus the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) occurs there alone.

However, when the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) appears in grammatical co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a word, because it possesses its own status as being manifested as the qualificand relative to its own meaning, there is no requirement for a relation that would determine its status as a qualificand. In that case, the relation—which is partially perceived through the word, such as a genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), applied to the qualifier—is also connected to the principal [the qualificand].

The meaning is that because it possesses a dual nature, it serves as an auxiliary to the qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) determined by the king and others, which is perceived when the words "king" and so forth are in proximity. However, the distinction is that in cases such as *rājñaḥ* ("of the king"), there is a cognition of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatva) determined by a general related entity, even without the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of another word.

For by the expression *rājñaḥ*, ownership being understood is made to imply possession (*svatva*) in the person precisely through the impossibility of its otherwise [being accounted for]; thus, since the relation is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), the nominative case ending is more intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) than the person.

And thus, from the word *rājñaḥ* [in the sense of] "belonging to the king," there arises the understanding that [the object] has the king as its owner (*rājasvāmikam*). For this very reason, there subsequently arises a desire to know the specific nature [of that object] through the question "What is it?", which is then resolved by words such as *puruṣaḥ* ("a man"). This is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *yasmād adhikam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.9), at page 494 of the Prakriyā-khaṇḍa of the Mahābhāṣya. However, when the intention is not to express the person (*puruṣa*) as a qualifier, then the form *puruṣasya rājā* ("the king of the person") also occurs; such is the general direction.

"—of the genitive [case] expressing a *kāraka*. This refers to the sense derived from the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛtī" (Pāṇini 2.3.65). In that regard, in examples such as "kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ" ("the act of Kṛṣṇa"), there is the power of agency (*kartṛtva-śakti*), while in "jagataḥ kartā" ("the creator of the world"), there is the power of objecthood (*karmatva-śakti*). The understanding (*bodha*) in these cases has already been explained previously.

As for the claim that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has a primary power (*śakti*) with respect to the relation [of agent and object], while there is *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) regarding these two meanings [the agent and the object themselves], and that the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.65) is what makes this known—that is not correct. For it is more appropriate that this rule serves to indicate the primary power (*śaktigrāhakatva*), since there is nowhere an instruction (*anuśāsana*) regarding a meaning that is merely secondary (*lākṣaṇika*). Even in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇasaṃjñā*) applies even to that which possesses the quality of being the substratum of the hamlet only by way of superimposition; thus, the locative case (*saptamī*) here has its primary power (*śakti*) alone.
This is clear from the inclusion of the term "tamap" (the superlative suffix) in the rule "ādhāro 'dhikaraṇam" (Pāṇini 1.4.42), as explained elsewhere.

As for the claim that the objecthood (*karmatva*) of the base-meaning of a *kṛt*-suffix is of a different class from the objecthood of the base-meaning of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), because a different kind of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is observed, that too is not correct. By the force of the grammatical rule prescribing correctness (*sādhutva-anuśāsana*) in *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65), the base-meaning of a *kṛt*-suffix exhibits an expectancy for an object in the form "of what? (*kasya*), as indicated by the presence of the genitive case; however, the base-meaning of a verbal suffix exhibits an expectancy for an object in the form "what? (*kim*), because the genitive case is absent.

For this very reason, in examples such as *pacan*, there is no demonstration of an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the meaning of the base of the suffix *śatṛ* (e.g., "what? because, by the prohibition of the genitive case in the rule *na loke* (Pāṇini 2.3.69)—[or rather, by the non-prohibition of the genitive in the view under discussion]—such [expectancy] is absent.
Thus ends the section on the genitive.

"—thus, the understanding is such. The specific manner [of this] has indeed been clearly stated in various places. Regarding the statement "in the case of objecthood (*viṣayatā*), it is by way of the definition (*lakṣaṇā*)," the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is mere cognition (*jñāna*); objecthood is the meaning of the accusative case ending. The base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed there as being inherent (*ādheyatva*). And that [objecthood] is construed with the meaning of the verbal root as its determiner (*nirūpakatva*). Consequently, in cases such as "he knows the pot" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), the understanding is: "cognition which is the determiner of the objecthood residing in the pot"—such is their view.

"—The restriction (*niyama*) applies to those [cases] under discussion. This is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Thus, the restriction—"the second case suffix (*dvitīyā*) occurs only for the object (*karman*)" and so forth—excludes only those [kārakas] currently under discussion, such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and others, but not the meaning of indeclinables (*avyaya*). Therefore, the derivation of case endings from indeclinables is established by the general rule.

And [the view that] number is the denoted meaning [of the suffixes]—namely, that the denotative capacity of the case-endings (*sup*) exists either by way of their being singular, etc., or by way of their specific forms such as *sut* and *aut*; and that the denoted meaning consists of singularity, duality, plurality, and so forth—is established through the grammatical rules "in the dual" (*dv-e-kayoḥ*, Pāṇini 1.4.22) and "in the plural" (*bahuṣu*, Pāṇini 1.4.21). In all cases, it is understood that the number is inherent in the meaning of the stem (*prakṛtyartha*).

In expressions such as "saṃpanno vrīhiḥ" ("the rice has ripened"), the use of the singular number occurs by superimposing the singularity inherent in the delimitor of the meaning of the base (prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka)—namely, *vrīhitva* (rice-ness)—onto the individual grains of rice. As for the claim that in the aforementioned usage the number is construed with *vrīhitva* and other such delimiters of the base-meaning itself, that is incorrect.

Because there is no evidence for abandoning the established rule that the meaning of the base (prakṛti) must be construed as the qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya), so too in cases such as "The Vedas are means of valid cognition" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*), the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) brings about the cognition of those very things [the Vedas] which possess the number inherent in the nature of being means of valid cognition. Its result, however, is the establishment of their status as belonging to a single class of means of valid cognition. It is exactly the same in cases such as "Cows are wealth" (*gāvo dhanam*). This is clearly stated in the *Pañcaviṃśati* Sūtra... [text fragment].

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "pañca-dāra-" (Pāṇini 5.4.73), it is stated that [the forms] beginning with *vibhakti* are not seen [as plural]. Furthermore, regarding words such as *dārāḥ*, it was previously explained that the plural number is used by superimposing plurality onto the parts [of the whole]. Regarding the phrase "restriction of the word" (*śabda-niyama*): the meaning is that a restriction serves to exclude the connection of the word bearing the technical name *vibhakti*—such as the second case (*dvitīyā*) and so forth—with any other sense than its intended one. Regarding the phrase "restriction of the meaning" (*artha-niyama*): [it refers to the exclusion of unintended meanings].
The meaning is that a restriction (niyama) serves to exclude the connection of the object (artha)—such as the *karman* case—and so forth, with other case-endings (*vibhakti*).

Regarding the phrase "nānṛtām iti"—[the word] "śrauta" and so forth [is used]. As for the statement "not in a case-ending (vibhakti)": although others proclaim that "there is no indication (lakṣaṇā) in a *sub*-case-ending," nevertheless, it is more appropriate to say that there is no indication in case-endings in general. This is because if one does not accept indication in a *sub*-case-ending, the rule regarding the reversal of restriction (*niyamavyatyaya*) and other such teachings would be rendered futile; furthermore, since [indication] exists even in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*-vibhakti), indication there too would lack any authoritative basis. —The phrase "dig" (direction/illustration)—means [this is merely one way of looking at it].
It should be understood that its meaning has been explained in the determination of the sense of the genitive case; thus all is auspicious. 1. (24).
Thus ends [the section] in the *Laghubhūṣaṇakānti*.
—0— Determination of the Meaning of Sub-words (Subarthanirṇaya) —0—

—The Determination of the Meaning of Nouns. Śrīḥ! Having thus defined the meaning of the case-suffixes, [the author], by way of occasion (*prasaṅgāt*), now defines the meaning of the noun which serves as their base (*prakṛti*), beginning with the words “one” (*ekam*) and so forth. “One” refers to the *jāti* (universal); this connects with the phrase “is the meaning of the noun. The meaning is that, between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), only one of the two is the denotative power (*śakya*) of the noun. This is because, as will be explained later, the removal of all objections applies to both of these two positions. The same applies hereafter.

"—the non-separation from the two-fold understanding. This means: whether [the word's power] resides in the universal (*jāti*) or in the individual (*vyakti*). The sense is that whatever establishes the oneness of the universal in the case of the power residing in the universal, that same [oneness] applies to the individual as well. He states the very [reason for] complexity: "For in this way..."—with the assumption that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base's own power, [it would follow that] in cases such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), because the connection of the case-suffix meaning with the individual would be untenable, [the suffix would have to denote] a qualified [individual].

(Positive concomitance is not observed). He states "moreover" (*kiṃ ca*) in order to refute, all at once, the view that [the word] has the capacity [to denote the individual]. Regarding "inhering in itself" (*svasamaveta*): "itself" refers to the individual by virtue of the word's capacity; "inhering in that" refers to the universal; and "being the locus of that" refers to another individual. The meaning is that there is an unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from such a relationship. [The phrase] "by logic" (*nyāyāt*)... [is not seen in the text from *nyāya* to *lakṣaṇāyāṃ vā*].

The meaning is that, according to the maxim "a cognition that has not grasped the qualifier does not proceed to the qualified," [the word cannot denote the individual]. Regarding the term *lakṣaṇāyāḥ*: it refers to the aforementioned *lakṣaṇā*. And thus, in both the case of denoting the individual and the case of *lakṣaṇā*, [the following] is established: the application of the case-ending to the meaning of the suffix is justified. This is because, according to the previously stated etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) alone is intended by the function (*vṛtti*), and since the individual is the meaning of the base through *lakṣaṇā*, the connection with the meaning of the case-ending is established. In reality, however, *lakṣaṇā* is inappropriate here.

Because cognition is observed even without a connection through logical necessity (*anupapatti-pratisandhāna*), and because in some cases it is observed that a word expressive of the mere possible meaning itself functions elsewhere through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), this is not the case here. Furthermore, although words are grasped as having their denotative power (*śakti*) in a universal (*jāti*) precisely through its being qualified by a particular (*viśeṣaṇa*), since the status of being a qualifier is untenable [for the universal], there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of the individual (*vyakti*) as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) in the form of an inference.

Furthermore, it has been argued that the application of a word refers to a universal (jāti) understood through a term devoid of [specific] suffixes and the like, which becomes the object of a cognition having the individual as its qualificandum, because its expressive power is grasped as a qualifier; but that too is not correct, because cognition arises even without the recollection of pervasion (vyāpti) and so forth. Moreover, since the word, like the sense organ, is a cause of indeterminate cognition (nirvikalpaka), the presentation of the universal from the word is itself indeterminate. Even the experience of the expressive power (śakti) regarding the aspect of the universal is itself devoid of any qualifying mode (niṣprakāraka). As for the "implication" (ākṣepa), it is simply the inference: "Cowness (gotva) is dependent on something [else], because it is a universal."

Nor is it correct to say that there is no violation of the rules of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) because the presentation of the word-meaning through its application serves as a cause for verbal cognition; for such a causal presentation is not universal. Furthermore, the genus (*jāti*) is not presented through the word itself. Nor can it be explained by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since comprehension occurs even without the knowledge of an apparent inconsistency (*anupapatti*). Nor is it tenable to define "implication" (*ākṣepa*) as being known through a single act of cognition, for we observe doubts regarding "fieryness" (*tejastva*) and so on when gold and other substances are perceived. This is evident even when the cognition "this is a substance" has arisen.

[The word] ‘sati’ is not seen here [in the verse], and furthermore, because of the absence of the cognition of "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva). Moreover, even if cowhood (gotva) is known through the same cognitive act as the particularity (vaiśiṣṭya) with respect to the cow, there would only be a collective apprehension (samūhālambana) of the form "the cow, cowhood, and the particularity," and not a qualified cognition (viśiṣṭabuddhi). If it is asked, "How then is there a cognition of the individual (vyakti) under the theory that the power [of the word] resides in the pure universal (śuddhajātiśaktivāda)?"—to this they reply: because the individual is the qualificandum (viśeṣya) in the apprehension of the power, the individual appears just as the universal appears as a delimiting factor (avacchedakatva) in the theory of the individual (vyaktivāda).

The apprehension of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*), however, takes the form "the word *go* has the genus (*jāti*) as its denotable object" (*gaur gopadaśakyā*), rather than the incorrect reading "the power [is in the genus]" (*śaktir vā*). And that apprehension occurs with respect to the genus alone, by means of the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) assisted by the maxim "that which is not grasped [cannot serve as a cause]" (*nāgṛhīte*), just as in the case of the statement "heaven has perished. Alternatively, the apprehension of the power may have the genus as its primary qualificand (*jātiviśeṣyaka*), taking the form "the cow is the denotable object of the word *go*" (*gaur gopadaśakyā*). Even though the genus is inseparable from its substratum, the genus alone is the denotation of the word.

Just as a face, even when not separated from its own location, is perceived in water and other media and is still understood by the word "face"—this is what must be understood here—the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) in this view is a property belonging to that universal (*jāti*). However, [according to another view], even in the absence of being the object of a convention, because there is a necessary relation between the universal and the individual in a general sense, the individual associated with itself qualifies the universal; thus, there is a cognition of the individual. As it has been said in the *Sarūpa* [Sūtra]: [Pāṇini 1.2.64].

In the Bhāṣya on Sūtra 1.2.64, it is stated: "Vājapyāyana [holds that the word denotes] the form" (*ākṛtiṃ vājapyāyanaḥ*; MaBh PraKha p. 90). This means that even in the absence of an individual (*vyakti*), actions such as bringing [an object] are impossible for the universal alone; therefore, they are accomplished through its association with the individual.

Others, however, maintain that because there is a permanent relationship between the universal and the individual, following the cognition of the universal from the word, the individual is manifested by way of memory—based on the principle that "that which is related to one [is remembered when the other is perceived]"—and that the Bhāṣyas situated in the *Sarūpa-sūtra* and elsewhere are solely intent upon this point.

—0kha— Others, however, [state] in the *Majjūṣā* (in the section on the investigation of the meaning of nominal stems, p. 12, l. 14): "Because there is no difference between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), even though primacy belongs to the universal alone, there is no logical impossibility in its connection with [properties such as] being a draught-animal (*vāha*) and so forth. Precisely because of that non-difference, universals and the like, which are the meanings of words such as 'cow' (*go*), possess the capacity to convey gender and other attributes residing in their substratum. This was stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *taddhitārthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.50). —0ka— (Mañjūṣā, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. ...).

386) "Alternatively—[of substance and form] because of non-distinction," as stated by the words "of substance and form" and so forth. Thus, non-distinction (*avyatireka*) has been explained. For this very reason, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra "jātyākhyāyām" (Pāṇini 1.2.58), non-distinction is stated in the passage beginning: "For by a word denoting a genus (*jāti*), both the substance (*dravya*) and the genus itself are expressed. For this same reason, [the rule] "sarūpa" (Pāṇini 1.2.64)...

In the Bhāṣya on Sūtra 1.2.64 as well, having raised the objection that if the genus (*jāti*) is the word-meaning, then because it is one, dual and plural endings would be unaccounted for; and having also raised the objection regarding the theory of the individual (*vyakti*) that in cases such as "one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa," one would feel satisfied after killing just a single Brāhmaṇa—it was stated: "For one who holds the genus to be the word-meaning, the substance is not not the word-meaning; nor, for one who holds the substance to be the word-meaning, is the genus not the word-meaning. Both are the word-meaning for both."

"For someone, one thing may be subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) and another primary (*pradhānabhūta*). (Mahābhāṣya, Prauḍhamanoramā-khaṇḍa, p. 99). From this, the non-distinction between genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*) is obtained; however, it is not the "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) position. Let the wise reflect that this commentary does not establish the "qualified" position whose basis will be stated later. [Regarding the phrase] "of the mention of *aṇ*"—this means in the rule *aṇudit* (Pāṇini 1.1.69). [Regarding the phrase] "because it is established by the treatise"—[this refers to the same].

Regarding the view that [words denote] the universal (*jāti*), the point is that since the two Vārttikas—"the mention of *aṇ* is not a general rule because it refers to the form" (*ākṛtigrahaṇāt*) and "or rather, there is no need for its commencement" (*anārambho vā*)—along with their Bhāṣya commentary (Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 373), have been rejected, the necessity [of the rule] applies only to the view that [words denote] the individual (*vyakti*). "—*tat-grahaṇāt*" means "because of the apprehension of the capacity" (*śakti*). "—*sambandhitāvacchedakasya*" means "of that which delimits the state of being related to the capacity," such as potness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth. "—*na caivam*" etc. (P.).

"And not even thus"—this refers to the apprehension that the aforementioned causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) might not be accepted; this apprehension extends up to the word "is to be suspected" (*śaṅkyam*), as the reading [of the text] is disjointed. This apprehension is prompted by the conceit that "the delimitor of the capacity to be denoted (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*)" belongs to that which is capable [of being denoted]. Even in the case of "non-causality"—as in the case of stickness (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth—and even in the case of "not being the object of definition (*alakṣyatva*)"—as in the case of bankness (*tīratva*) and so forth—it is possible here as well; for even though potness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth may not themselves be directly denotable, it is still possible for them to be the delimiters of the capacity to be denoted.

For instance: just as the state of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) in the apprehension of a relation is the regulator for the manifestation of the relata, so too is the state of being its delimitant (*avacchedakatva*) the regulator for the manifestation of the property (*dharma*). Just as, in the case of an elephant-driver and the like, the apprehension of the relation with the elephant is the regulator for the presentation [of the object] as "elephant-driver-ness" (*hastipakatva*) and so forth. For this very reason, there is the presentation of a jar through "jar-ness" from a staff, and of a staff through "staff-ness" from a jar.
