By this, the view that there is a denotative power (*śakti*) even in the delimitant of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is refuted, because it lacks a result. (P. 02-0)

Because of the absence of a result [otherwise] similar [to the primary one], just as in the apprehension of a word's power (*śaktigraha*), there is the manifestation of all individual instances (*vyakti*) subsumed under the delimitor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), so too in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there is the manifestation of all those subsumed individual instances.

If it is objected: "In the view that the individual instance alone is the denotation (*śuddhavyaktipakṣa*), since individual instances are infinite, would there not be the undesirable consequence of a plural ending in expressions such as 'one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa' (*na brāhmaṇam*)," we reply: No.

There is no fault in the use of the singular number because the number residing in the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is superimposed upon the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). And "being the delimitor of denotability" consists in appearing as a mode (*prakāratā*), specifically called the "delimitorship of the qualificandhood" (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatā*) which resides in the denotable object. Furthermore, in the apprehension of the word-potency (*śakti*) for words such as "jar," it is potness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like that constitutes this [delimitorship], not substanceness (*dravyatva*) and the like; therefore, there is no cognition of substanceness and so forth as the mode from those words.

For this very reason, although the word *ākāśa* lacks a direct denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to being the substratum of sound, there nevertheless arises a cognition of it in that very form. This is because the apprehension of a relation having a qualified object as its content is the cause of a cognition having that same qualified object as its content; so says the author of the *Maṇi* (Raghunātha Śiromaṇi). In reality, however, the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is either an impartite adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) consisting of that word-form, or a universal (*jāti*) consisting of that word-form; by means of this, the usage "ākāśa is the substratum of sound" is rendered logically consistent.

And this position of the pure individual (*śuddhavyaktipakṣa*) was stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sūtra* "sarūpa" (Pāṇini 1.2.64): "The *vyaṅ* [suffix] denotes a substance (*dravya*)" (Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 94). Here, by the word "substance," every entity whatsoever that is expressed by a word as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is understood to be endowed with the properties of a substance. And that [entity] is either endowed with its primary properties or endowed with those properties figuratively. As it has been said: "Where a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is employed to indicate a thing..."

"That object which is intended to be expressed as something to be differentiated is called a substance (*dravya*)" (Vākyapadīya III, Bhūyo’rthasaṃkhyāna-kārikā 3). The meaning is that a "substance" is an entity capable of being referred to by pronouns such as "this" or "that. Another definition is provided by the phrase "as something to be differentiated," which means "as a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) determined by something [else]. By the word "intended," it is stated that this is a definition of the referent of a word in general. Consequently, even universals (*jāti*) and the like possess the status of substance when they are intended to be expressed as the qualificand.

Furthermore, because the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)—namely, action—is referred to by words such as *kim* ("what"), and because it is qualified by terms such as *sukham* ("pleasure"), and because in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) it is qualified by number, it possesses the very nature of a substance (*dravyatva*). As for the rule "And that which is contradictory... (*vipratiṣiddhaṃ ca*, Pāṇini 2.4.13), the term "substance" (*dravya*) refers, by implication, to the substance as it is well-known in other systems; this is the general direction.

Others, however, maintain that although the power [of a word] is grasped by taking the genus as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), in reality what is cognized is the individual qualified by that genus; yet it is not cognized under the aspect of that property. This is the doctrine of the "pure individual" (*śuddhavyaktivāda*). For example, in cases such as "He who wears white clothes is Devadatta," even though the power of the word is grasped with respect to Devadatta as indicated by the white clothes, there is no manifestation of those clothes in the cognition produced by the word "Devadatta"; the same applies to the genus and so forth.

This is precisely what constitutes the character of a *upalakṣaṇa* (indirect indicator) for a genus (*jāti*) and so forth: having enabled all its own substrates to become objects of the apprehension of their own essential nature and capacity, it itself becomes an object of the apprehension of capacity while remaining non-objective to cognition. For example, in such cases as "Devadatta’s house has crows," the crow—serving as an indirect indicator—distinguishes that house from others by means of its own [presence], such as the presence of grass and so on. Similarly, the genus, having presented the individuals, distinguishes those individuals (as indicated by itself) from others.

According to this view, the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) is as follows: that which is the substratum of potness (*ghaṭatva*) is the denotation (*śakya*) of the word "pot. By the pronoun *tat* [in the compound *tatpada*], there is a reference to the qualificand alone. This is precisely the meaning of the statement "the pot is the denotation of the word 'pot. It is with this very intention that, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "dhruvam apāye" (Pāṇini 1.4.24), the objection regarding the lack of fixity (*adhruvatva*) in examples such as "he fell while running" (*dhāvataḥ patitaḥ*) was raised and resolved by the principle that "even that which exists may not be intended to be expressed" (*satopy avivakṣā bhavati*).

With the intention of explaining that "only the substance characterized by the action of going (*saraṇakriyā*) is intended here as the *apādāna*," as stated in the *Pradīpa* on the *Mahābhāṣya* (Prakriyā-kaumudī, p. 249): "'Only the substance characterized by the action of going is intended as the *apādāna*,' and having considered this, he cites the statement of the elder [grammarian]: 'It has been said' (*tad uktam*). Even in cases such as 'not a Brāhmaṇa' (*na brāhmaṇam*), there is no fault, because the state of being characterized by Brāhmaṇahood (*brāhmaṇatva-upalakṣitatva*) exists in all individual instances."

The singular number, however, is to be justified as before. In this view, by resorting to the distinction of the substance through its form as a qualifier of the common locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the formation of compounds such as *vīrapuruṣa* is established by relying on a coordinate compound (*sāmānādhikaraṇasamāsa*). There is no synonymy between these two words; for there is synonymy only when both words convey the same individual entity (*vyakti*)—that is, when they signify merely the same object of cognition—since the word *vīra* also brings about the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the person (*puruṣa*).

For this very reason, the simultaneous usage of expressions such as "the cow is white" (*gauḥ śukla*) is also justified. Introducing the position that [the denotation] consists of two [factors], he states the final conclusion (siddhānta): "In reality, however... and "...the qualified [entity] is the denotation," according to the Bhāṣya. In fact, it was already stated previously that the position of the qualified [denotation] is not obtained from this Bhāṣya. If one asks, "How then is the position of the qualified [denotation] established?"—listen: the determination of the word's power (śakti) with respect to a bare genus is not possible, because among the factors for determining that power, the primary ones—namely, practical activity (*vyavahāra*) consisting of leading, bringing, and so forth—are obstructed in that case.

Nor should it be argued that the determination of that [meaning] may reside in the individual instance (*vyakti*) alone; for it is impossible to grasp the meaning in every individual instance because they are infinite. Furthermore, if the apprehension of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*) were restricted to one particular instance, there would be no cognition of any other instance. If, on the other hand, one were to accept that an instance not actually present within the scope of that [power-apprehension] could still be its object, then even a horse would appear from the word "cow. If, however, one maintains that the apprehension of the power with respect to a specific instance is the cause of the verbal cognition of that instance, then there is a logical inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*).

Furthermore: [In the case] of another individual elephant-driver (*hastipaka-vyaktyantara*), because one has grasped the relationship with an elephant, even for that driver who has not previously grasped it, there would arise a memory of the sight of an elephant; therefore, it must be postulated that the knowledge of a relationship in one individual is not the cause of the cognition of another individual. Furthermore, if all words were to denote merely the individual (*vyakti-mātra*), [the following would occur].

Otherwise, the co-usage of [words] such as "this is a cow," "white," and "red" would be untenable, because they would be synonyms. Therefore, one must maintain that the apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śaktigraha*) occurs with respect to individuals qualified by the genus and so forth—namely, all individuals that are subsumed under that genus—since we observe that through such an apprehension of the power, there arises a cognition of all the individuals. Regarding the aspect of the individual...

In the view of Vyāsa, the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) consists in a cognition whose qualificandum-ness is not delimited by anything other than the delimitor of the power’s denotability and which possesses the universal as its qualifier; thus, the comprehension of all individuals that are the substrata of the universal becomes possible. And so, the acceptance of "universal-characterized" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*) proximity for this purpose is entirely redundant.

Furthermore, if that were accepted, there would be the undesirable consequence of omniscience, because through the "universal-characterized" proximity of knowability (*prameyatva*), there would result the cognition of all things—properties, substrata, and their specific relations—in their respective forms.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because, by virtue of being the locus of a property residing in itself (*svavṛttidharmāśrayatva*), only a cognition qualified by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) is produced.

Enough of this, as it has never been observed anywhere that a word functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*) due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). In that regard, the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in both the qualifier and the qualified. It should be understood here that "being the delimiting factor of expressibility" (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) consists in being a qualifier within a portion of the expressed meaning. He resolves the contradiction with the words "and of the term 'one'. This is the intended meaning: according to the view that [words denote] a universal (*jāti*), words such as "cow" possess expressive power in both respects.

In the causal relation for the apprehension of power (*śakti*), only the property of having a genus (*jāti*) as the qualifier (*prakāraka*) is included; thus, there is a single causal relation by including only this one factor. There is no inclusion of the property of having an individual (*vyakti*) as the qualificand (*viśeṣyaka*). For this very reason, power is "crooked" (*kubjī*) with respect to the individual portion, because in that portion there is no requirement for the cognition produced by that [power]. The intended meaning is that it is on account of this alone that the conventional usage "power resides in the genus" is maintained. This is the sense of the phrase "in the knowledge of power. The underlying point is as follows: (L. 02)

The point is this: [the latter view] is abandoned due to parsimony (*lāghava*). In the cognition "this is a jar" (*ghaṭa*), parsimony is achieved by taking the causal efficiency (*karaṇatā*) to reside in the knowledge of the power (*śaktijñāna*) as having the nature of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). However, [in the alternative view], the causal efficiency residing in the knowledge of power would have as its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) the knowledge of power as having the nature of "the knowledge of the power qualified by jar-ness. Consequently, one would have to introduce the jar itself and its qualification—that is, its specific character—as additional factors, resulting in great complexity (*mahāgaurava*).

This very theory of the expressive power residing in the genus (*jāti*) is also accepted by the Gurus (Prābhākaras). Otherwise, if expressive power were admitted to reside in the genus alone, their doctrine that the expressive power of words resides in [the word as] connected with an action (*kāryānvita*) would not be established; for it is only individuals that are connected with an action.

Now, if it is argued that in the cognition produced by a word such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), the causality [of the word] consists in the knowledge of its power residing in the genus "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), then one might object that just as there is the cognition "the jar exists" (*ghaṭo'sti*), there would likewise be the cognition "jar-ness exists" (*ghaṭatvamasti*). Therefore, [it must be held that] the causality consists in the knowledge of the power residing in the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). To this we say: no.

This is because it is accepted that, with respect to a cognition having "potness" as its qualifier (*prakāra*), the cause is the knowledge of the power (*śakti*) residing in potness, provided that potness is not qualified by anything else. Since a pure [potness] cannot be expressed [by words] in that context, it is denoted by the word "potness" (*ghaṭatva*). (The portion from "ghaṭa" to "paramārthatas tu, ni" is not observed.)

[Objection: But in this view, all words would possess all three genders, since the non-denotative nature of gender is equal everywhere. [Reply: No—this is actually untenable because it is overly complex (*gaurava*). Furthermore, this method is intended to refute the theory of the universal-characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*); however, that is impossible, for if the substantive portion (*viśeṣya-aṃśa*) were not included within the scope of the delimiting condition of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), there would arise the absurdity of cognizing a horse and so forth as a cow.

Nor should it be said that only a specific modehood (*prakāratā*) is being posited; for that [modehood] is difficult to ascertain, as it must be understood by the very expression "as determined by a qualificandum-ness residing in a cow" (*viśeṣyavattā*). Moreover, if that were posited, there would be no cognition of another individual cow, because the [required] modehood residing in that [other cow] would lack the corresponding determiner (*nirūpaka*). (Note: In the manuscript, the phrase *tanniṣṭhaviśeṣyatāyām* appears to have been deleted.)

However, if it is considered that there is no fault here because the property of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) in the portion of the qualificandum is introduced as not being delimited by anything other than the qualifier (*prakāra*), then it should be understood that this effort is in vain. Regarding the phrase "the pair" (*dvikamiti*): the meaning is that in the rule prescribing the nominative case, the term "prātipadikārtha" (the meaning of the nominal stem) includes the pair consisting of the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*).

—04—In this regard, [this subject has been stated twice in this Mātṛkā]. The truth is this: among the three positions, it has been established that the position of the universal (*jāti*) alone is both simpler and more logical. More may be understood from other sources. Alternatively, substance (*dravya*) itself, being of the nature of Brahman, is denoted by all words because of its eternity; its differentiation is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), and thus there is synonymy (*paryāyatā*). A universal, however, is not eternal, according to the Vedic revelation: "That through which fire possesses the nature of fire. —01—

This point is also clarified elsewhere: in words such as *guṇa* (quality), where the designations "quality" (*guṇa*) and so forth refer to other qualities and actions, the [denotable] capacities (*śakya*) are, respectively, the qualities and so on. Since their eternality and unity are accepted, there is neither infinity (*anantya*) nor deviation (*vyabhicāra*). In that regard, concerning the scope of the technical name (*saṃjñā*), the capacity belongs to the individual (*vyakti*) alone; and because that individual is one, those two [faults] do not apply. Nor does this lead to the consequence of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpa*). This is because the individual itself appears through two modes of objectivity (*viṣayatā*), namely as the qualifier (*prakāratā*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*); thus, there is no fault. This too is clear elsewhere.

In the case of words where qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are predominant [i.e., *guṇya* and so forth], the universals (*jāti*) residing in those qualities and so forth are the denotable meanings (*śakya*). Alternatively, even in the case of words where the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) and so forth are predominant, the universal alone is the denotable meaning. Since that universal possesses the property of residing in substances and so forth through a transitive relation consisting in "residing in that which resides in its own substratum," the cognition of substances and so forth is possible. In that regard, concerning words that are proper names such as *Ḍittha*, the universal residing in the word *Ḍittha* is the denotable meaning.

Because words such as "ḍittha" are distinct due to differences in their utterance by Śuka and others, or because they are determined as such, [the universal] resides in multiple individuals. And since that [universal] resides in a substance through its relation to being denotable by its own substratum, there is the cognition of the substance.

As for the claim that because the body differs according to the distinctions of stages such as childhood and youth, the universal (jāti) residing in that body—such as "Devadatta-ness" (ḍitthatva)—is itself the referent of words like "you" (tvad), that is not so, because there is a lack of evidence. Furthermore, if this were the case, it would lead to the impossibility of a name (saṃjñā) being applied to a single substance, which will be demonstrated later. [The phrase] "residing in those respective words" [is used]; for this very reason, expressions such as "the word is masculine" are logically justified.

"And that [gender] is also denoted by it" means that gender (*liṅga*) is also denoted by the nominal stem (*pratipadika*). The meaning is that, just as that which is the object of the apprehension of word-potency—whether as the delimitor of the substratum (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), as co-located with the delimitor of the substratum, or as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—is the object of cognition, so too is gender. For this very reason, there is the experienced cognition: "a jar qualified by masculinity."

Nor is this the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), because according to the maxim "the meaning of the base and the suffix," that [suffix] would result in being the predominant factor. Furthermore, gender is understood even from words such as *vāk* and others, even without a suffix. For this very reason, in the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 1.1.43), the phrase *puṃsi* means "when the base is a word in the masculine gender. Similarly, in the rule *striyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.3), the meaning is "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) occurring therein [in the feminine]. [The same applies to] *prātipadikārtha* (Pāṇini 2.3.46).

In the sūtra [Pāṇini 2.3.46], the word *liṅga* also carries the meaning "occurring therein. However, if the nominative case (*prathamā*) itself were to signify gender (*liṅga*), then in examples such as *ghaṭena*, there would be no possibility of that cognition [of gender] arising. Now, one might object: although worldly masculinity (*puṃstva*) and so forth—defined by characteristics such as "one who possesses breasts and hair is a woman; one who is hairy is remembered as a man," and "that which is the absence of both is the neuter"—are possible in the case of sentient beings, they are contradicted in the case of insentient objects. Consequently, there would be no occurrence of suffixes such as *ṭāp* in words like *ghaṭa*.

Furthermore, in cases such as *dārāḥ* (wife/wives), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would not occur because the referent lacks masculinity; therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya states the gender by saying "satva... and so forth. The state of equilibrium (*sāmyāvasthā*) consists in the existence of the qualities (*guṇa*)—namely the primary qualities (*prākṛta*)—in a state of balance. For this very reason, even when there is the presence of increase (*utkarṣa*) or decrease (*apakarṣa*), when one intends to express merely the persistence in a state of equilibrium, it is neuter. This is the meaning of the maxim "the neuter is used in the sense of generality" (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*). Since these three states exist in every category of object (*padārtha*), this [neuter gender] is a purely positive concomitant (*kevalānvayi*).

This is because the conventional designations "this is an individual," "this is a thing," or "this is an object" are everywhere unobstructed and extensively prevalent. —02-0-2— "That very [form]" means precisely that which consists of the nature of femininity, masculinity, and so forth. (L. mama) [This is my [view]. The meaning is: in the form of femininity, masculinity, etc. itself.

[Objection: But surely, according to the reasoning already stated, since there is a difference of words due to the difference of genders within a single word, how can there be the conventional usage of a single word such as *taṭa* having multiple genders? To this, he says: "Of some... and so on. The phrase "due to gender" means that for words such as *taṭa* and the like, [the gender is inherent]. And the phrase "if this were so" means: if gender were resident in the word itself. For if gender were resident in the object (*artha*), then because the object would be qualified by femininity and so forth, the word for the referent—such as *padārtha*—would undergo grammatical operations conditioned by those respective genders; this is the intended meaning.

"—it is established. (In the manuscript L, the portion from "copa" to "bhavaḥ" is not seen. Otherwise, because a single entity would possess only one form, the distinction of gender would be untenable. My point, however, is that the distinction of words is indeed real, due to differences such as pronunciation and so forth. —"By way of determining the object"—this is to be understood through the relation of being denotable by its own substratum.

"—The word *paśu* does not denote a female" means that, by the force of the rules on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*), it possesses masculinity; this is the implied sense. "—It might be suspected of being common [to both genders]" means that, just as words such as *vyakti* (individual) and so forth include jars and other objects qualified by masculinity, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the word *paśu* would also include goats and the like. "—Due to a lack of evidence" means that since gender is based on worldly convention (*laukikatva*), the rules on gender have been rejected [as authoritative]; therefore, what was stated previously is not a valid proof for that.

He states another reason for its lack of authority, namely the contradiction with Śruti: "As [one follows] a thief who has entered a cave like a beast" (*Paśvā na tāyu guhā catantam*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 9.12.65). And because of the observation [of the word *nārī* as feminine]. The sense is that it is not due to non-existence or non-observation, but rather because of the observation of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) by means of this [word]. Since the [form] can be explained away as being Vedic (*chāndasa*), he says: "In Mīmāṃsā. [The phrase] "because it is intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣitatvāt*)—and this reason is consistent only with the state of having both genders (*ubhayaliṅgatva*), but not with permanent masculinity; such is the sense.

He states [the following] independently: "—2In reality, however—2. To establish the Vedic usage, he says: "—2Even in the Vedabhāṣya—2. The meaning is that if [the word] were to possess all genders, then stating it in this way would be purposeless.

But surely, since the word *padārtha* is eternally masculine, it would follow that it applies to a she-goat; therefore, he says: "But in the present case... The word *tu* indicates a distinction. [This refers to the rule: "Or rather, a goat [is to be sacrificed], because of the wording of the mantra," etc. (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.8.31).

Regarding the rule *agnīṣomīyaṃ paśumālabheta* ("One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma") [Mīmāṃsāsūtra 6.8.30], the meaning of the sūtra is that just as in the mantra *chāgasya vapāyā medasaḥ* ("of the goat's omentum and fat"), the mention of "goat" (*chāga*) qualified by the masculine gender excludes other animals, so too it excludes other genders. In reality, however, gender (*liṅga*) is grounded in the object itself. Thus says the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ekārthe* (Pāṇini 4.1.3): "In the case of a single referent... [Mahābhāṣya, Vol. II, p. ...].

296) "Because of the difference in words, a difference in gender is observed, and because of the difference in phonemes. Kaiyaṭa explains that the meaning is as follows: from the observation of a plurality of words—such as *puṣyaḥ*, *tārakā*, and *nakṣatram*—it is seen that gender is based on the object (*arthaniṣṭha*). Furthermore, in cases such as *kuṭī* and *kuṭīra*, even when there is the addition (*upajana*) of the phoneme *r* (or, according to another reading, its removal), a difference in gender is observed. For this very reason, it was stated in the introductory portion of the Mahābhāṣya on the sūtra *striyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.3).

294 (Dvikha): It has been stated that the contraction (*saṃstyāna*) and expansion (*prasava*) of color, taste, smell, touch, and sound constitute the gender-mark (*liṅga*). For color and the other qualities do not reside in sound. However, the expression "the word is masculine" should be understood either through the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the denoted object and the denoting word, or because it ends in the suffix *ac* (forming a noun from a verbal root).

Now, if the indicator (*liṅga*) were grounded in the object, then since the Self (*ātman*) is not an indicator, the conventional usage "the Self is Brahman"—which implies a distinction characterized by being an indicator—would be untenable. If it is argued that there is no fault because, when the indicator is grounded in the word, the Self is not an indicator [of itself], we say: no.

Since the Self is superimposed upon itself, the indicator belonging to the scripture exists there [in the Self] through a mediated succession; thus, the conventional usage "the Self is Brahman" and so forth is established.

Nor does it follow that a single word cannot possess two or three genders on the grounds that contradictory properties such as accumulation (*upacaya*) and so forth cannot coexist in a single object; for if these properties were inherent in the word itself, one might argue that there is no fault because the word would differ according to those contradictory attributes. However, this must not be said, because—by the authority of lexicons, the usage of learned elders (*āpta*), and other sources—the contradiction simply does not exist. In that case, a certain word is capable of denoting an object qualified by only one gender.

Whether [the suffixes apply] to a single meaning qualified by two genders or qualified by three genders is to be determined from the rules on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) and other sources. The phrase "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) occurring in the feminine" means "from a nominal stem occurring in a meaning qualified by femininity. By this, the view that one superimposes the gender residing in the meaning onto the nominal stem and thus employs expressions such as "from a nominal stem occurring in the feminine" is refuted.

Thus, by the word *madhu* (honey), only nectar and the like are expressed when characterized by both the masculine and neuter genders; however, when characterized by the masculine gender alone, it may also refer to the month of Caitra and so forth—this too is to be determined from that very source. Regarding these technical genders (*liṅga*), there is a technical convention (*saṃketa*) similar to [the rules for] vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) and the like. As it is said: "One must certainly accept some established doctrine (*svakṛtānta*)," as stated in the Mahābhāṣya on the rule *striyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.3).

"Therefore, it is not possible for grammarians to rely upon worldly *liṅ* endings; some established doctrine (*svakṛtānta*) must necessarily be accepted. This is the Bhāṣya. Now, one might object: "By the principle of the artificial versus the non-artificial (*kṛtrimākṛtrimanyāya*), only that which is technical (*śāstrīya*) should be understood in the rules (*pradeśa*). If this is argued, we say no.

The designation *liṅghu* (masculine, etc. is joined with the technical term *saṃjñā*; because the technical terms for "heavy" (*guru*) and so forth are applied starting from the masculine, and because even worldly gender (*laukika-liṅga*) is accepted as a causal factor when the application of grammatical rules (*natvādi-śāstra*) occurs; furthermore, while the conventions of "masculine" and so forth proceed in order to include other meanings within the technical term for number (*saṃkhyā-saṃjñā*), they do not proceed for the purpose of excluding other meanings. In that regard, when it is impossible in the worldly sense, the operation must take place according to the technical sense alone.

But when that [gender] is possible, [the gender] resides in the worldly [object] as qualified by the scriptural [context], through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and not in the [gender] alone; for in cases such as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the worldly masculinity is not intended to be expressed by the suffix and so forth, because the gender is grounded in the object itself. Thus, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that there is no sacrifice by a woman.

Nor should it be argued that this is inconsistent because the *liṅgānuśāsana* (treatise on gender) states "there is no [word] ending in *u* for females," and because the *uktānuśāsana* (treatise on suffixes) indicates that words ending in *u* possess only masculinity, and thus [the word *apasu*] is intended to have permanent masculinity; for such an argument would result in the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the term would become common to all genders, just like the word *padārtha*.

From the observation in the *Ṛgveda* (ṚV 1.162.3) that "the life of cattle, the guidance of cattle, for cattle, for men," it is determined that the word *paśu* does not necessarily denote a male. Furthermore, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has rendered the aforementioned rules on gender unnecessary by showing that gender is merely worldly (*laukika*) and so forth. [As stated in the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*: "The goat [is the victim], because of the wording of the mantra," etc. (MīmS 6.8.31)].

(Sūtra 31: Furthermore, according to the principle of the final section of the sixth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras], just as in the case of selecting a specific animal in the form of a goat, there is a presence of evidence for grasping the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the mantra-text regarding the worldly masculinity [of the sacrificer]; for in the mantra "of the goat's omentum" (*chāgasya vapāyāḥ*), the form "of the goat" (*chāgasya*) cannot apply to an animal other than a goat, nor can it apply to a female. This is because the word "goat" (*chāga*), ending in a vowel, has its conventional denotative power (*śakti*) restricted to that which is characterized by both worldly masculinity and technical (*pāribhāṣika*) masculinity.

Just as in the case of the injunction "There are two rams for Sarasvatī," where—by the rule that the base of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) [indicates] "that which belongs to the deity"—the mention of two is established through *ekaśeṣa* based on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "that indeed is a divine pair," so too is it here. Furthermore, if gender were inherent in the word itself, then its connection with the meaning would involve a cumbersome relationship consisting of the aforementioned indirect succession; moreover, this would result in a lack of natural consistency in rules such as Pāṇini’s *puṃyogād ākhyāyām* (4.1.48).

Since the meaning of the word *napuṃsaka* is already established in common worldly usage (*laukika*), it is appropriate to accept that same meaning for the technical term (*śāstrīya*) as well, in order to maintain consistency between them. Furthermore, this is because it would contradict the commentary on the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23), which states that there is no such thing as a word called *napuṃsaka*.
If it is asked: "In that case, how can there be a non-differentiated usage of the expression 'from a neuter nominal stem' (*napuṃsakāt prātipadikāt*)?"—the answer is: No.

It should be understood that because [the word] expresses a neuter meaning, and because the word itself is not distinct from that [meaning], it is neuter. Some say: "These three genders exist as inherent classes (*jāti*) in certain things, which are not contradicted by contradictory classes such as those of the cow, the buffalo, and so forth" (*Vākyapadīya* III. liṅgasaṃgrahakārikā 4). They thus claim that masculinity and the other two are three classes. The exposition and refutation of that [view] should be determined from the *Mañjūṣā*. That refers to gender and so forth. According to the maxim "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise," he says: "from that alone"—that is, from the suffixes themselves.

[Objection: Surely, for grammarians, understanding will arise from the recollection of the elided case-ending; therefore, he says: "for one who does not know the suffix," and "because it is observed [otherwise]."

Nor should it be argued that there is the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating the expressive power (*śakti*) for an infinite number of bases (*prakṛti*); for such complexity is not a defect when it pertains to the result (*phalamukha*). Furthermore, we observe that even from a base alone, a meaning such as number is understood by one who has already grasped the power of that suffix to denote number. As for the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would follow if the meaning were expressed by the base, it should be avoided by following linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) and through the force of intention (*tātparya*). "In these views" refers to the views concerning [the denotation of] three and so forth.

He states the meaning of the phrase "for this very reason" as follows: "of the suffix alone. Regarding the object that is merely number, he says: "it is either indicative (*dyotikā*) or expressive (*vācikā*)" (Pāṇini-vārttika II. 1.64). Alternatively, the second half [of the verse] means that the aggregate [of the base and suffix] is the denoter of the object possessing number. This is the meaning: mere number is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

"The fourfold group ending with the *kāraka* is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The truth of the matter here is this: although all these positions are clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the *Anabhihita* sūtra (Pāṇini 2.3.1) and elsewhere, nevertheless, the view that "the fivefold group is the meaning of the nominal stem" is superior. This is because all [five] are experienced as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Nor should it be argued that if all five were the meaning of the nominal stem, the causal relationship—wherein the presence of a case-ending (*sup*) is the cause for a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the nominal stem—would be undermined. [This is not so,] because...

This is because such an undesirable consequence is accepted. Since it is only a substance (*dravya*) qualified by genus (*jāti*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and the capacity for grammatical relations (*kārakaśakti*) that is understood, a cognition in which the meaning of a case-ending (*subartha*) is the qualifier is as non-existent as a sky-flower; therefore, enough of this.

Having stated the fivefold meaning of the nominal stem (*parātipadika*), he states that the word (*śabda*) also has that as its meaning: "The word, first of all... (the *iti* is not present). "'Because of the accompaniment by the word' (*śabdānugamāt*)" means because it has the word as its object. "'Interwoven' (*anuviddham*)"—the construction is: every cognition appears as if interwoven with the word. By the use of the verb "appears" (*bhāsate*) in the latter half [of the verse], it is indicated that since the word appears in the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), the word appears in every cognition that consists of a primary apprehension (*vyavasāya*).

"—*viṣṇumuccāraya*—2" and so forth. Likewise, in the case of "utter the word *go*," according to the aforementioned method, the meaning is simply "utter the word *go*. {Therefore, even in the case of a word} there is indeed activity [of the speaker], as is clear elsewhere. —"*That too is the meaning of the nominal stem*"—2. This is the intended sense: according to the view that there is identity (*tādātmya*) between the word and its object, since one does not perceive an absolute distinction between the word and its object because words such as "pot" are applied to the object just as they are applied to the word itself. For this very reason: "The single-syllabled *om* is Brahman," and "The two-syllabled name *Rāma* is the breaker of the pride of the wielder of the Pināka bow."

In such instances as "The breaking of Bhārgava’s pride and the breaking of Vālin’s valor, followed by their slaughter in a most fierce battle—alas, alas! Their destruction! there is a cognition of the meaning through the medium of the word. For this very reason, the three—the word "jar," the object "jar," and the cognition "jar"—possess a single form. However, in the view that the word and its meaning are distinct, there is no fault, because on the strength of experience it is postulated that the very causal complex for general cognition possesses the capacity to manifest the word.

As for the claim that after the cognition of the object, the word—recalled by way of its having a single relation with that object—appears in the cognition [of the object], and for this very reason they say, "Only when the individual object has been seen is it capable of causing the name to be remembered," that is not correct; because the appearance of the word in perception is untenable. For it is impossible for that [word] recalled after the cognition of the object to appear in the *vyavasāya* (the primary perceptual judgment). However, according to your own view, its appearance in the *anuvyavasāya* (the subsequent reflective awareness) might be established, but not in the *vyavasāya*.

However, according to the method stated by me, the manifestation of the word (*śabdabhāna*) is possible in both of these two positions. And that word, in rules such as *agner ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33), is understood as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) because of the sublation of the grammatical operation (*kāryabādha*) regarding the meaning in the technical treatise (*śāstra*).

Indeed, a word that lacks the capacity for denotation cannot be made to possess it—even by a hundred arguments—as is seen in the case of words such as "Rāma. In expressions such as "Rāma was" or "Duṣyanta was," the understanding produced is not that the referent of the word "Rāma" possessed the word "Rāma" through the relation of denotability; rather, it is of the form: "the one denoted by the word 'Rāma' existed. For this very reason, in cases such as "This very person is Devadatta," the meaning is: "This very person is the one denoted by the word 'Devadatta'."

For this very reason, even when Devadatta—the denoter of the cognition—is in contact with the eye, there occurs the conventional usage: "Devadatta is not known," and so forth. Furthermore, if [the word] were not the denotable, then the logical school's (Tārkika) doctrine—that "denotability" (or "denotative capacity") is a property of absolute positive concomitance (*kevalānvayin*)—would be inconsistent; such is the direction of the argument. [The phrase] "because it is not distinct from capacity" means that there is no evidence for its being distinct from capacity. [The phrase] "by the non-apprehension of capacity" means by the non-apprehension of a capacity distinct from the word. [The phrase] "because of its lack of utility" means...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of verbal comprehension even from a word that is semantically potent (*śakta*) but whose function is not known—this is because of the absence of semantic potency (*śaktyabhāva*). The meaning is that although imitation words (*anukaraṇa*) are grammatically correct (*sādhūni*), since they lack semantic potency, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not possible. (1) (25)

"—The word also"—(Vai.Si.Kā. 26)—means that the word which is to be imitated (*anukārya*) is also [included]. Likewise, he states the meaning of the word: "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). He states the established referent: "presented (*upasthita*). "There is a difference between the object to be imitated and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*). And the proof of their difference is seen in cases such as "paṭaditi kuru," where there is a distinction based on being composed of sounds (*dhvani*) versus being composed of phonemes (*varṇa*), and in cases such as "bhuvo vuk" (Pāṇini 6.4.88), where the suffix *su* and others are produced. For this very reason, [it is stated] "in the sense of matup, the suffix cha... (Pāṇini 5.2.95).

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *Pāṇini 5.2.59*, regarding the rule "The suffix *cha* is used after [words] denoting hymns (*sūkta*) and chants (*sāman*) when the sense is 'pertaining to' (*mataḥ*)," it is stated: "That word *asyavāma* which is recited in the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*), for that very reason—namely, because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—the suffix *cha* is established in the sense of the word *asyavāmīya* and others, which is the meaning of the base of this suffix.

Now, one might object: "But even in the view that there is non-difference (*abheda*), the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between a thing and itself is impossible. To this, he says: "In the case of non-difference... [and] "in the case of perception, with respect to the object... [implying that such a relationship is possible where there is difference].

The point is this: just as in the case of visual perception (*cākṣuṣapratyakṣa*) in the form "this is a jar," where the object is the cause by way of the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), such that the causal relationship is established through a cognition residing in the object; likewise, in the case of auditory perception (*śrāvaṇapratyakṣa*), the object in the form of sound is the cause by way of identity, [the effect] being [the perception] through the relation of being its object (*viṣayatā*).

And likewise, since the presentation (upasthiti) of a word—which consists of auditory perception—is produced by that word, and since such a presentation is a cause of verbal cognition (śābdabuddhi), it follows that the word has that [presentation] as its object. This is the justification. Thus, the point is that in both ways, the word is the object of verbal cognition.

"—In order to prevent over-extension" means: in order to prevent the cognition of *ākāśa* (ether), which is presented [to the mind] from the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). "—Because it possesses occurrence as its substratum" means: because sound has its locus in that [ether] through that very relation; such is the sense. (Note: The portion of the manuscript from 'sambandhena' to 'tatsaṃbandhena' is not observed.)

"—2 *nirūpakatā*—2 || —2 *tathā ca* etc.—2 || Since the object (*artha*) is the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of the function residing in the word, the sense is that the object possesses the function through this relation, while the word possesses it by being its substratum (*āśrayatā*). Because of the complexity [of this view], he says: —2 'of the relation'—2; and 'of itself'—2. The sense is that there is comprehension because the word is remembered through the cognition of the object, according to the principle of being a single related term (*ekasaṃbandhī*). In reality, however, this is incorrect, as was stated previously. —0 *grāhyatvam*—2 (Vākyapadīya I.1.75)."

55) *Grāhyatva* (the state of being apprehended) is the state of being the object of apprehension (*grahaviṣayatva*). *Grāhakatva* (the state of being an apprehender) is the state of being the producer of apprehension (*grahajanakatva*). The sense is that just as a lamp, while illuminating objects such as a jar, also illuminates itself, so too does the word. [Regarding the phrase] "disregarding the state of being an object": thus, by including the objective state (*viṣayatā*) such as the state of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) within it, from the word there arises a cognition in the form: "The jar is that which possesses a qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a qualifier-ness residing in jar-ness (*ghaṭatvaniṣṭhaprakāratānirūpitaviśeṣyatāvān ghaṭaḥ*)," and so forth.

—02— Because the word *ghaṭa* (pot) has its expressive power (*śakti*) restricted to that which is delimited by the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatva*) as determined by the modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in potness (*ghaṭatva*), etc.; for the apprehension of that power (*śaktigraha*) occurs precisely in that manner. For this very reason, in the view of those who maintain that the primary meaning is not abandoned (*ajahatsvārthavṛtti*), the *Mahābhāṣya* employs the term "non-abandonment of one's own meaning" (*jahatsvārthatva*) with respect to compounds such as *rājapuruṣa*, because in such a compound, there is merely the relinquishment of the qualificandhood residing in the king (*rājan*) as it would appear in a sentence (*vākyīya*). Therefore, even a cognitive object (*viṣayatā*) is a word-meaning (*padārtha*) by virtue of the word’s expressive power. However, some say that this verse merely elucidates the cognitive object residing in the word itself.

Others, however, maintain that in cases of non-difference, imitation (*anukaraṇa*) brings about the object of imitation (*anukārya*) through similarity; and although it is thus presented, its connection with the word of imitation occurs by way of being either the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) or the sub-correlate (*anuyogitva*) in verbal cognition. Furthermore, due to the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), the fact of being produced from imitation (*anukaraṇajanyatva*)—rather than the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛttijñāna*)—is the defining property (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the status of being a verbal cognition (*śābdatva*).

For this very reason, there is no production of case-endings (*vibhakti*) in expressions such as *bhūsattāyām* ("in the existence of the root *bhū*"), because they lack meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) in the form of being denotative through a function (*vṛtti*). This is because such meaningfulness is restricted [to those that possess a specific function]. For this same reason, Kaiyaṭa stated in the commentary on the rule *maitau cha* (Pāṇini 5.2.59): "They say that an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), even when uttered in reverse order, becomes a communicator of the original (*anukārya*) by virtue of its similarity to it. (2) (26)

"—Because of the absence of meaningfulness (arthavatvābhāvāt)"—the meaning is: because of the absence of being a producer of the cognition of meaning through its function (*vṛtti*). The point is that, since the *arthavat* rule (Pāṇini 1.2.45) refers only to such meaningfulness, there is an absence of the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*). "—Otherwise"—means: if one does not accept the intention of non-difference (*abhedavivakṣā*). "—Because of the transgression of a prohibition"—means: because of the transgression of the prohibition which results from the restrictive rule that "an affix must necessarily follow [something]."

"—the consequence of ungrammaticality. This means that under the view of difference (*bhedapakṣa*), because [the word] possesses the aforementioned meaning and thus falls within the scope of the defining condition (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) for the rule prescribing the technical designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*), there arises the consequence of ungrammaticality due to the failure to apply that [designation]. (V1,2. *aprayuktā*) However, under the view of non-difference (*abhedapakṣa*), since it lacks the aforementioned meaning, it does not fall within the scope of that defining condition; consequently, because the designation is not obtained, there is no ungrammaticality. (P.V1,2. Regarding this:)

In this regard, however, it is not observed that the doctrine of non-difference (*abheda*) is universal; rather, the doctrine of difference (*bheda*) alone is universal, while the doctrine of non-difference occurs only in certain instances, such as in the case of the root *bhū* meaning "existence" (*sattā*). Or rather, even there, the doctrine of difference alone prevails. The non-arising of the manifestation [of the object] follows from the specific instruction that *bhū* means "existence" and so forth. Consequently, since the representation of the original (*anukārya*) is achieved through power (*śakti*) itself, one need not accept the representation of the form of the original based on similarity (*sādṛśya*). Furthermore, the nature of imitation (*anukaraṇatva*) consists in being the object of an utterance whose primary intention (*tātparya*) is directed toward the sound-form alone.

In the case of the co-occurrence [of the term] *padārthaviparyāsakṛt* (or *viparyāsi*), as in the example from the commentary on Sūtra 1.1.44 (*na vā*)—"he says 'cow' (*gaur iti*)"—there is no status of being an imitation (*anukaraṇa*). This is because, by virtue of functioning as a qualifier, it possesses a meaning and lacks the intentionality of referring to the mere sound-form alone. Rather, it is simply a restatement (*anuvāda*).

For this very reason, when one person, intending to say "Bring the cow," says "gaurānaya," and the other, not having heard it correctly, asks the first person, "What did he say?", and the first person replies, "He said 'gauḥ'," the listener proceeds to act precisely because of the understanding of the meaning derived from that [reproduction]. As for the claim that the understanding arises from the reproduced word (*anukārya-śabda*) as remembered by the listener, that is not tenable; for the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that only a word that has been uttered possesses the capacity to convey meaning. Furthermore, the evidence (*māna*) for the fact that the particle *kvi* sometimes indicates the nature of being a reproduction is found in the rule: "And a reproduction [is treated as its original], except when followed by *iti*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.62).

(1-4-62) is the very sūtra itself. Thus, in the case of an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), the meaning does not appear either as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as a qualificand (*viśeṣya*). In the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), however, the meaning certainly appears as a qualifier; this is the distinction between the two. As for the meanings of the nominal stems beginning with *sarva*, they should be determined from the *Mañjūṣā* (specifically the *Laghumañjūṣā*, in the section on the investigation of the meaning of nominal stems, pp. 1154–1155). They are not written here for fear of prolixity and because they do not assist the present work. (27) — *Śivam* — thus ends the *Laghubhūṣaṇakānti*.
— The Determination of the Meaning of Names—
Śrī—
The Determination of the Meaning of Compounds.

When the general meaning of "name" (*nāman*) has been explained—[as noted in the variant reading] "a contraction"—I shall now explain the specific meaning of names in the form of compounds (*samāsa*), which is the meaning of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). To that end, I first state the division [of compounds], beginning with the rule: "A case-ending [ending in a *sup* suffix] [is compounded] with a word ending in a *sup* suffix" (Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudī 28).

"—The compound (*samāsa*) is of six kinds"—thus [it is said]. Furthermore, "the state of being a compound" (*samāsatva*) is, according to one view, the possession of the status of a compound-word (*samāsapada*) through a specific conventional relation. Another [view] holds that it is the state of being a collection of nouns (*nāman*) with identical case-endings (*vibhakti*) where the preceding member is a noun; however, that is not correct, because it would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as *dadhi-madhuraṃ* ("sweet curd"), since there is no coordination of case-endings there. In that case—by means of the coordination of case-endings...

If it is argued that understanding arises through subsequent investigation (*anusandhāna*), this applies equally to compounds such as *rājapuruṣa* as well. Furthermore, the claim that understanding arises for one who does not recognize the elision (*lopa*) is the same in both cases. Moreover, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the composite expression *ivārtham* within the sentence *śruter ivārtham* (Pāṇini 1.4.96). Finally, there is over-extension to compounds consisting of verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) such as *paryabhūṣayat* and *pacatabhṛjjata*. This is the summary. Since the designation of "compound" (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) is established for the aggregate according to the maxim "the completion of a sentence occurs in the aggregate," the inclusion of the word *saha* ("together") for that purpose would be redundant.

On this point, some maintain that the reading of *nityādhikāre* (in the section on obligatory rules) is necessary for the sake of making the compound obligatory; others, however, do not accept this. For they argue that since compounds are not observed in cases such as *abhiprabharad-dhṛṣata*, Dīkṣita and others have accepted that the rule is optional by virtue of the *nityādhikāra*. Furthermore, even for the compound prescribed by the rule *saheti vibhakta-sūtra*, the division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) serves the purpose of achieving the desired result, and thus its obligatoriness is not required.

If it is argued that, because of the rule for compound formation beginning with *avyayam* (Pāṇini 2.1.6), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the optionality of *saha*—just like that of *sup*—should be understood from that very indication, we say no.

In the case of *anuvyacalat*, [the form] *vinā acalat* is not observed by this very rule (as it is not seen in the commentary on the sūtra). Nor should one suspect that because the mention of "nitya" (invariable) is rejected in the *Vārttika*, its prohibition is established even though [the rule] would otherwise be optional for the sake of obtaining the application; for although that rejection of the mention of "nitya" results in the rule being optional within the scope of the *yoga* "supā" (Pāṇini 2.1.4), such as in the case of *avāpyaśva*, there is no evidence for this being the case here. Furthermore, because a usage containing a *yaṇ*-substitution is non-existent [in this context]. Now, if it is argued: "If the compound formed by the word *saha* according to the aforementioned method were invariable (*nitya*), why is it not applied in cases such as *abhipramare*?"—if so, the answer is: No.

This is because the division of the *yogavibhāga* is intended for the sake of establishing the desired result; for in the Vedic language (*chandas*), the compound with *saha* is accepted only in cases where elision occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.68], *halṅyābbyo dīrghāt...* etc. Otherwise, if it were a compound with a verbal suffix ending in *a*, it would result in the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which would lead to the undesirable consequence of hearing a case-ending (*sup*) pronounced. By this, the objection that "if there were a compound in forms such as *prakurvīran*, the elision would not occur" is refuted; for in the Vedic language, since one follows what is observed, such a consequence is impossible. Therefore, the rule for *saha* is indeed obligatory; for this very reason, [the word] *sub* functions as its prescriptive element.

But if this were so, the reading of "udāttavati" and so forth within the section on *tatpuruṣa* compounds (as found in the Vārttika, though not seen here) would be redundant; therefore, that reading is for the purpose of assigning the technical name *tatpuruṣa*. For this very reason, in cases such as *punargavaḥ*, the suffix *ṭac* is established by the rule "avyaya-pravṛddhādibhiḥ" (*pravṛddhādīnāṃ ca*, Pāṇini 6.2.147).

But in this case, in examples such as *anuvyacalat*, there would result the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārthe* (Pāṇini 6.2.2). To explain: since *acalat* is accented on its first syllable, the condition *udāttavataḥ* (of that which possesses an acute accent) applies for the formation of a *tatpuruṣa* compound; however, because the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28), which causes the elision [of the accent] of the following finite verb, takes precedence, the elided accent of the *tiṅ* ending prevents the presence of a *tiṅ*-ending word possessing an acute accent immediately following it. Consequently, no *tatpuruṣa* compound is formed here. Rather, the compound is formed solely by the application of the rule *saheti yogena* (Pāṇini 2.1.4).

For this very reason, there is the constant hearing of the form containing the *yaṇ* [substitution]; and since that [form] is devoid of any specific technical designation (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*), it possesses only the accentuation of the final member of a compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*). Consequently, by way of distinction, in the word *acalat*, the compound is a *tatpuruṣa* formed by the rule "anorgatimātā tiṅntena" (Pāṇini 2.2.18), which applies the rule "gati-gatā" (Pāṇini 8.1.70) to render the preceding element unaccented (*anudātta*). In that case, the accentuation of the final member of the compound is not desired. (Regarding the rule "tatpuruṣe tulyārthe"...).

Because, according to the method stated, that [compound] lacks the designation of *tatpuruṣa*. Regarding the Vārttika on Pāṇini 6.2.147, since the word *ādi* in the previous Vārttika signifies "type" (*prakāra*), terms such as *udāttavat* and others are included as its specific instances. Alternatively, it should be understood that the author of the Vārttika, Kātyāyana, considering this very point already established to be difficult to grasp, initiated the statements beginning with *gatimatā* and so forth; this meaning is clear from the Bhāṣya (L.P. (1) (28) [Note: The division stated by the ancient grammarians is subject to the fault of being under-extensive (*avyāpti*).

If, however, compound (*samāsa*) is of two kinds—namely, that which is devoid of specific technical designations, such as *suptup* [Pāṇini 2.1.4], and that which is endowed with specific technical designations, such as that prescribed for *bahuvrīhi* [Pāṇini 2.2.23]—then it is the latter. This is fourfold, due to the division into *avyayībhāva*, *tatpuruṣa*, *bahuvrīhi*, and *dvandva*. Among these, the status of being an *avyayībhāva* and so forth belongs to the *avyayībhāva* and other compounds by virtue of their connection with specific technical designations; or rather, it is a specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*). It does not consist in being "predominantly the sense of the first member" (*pūrvapadārtha-pradhānatva*) and so on.

In cases such as *śākaprati*, the deviation [from the rule] is evident in the root text itself. However, there is no obstacle to accepting it as a general rule (*utsarga*). Regarding that, the first example is *bhūtapūrvaḥ* ("formerly been"), which is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā*. Here, *pūrvam* is an adverbial adjunct (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) signifying occurrence at a prior time; the meaning of the root *bhū* is either existence (*sattā*) or origination (*utpatti*). Thus, the cognition is: "that which is the locus of existence, etc., occurring at a prior time. Although the state of being prior is already expressed by the word *pūrva*, the suffix *-ta* (niṣṭhā) is used to indicate its pastness (*atītatva*), following the maxim "what is twice bound is more secure" (*dvirbaddham iti nyāya*).

Thus, [in cases such as] "vispaṣṭaṃ paṭuḥ" (clearly clever) and "vispaṣṭaṃ mṛduḥ" (clearly soft), the word *vispaṣṭam* is neuter because it functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatayā*) for the quality of clarity (*paṭutva*). The understanding is that it is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the quality of clarity, namely "one whose clarity is manifest. It should be understood that this principle may be inferred (*ūhya*) in other instances as well. Consequently, it is not appropriate to assume that the classification [of compounds] is merely conventional (*prāyikatva*), nor is it appropriate to maintain the definition stated [previously]. Here, [the compound] is one where the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is predominant.

(There is an additional reading: *śodhaphādvayam*) In examples such as *adhihari bhaktiḥ* ("devotion toward Hari"), there is a sequential understanding that "devotion has Hari as its locus" (*haryadhikaraṇikā bhaktiḥ*), and so forth. In this case, the particle *adhi* and others are denoters (*vācaka*) of the meaning of the locative case and so on. For this very reason, the general rule (*utsarga*) that "the meaning of the preceding word is the object of the gift" (*pūrvapadārthapradāna*) is maintained. If they were merely indicators (*dyotaka*), then since it will be stated later that the indicated meaning is necessarily a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the failure of that rule would be evident. By this, [the view that] in cases like *upakumbham* ("near the jar"), particles such as *upa* have a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "in proximity to that," and the word *upa* itself conveys the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

The view that [the suffix] is a *grahaka* (perceiver) is rejected; for, in cases such as *prajayati*, there would be a cognition where the expressed meaning is a qualifier, while in cases such as *upakumbham*, there would be a cognition where the expressed meaning is the qualificand. This results in the unwarranted complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating two distinct causal capacities for the expressed meaning.

"—2 It is that in which the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*) is predominant—2. For example: *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ* (one who has resorted to Kṛṣṇa), etc. (V1, 2. Examples). This is because the understanding arises in sequence as 'the agent of resorting whose object (*karman*) is Kṛṣṇa,' and so forth. However, in cases such as *mahatkaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ* (resorted to a great hardship), there is no compound formation due to a lack of semantic compatibility (*asāmarthya*); this and more is explained at length elsewhere. In the case of *māsajātaḥ* ('born after a month'), both in the compound and in its analytical explanation (*vigraha*), there is indeed predominance of the meaning of the final member, in accordance with the requirement that the meaning of the compound be conveyed by those two."

Nor should it be argued that even in the case of a *vigraha* (analytic expansion), the use of the genitive case is untenable because the word *jāta* functions as a qualifier, since [the rule for the genitive] is prescribed specifically for qualifiers. This is because, in accordance with the requirement that the *vṛtti* (compound) and its *vigraha* must have the same meaning, when one intends the *vigraha* to convey the meaning of the *vṛtti*, the reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship does not affect the persistence of the genitive suffix—a grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*)—which was already produced in the prior state of neutrality.

Objection: Let the analysis (*vigraha*) simply be "born of a month" (*māsasya jātaḥ*). In this case, the compound and its analysis would have the same meaning. Nor should it be argued that the rule "the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhī*, Pāṇini 2.2.8) is redundant; for by the restrictive rule that "time-measures are compounded only with the thing measured, and not the thing measured with the time-measure," that rule serves a purpose by excluding the formation of *jātamāsa*. Reply: This is not so—

This is because, according to the authority of the *Mahābhāṣya* (Pra-kha-pṛ. 420), which provides the analysis (*vigraha*) "of one born for a month" (*māso jātasya*), it is accepted that in a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) between a delimiter (*paricchedaka*) and a delimited (*paricchedya*), the genitive case occurs only when there is a delimitation (*pariccheda*). Consequently, such an analysis is impossible [in the case of *tantūnāṃ paṭaḥ*]. Similarly, in a co-utterance between a part (*avayava*) and a whole (*avayavin*), the genitive occurs only from the word denoting the part, based on the relation of being a part (*avayavatva*), as in "the cloth by means of the threads" (*tantunā paṭaḥ*). (Vārttika 1.2.64)

In expressions such as "of the threads" (*tantūnām*), however, the genitive case denotes the relationship of produced and producer (*janyajanakabhāva*). [The meaning is: "the cognition was born, delimited by a month. It should be understood that the state of being delimited for that which has been born is due to its being the locus of the production of that which is to be delimited.

When the relation of qualifier and qualified is reversed and included [within the compound], the *bahuvrīhi* has its denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward the relation of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), etc., as well as toward the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*) which serves as the locus of that relation—as in the case of "citragu" (one who possesses brindled cows). This is because there is a cognition of the referent of another word as being qualified by the brindled cows through the relation of ownership. Alternatively, it is the very meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), in the form of a relation, that is the denoted object (*śakya*) of the *bahuvrīhi*. Nor... [text fragment]

Objection: Since the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is of the nature of non-substance (*asatvarūpatā*), it must be said that in expressions such as *citraguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows"), the grammatical operations pertaining to gender and number would be untenable. Reply: This is not so, because this relation—like a quality expressed by a word—is dependent upon a substance; thus, its connection with the gender and number of that [substance] is accepted. And in this way, the compound does not denote a relation that is explicitly expressed; rather, it denotes the very identity (*tādātmya*) of the relata themselves.

In this regard, although a relation resides in two relata, because the other relatum—the form of the cow—is presented by the word itself as a qualifier and possesses primacy, it is established that the owner alone is the substratum; consequently, the gender and number belong only to him, and not to the meanings of the constituent members of the compound. Furthermore, since there is no relation between the relation and its relata distinct from their own essential natures, it should be understood that the relation culminates in identity with the relatum, owing to the very nature of the word’s expressive power (*śabda-śakti*).

Just as in the expression "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śukla*), there is no intention to express a distinction here; however, in the case of the sentence, the intention is indeed to express a distinction—this is another point. Furthermore, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is of two kinds, based on the distinction between "possessing that quality" (*tadguṇa*) and "not possessing that quality" (*atadguṇa*); this is explained in detail elsewhere.

"—it is one in which both members of the compound are primary. This is because, in an *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction) compound, the collective whole (*sahitya*) functions as a qualifier; and this collectivity is what is denoted by the power of the entire aggregate. As for the claim that it is indicated (*lakṣya*) by the final member alone—that must be refuted by the objections to be stated later, such as the consequence that the final member alone would incur the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Nor is it correct to say that it is indicated by the aggregate, for—as will be explained—it is perceived even without the recognition of any such logical inconsistency.

If there were no manifestation of *sāhitya* (concomitance) in an *itaretara-yoga-dvandva* (mutual conjunction compound), then—due to the absence of any delimitor (*avacchedaka*) suitable for the connection with duality (note: the three sentences beginning from "dvitvānvaya" have been omitted)—there would be no connection with duality. Therefore, the manifestation of *sāhitya*, which serves as the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*), is necessary. In a *samāhāra* (collective) compound, however, that [duality] is the qualifier (*viśeṣya*). For this very reason, he will state that there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) regarding the predominance of both word-meanings in a *samāhāra-dvandva*.

In reality, even in the case of *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction), as in the case of *samāhāra* (aggregation), the coexistence (*sāhitya*) is itself the substantive (*viśeṣya*). For this very reason, in the commentary on the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.29), having raised the objection that the *dvandva* compound prescribed for the sense of *ca* should likewise lack gender and number, the objection is refuted by the statement: "By the very nature of word-potency, like adjectives (*guṇavacana*), [the compound] takes its gender and number from the substratum (*āśrayataḥ*). (Mahābhāṣya, Prauḍhamanoramā edition, p. 463).

Furthermore, if in the case of *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction) the coexistence (*sāhitya*) denoted by *ca* were to function as a qualifier, then the doubt regarding its being devoid of gender and number, along with the subsequent refutation of that doubt, would result in an inconsistency. Nor should one suspect that this Bhāṣya refers to the *samāhāra* (collective) type of *dvandva*; for in that case, since the singular number and the specific gender are established by direct rule (*vācanika*), it would be impossible to maintain that [the compound] is intended to express that [coexistence]. Moreover, [the collective compound] lacks the capacity to adopt the gender and number residing in its substratum. For this very reason, [the author of the Bhāṣya states]: "The word *gauḥ* [is used] for the feminine... (Sūtra).

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *gostriyoḥ* (P. 1.2.48), regarding the example *kukkuṭamayūryau*, it is stated that one must state a prohibition for the case of a *dvandva* compound, having raised the objection that the short vowel [of *mayūrī*] would apply by virtue of that sūtra. Kaiyaṭa has explained that because the meaning of the constituent part—the referent of the word *mayūrī*—is subordinate (*aprādhānya*) within the collective sense (*samāhāra*) of the compound, and because it is designated first [in the *upadeśa*], it is an *upasarjana*. (This is also stated by Kaiyaṭa.)

However, if *samāhāra* (collective compound) were a distinct category [of *dvandva*], then because the meaning of the constituent members (*varti-padārtha*) would be primary, they would lack the status of being subordinate (*upasarjana*), which would result in an inconsistency with the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa. Furthermore, just as in a *bahuvrīhi* the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, here too it is appropriate that the meaning of the conjunction (*cārtha*) itself should be predominant. In that regard, in examples such as "dhava and khadira trees," where there is mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the aggregate has its constituent parts manifested as distinct.

The summarized meaning [of the rule] is as follows: In cases such as *pāṇipādam*, where there is a collective compound (*samāhāra*), the meaning of the compound is a collection in which the distinction between its constituent parts is not manifested. The manifestation of the distinction between constituent parts consists in the attribution of the number belonging to those parts; the opposite of that is the non-manifestation of the distinction between constituent parts. Consequently, in the former case (the dual), there are the dual and plural numbers, while in the latter case, there is only the singular. Furthermore, the section concerning "behaving as a single unit" (*ekavadbhāva*) serves precisely as the restrictive rule.

In both types of *dvandva* compounds, even the collective aggregate (*samūha*), which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), is not distinct from its constituent parts; for this is expressed by the very words themselves, as in "the *dhava* and *khadira* trees. However, when the aggregate is distinct from its parts—as in "a herd" (*yūtha*) or "a forest" (*vana*)—it is expressed by entirely different words, such as "king’s herd" (*rājayūtha*) or "forest of trees" (*vṛkṣavana*). By this, the distinction that in *itaretarayoga* the aggregate is non-distinct [from the parts] while in *samāhāra* it is distinct is refuted.

The designation "predominant in the meaning of both members" is logically justified precisely because there is no difference between the aggregate (*samūha*) and its constituents (*samūhin*). In expressions such as *pāṇipādaṃ vādayati* ("he plays with hands and feet"), the status of being the object of the act of playing is also established in reality because the aggregate is non-different from the hands and feet. However, in cases such as *pāṇipādam*, the aggregate does not appear [as a distinct entity], due to the requirement of connecting it with the status of being the object of playing. As for the dual number and so forth, the view that they do not occur because the section on "treatment as a singular" (*ekavadbhāva*) teaches their ungrammaticality is not tenable.

This is because there is no instruction anywhere that would indicate such a meaning; furthermore, since the section on "treatment as a single unit" (*ekavadbhāva*) serves as a restrictive rule, there is no rule that prescribes singularity [as the meaning of the dual]. If it is argued that the section itself functions as a prescriptive rule, then the same would undesirably apply to the maxim *saṃjñāparibhāṣā*. Moreover, the statement in the root-text—that there must be a manifestation of collective association (*sāhitya*) for the sake of the application of duality in a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga*)—is also incorrect. This is because, even when duality and so forth are connected to multiple properties that delimit the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*), there is no impairment of the requirements of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and semantic compatibility (*yogyatā*).

In some cases, although the number is pervaded by the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*), there is no evidence for assuming that [pervasion] everywhere. For me, however, this fault does not arise; because it is accepted that the relation of duality and so forth, which does not reside in each individual, resides in the aggregate (*samudāya*), and because it is admitted that the aggregate appears as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), duality and so forth appear in the aggregate alone. Even in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) in expressions such as *ghaṭau*, just as in a *dvandva* compound, the connection occurs with the aggregate itself as the qualificand. This is because the aggregate is the qualificand, etc. (P. 01-0).
Precisely because it is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), in cases such as "Agni-Soma," the status of the deity belongs to the aggregate as a whole, which is non-different from the collection.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that in expressions such as "Caitra and Maitra go," the verbal suffix must be held to denote a collective (*samūha*)—both for the purpose of the number assigned by the suffix being construed with that collective and for that collective to serve as the primary referent (*viśeṣya*). For if that were the case, then just as in the expression "the collection of Caitra and Maitra," one would expect the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in "Caitra and Maitra go" [yielding *caitrasya maitrasya ca gacchataḥ*]. This objection is invalid, because the genitive is not applicable here; its application is based on the cognition of a collection as something distinct from the individuals, which is not the case here. Since the collection is perceived as non-different from the individuals, the conditions for the genitive do not arise.

However, there is no compound in the case of *samuccaya* (conjunction) and *anvaya* (succession). In examples such as "Worship both Īśvara and the Guru," although the action is connected to the Guru who is accompanied by *ca* (and) and to Īśvara who is accompanied by [the same], there is no occurrence of the function (*vṛtti*) of multiple *subanta* words in the sense of *ca*, because Īśvara alone is connected to that which is delimited by a single property (*ekadharmāvacchinna*). This is because of the expression "delimited by a single property. In reality, even if the act of worship is divided [between the two], there is no fault.

In this case, after one [word] has been connected with the action alone, the other [word], accompanied by another, is subsequently connected through repetition (*āvṛtti*).
