In the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*), as in "Caitra and Maitra cook," there is always the use of the verb in the singular number only; for since only one [agent] is connected in isolation, and because there is the cognition of a mere aggregate whose internal distinctions have not yet emerged—even when accompanied by "and" (*ca*)—the use of the dual or plural numbers is inappropriate. Furthermore, in the case of subsequent mention (*anvācaya*), such as "Go beg for alms and bring the cow," there is no compound (*samāsa*).

In the expression *ca* (and), both the status of being incidental (*ānuṣaṅgikatva*) and the concomitance with the other [action] appear in relation to the bringing of the cow (*gavānayana*) which is co-uttered. Incidental status consists in being produced by the result that brings about another [action]. Thus, its being pervaded (*tadvyāpyatva*) follows as a consequence. Consequently, the cognition arises: "the bringing of the cow is incidental and accompanied by begging for alms. In this way, it is clearly evident that the meaning of *ca* does not reside in either of the two [actions individually]. Furthermore, there is no such usage as "cut the dhava and khadira trees—look! (or "see").

It should be understood that a *dvandva* compound is grammatically correct when there is a concomitance (*anvaya*) with the other [member] alone, as delimited by a single property (*ekadharmāvacchinna*) within the conjoined [members]. Having refuted the classification [of compounds] by failing to include examples such as ‘*bhūtapūrva*’ and others, he states that the definitions—such as "the predominance of the meaning of the first member" (*pūrvapadārthapradhānatva*) and so forth—are flawed due to under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*). He further points out the defect of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*) regarding those very definitions, stating: “And because of impossibility” (*asaṃbhavacca*). By suggesting that these definitions are impossible, he states the possibility of their expression; this is the reading [in the text], for it is only thus that the connection is coherent. [He explains: “Because of the state of having occurred previously” (*bhūtapūrvyāt*).

"Prior"—that is, during the stage of prior action before the formation [of the compound]; "having existed previously" (*bhūtapūrva*) means the state of having existed before; [the term] is derived from that. Thus, the meaning is that by taking the predominance of the prior member's meaning and so forth as they exist in the sentences that constitute the respective processes of compounding, those respective linguistic usages apply even to the compounds themselves. He states this very point: "not a definition of these," etc.—"these" refers to the predominance of the prior member's meaning and so forth; "not a definition of the compounds" means not a definition of those respective compounds.

In that regard, according to the view which accepts a specific power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) as the means of establishing a single meaning—following the method to be explained in the root text—the sense is that, by accepting that the function (*vṛtti*) is "abandoning its own meaning" (*jahatsvārthatva*), the individual words would be rendered meaningless, and thus the referent of the preceding word and so forth would not be established. "In the same way" means "like a line-drawn cow (*rekhāgavaya*) and the like. (21/2) (291/2)

—2 “The conclusion is thus”—2. This is clearly stated in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa* and other works. In reality, just as in the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*), so too in the theory of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), the doctrine of the operation of the derivative form (*vṛttivarttanavāda*) is possible under both views: that which abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārtha*) and that which does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārtha*). To explain: just as the sentence, the derivative form (*vṛtti*) is produced by the grammatical treatise for the purpose of denoting the meaning; indeed, even the expression of the meaning is brought about by the author of the treatise. And thus, regarding the rule "A *dvandva* compound occurs when there is the sense of *ca*" (Sūtra 2.2.29), [the word] *anekaṃ*... [is used].

The meaning is that multiple *subanta* (inflected nominal) words function in the sense of conjunction (*cārthe*), and those functioning in the sense of conjunction receive the technical designation of *dvandva*. Similarly, multiple *subanta* words function in the sense of another word (*anyapadārthe*), and those functioning therein receive the designation of *bahuvrīhi*; this is the meaning of the rule "anekamanyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24). The same applies elsewhere. Since there is no simultaneous prescription of multiple operations directed toward a single objective, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Therefore, because it has been stated that the operation [of conjunction] occurs in the sense of conjunction and so forth specifically within the constituent words themselves, the non-employment of the particle *ca* and the like is established; thus, that [non-employment] is not the result of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning).

But, one might object: according to this view, since the meaning (*artha*)—just like the word (*śabda*)—is dependent upon the treatise (*śāstra*) and is thus a product of the treatise, it would be impossible to know the meaning of words from common usage (*loka*). Consequently, it would be impossible to state the definition of *vṛtti* as "the state of being a collection of that which possesses *vṛtti*. If you ask, "What then is the definition of *vṛtti*?"—we say: no.

Because its definition was stated in the Bhāṣya itself in the passage beginning with "vṛtti is the expression of another's meaning" (*parārthābhidhānam vṛttiḥ*) [Mahābhāṣya, Prauḍhamanoramā-khaṇḍa, p. 328], according to the rule "the operation concerning words is dependent on their mutual capacity" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*, Pāṇini 2.1.1). And its meaning is as follows: when a word such as *rājan* (king), which has a subordinate meaning, expresses its meaning through another word—such as *puruṣa* (man)—which has a primary meaning, and that [subordinate] meaning is grasped as a qualifier of its own [primary] referent, that is *vṛtti*.

Alternatively, the meaning is that *vṛtti* is that operation wherein a person or other entity intended for the sake of another—that is, for the purpose of being given—is grasped as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of its own meaning by means of subordinate words such as "king. This is the underlying idea: in expressions such as *rājapuruṣaḥ*, the meaning of the king—which was not yet integrated (*anāskanna*) into the meaning of the word *puruṣa* during the stage of the sentence—is integrated by the word *rājan*; or the meaning of the person, which was not yet integrated into the word *rājan*, is integrated. That is to say, one's own meaning is presented as conjoined with those [other meanings].

By this much alone, the linguistic convention of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning) applies even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*. In such a compound, the principal word (*pradhānapada*) is indeed the entire complex (*samudāya*), while the constituent words (*ghaṭakapada*) are non-principal. In that context, the principal word conveys its own meaning either by subsuming the meanings of its parts, or the parts convey their own meanings by subsuming the meaning of that [principal]. And the primacy of the complex arises from its capacity to convey another referent (*anyapadārtha*) which is the principal element, though it is presented through the parts.

Even in a *dvandva* compound, there is a cognition of the "concomitance" (*sāhitya*)—which is presented by the collection of the principal words—as it encompasses the meanings of the individual members. Alternatively, through the two members encompassing their respective meanings, the concomitance—which takes the form of a collective whole (*samūha*) in both types of *dvandva*, namely *samāhāra* and *itararetara*—is the grammatical predicate (*viśeṣya*). In the first case, it is a collective whole in which the distinction between the members is unmanifest; in the latter, the distinction between the members is manifest. Thus, there is no failure to produce the dual number and so forth.

Now, one might object: this formulation regarding the denotation of another's meaning is improper, because by accepting that the function (*vṛtti*) is "abandoning its own meaning" (*jahatsvārtha*), there would be no such thing as a meaning belonging to another; furthermore, it would entail the loss of the eternality of the relationship between word and meaning. Moreover, if one accepts that the first member of a compound abandons its own meaning, it would follow that from expressions such as *rājapuruṣa* ("the king’s man"), only the "man" and so forth would be understood. To this we reply: no.

There is no fault even if one accepts the *jahatsvārtha* (renunciation of its own meaning) theory—by abandoning the mere status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) residing in the meaning of "king" and so forth, which constitutes the word’s own meaning and is opposed to the presentation [of that meaning] as a qualifier (*guṇabhūta*) of the principal referent. Alternatively, let there be a total abandonment of the word’s own meaning by the subordinate term; in the compound (*vṛtti*), the word "person" (*puruṣa*) alone, through its connection with the word "king," conveys the person who is related to the king.

Just as there is the conventional usage of "a basket of campaka flowers" (*campakapuṣpapuṭa*) and so forth, even though the campaka flowers themselves are not the basket, by virtue of being permeated by their fragrance—so too are such usages as "the meaning of the word *rāja* (king) is a qualifier of the person" and "the meaning of the preceding member [of a compound] is [the primary referent]. And in this view, *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning) consists in the two meanings conveyed by the two words becoming conveyed by a single word.

In the case of a non-worldly sentence (*alaukika-vākya*), however, that [superimposed meaning]—which, according to the method to be explained, is superimposed even when it is subordinate to the negation (*abhāva*)—is indeed one that does not abandon its own primary sense (*ajahatsvārthā*). This is based on the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samaratha* Sūtra (Pāṇini 2.1.1): "A beggar, having obtained a second alms-offering, does not discard the first; he proceeds only for the sake of accumulation. If it is objected: "In this view, since words such as 'king' convey their own meaning as delimited by its status as a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), how can there be an appearance [of that meaning] as a qualifier of another?"

By virtue of the power of the qualified denotation (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*), [the word] accepts a qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatā*) determined by another only when there exists a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) that has its own word-meaning as its locus. In that case, because there is no distinction, that qualifierhood resides only in the complete entity presented by the word "king" (*rāja*) and so forth. And thus, since even that which is the qualificandhood constituting its own word-meaning appears merely as a qualifier, there is no further connection of a qualifier to it.

For it is accepted that a word’s connection [with another] occurs only when it is presented as a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) by its own form (*svarūpataḥ*) and as possessing a qualification (*vaiśiṣṭyena*). In the sentence "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), however, there is a distinction: while the presentation produced by the words presents [the man] as a qualificand by its own form, it also appears as possessing a qualification; thus, the connection with the qualifier is established. Therefore, in the view that the compound functions as a single unit (*vṛttivarttanavāda*), it is proven that there is a state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) in both positions—both the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning one's own meaning) and the *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning one's own meaning).

By this, the statement in the *Mūla* (the *Kāśikā*)—that "in the *jahatsvārthā* [view], there is *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning), whereas in the *ajahatsvārthā* [view], it is merely the removal [of syntactic separation]"—is indeed to be questioned. This is because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*. For in that [work], after describing the specific distinction produced by *ekārthībhāva* as consisting in the absence of numerical distinctions and the absence of conjunction (*yoga*), it poses the following alternative: "Now, regarding this distinction produced by *ekārthībhāva*, is the denotation of meaning by words natural (*svābhāvika*), or is it based on formal rule (*vācanika*)? (Mahābhāṣya, Prauḍhamanoramā-khaṇḍa, p. 331). (L.P.)

Having established the position that [the compound] is inherent (*svābhāvikatva*), he then states the position based on the explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*) with the passage: "Now, as for those who maintain that there is a function (*vṛtti*), what do they say? Is the function the expression of another meaning (*parārthābhidhāna*)? Then it is asked: "Now, for those speaking thus, does the function consist in abandoning its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā*), or not abandoning its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*)? By this, it is understood that having introduced the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), two positions are presented within that very context. [This is discussed under] Pāṇini 2.1.48: *vāpyaśca* in the sense of a name (*saṃjñāyām*).

In the compound [formed by] *sup sup* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), the function (*vṛtti*) is one where the individual meanings are abandoned (*jahatsvārthā*), whereas in the compound [formed by] *sup sup* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), the function is one where the individual meanings are not abandoned (*ajahatsvārthā*). With this intention, both of these two functions were stated by the author of the Bhāṣya in the rule *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam* (Sūtra 1.1.19); therefore, there is no contradiction with that. Alternatively, it should be understood that its justification lies simply in the fact that the preceding member abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthatva*). Regarding the phrase "of the words": the meaning is "of the preceding and succeeding members. Regarding the phrase "by the power of the compound itself": [it means] by the expressive power of the compound alone.

The meaning is that, according to the view that "words are composed of parts," since it is established by the experience of all people that even children who do not know the power of the individual parts (*avayava-śakti*) or their respective secondary significations (*lakṣaṇā*) understand a word through the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*) alone, that [power of the whole] is necessary. Regarding the phrase "in words such as *vṛṣabha*": the meaning is "in those ending in suffixes that do not alter the original meaning" (*svārthika-pratyaya*). The intention is that only a sequence (*ānupūrvī*) qualified by the absence of being a constituent of any other sequence can serve as the delimiting factor for the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).

For this very reason, although the phonemes *ra* and *a*—which denote Agni and Nārāyaṇa respectively—are present in the words *rāma* and so forth, no cognition of those [deities] arises from the wholes [of the words]. In a sentence, however, the constituent words are indeed meaningful; for instance, regarding the meaning "a person related to a king," the word-potency (*pada-śakti*) is more parsimonious than the postulation of a potency for the wholes in expressions such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* or *puruṣo rājñaḥ*.

Having taken up the superimposed meaning within the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), each constituent—such as the case-ending and so forth—is treated as a word (*pada*) precisely through the superimposition of the meaning that existed prior to the compound formation (*vṛtti*). It is by means of this very superimposition that the application of rules such as *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *a*) occurs in cases like *supanthāḥ*. Otherwise—if the constituent parts, such as the words *rāja-* and so on, were to convey their own literal meanings [rather than the superimposed meaning]—[the grammatical operations would fail].

The meaning is that because [the base] is present as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), [the objection] does not arise. Since it is unavoidable (*durvāratvāt*) [to admit the presence of the base], the assumption of a distinct power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) for the whole is redundant. For nominal stems (*prātipadika*), meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) exists only through superimposition (*āropita*). The mere fact that a certain cognition arises from the power of the whole does not suffice to prove the meaninglessness (*anarthakatva*) of the constituent parts; for if that were so, since a certain cognition also arises from a sentence by means of its distinct power, one would consequently have to conclude that the constituents of the sentence are likewise meaningless.

Furthermore, for those who possess only the analytical investigation necessary for the application of the scriptures, it is impossible to speak of either the ignorance of that [meaning] or of a cognition arising solely from a specific collective power (*samudāyaśakti*). Moreover, this is because of the non-contradiction with the statement by Bhartṛhari: "The *jahatsvārthā* [type of compound] occurs only where the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) contradicts [the literal meaning]," which implies that the collective power exists only in cases where it is opposed to the meaning of the individual parts, as is the case with the *rathantara* and other such [names].

In that case, although the two words would be devoid of meaning through the superimposition (*āropa*) of the agency of crossing upon the chariot-maker, one should understand that the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) is nonetheless maintained. However, in compounds such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man), such a superimposition cannot be asserted, because there is no contradiction with the actual meaning. Furthermore, even under the theory of "abandoning one's own meaning" (*jahatsvārtha*), there is no purpose in abandoning the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) in cases like *rājapuruṣa*. Moreover, if [the compound were] "abandoning its own meaning," it would follow that only the person [in general] would be brought, which contradicts the *Bhāṣya*.

If both [alternatives] were equally purposeless, it would have to be stated by the author of the Bhāṣya that "the bringing of either one does not follow. And thus, in the Vṛtti, the passage beginning with *ānupūrvyantareṇa*—namely, "there is no purpose for the restriction"—is to be understood (*bodhya*). This is what was stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya. That Bhāṣya has been cited. He concludes what was stated by Śaṅkuka with the words *tathāca*. For those who maintain this view, the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is easily established; so it has been explained.

—2 Because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). —2 It must be stated that there is a threefold nature of the denoted meaning (vācya-traividhya). Although it is stated in the Bhāṣya that "the denoted meaning consists of difference (bheda), relation (saṃsarga), and capacity (sāmarthya)," nevertheless, the intention of the Bhāṣya regarding the definition of the denoted meaning in a compound (vṛtti) is that there is a threefold nature of the denoted meaning, namely: (1) presenting an object characterized by difference; (2) presenting an object characterized by relation; or (3) presenting an object characterized by both. This is the meaning of "there is a threefold nature of the denoted meaning. —2 Regarding its being the denoted meaning (asyā vācyatve). —2

The meaning is: "if difference (*bheda*) is not denotable" means if only the relation (*saṃsarga*) is denotable. [The example] "like 'the king is beautiful'"—the meaning is that, just as qualifiers such as "beautiful" are connected through coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the qualificand even though they do not enter into the primary denotation (*vṛtti*), so too there would be the consequence of connecting qualifiers such as Devadatta through the relation of difference, even though they do not enter into the primary denotation. "The contradiction" means that in the cognition of "not being the king's" regarding the aforementioned object of definition, the cognition of "being different from him" is contradictory. "This is the sense" means... [end of fragment].

Therefore, the distinction must be stated. However, in this view, the relation (*saṃsarga*) is what is to be inferred. [The author] says that in this very view, the relation itself is the denoted meaning: "by means of the connection with the king. In this view, the cognition is precisely "one who has a connection with the king"; the exclusion of those not belonging to the king, however, is to be inferred. In both positions, the inference of one or the other follows from their necessary concomitance (*samanaiyatyāt*).

He states the position that both [the individual and the relation] are denotable (*vācya*) with the words "vinigamanā... and so on. The term "asvāmike" means in the absence of an owner; "rājāsvāmike" means in the case where there is no king as owner. The phrase "prayogāpattiṃ ca" means that because of the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of Vyāsa and others, the relation cannot be an object of inference. Regarding the phrase "iti bodhaḥ": in reality, neither of these two is denotable, because we do not experience them as such in our cognition, and because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, it is impossible to establish that difference (*bheda*) and so forth are denotable in a *dvandva* compound.

Furthermore, if difference (*bheda*) and relation (*saṃsarga*) were to appear [in the cognition], then because they are defined by their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), it would necessarily follow that the preceding member of the compound must also be an object of cognition. Consequently, this method would result in a contradiction with the *Mahābhāṣya* (on *Pāṇini* 2.1.1), which aims to establish that the first member of a compound does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārtha*). For in that passage, beginning with "Is it difference or relation?", every possible alternative occurring in the discourse is explicitly indicated as its own [position].

In such cases as "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) and "the king’s horse" (*rājñaḥ aśvaḥ*), every [word] is applied accordingly, and even the owner (*svāmin*) is employed—as in "the king’s man and the wife’s [man]" (*rājñaḥ puruṣo bhāryāyāśca*). When "king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*) is said, the word "king" excludes other owners from the man, and the word "man" excludes other kings from the man. Thus, when both [words] are mutually not delimited [by other referents], if the word "king" abandons its own primary meaning (*svārtha*), then let it abandon it if it so desires—this is what has been stated. By this, the abandonment of one's own meaning (*jahatsvārthatva*) in the two theories of *vedasaṃsarga* (the connection of meanings) is clearly established. (L.P.: *labhyate* is not present).

If it is asked: "Since these two [words] are not denotative [of their own specific meanings], why is it that we do not have the expression *rājapuruṣo 'śvaḥ* (‘the king’s man is a horse’), just as we have *arājñaḥ paruṣo 'śvaḥ* (‘the man who is not a king’s is a horse’)? — the answer is no, because of the force of syntactic unity (*ekārthībhāva*). In the view known as *jahatsvārtha* (where the word abandons its own meaning), which consists in the relinquishing of the status of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) inherent in itself, it is impossible for something to function as a qualifier in another context if its capacity has not been grasped as such while it was already known as a qualifier in one context. This is just as, in the case of the sentence “The jar and the cloth are substances,” the word *dravya* (substance) in that sense does not apply when the phrase “the substance is the cloth” is used, because the word *dravya* there functions as a qualifier referring specifically to the jar.

Similarly, just as in the case of "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣe*) and "belonging to the wife" (*bhāryāyāśca*), [it is understood that] *rājapuruṣaḥ* belongs to the wife. By the force of that [connection], when the capacity [of the word] has been grasped through the qualification by a single qualifier, or when it is known as such, then, with respect to the non-qualifier (*aviśeṣya*), [there is a connection] through a relation belonging to the same class (*sajātīya*).

[The connection] is not seen in the form of [the primary meaning’s] abandonment, because the connection with another qualifier is not established—just as, for example, one does not say "the pot of substanceness" when the intended meaning is "the pot is a substance. In every respect, however, according to the view that the compound is *jahatsvārtha* (abandoning its own meaning) in the sense of abandoning the meaning of the prior member, due to the proximity of the word *rāja-* in the compound, the word *puruṣa-* itself [denotes] one who possesses a connection with the king, [and thus] one who possesses a connection with an owner other than the king.

The connection of "king" (*rājan*) with its own [internal] object is not seen; nor is that specific individual person (*puruṣa-vyakti*) brought to mind. Therefore, there is no connection of "king" with its own [internal] object because the referent of the word "king" is absent [in isolation]; nor is there a connection of the word "person" with its own owner. As it is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.1): [MaBh Pra-kha-pṛ. 330, Bhā-pa].

"Now, when it is said, 'Bring the king's man,' the king turns the man away from other masters; thus, [the phrase] 'The king turns the man away from other masters. Because of the intention to express a connection with those of the same class (*sajātīya*), the usage 'The king's man is the wife's'—which conveys a relationship such as being an object of the wife's affection toward one qualified by the relationship with the king—is indeed desired, just like the expression 'The king's man is handsome.'"

[Objection: But if the primary object (*pradhāna*) possesses a qualifier in this way, would it not follow that the linguistic usage "the function [of the word]" (*vṛtti*) is abolished? For, according to the stated method, because it is a qualifier of a qualified [entity], it lacks the status of being a qualifier of the primary object alone. [Reply: This is not so.

In that case, the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*)—which is itself determined by the mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in the beautiful person—is simply "humanity" (*puruṣatva*), because "the qualified is not distinct from the qualificand. It is with this intention—that the relation to the king is not [the delimitor]—that such linguistic usage occurs. Thus, in all cases of cognition having a qualified entity as its object, the status of being a delimitor of the qualificand-ness and so forth resides only in the property residing in the qualificand.

Objection: "In this view, since the meaning is already expressed by the word *puruṣa* alone, the employment of the word *rāja* (king) is redundant. Reply: This is not so; for while the word *puruṣa* has such a meaning, the word *rāja* serves to indicate its specific intended sense (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Furthermore, even though [the specific identity] is not established by other means of knowledge, that which is employed [in the compound] serves as the means for determining a particular individual, just as in the case of "The moon is the most excellent light" (*prakṛṣṭaprakāśaś candramāḥ*). In this view, the apprehension of the word-power (*śaktigraha*) takes the form: "The word *puruṣa* joined with the word *rāja* denotes a particular individual qualified as a person [belonging to the king]."

In this view, in examples such as *mahārāja*, one should understand that the substitution of *ā* in the first member (*mahat*) is based on its having been meaningful by way of its prior state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*).

(31/2) [301/2] Regarding the phrase "only of the theory of mutual expectancy" (*vyapekṣāvādasyaiva*): for those who maintain that theory, "mutual expectancy" (*vyapekṣā*), which consists of a reciprocal requirement (*parasparākāṅkṣā*), is what constitutes "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) in the rule "A grammatical operation concerning words is dependent upon capacity" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*, Pāṇini 2.1.1), and not "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*). As it is stated in the Mahābhāṣya (Pra. Khaṇḍa, p. 332): "Some say that capacity is mutual expectancy; that which has a mutually expected meaning is 'capable' (*samartha*)."

The intended meaning is as follows: in a sentence such as "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), where the king and the man are mutually expectant of one another, the case-ending following the word "king" (*rājādi*) expresses the relation (*sambandha*). This is also the case in a compound such as "king-man" (*rājapuruṣa*), where [the two members] are presented separately (*pṛthagupasthitayoḥ*).

When two [meanings] are presented—[and no distinct relation is perceived between them], as in the case of "the king is handsome" (*arāja sundara*) and so forth—their relation is not denotable by the whole (*samudāya-śakya*), nor is that presentation of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭopasthiti*) the restrictive factor; for the cognition of that [relation] occurs only after the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the two presented meanings has arisen. Furthermore, the apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) takes the form: "this [word] is expressive of the relation between these two presented meanings."

In expressions such as *vāpy-aśvaḥ* ("a pond-horse"), because the relation denoted by the locative case is part of the specific denotation (*viśiṣṭa-śakyatva*) [of the compound], the word *vāpī* does not function with respect to the meaning of the locative; therefore, it lacks the status of being a *pragṛhya*. For this very reason, the designation of the entire aggregate as a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) is established. (This is established. In this view, even when there is a complex formation (*vṛtti*), since the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) remains identical to that in the sentence, there is a cognition of the relation of difference. This is because, due to the distinction between words, there is a distinction in linguistic convention (*vyutpatti-bheda*); specifically, the respective conventions are postulated solely on the basis of expectancy.

For this very reason, there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending, because its meaning is understood from other sources alone. For this same reason, no specific number is apprehended here. Since the presence of a case-ending that contradicts what is observed in the sentence is also maintained in the compound (*vṛtti*), there is no conflict with the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) regarding the non-difference relation (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meanings of two nouns. For this very reason, in expressions such as "dadhi ha(dra-)ṣṭe" (curd, look!), there is a relation of non-difference. Even for one who does not know the elision of the case-ending, understanding arises through worldly convention (*lokavyutpatti*) based on the instruction provided by one who knows it.

However, in the absence of such an instruction (upadeśa), there is no fault, because the lack of that [instruction] implies a lack of knowledge regarding its derivation. Furthermore, since the meaning of the case-ending (vibhakti) must be construed with the very meaning conveyed by the base (prakṛti), in expressions such as "rājapuruṣaṃ paśya" ("see the king's man"), the cognition of the objecthood (karmatva) pertains to the qualified entity; this is also due to the requirement of the *parāṅgavadbhāva* rule. Even in compounds and the like, semantic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) alone constitutes the capacity for relation (*sāmarthya*). Otherwise, a discrepancy would arise—namely, that there is semantic expectancy in the *parāṅgavadbhāva* state while there is unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) in compounds and so forth—as is clear elsewhere.

Even in a *karmadhāraya* compound, the relation between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is established through mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). In avyayībhāva compounds such as ‘upakumbham’ and in tatpuruṣa compounds, there is mutual expectancy between the preceding and following members by accepting that particles (*nipāta*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). In cases such as ‘niṣkauśāmbi’, there is mutual expectancy either by accepting that prefixes like *nis-* signify meanings such as "having gone beyond" (*krānta*), or by applying the principle of the "part of a word" (*padaikadeśanyāya*). In instances such as ‘dvidaśāḥ’ and ‘saptaparṇa’, [there is mutual expectancy] between the sense of the case-ending (*sub-artha*) and the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

The same applies to the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Even in a *bahuvrīhi*, there is a mutual connection between the two word-meanings—such as "variegated" (*citra*) and "cow" (*go*)—which are already mutually related through their expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) with the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) expressed by the compound itself. Furthermore, the fact that the external referent is denoted by the entire compound follows from the authority of the grammatical rule: *anekam anyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.24). Similarly, in a *dvandva* compound, the collective sense (*sāhitya*) residing in the aggregate is established by the authority of the rule: *cārthe dvandvaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.29).

The distinction between manifested (*udbhūta*) and unmanifested (*anudbhūta*) [gender] accounts for the use of the singular, dual, and so forth; this position too belongs only to the proponents of the theory that the *vṛtti* (compound) arises from the *varttana* (the constituent words), as it is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya itself. It should be understood as belonging only to one who believes that the *vṛtti* is produced from the sentence (*vākya*) alone. [This is because it is] "contrary to the reasoned Bhāṣya"—meaning, because it is contrary to reason and contrary to the Bhāṣya.

This is the [proposed] state of affairs: because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to establish through specific rules (*vacana*) the properties of those [compounds] to be discussed hereafter—such as the non-comprehension of numerical distinctions, the absence of connection with qualifiers, and so forth—which are produced by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). For even when elision (*luk*) occurs in forms such as *dadhi*, the non-comprehension of a specific number persists, and thus elision cannot be the cause of that non-comprehension. Furthermore, in cases such as *dvau avitau*, the elision does not occur even though the [condition for it] is otherwise present.

Furthermore, in introducing a new rule in the form of the governing heading *vibhāṣā* for the sake of excluding even synonymous sentences, you alone incur the burden of complexity. Moreover, this contradicts the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *tasya bhāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.119), as is clear elsewhere. Furthermore, there is no evidence that the entire compound is the denotative power (*śakyatva*) when its constituent relationship is already required; rather, by the maxim *śiṣyamāṇaṃ lupyamānārthābhidhāyi* ("that which remains expresses the meaning of what has been elided"), it is more appropriate that the denotative power resides in the first member of the compound.

If it is argued that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), then in cases such as *vāpyaśva*, there would likewise result the status of being a *pragṛhya*—just as in *somo gaurī adhiśrita*—and furthermore, because the composite lacks semantic meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), it would fail to attain the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

By the statement, "The mention of 'that cause' (*tannimittagrahaṇa*) must be made," which means that whatever is the cause for the meaning of the vocative is itself treated as if it were a subsequent member (*parāṅgavat*), the status of being a subsequent member is excluded for examples such as *ṛtena mitrāvaruṇau*. Furthermore, because the *samartha-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding semantic connection) applies there, there is no purpose [for the aforementioned provision] in that context. In cases such as *ṛtena mitrāvaruṇau*—[this refers to the portion containing the suffix *ghat*].

The statement by Kaiyaṭa (*Suvāmantrite parāṅgavat* [Pāṇini 2.1.2], Mahābhāṣya, Pradīpa, p. 351)—that semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) exists solely through the medium of action (*kriyā*)—is not tenable. This is because the Bhāṣya (Mahābhāṣya, Pradīpa, p. 332) explicitly states that mutual expectancy itself is the referent of the term "semantic competency" (*sāmarthya*). Otherwise, compounds such as *sarvo mṛttikayā* ("all with clay") would result, since the condition of such [action-mediated] expectancy would be present there as well.

Therefore, it is not proper to adopt the view that semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) is characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), as this contradicts both logic and the Bhāṣya. Now, one might object: "Even if the theory of mutual expectancy avoids the formation of compounds in cases such as *draṣṭum gataścaitraḥ* ('Caitra has gone to see') and *kṛṣṇam śrito gurukulam maitraḥ* ('Maitra has resorted to the teacher's house for Kṛṣṇa'), because there is no semantic capacity characterized by mutual expectancy there, the theory of the Siddhāntin—which maintains that semantic capacity is characterized by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*)—would still result in the undesired formation of a compound. If this is raised, we say: No.

Because, due to the mutual connection between *kṛṣṇa* and *āśrita*, even the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) based on syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is impossible. [This concerns] the technical designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*), etc.; [it concerns] that which is "capable" (*samartha*), i.e., the word possessing semantic capacity, such as *rājapuruṣa*, which serves as its substratum. He states that very thing: "The semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) of multiple words is their integration into a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). This is because of the *Mahābhāṣya* on Sūtra 2.1.1 (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), which states: "In a sentence, words have separate meanings; in a compound, they have a single meaning. (Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. ...).

And *ekārthībhāva* (the state of having a single unified meaning) consists in the capacity of words—which are observed in common usage to have as their objects distinct meanings arising from each individual word—to generate a single presentation (*ekopasthiti*) based on a single power (*ekaśakti*) whose object is a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭaviṣayaka*).

If it is objected: "Since the words in a compound are different from the corresponding words in a sentence, how can they possess that [sentence-word] nature?"—we say no; for even if those [compound words] lack that nature, words similar to them do possess it. Alternatively, according to the view of those who maintain that words denote the effect (*kāryaśabdavādin*), the function (*vṛtti*) is produced from the sentence itself; thus, the "nature" belongs to the cognition. As for the mention of the *cvī*-suffix, it is intended to indicate that just as the usage of existence regarding sentence-words is figurative because such words do not exist [as independent entities], so too is the usage of "having a single meaning."

The phrase ending with "dṛṣṭānām" (of those seen) is intended to exclude the state of having a unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) in that which ends in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*), because case-suffixes are not observed in the world as such [independently], and because there is no other word that denotes the meaning expressed by a case-suffix. In the case of *aupagava* and the like, although the suffixes themselves are not observed as such, there is consistency because the word *apatya* (offspring), which denotes the meaning of "offspring," is observed as such in expressions such as *upagor apatyam asti* ("there is the offspring of Upagu"). It is for this very purpose that the expression "any word whatsoever" (*yatkiñcitpada*) was stated.

The statement of the reason is "by means of the capacity [to denote] a specific object. For this very reason, the teacher Kaiyaṭa (in the *Pradīpa* on the *Mahābhāṣya*, Pra. Khaṇḍa, p. 321) states: "A distinct collective meaning, conjoined with the meanings of the individual parts, comes into being; in relation to that, it is called 'unification of meaning' (*ekārthībhāva*), because, like 'dust and water,' it has attained a state of non-distinction."

This is the point: although in a sentence (*vākya*) there is a cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*)—in which the qualifier and the qualified stand in a relationship of mutual dependence (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*)—arising through the power of the sentence based on expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), even when the word-meanings are understood individually by means of the words; it is not so in a compound (*vṛtti*). Rather, in a compound, the cognition of the word-meanings arises precisely through the powers of the constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*), aided by the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*) based on expectancy, and by virtue of a specific awakening factor (*niyata-udbodhaka*); this resulting cognition has as its object the qualified entity characterized by the relationship of qualifier and qualified. Therefore, in that case, there is the apprehension of the power of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-śakti-graha*).

Thus, the word *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man") is endowed with a specific power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) regarding a person and so forth who possesses a relation to the king; by the maxim of "distinguishing between what is already obtained and what is not" (*prāptāprāptaviveka*), this [power] culminates in the aspect of the relation and in the aspect of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*). Since the presentation of the king and so forth is possible through the established powers of the constituent parts themselves, the qualification "rooted in expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣāmūlaka*) ensures that expressions such as *nityo ghaṭaḥ* ("an eternal pot") do not possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) by virtue of having a unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). This is because there is an absence of expectancy for the "potness" (*ghaṭatva*)—which is presented as a qualifier—to relate to its own qualifier.

For this very reason, even a sentence such as "a jar is eternal" (*nityo ghaṭaḥ*) is not [an instance of that]. And this extraordinary power (*alaukika-vidagraha*), which establishes the state of having a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), is superimposed [upon the words] even when there is no apprehension of the extraordinary form. This is because of the authority of the rule "A grammatical operation concerning words applies to what is meaningful" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*, Pāṇini 2.1.1), which means that the designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) and so forth is resorted to based on semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). Furthermore, the designation of a compound and so forth occurs only in the extraordinary form (*alaukika*).

For this very reason, when the designation of a compound (*samāsa*) applies there, the elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktiluk*) is established through the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which is based on the criterion of having meaning (*arthavattva*). By the force of rules such as "the sixth [case-ending]" (*ṣaṣṭhī*, P. 2.2.8), in order to justify the occurrence of the sixth case-ending and others—which are based on the presentation of non-difference (*abheda*)—the quality of having separate meanings (*pṛthag-arthatva*) is superimposed upon the non-worldly sentence (*alaukika-vākya*). Since both [qualities] are conceptual (*kālpnika*), there is no contradiction between them, owing to the authority of the grammatical tradition (*smṛti*).

Furthermore, this capacity for a compound (*vṛtti*) to possess a specific meaning is established by common worldly usage (*loka-siddha*), because there is no formal rule (*vidhāna*) for such meanings in the grammatical treatise (*sāstra*). This is also evident from the fact that meanings are not explicitly seen in rules such as *acatura-avicatura-* (Pāṇini 5.4.77). As for rules like *cārthe dvandvaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.29), these merely restate the compound formation already established in common usage regarding the sense of conjunction (*cārtha*) and prescribe the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "dvandva" alone. Otherwise, there would result a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), as the rule would have to state: "several inflected words (*subanta*) function in the sense of conjunction, and that [group] is designated as a dvandva."

Furthermore, there is the complexity of having to formulate a new *vibhāṣā* (optional) rule in order to exclude sentences that have the same meaning as the compound itself; for me, however, that [rule] is merely a restatement of an established fact conceived by the author of the grammar: namely, that a *samāsa* occurs when there is *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning), whereas a sentence occurs when there is *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy). And according to this view of naturalness (*svābhāvikatva*), words such as *śrotriya* and *kṣatriya* are indivisible and eternal (as stated in Vākyapadīya III, Vṛtti on verse 54: "The words *śrotriya*, *kṣatriya*, etc., are indivisible and eternal"). The operation of the grammatical system proceeds with respect to these words, which are like a "line-drawn cow" (*rekhāgavaya*) constructed for the purpose of their formal description. As it has been said:
"For the sake of comprehension by the ignorant, various means [of expression] are employed for practice;

because they are different words, there is an absolute difference between the sentence and the compound. (Vākyapadīya III, Vṛtti-saṃgraha 49). It is precisely by resorting to this view that the author of the grammatical treatise prescribes the elision of the suffixes *yukta* and so forth in cases such as *goratha*. However, the common worldly sentence *go yukto rathaḥ* is merely a synonym (*paryāya*) for the compound. "Just as a word is established in reference to an object qualified by a tree or the like..."

"Even a word such as *nīlotpala* (blue lotus) functions through two parts" (Vākyapadīya III. vṛtti-sāra 53). "Through two parts"—that is, through two imagined aspects (*kalpitābhāga*). However, for children whose basis is similarity, we say that these very words situated in the sentence are the constituents of the compound. It is precisely based on this that the technical term *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning) is employed. In this view, since words possess a nature consisting of individual meanings, their absence would result in the collapse of that [integrated] nature.

"Likewise, the distinction between *rūḍhi* (conventional) and *arūḍhi* (non-conventional) is also made for the sake of understanding" (*Vākyapadīya*, III, vṛtti, verse 55). The phrase "by the authors of the treatises" implies "for the sake of the unlearned. In this regard, in cases such as *paṅkaja* ("mud-born"), because one understands the meaning of the sentence and yet perceives a different referent, there is *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-conventional). In cases such as *saptaparṇa* ("seven-leaved"), although there is sometimes a correspondence with the meaning, since that correspondence is absent when the leaves have fallen, it is merely *rūḍhi*.

Furthermore, in cases such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), because there is a correspondence with the meaning of the sentence, there is *yaugikatva* (etymological character), and so forth; the intended sense is that these are merely conceptual means of instruction. By this [the author]...

In the view that the word is indivisible (*akhaṇḍatvapakṣa*), there would be a contradiction with the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "In a sentence, words have distinct meanings; in a compound, they have a single meaning. The claim that "words themselves do not exist" is refuted, because even though at the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) words exist as mere substitutes for a line-drawing cow (*rekhāgavaya*), there is no subverting evidence against their existence. As for the point regarding the rule *samartha* (Pāṇini 2.1.1), where "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) also includes independence from others (*itara-nairapekṣya*).

By the term *padavidhi* ("rule concerning a word"), there is meant a rule that has a word as its locus (*uddeśya*), such as the technical designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) and so forth, as well as rules that effect the status of being a word (*padatva*), such as "the third case [is used] for the agent and the instrument" (*kartṛkaraṇayostṛtīyā*, Pāṇini 2.3.18). Therefore, by repetition, the meaning of the Sūtra is also: "That which is enjoined by a rule having a word as its locus—namely, a compound and the like—is dependent upon semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting of 'unification of meaning' (*ekārthībhāva*)," and "that which is enjoined by a rule effecting the status of being a word—the third case and so forth—has as its meaning semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting of independence from others."

Therefore, in cases such as "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), the meaning "one should sacrifice with rice" is established independently of anything else, and furthermore, only that which is of the same class (*sajātīya*) is understood [as the instrument]. Consequently, expressions such as "he makes a pot with a wheel by means of a staff" (*cakreṇa daṇḍena ghaṭaṃ karoti*) would not be ungrammatical (*asādhutā*). To this, [the author] replies: "That is not so."

Because it is not stated in the *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, in cases such as *paśyan mṛgo dhāvati* ("seeing, the deer runs") or *pacati bhavati* ("he is cooking"), even though there is an absence of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) that conveys the capacity you have described, it is possible—even by logical necessity (*nyāyataḥ*)—to understand the objecthood (*karmatva*) and so forth as being independent of anything else, since the qualifier has the effect of excluding connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). This is because there is no difference in result [between your view and ours] even in examples like *vrīhibhiḥ* ("with rice"). Moreover, it is impossible to provide a definition for "homogeneity" (*sājātya*). [This concludes the discussion on] "kṛt and taddhita... (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.46).

Because [the suffix] *kṛt* is conditioned by an *upapada*, it is a rule (*vidhi*) whose locus is a word (*pada*); thus, when the *samartha-paribhāṣā* is present, that [suffix] operates only in the domain of *ekārthībhāva* (syntactic unification). For this very reason, it is stated clearly in the Mahābhāṣya on the sūtra "tatra upapadam" (Mbh. Vol. II, p. 120; Pāṇini 3.1.92): "In the case of 'he makes a large jar' (*mahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti*), the suffix *aṇ* does not occur."

Since words such as *pācaka* (cook) are also conventionally treated as having their application based on an action rooted in the relationship between an action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*), and since the property of having a relation as the ground for application is observed only in the case of a compound (*vṛtti*), this much alone constitutes being a compound. For this very reason, when there is an intention to express the connection with an operation (*vyāpārānvaya*), one does not say "the beginning is a cook" (*ādiḥ pācaka*) as one might say "the beginning cooks" (*ādiḥ pacati*); this is because secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) arise from nominal stems (*subanta*). Because it is a rule dependent on words (*padavidhi*), this technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) applies only when there is a state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

In the case of a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix, such as "Sundarasyaupagava" (the son of Upagu of Sundara), it is clear that the compound (*samāsa*) is a rule whose locus is the individual words, in the sense of "the offspring of Sundara's Upagu. As for *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one of identical forms), its status as a *vṛtti* (grammatical formation) is only figurative, being an exception (*apavāda*) to [the general definition of] *vṛtti*; for here there is no *ekārthībhāva*—that is, the state of having a single unified meaning—among the meanings presented by the separate words.

Regarding the *dhātu* (verbal root) that begins with *san* and so forth, although *san* and the other affixes do not have rules whose objects are words (*pada*), there is the statement in the Mahābhāṣya on *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.1): "The mention of 'optionally' (*vā*) is redundant because *san* is compulsory; here there are two [conceptions]: the *vṛtti* and the sentence (*vākya*). (Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. ...).

327) "[Because] *ekārthībhāva* (the state of having a single unified meaning) is the domain of *vṛtti* (grammatical formation), while a sentence (*vākya*) has as its domain *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy), there is no possibility of a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) due to their having different meanings"—thus [states] Kaiyaṭa and others, citing the *Mahābhāṣya* (Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 327): "By that [term] *ekārthībhāva*, [examples such as] *pipaṭhiṣati* (desires to read) and *gantum* (to go) [are explained]. In reality, however, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from a group of identical words) does not possess the status of a *vṛtti*; therefore, its definition is stated only in four ways:
"A son born to a Vaiśya woman from a Kṣatriya father is known as a Māhiṣya;
a son born to a Vaiśya woman from a Śūdra father is called a Karaṇa."

"A son born from a Māhiṣya father and a Karṇī mother is called a Rathakāra. This refers to the postulation of that [compound], namely, the postulation of a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*). The phrase "the Sūtra is established by logic alone" means, in my view, that it is established for one who maintains that semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) is characterized by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). The phrase "because it is a part of the word-meaning" refers to its connection [with the other members of the compound].

[Objection: "But surely, even if it [the qualifier] is only a part of the word-meaning, it still possesses the status of being the meaning of the word *rājan* (king); thus, even according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there would indeed be a connection with qualifiers and so forth. [Reply: This is not so—because when there is a connection with a qualifier, the relevant factor is either that the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is not the object of a grasp of its power (*śaktigraha*) as being a qualifier of something else, or that there is the cognition of the qualificand as not being a qualifier of anything else; since this is the governing principle, there is no fault. It is precisely based on this that the grammatical maxim arises: "A word-meaning connects with a word-meaning, but not with a part of a word-meaning."

In reality, in a compound (*vṛtti*), the specific feature consisting in the connection of one qualifier with another qualifier is not caused by *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning). This is because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*): even when *ekārthībhāva* is absent—as in "Devadatta’s teacher's family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*) or "pot" (*ghaṭa*)—one observes the presence or absence of the connection of another qualifier in the qualifiers "teacher" (*guru*) and "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Furthermore, this is not stated in the *Bhāṣya*. As for the claim that "this specific feature is indeed caused by *ekārthībhāva*," [it is incorrect].

In cases such as *devattasya gurukulam* ("the teacher's house of Devatta"), a compound occurs because there is a constant requirement for a correlative (*nityasāpekṣatva*), and it has been established elsewhere that in instances of constant requirement, both types [of compounds] are permissible. However, in cases like *rājapuruṣa* ("the king's servant"), since the king and so forth do not have a constant requirement for another related entity, the rule states that a compound does not occur when a qualifier is itself qualified. This is incorrect; for if one were to use the expression *śivabhāgavata* in the sense "Lord Śiva’s devotee" (*asya bhaktiḥ*), the compound would not be valid according to that rule regarding the meaning of the devotee (*bhaktārthe*).

Because the word *bhagavat* lacks dependence on any other constant correlate (*nityasambandhyantara*), therefore it is logical that in its expressive function (*gamakatve*) there is a connection with a qualifier, but not in its non-expressive state (*āgamakaratve*). Furthermore, it should be understood that "expressiveness" (*gamakatva*) is the capacity to produce such a cognition, as is clear from various passages in the Bhāṣya. Precisely for this reason—that it is established by reasoning—it must be stated; that is to say, it must be established through verbal expressions. ||5|| (32)

"At the root [of our system], this is established by reasoning" (Vai.si.kā. 33). This is the underlying point: since in a *vṛtti* (compound) there is the cessation of the distinction between the individual members due to the emergence of a single unified meaning (*ekārtha*), and because of the absence of the particle *ca*—which, as a basis for distinction, expresses a sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*)—there is no possibility of using *ca* and other such particles even as that which is expressed (*dyotya*). Furthermore, this [emergence of a single meaning] is itself produced by the state of becoming a single referent (*ekārthībhāva*).

Because the conjunction (*samuccaya*) is expressed only when its members are presented separately, and because such separate presentation is absent due to the lack of "single-meaningness" (*ekārthībhāva*), [the word *ca* is not used]. Even in common worldly usage, the term "collection" (*samūha*) is applied only when things known separately occupy a single location. As for the claim that the root meaning [of the rule] is that the word *ca* is not employed because the meaning has already been expressed by the compound, according to the maxim *uktārthānām aprayogaḥ* (there is no employment of what has already been stated)—that is incorrect; for even though the collection, being a substantive entity (*satvabhūta*), is denoted as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) by the compound, the word *ca* is still employed for the sake of conveying it as a non-substantive entity (*asatvabhūta*) functioning as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

This is because [the meaning] is difficult to avoid. Nor should it be argued that if the meaning of *ca* (*cārtha*), which is of the nature of non-existence (*asattvabhūta*), were not denoted by the compound, then the rule “*dvandva* is used in the sense of *ca*” (Pāṇini 2.2.29) would be untenable, since such a denotation is thereby obtained. For the status of being the meaning of *ca* (*cārthatva*) is possible through the superimposition (*āropa*) of similarity upon the collection (*samūha*) not denoted by the compound. Just as in the case of *dvandva*, there is a cognition of a collection according to both the view that it is with parts (*sakhaṇḍa*) and the view that it is partless (*akhaṇḍa*), as was explained previously regarding the collection. This applies to [the particles] *vā* and so forth as well.

The meaning is as follows: since words such as *iva* function as indicators of similarity (*sādṛśya*) based on a distinction [between the object of comparison and the standard], that distinction is concealed by the force of "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) within a compound; consequently, in a compound (*vṛtti*), there is no employment of *iva* and the like, which indicate similarity rooted in that very distinction. However, in a sentence (*vākya*), because the distinction is present through its manifestation, the employment of *iva* and so forth certainly occurs. Regarding the phrase "and of those mentioned previously": this refers to words such as *krānta* (in the example *niṣkauśāmbi*, etc.).

In reality, the absence of the use of words such as *krānta* (gone) in a compound (*vṛtti*) is not caused by their lack of *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning), because this is not stated in the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, it is impossible for the absence of *krānta* and other such terms in a compound to be caused by *ekārthībhāva* in the sense of being the generator of a single presentation (*ekopasthitijanakatva*). If one asks, "How then is there no use of them in the compound?", the answer is: because in a compound, words preceded by *ni-* and others function with the meaning of *krānta* and so forth; thus, the meaning is understood from that very [compound] through the maxim of the "part of a word" (*padaikadeśanyāya*). Consequently, the non-usage of those terms is established by the maxim *uktārthānām aprayogaḥ* ("there is no usage of what has already been expressed").

There is no fault here, because the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the entire compound [“go-svāda”] is accepted in the sense of a specific class (*jāti-viśeṣa*). This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule “*saṃkhyā-vyayādeḥ*” (Pāṇini 4.1.26); this should be understood.
Nor is there a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) there; the ellipsis [to be supplied] is “of the second member (*uttara-pada*) in the sense of another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*)”.

Nor should it be argued that if the word *go* (cow) were to indicate the owner of the cow through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of its own primary meaning, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the word *citra* (variegated) not connecting with the referent of the word *go*, because [the indicated meaning] is only a part [of the whole]. This is not a fault, because the word *citra* serves to apprehend the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*), and thus the indication of the owner of the variegated cow occurs through the word *go* alone. "—2prāptodeti—2" refers to the phrase beginning with "even so. —2tadasaṃbhavāt—2 means "because of the impossibility of indication. He demonstrates that very point with —2prāptiti—2. —2itibodottaram—2 means "after the cognition of the primary meaning."

"—the village related to such water. The meaning is that the relation of such water with the village consists in its being the object of an attainment (prāpti) whose agent is [the village] itself. This is because, according to his view, it would follow that the resulting cognition would be precisely this: "The village is related to the water which is non-different from the agent of the attainment. "The term 'object' (karman) would [be required]"—this is because of the principle: "When grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is possible, it is improper to resort to a lack of coreferentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya). He states this very point with the words "otherwise" (anyathā), meaning: in the case where non-difference is not admitted.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the object (*karman*) is indicated by the *kta* suffix in the word *prāpta*, which has the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*)? Furthermore, the water (*udaka*) would be construed with the attainment (*prāpti*) through a relation of identity (*tādātmya*), which is the nature of the agent. Moreover, since there is the grammatical rule "the meaning of two nouns [is construed together]," let there be a restriction in the present case; therefore, he says: "of the attainment" (*prāpteḥ*). "And because of the impossibility of syntactic connection" (*anvayāsaṃbhavācca*)—this means that there is no possibility of a distinct syntactic connection between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root without mediating the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhakti*). This is likewise because of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

In expressions such as *śobhanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks beautifully"), because those two [the adverb and the verb] are construed even without mediating through that [the object], [the author says] "by way of distinction" (*bhedena*). Otherwise—[if one were to claim] that the meaning of the noun is not construed with the meaning of the verbal root by means of the relation of agency (*kartṛtā*)—there would be the undesirable consequence of non-construction (*ananvayāpatti*). And thus, the sense is that this [unwanted] usage would result.

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should also be understood that if one were to resort to *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) for the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) in the case of [the word] "water" (*udaka*), then since the agent in the form of water would not be expressed, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) would follow from it; consequently, because of the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the formation of a *bahuvrīhi* compound would be impossible. [The phrase] "by virtue of being the meaning of a noun" (*nāmārthatvena*) means "by virtue of being the object that is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the cognition produced by a noun. In the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the term *nāmārthayoḥ*, the meaning is "of those two objects which are the qualificands in the cognition produced by a noun. [Otherwise, there would be the fault of] "non-connection" (*ananvaya*).

Otherwise, there would be a violation of the principle stated in the *Nirukta* (A. 1, Pāda 1): "Names have substance as their primary referent. Furthermore, it should be understood that in your view, since "attainment" (*prāpti*) is the substantive, it cannot be connected with water (*udaka*), as the agent [of attainment] is only a partial factor (*ekadeśajñatva*). 6. (33)

"—of the mere word *citra* (variegated), etc."—this is the reason for the occurrence of two distinct cognitions. When there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for the word *citra*, the denoted meaning (*śakyārtha*) of the word *citra* becomes a part of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyaikadeśa*), and therefore the meaning of the word *go* (cow) cannot be construed with it, according to the linguistic rule: "the meaning of a word [is construed] with the meaning of a word. Similarly, when there is *lakṣaṇā* for the word *go*, the denoted meaning of the word *go* becomes a part of the indicated meaning, and thus the meaning of the word *citra* cannot be construed with it. By the phrase "etc.," the meanings of the words *go* and *citra* are both included.

"—*citragu*—the meaning is 'a cow non-different from the variegated. The point is that the word *citra* (variegated) serves to bring about the apprehension of the intended sense (*tātparya*). —'Only through direct relation'—the point is that since the word *go* (cow) denotes a substance (*dravya*), its referent (*artha*) is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*); therefore, qualities such as 'variegated' are construed with it only by means of that [substance]. —'*Yaugika*s'—refers to words such as *prāpta* (obtained), etc.

"—'The repetition of the word *bodha* (understanding)'—the meaning is that it is the object (*karman*) of the attainment (*prāpti*) whose agent (*kartṛ*) is water. —'Mutually'—the meaning is that when words such as 'water' are used in close proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*), the very word 'attainment' (*prāpti*) itself, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), signifies 'the object of the attainment whose agent is water. —'By remaining in that same state'—"

The meaning is that, because there is an absence of any decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*)—namely, whether it is the word *udaka* occurring in proximity with the word *prāpta*, or the word *prāpta* occurring in proximity with the word *udaka*—not even one of the two is established. Nor should it be argued that, despite the lack of a decisive criterion, both are established alternatively, thereby achieving our desired goal; for even in that case, it would result in the hearer having two successive cognitions.

"Due to conformity with the meaning of the suffix"—that is, due to conformity with the connection of that [suffix's] meaning. "Of the proximate word-meaning"—this must be supplemented by "of the preceding word-meaning. Otherwise, as will be stated later, in cases such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the genitive case-meaning connecting with the "man" (*puruṣa*). "For thus"—that is, for if one accepts that the capacity to convey the qualified meaning resides in the final word alone through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

He states the impossibility itself: "—2 *anekam iti* —2" (because of contradiction). [The reading "because of prescription" (*vidhānāt*) is a scribal error. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); for instance, in cases such as *sarvaka*, the suffix would deviate from its position by occurring in the middle. Furthermore, in examples such as *dadhi bahupaṭurdadāti* ("he gives curd that is very clever"), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the plural meaning (*bahutva*) attaching to the curd (*dadhi*), and there would be the failure of the meaning to attach to the word *paṭu*. It should also be understood that in examples such as *dadhi iyaddadāti* ("he gives so much curd"), there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix *vatup* attaching to the curd.

He says "moreover" (*kiñca*) according to the reasoning already stated. He raises an objection with "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*). "This has been explained in detail elsewhere. According to the stated method, there is the cognition of a qualified object through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the jar and so forth. One should also understand that even the contradiction regarding the etymology of the word "cognitions" (*pratyayānām*) does not apply; for the preceding phonemes are useful as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). However, if one were to accept this consequence, then since everything could be resolved in this manner, it would follow that specific discourse (*viśiṣṭakathā*) would be abolished.

If it is argued that, since words such as *ghaṭa* (pot) convey a meaning even when there is no multiplicity of their constituent parts or their secondary indications (*lakṣaṇā*), a specific denotative power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) must reside therein—this is equally applicable to *vṛtti* (compound). Even if some understanding arises from knowledge of the parts or secondary indication during a *vṛtti*, it does not possess the status of a [primary] word, nor is it a grammatical property (*dharma*), because that would contradict the rule *anekam* (Pāṇini 2.2.24). Furthermore, nowhere is the derivation of a word based on secondary indication seen in the Sūtras, and this would result in the collapse of the view that grammar is the means for grasping denotative power; the details of this are found elsewhere.

"—the justification by means of the established power [of the parts]—means that there is an abandonment of the etymological derivation based on the power of the established parts. —The followers of the *vyapekṣā* theory—refers to those who follow the proponent of *vyapekṣā*. The position of the proponents of *vyapekṣā* as established in the *Bhāṣya* has already been stated previously.

Nor should it be argued that if the word *rāja-* were to have a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of 'one related to the king,' there would result the formation of a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *rūṣa-*."

Because the status of *karmadhāraya* is accepted only in those cases where, given that the meaning of a constituent member of the compound is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is the indication of a single case-ending for both words in the non-standard (*alaukika*) analytical statement (*vigraha*). By the inclusion of the "sati" clause [in the definition], there is the exclusion of examples such as ‘citraguḥ’ and ‘pañcaphalī’ (from the root-text), because in those cases the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) or a collective (*samāhāra*) is the qualificand, and thus the meaning of the constituent member of the compound lacks the status of being the qualificand. For this very reason—namely, because the word ‘rāja’ and so forth possess a meaning qualified by that [other factor].

"—by virtue of expressing that meaning—" || —The reason for [using] the term *ghañ* and so forth is that it functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward things similar to that [action], etc. || —"One who possesses a connection with the king"—this cognition arises according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), wherein even the relation (*saṃsarga*), which is the meaning of the genitive case, appears precisely as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*). And this is logical, whereas the view that "one possesses a king by way of the relation of ownership" (*svatva-sambandhena*) is not correct, as is clear elsewhere. || —"From those"—that is, from words such as *paṅkaja* ("mud-born"). ||

"—2na ceti—2" means "it is not so," that is, "indeed not. Here, in words such as *paṅkaja* ("lotus"), "non-apprehension of *śakti*" means non-apprehension of the power residing in the individual components [of the compound]. "—2lakṣaṇāyeti—" (or *lakṣaṇayeti*) means: since *lakṣaṇā* consists in a relationship with the primary meaning (*śakyasambandha*), if *śakti* is not apprehended, *lakṣaṇā* cannot be apprehended either; this is the meaning. "—2sambhavatīti—" (is possible): the ellipsis is "therefore, the acceptance of a specific *śakti* in those [words] is possible. "—2ata eva—" means precisely because *lakṣaṇā* is not apprehended when *śakti* is not apprehended. This connects with the phrase "nor can it be said... (*nāpi... vācyam*).

"—only in the case of the word *udaka*. The meaning is this: the word *udaka* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in the sense of the object of attainment whose agent is itself, and the word *prāpta* serves as the indicator of that intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka-nimitta*). — "The meaning of the proximate word": this should be explained as before, namely, as the meaning of the preceding proximate word.

The Naiyāyika states his own view: "Atirikta" (distinct) means having the nature of desire and so forth, which is distinct from the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*). "Viśiṣṭe" (qualified) means qualified by the phonemes *gh*, *a*, *ṭ*, and *ṭ*. He also speaks according to the fundamental method: "Bodhakatva" [is absent] because of its non-existence, that is, because it is not experienced. "Sā" refers to *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Even assuming [the opponent's position], he says: this is also an illustration of the status of being indicative (*lakṣaka*) according to other schools of thought. "Arthavattvābhāvena" means by the absence of the capacity to present a meaning through a linguistic function (*vṛtti*).

The meaning is that although a portion [of the compound] possesses the status of being a base (lakṣaṇārūpavṛttimat), the compound as a whole lacks the status of being a base; therefore, that designation of "nominal stem" (prātipadika-saṃjñā) does not apply.

[Objection: But surely, since a compound (*samāsa*) presents a qualified meaning through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), it indeed possesses the aforementioned meaningfulness (*arthavattva*). To this, he says: "In the compound-sentence" (*samāsavākye*). This means "in a sentence in the form of a compound. Since they [the grammarians] define a word as "that which is expressive" (*śaktaṃ padam*) and a sentence as "a collection of words" (*padasamūho vākyam*), this is stated according to that system. However, it should be understood that in reality, even a single word can function as a sentence, as was previously established by the principle of "a part of a word" (*padaikadeśanyāya*). [The phrase] "let it be for the sake of the restriction" (*niyamārtham astv iti*)... [is used].

The meaning is "in order to prevent [the application of] a sentence."—2By virtue of the necessity of being meaningful—2 by virtue of the necessity of a word that conveys that [meaning].—2"It implies"—2 this is the ellipsis for the sentence: "And that [implication] is untenable without a specific denotative power (viśiṣṭa-śakti). This is also an illustration: in cases such as *kaṇṭhe kālaḥ* ("Black on the neck") and *dāsyāḥ putraḥ* ("The son of a slave-girl"), since the case-ending is heard without elision (*aluk*), there is no evidence for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*); consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of the connection of qualifiers [to the primary sense]. Nor can it be argued that even in those cases, the word *dāsī* has a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in its relation to [the son].

This is because there is no experience of [the meaning] "the relative of the slave's relative. Furthermore, there can be no secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for that which ends in a case-suffix (*vibhakta*); for in your view, it lacks primary denotative power (*śakti*), and because even the meaning of the case-suffix, as a word-meaning, appears only as a relation (*saṃsarga*) in your system. It should also be understood that the two grounds for secondary indication—conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or a specific purpose (*prayojana*)—are absent here.

As for the view that, in order to avoid inconsistency (*avairūpya*) in all compounds, the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs only in the final member (*uttarapada*), and that its status as a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) also belongs to that alone—such as in "rājapuruṣa" and so on—and thus there is no suspicion of it being a *karmadhāraya* compound, [the author] refutes that with the words "Moreover, if this were so": the meaning is, if one accepts signification in the final member. "The consequence of non-connection" (*ananvayāpattiḥ*): the word "of the master" (*svāminī*) is to be supplied. "Because of being the base" (*prakṛtitvāt*): this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). For if only that [final member] were the nominal stem, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) situated in the preceding member would not occur.
