Because the mere final member [of the compound] ends in a suffix, it is precluded by the rule "not being a suffix" (*apratyaya*), and because it cannot be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); and because the meaning of the word "citrā" as intended to convey the sense of the referent—namely, the object consisting of a cow non-different from Citrā—is composed of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) "the owner of a cow non-different from Citrā," there would be the consequence of breaking the established capacity of words like "citra" to convey the intended sense in cases such as "citrā-guḥ," which was previously established in examples like "prāptodakaḥ."

In that case, because the intended meaning [of the sentence] is not constituted by the literal meanings of words such as "attained" (*prāpta*)—since the literal meaning of "attained" is non-different from water, and thus the indicated meaning of "the object of attainment whose agent is water" is not included therein—the status of being grasped through the intended meaning [is absent]. Furthermore, this status of being grasped through the intended meaning exists at the stage when the literal meaning is not yet constituted by itself... (P. 02-02) ...at that time.

Just as in the state of primary denotation (*vācyārtha*), there is the capacity to awaken a cognition in which the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*) has been established, so too in the state of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or even in the state of specific power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*), there is such a capacity to awaken a cognition in which the qualifier-qualified relationship has been established. And this [capacity] exists in cases such as *prajayati* and the like; however, it is also absent in the present case.

The meaning is as follows: [the rule] "bodhyam" (is to be understood) because there is a deviation from the general principle (*avyabhicārāt*). In expressions such as *ardhapippalī* ("half a pepper"), although the word *pippalī* denotes the relation to the pepper through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—and thus the relation is presented—the object denoted by the word *ardha* (the half) is presented by that very word *ardha* itself as a half. Consequently, it is this [word *ardha*] alone that, being primary, connects with the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*). Furthermore, since that [meaning of the case-ending] is not in immediate proximity to the suffix (*pratyaya*), there is a deviation from the established grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*). It should be understood, however, that this deviation does not apply if one takes the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) as part of the entire compound *ardhapippalī*.

"Let it be that the derivation [of the suffix] is indeed based on the sense of 'proximity' (*sannihita*) and so forth; however, the status of being a *prakṛti* (base) is not required. Consequently, in cases such as *ardhapippalī*, since the subsequent member conveys a qualified meaning through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is no inconsistency with the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) for the suffix. With this intention, he says: 'na ca' ('nor...'), which connects with the word 'vācyam' ('must be stated'). Regarding the phrase 'tatrāpi': the meaning is 'even in cases such as *ardhapippalī*'. He states the very rule based on the grammatical injunction: 'tathā ca' ('and thus...')."

Nor should it be argued that if the base (*prakṛti*) were not included in the definition of *vyutpatti*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the sixth-case meaning (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) being construed with "man" (*puruṣa*) in expressions such as "the king’s man" (*arājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*); for what is intended [by the definition] is that suffixes denote a meaning residing in the immediately preceding word-meaning, and so forth.

"—2Because of the subsequent instruction—2. Thus, even according to the method you have stated, that [position] is far from tenable; this is the sense. Furthermore, in examples such as "the dhava and khadira trees," there would be the undesirable consequence of the number two not being construed with the *dhava* tree (note: the phrase "due to the necessity of the function residing in the *dhava*" is not observed in the manuscript), because figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not accepted in that case.

Now, it might be argued that there is no fault in cases such as *dhava-khadira* or *vīra-aśoka*, because of the rule: "Whatever compound is taught, it denotes its own meaning as residing in either of those two meanings [of the members] that constitute it," and because factors such as semantic compatibility (*yogyatā*) serve as the determinants [of the specific relation]. Furthermore, there would be no fault in cases such as *ardha-pippalī* or "see the king-ruru deer. If this is said, we reply: No—because it would involve the unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating a different rule of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*).

Moreover, a compound formation is necessary here in accordance with the requirement that the compound must denote a collection of word-meanings whose connection to a single action is invariably concomitant with the state of being compounded. For this very reason, particles such as *iva* or *ca* are not used in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) in these instances.

"Let it be that the etymological derivation (vyutpatti) is indeed 'of the meanings of the base' (prakṛtyartha), etc.; however, in that context, the property of being the locus of the status of a base (prakṛtitvāśrayatva) in the phrase 'of the meaning of the base' does not exist by way of the relation of pervasion (paryāpti); rather, it exists by way of the relation of identity (svarūpa). And since that [relation] is common to both the whole and its parts, there is no fault in cases such as 'half-a-pippalī' (ardhapippalī). With this intention, he says "abhe" [in the verse]. [The commentary explains: "[In the sense of] the locus of the status of a base"—that is, [the meaning] "of the locus of the status of a base. [He says] "because of the consequence of [unwanted] application" (anvayaprasaṅgāt); the implication is that even without resorting to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

If, however, one accepts that there is a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) of a word denoting a qualified entity upon its constituent part, then this is precisely what we desire. One might object that the aforementioned fault is avoided by the assumption that the case-suffix meaning is construed with the referent of the base which serves as the qualificand; to this, he says: "And not... and "...because of the [unwanted] consequence. If, on the other hand, it is argued that—by virtue of proximity—the case-suffix meaning is construed with the referent of the base (which is the qualificand) as determined by that very suffix, [then the following applies].

It should be noted that in such cases as "unripe blue" (*apākānnīla*), there is no room for error. As for the claim that "being a base" (*prakṛtitva*) consists in being the word immediately preceding an affix, and since this exists in a word like *citragu*, the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is connected to that [base] through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—that is incorrect. For in a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the meaning of the prior member is predominant, such as *ardhapippalī* ("half a pippalī"), there would be no way to avoid the fault. Even if one assumes secondary signification in the subsequent member, the connection of the case-meaning with the object of the word "half" (*ardhapada*) would still not be possible.

Furthermore, [the definition would suffer from] non-pervasion (avyāpti) regarding words such as *paṭu* and *sarva* in compounds like *bahupaṭuḥ* and *sarvaka*; and it would result in over-pervasion (ativyāpti) regarding words like *dadhi* in examples such as *dadhi iyad dadāti* and *dadhi paṭurdadāti*, because those words (*dadhi*, etc. would then be considered the bases (*prakṛti*) of the suffixes. Moreover, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that the prefix (*upasarga*) in *vyatise* would be the base of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

Therefore, being a *prakṛti* consists precisely in not being sublated by the application of a suffix (*pratyaya*), and being the meaning of the *prakṛti* consists in being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the specific cognition produced by it. This [status] does not belong to the final member alone in a compound (*samāsa*), nor to the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*). Thus, even if one were to resort to indication (*lakṣaṇā*), that [explanation] would remain untenable. Nor can it be said: "Let the status of being a *prakṛti* be as established by the tenets; however, its being the meaning [of the *prakṛti*]... (P.)

The view that being the object of a secondary (lakṣya) meaning consists merely in being the object of the cognition produced by that [word], and not extending as far as being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), thereby avoiding any fault in cases such as *ardhapippalī* ("half-a-pippali") or *pākān nīlaḥ* ("blue from cooking"), is now refined: "And that which..."—the phrase "produced by that" means "produced by the base (*prakṛti*)"; and "and that here"—means "in all instances," such as *pākān nīlaḥ* and *citraguḥ*. It is "not contradictory."

The meaning is that [the property of] being an object (*viṣayatā*) is common to both the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Regarding "by means of inherence" (*samavāyena*): the meaning is that words reside in space (*ākāśa*) through the relation of inherence. Regarding "by means of a function (*vṛtti*) [of denoting] the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*") (*vṛttyā prakṛtyarthatvasya*"): since you do not accept either primary denotation (*śakti*) or metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for a qualified base, there is an absence of knowledge of the meaning produced by such a base through any function; thus, the impossibility [of your position] in your own view is quite evident. This is the intended meaning.

If, however, one accepts that the word has its denotative power (*śakti*) in the qualified sense according to the Siddhānta view, and further accepts—by way of *vṛtti*—that the object of the cognition produced by such a base (the qualified) possesses the status of being the referent, then there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the case-ending meaning (*vibhaktyartha*) being construed with "mud" (*paṅka*) and so on in expressions such as ‘paṅkaja’ (“mud-born”) and ‘rājapuruṣaṃ paśya’ (“see the king’s man”).

—2. [The objection: "By the stick" (*daṇḍena*)—here, the suffix *su* follows the word *kṛṣṇa*; the word preceding that suffix is *kṛṣṇa*. Since the quality of being the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatva*), defined as the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) of the cognition produced by that [base], exists in *kṛṣṇa*, there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the third-case meaning [instrumentality] being construed with it. If, however, this is refined such that the meaning of the base is defined as the state of being the qualificand of the cognition produced by the word immediately preceding the suffix whose meaning one intends to construe through proximity (*pratyāsatti*), [then the fault is avoided].

Even if the aforementioned defects are removed, one should understand that there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "bahu-paṭuḥ sarvakaḥ" and the like. [The phrase] "residing in the meaning of the word being compounded" should be intended to mean "residing in the meaning which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the word being compounded. Otherwise, in examples such as "rājapuruṣaṃ paśya" ("see the king's man"), there would be the undesirable consequence of the case-meaning (*vibhaktyartha*) connecting even with the meaning of the word "king," which functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). [The phrase] "from the base (*jāti*)" [refers to] the suffixes *su* and so on, which by virtue of the grammatical rule "after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), *su* etc. occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) and so forth," are obtained through proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Of these suffixes...

The meaning of the direction [in the verse] is as follows: because of the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that a suffix conveys its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), there would result a violation of both the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of those two—the base and the suffix—and their mutual connection with the meanings of the base and the suffix as thus obtained.

"—2 *prātipadikārthaprakāraka*—" || One should also supply "*bhedasaṃsargaka*" (having difference as its relation). By this, in cases such as "he cooks slightly" (*stokaṃ pacati*), there is no defect even if the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—such as "slight" (*stoka*)—is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) through non-difference (*abheda*), without the representation produced by the case-ending (*vibhakti*). "—2 *vibhaktijanya*—" || This refers to "*tadvihita*" and so forth. As for the claim that the cause is the representation produced by the suffix prescribed for that [nominal stem], that [would apply] because the word "puruṣa" also conveys a meaning.

Because it is a suffix (*pratyaya*), [the definition] is inconsistent. However, the claim that "being a suffix consists in having the status of the word *pratyaya* through a relationship based on convention" is difficult to maintain according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the application of words is threefold. Furthermore, being read in the section on suffixes (*pratyayādhikāra*) is over-extended to items such as the word *ādeśīya*. It should be understood, however, that if one accepts a specific universal (*jāti*) as the nature of being a suffix and thereby posits a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) accordingly, then the desired conclusion is reached.

He prevents the deviation of the stated causal relationship [between word-meaning and case-meaning] by stating: "The rice is white. The point is that there is non-difference between the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) meanings, because another linguistic rule (vyutpatti) is postulated: "In a cognition where the meaning of the nominal stem is the qualifier (prakāra), the cause is the presentation (upastiti) produced by the case-ending whose meaning is the nominal stem-meaning. [The term] "of that" refers to the meaning of the nominative case.

In cases such as "śubhreṇa taṇḍulena" (with white rice), regarding the cognition of non-difference (*abheda*) through a meaning other than that of the noun, the causal factor is simply the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by nouns bearing the same case-ending. Thus, because a different rule of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) is postulated, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the cause-and-effect relationship involving difference (*bheda*) here either. Furthermore, with the intention that the second case-endings following the qualifying words serve the purpose of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) rather than expressing non-difference, he says: "śubhreṇeti."

And thus, the meaning is that in the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) constructed by the aforementioned non-difference (*abheda*), the state of having a meaningful case-ending (*sārthakavibhaktitva*) is included. [The phrase] "the case-ending has a non-lexical meaning" (*vibhaktir abhedārthā*) follows from this. For this very reason, the author of the *Bhāṣya* states regarding the rule *anabhihite* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.1): "In examples such as 'make the mat formidable' (*kaṭaṃ bhīṣmaṃ kuru*), the second case ending occurs after words like *bhīṣma* because of their coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *kaṭa*. Alternatively, it is a subsequent [explanation].

In this view, according to the principle of the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, each word is connected directly with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), and thus [the words] possess the status of being instruments (*karaṇatva*). Consequently, this is merely the implied (*lakṣya*) object of the causal relation constituted by the verbal root. As for their mutual connection, that is a subsequent matter (*pārṣṭhika*), which is another point. For this very reason, the Commentator says: "Even though the accusative case is not expressed [by a suffix], *bhīṣma* and the others are also the object" (on Pāṇini 2.3.1, Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 478). This is what is meant by "non-differentiated connection" (*abhedānvaya*).

It is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sarvādi* rule (*Pāṇini* 1.1.27; Ma.Bhā.Pra.Kha.Pṛ. 203–214) that in a construction involving non-difference (*abhedānvaya*), grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) belongs only to two nouns that possess identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktika*). Furthermore, it was previously established that a subsequent noun consists of a nominal stem (*nāman*) together with a case-ending (*vibhakti*). Even in cases such as *taddadhi paśya* ("look at that curd"), the condition of having identical case-endings is maintained by taking the elided case-ending (*luptavibhakti*) into account. For one who is unaware of the elision of the case-ending, there is likewise an ignorance of that specific grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*). However, through formal instruction (*upadeśa*), knowledge of this is easily accessible to both [the learner and the teacher].

In expressions such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king’s man"), because the case-ending (*vibhakti*) has been elided, there is a difference in case-endings; thus, there is no identity of case-ending (*samānavibhaktikatva*). Identity of case-ending consists in possessing case-endings that have the same referential meaning (*sāmānārthaka*); therefore, there is no fault in cases such as *rājñaḥ sutasya dhanam* ("the wealth of the king’s son"), because in one instance the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has the sense of being produced (*janyatva*), while in the other it has the sense of ownership (*svatva*), and thus the condition [of identical meaning] is absent. Furthermore, identity of gender (*liṅga*) and number (*vacana*) are not required for non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*). (L.)

In this regard, [the definition] fails due to exceptions (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "The Vedas are authoritative," "The villages are on the Godāvarī," "That which is similar to that is called *tulya*," and "For that which is coolness is its very nature" (Raghuvamśa Mahākāvya, Fifth Canto, verse 54). This has been explained in detail elsewhere. The intention is that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because of the previously established etymology. In reality, however, in examples such as "Make Bhīṣma a mat" (*bhīṣmaṃ kaṭaṃ kuru*), the mat qualified by the attribute of being Bhīṣma-like is the *karman* because it is the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) of the action of making.

In that regard, an objection is raised: since the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is not distinct from its primary constituent (*pradhāna*), when that [objecthood] residing in the primary is expressed by the second case (*dvitīyā*) following the word *kaṭa*, the objecthood residing in the qualified entity is already expressed; thus, the second case would not apply after words such as *bhīṣma*. Anticipating this, one solution stated in the Bhāṣya is that because the objecthood residing in the qualified entity cannot be conveyed without a coreferential qualifier (*samānavibhaktika-viśeṣaṇa*), even though the capacity for objecthood (*karmatva-śaktimatva*) is expressed for *bhīṣma* and the others, the second case still applies. This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of that [passage].

If the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is the object (*karman*), then the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) must also be that [object]; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement "the qualified is the object. Now, one might object: "In cases such as 'the earring-wearer is wise' (*kuṇḍalī paṇḍitaḥ*), if wisdom (*paṇḍitatva*) is construed with the qualified, then wisdom would also have to be construed with the qualifier, such as the earring; and since that is sublated (*bādhita*), the aforementioned cognition of the qualified would be untenable. This is not so—

Just as in cases such as "The crested one [Śiva] has his crest destroyed" (*śikhī dhvasta*), even though there is a sublation of the connection between the destruction and the particular [the crest], there is a cognition through the superimposition (*āropa*) of the destruction residing in the qualifier [the crest] onto the qualificand [the person]; so too here, although there is a sublation of the connection with scholarship in the qualifier, the cognition of the qualified entity is established through the superimposition of that [scholarship] onto the qualificand, such as the earrings. And thus, in this case, the knowledge possesses the nature of error (*bhramatva*) regarding that part. However, where there is no sublation, there is no error even in that part; as in the present example, "Bhīṣma is the mat" (*bhīṣmaṃ kaṭam*), and so forth.

Furthermore, the demonstration here that [the accusative] expresses a qualified object-status (*viśiṣṭakarmatva*) implies that the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is required in both instances; this is also established by the qualification [in the rule]. According to the principle that "suffixes are connected with the meaning of their base" (*pratyayānāṃ prakṛtyarthānvayitvam*), there is also a connection with the meaning of its own base as qualified by the qualifier. In this view, from the word expressing the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇapada*), there arises a presentation of that [object] unassociated with object-status (*karmatva*) and so forth. However, since the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is perceived as being characterized by that [qualifier], it is the qualificand itself that is understood as the object.

Likewise, in the case of cognition (*bodha*), the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) and others, as well as the qualifier and the rest, are also auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*). Therefore, due to the impossibility of such semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), a compound (*samāsa*) is not possible. For this very reason, it does not occur in cases such as "made with white rice" (*śubhreṇa taṇḍulena kṛtam* → *śubhrataṇḍulena kṛtam*). Now, even if a compound is possible under the view that the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) possesses the status of the object (*karmatva*) according to the aforementioned method, one might—intending the connection of each [attribute] individually with the action according to the logic of the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*—argue: "The mat is also the object, and the terrifying [qualities] and so forth are also [the objects]" (*kaṭo'pi karma bhīṣmādayo'pi*). [This is addressed in the Mahābhāṣya on *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1), Prākṣiptakhanda, p. ...].

If it is argued that in the second alternative mentioned in the Bhāṣya, the formation of the compound is indeed untenable because both the qualifier and the qualified, being connected to the action in this view, function as instruments (*karaṇa*), and thus lack mutual connection due to a deficiency of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), we say: no.

This is because the objection—"In that case, [the rule] would apply even to *karma* [objects], and thus to Bhīṣma and others as well"—is answered by the *Mahābhāṣya* itself under the rule "anabhihite" (*Pāṇini* 2.3.1, *Mahābhāṣya*, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 478). The point is this: in this view, since both [the mat and the quality] possess the status of being an object (*karman*), even though the accusative case following the word *kaṭa* expresses the objecthood residing in the mat, an accusative is used after the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) as well in order to convey the objecthood residing in the qualifier. In that context, the production denoted by the root *kṛ* belongs to the quality only through the medium of the substance; likewise, the status of being an object for [actions such as] giving and so forth [is understood in the same way].

Karma (the object) is not perceived as a direct indicator [of the action], but rather through the medium of a substance (*dravya*). Thus, just as the locus of the fruit (*phala*) is directly the substratum, so too the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and so forth belongs even to the locus of the fruit through the medium of a substance. And in this view, the qualifier is a distinct indicator by virtue of its possession of a specific power (*śakti*); however, because qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are non-different from the substance, that power is not specifically grasped in the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). In this view as well, as in the previously mentioned view, the connection with the action occurs only after the mutual connection between the qualifier and the qualified has taken place.

Nor is there a loss of the rule regarding the connection of factors (*kāraka*) with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). For those factors that produce the action directly are connected with it directly; however, for those that produce it through another medium, their connection with the action occurs through that medium. Thus, since this is indeed the rule, there is no loss of it. By this, the objection that [the connection] contradicts the principle "and because subordinate elements (*guṇa*) exist for the sake of another" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.22) regarding mutual connection is refuted. This is because, according to the aforementioned method, the relationship of quality and qualified (*guṇaguṇibhāva*) exists, and thus there is an absence of equality [between the factors]. And this alone is logical.

But it is not the case that first there is a cognition of the connection with the verb for both [the object and the agent], and then a subsequent (pārṣṭika) cognition of their mutual connection; for that would involve the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava) in postulating two separate cognitions, and because such a sequence of cognition is never experienced.

Furthermore, there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether the primary syntactic connection with the verb is for the sake of the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the case-ending, while the compound itself attains correctness by taking its primary mutual connection, and the case-endings attain correctness by taking a subsequent connection; or whether the compound itself attains correctness by taking its primary mutual connection, while the case-ending attains correctness through its subsequent connection with the verb. Indeed, this construction of alternative views is intended solely to justify the use of the accusative case.

Just as the author of the Bhāṣya [Patañjali] assumes the division into *prakṛti* (base), *pratyaya* (suffix), and so forth for the author of the Sūtras [Pāṇini], there is no difference here in the understanding [of the meaning]. Because a compound would be ungrammatical (*asādhutva*) by virtue of its subsequent syntactic connection (*pārṣṭikānvaya*), there is no compound formation for vocative forms such as in "rājabṛndāraka" and the like. {For this very reason} in this case, one must proceed with a sentence of equivalent meaning. And since the object intended here is understood through a sentence, it is never understood through a compound. The address to a constituent part is understood through a sentence;

This accords with what is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra "naṅi saṃbuddhyoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.8; *MaBh*, Tṛtīyakhaṇḍa, p. 378), namely that there is a vocative address to the aggregate (*samudāyasaṃbodhana*) in the case of "samapsne. Kaiyaṭa also [holds this view], stating that when two parts have distinct meanings are being addressed, there can be no mutual capacity (*sāmarthya*) characterized by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

The intention of the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa is that since the meaning of the vocative case is a restatement (*anuvādya*) and thus connects with the predicate (*vidheya*), and since the action (*kriyā*) is itself the predicate, both [the vocative and the noun] connect with the action; consequently, there is no mutual connection between them, and thus the possibility of "single-meaningness" (*ekārthībhāva*) does not arise. In your view, however, since it can be argued that even here—as in examples such as *nīlam utphalam*—there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) through a subsequent connection (*pārṣṭikānvaya*), the inconsistency with the Bhāṣya and other works is quite evident.

Therefore, according to the method stated by me, in cases such as "anīlam utphalam" (a blue lotus), although each member possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) for the sake of producing its respective accusative case-ending, there is indeed semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) because only those members that are mutually related are connected with the verb; thus, there is no impossibility of forming a compound. In the case of the vocative, however, the vocative case-ending occurs in both instances only when each member individually faces [the speaker]; therefore, it is not equivalent to a qualifying case-ending, and the aforementioned method does not apply there.

In the third alternative mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*—namely, that the mat (*kaṭa*) itself is the object (*karman*) because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Bhīṣma and others—the accusative case ending is applied to "Bhīṣma" and so on, even though they lack the status of being the object themselves, by virtue of the object-status residing in their own qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Kaiyaṭa explains: "Just as those who are the dear friends of the Lord, though themselves poor, partake of the fruit [of wealth] solely through the Lord's wealth, so too [is it here], because they share the same welfare and security (*ekayogakṣema*) as Him. (From the *Mahābhāṣya-pradīpa*, Pratyāhāra-khaṇḍa, p. [X]). This refers to the rule *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1).

480) This is the intended meaning: what is called grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the capacity to convey a single referent. If there were a difference in the powers (*śakti*) of the qualifier and the qualified, then, due to that difference in power, there would be a difference in referents, and thus the unity of referent would be destroyed. Therefore, qualifiers that are non-different from [the qualified] possess the same power as the qualified; hence, they must have identical case-endings. Just like being the locus of the result (*phala*), so too is coreferentiality a regulator of those respective powers.

And thus, since the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final conclusion (siddhānta) form a single coherent statement, even in this view, it is appropriate that the cognition of the connection with one element occurs only when there is already a mutual connection [within the compound], according to the method described above. It is clear elsewhere that the established conclusion (siddhānta) regarding the *aruṇā* section is likewise exactly so. Now, an objection may be raised: "In this case, in expressions such as ‘nīlaghaṭam ānaya’ (‘bring the blue jar’), since the objecthood (*karmatva*) exists according to the stated method, would not the accusative case ending follow the word ‘nīla’ etc. within the compound? This is not so—

Because the case-ending (*sup*) of the word *jāta* is elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), and because the compound presents only the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), that [quality] residing therein is already expressed by the very case-ending of the subsequent qualified term. Therefore, since the three positions stated in the Bhāṣya can be explained in three ways in examples such as *śubhre taṇḍulena*, it is not appropriate for the author of the root-text (*mūlakṛt*) to assume that the case-ending of the qualifier serves either to indicate grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) or to express non-difference (*abheda*), as there is no evidence for such a claim.

Because there is no secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) in a case-ending, and because even through secondary function there is no denotation of that meaning; and because there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) for a qualifying case-ending even when used for the sake of grammatical correctness; and as for the claim that in cases such as "white rice" (*śubhraḥ taṇḍulaḥ*), the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is construed with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—which is the primary sense of the case-ending—by way of identity (*abheda*), that too is not tenable.

This is because the rule "the finite verb [is used] when there is coreferentiality" (*tiṅ samānādhikaraṇye prathamā*) and so forth teaches that a finite verb is grammatically correct only when it is connected to the action by way of its meaning as the agent or object. Furthermore, the claim that there is a connection through the relation of identity (*abhedasaṃbandha*) is also incorrect, since that [identity] lacks the status of being a relation; this was established in the discussion on the primary case-roles (*kāraka*). The phrase "having the same meaning as a compound" (*samāsasamānārthaka*) is used because, although in cases such as the *bahuvrīhi* there may be a reversal regarding the aspect of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*), there is no evidence for a reversal regarding other aspects. This will be explained further below. "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) means from the sentence (*vākya*).

Regarding the statement "between the meanings of two nouns having the same case-ending," since non-difference (*abheda*) does not extend [to the relation] due to the presence of case-endings as previously stated, he says: "devoid of contradictory case-endings. For this very reason—namely, because in a compound (*vṛtti*) the acceptance of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) results in a presentation that is not distinct [from the individual members]. As in the rule: "The first portion belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*. This is the intended sense.

In this context, the meaning of the sentence is not that "the first [act] is the consumption by the *varṣaṭkartṛ*," nor is it an injunction prescribing priority with respect to consumption; for, due to the force of *ekārthībhāva* (syntactic unification), it is impossible for there to be a relationship of subject and predicate between consumption and priority when both are conveyed by a single word. Rather, the injunction pertains to a distinct act of consumption denoted by the compound *prathamabhakṣaḥ*, while the priority is obtained through the force of the sense (*arthāt*).

And thus, where in a single instance both the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer and another person are entitled to consume the Soma—on account of the *vaṣaṭ*-call and by virtue of their respective designations (*samākhyā*)—there the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer alone should consume it first. Accordingly, Jaimini states: "And one should consume [Soma] because of the *vaṣaṭ*-call" (*Jaiminisūtra* 3.5.31). [This principle of] "single-streamedness" (*ekaprasaratā*) precludes disjunction and lack of syntactic connection.

This means "the capacity consisting in the generation of a single qualified presentation. Regarding the phrase "because of the consequence of breaking [the unity of the sentence]": since separate presentation is required when there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by way of the relation between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), the meaning is that such a connection would result in the breaking of the "single flow" (*ekaprasaratā*)—which is defined as the aforementioned capacity. This applies even to the expression "one cooks the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with three parts," where the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) is also to be supplied.

The meaning is as follows: In the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*), after describing the sacrifice through the cutting of eleven limbs—beginning with "He cuts from the heart into the fire, then from the tongue, then from the chest"—it is stated: "He cooks the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with three limbs. In that context, the sense is not that the *sviṣṭakṛt* is to be offered three times with just any one limb as determined by the context; for since the term "with three limbs" (*tryaṅgaiḥ*) is a single compound word (*samasta-pada*), it is impossible to establish a relationship between a subject and a predicate (*uddeśya-vidheya-bhāva*).

However, because of the prohibition of offering (*avadāna*) from three limbs in the primary sacrifice by the rule "but not from the two last nor from the head" (*na antyayoḥ avadyati na śiraḥ*), the *sviṣṭakṛt* must be offered with those very same limbs; therefore, here too, as before, there is indeed an injunction of a qualified limb. Consequently, in the *vṛtti*, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by way of the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*). For this very reason, there is no compound with the dative case prescribed by the rule *caturthī cāśiṣi* (Pāṇini 2.3.73). Indeed, in the domain of benediction (*āśis*), as in the example "may it be well for the guest" (*vimāya bhadraṃ bhūyāt*), the relationship between the subject and the predicate is understood.

Haradatta and others maintain that in a compound (*samāsa*), however, there would be no such comprehension [of the relation between subject and predicate]. In reality, the absence of connection by way of the relationship between subject (*uddeśya*) and predicate (*vidheya*) is not caused by *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning). This is because it was not stated so by the author of the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, being the subject and being the predicate are suggested by the proximity of the words *yat* and *tat*; and since in a compound, words such as *ṛddha* (prosperous) cannot be construed with the word *yat*, there is no connection by way of the relationship between subject and predicate.

Furthermore, even though there is a state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), because such a connection is absent in cases like *ghaṭam* and the like, and because such a connection exists in compounds like *abhyāsalopaśca*, the [intended] function is not established by that alone. Moreover, in cases such as *lohitoṣṇīṣāḥ* ("those with red turbans"), since turbans are already obtained through another sentence such as *soṣṇīṣāḥ*, the cognition of "redness" occurs precisely by aiming at the turbans according to the maxim of "discrimination between what is obtained and what is not obtained" (*prāptāprāptavivekanyāya*). Therefore, the application of the compound in that cognition is not incorrect.

Furthermore, in the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57), the Vārttika states, "because both are qualifiers," or "because both are the qualified"; thus, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), it is observed that the referent of the two words [in the compound] is the subject (*uddeśyatva*) and the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) is the predicate (*vidheyatva*).

For this very reason, such compound sentences were not cited by Mammaṭa, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* (in the seventh chapter, the "Chapter on Defects"), under the defect of "corrupted syntax" (*cyutasaṃskṛti*), but rather only under the defect of "unconsidered predication" (*āvimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa*). The seed of its defectiveness lies solely in the aversion of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) resulting from the abandonment of the general rule that there must be a syntactic connection between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) as they are presented separately. Furthermore, in the example cited, there is no compound with a word ending in the dative case which is the object of a benediction (*āśis*).

Even in the case of *vipra* and *bhadra*, because they lack mutual semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) due to their connection with meanings that are mutually exclusive, there is no such understanding [of the compound] from the outset. Therefore, for one who is proficient in that manner regarding compounds and the like, that understanding certainly arises. This is because, even when a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is presented, there is no obstacle to accepting [the presence of] the status of being a qualificand (*uddeśyatā*) and so forth in the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the rest, just as one accepts the status of being a mode (*prakāratā*) and so forth.

For this very reason, there is no inconsistency with the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *dvitīyāṭaussvena* (Pāṇini 2.4.34), which intends to address both the concern regarding the replacement by *enad* etc. in examples such as *etacchritaḥ* and its subsequent resolution based on that replacement not being motivated (*aprayuktatva*). Otherwise, if followed by your reasoning, there would be the consequence of inconsistency, since an *anvādeśa*—which consists of the re-introduction of an element already employed to prescribe one operation for the purpose of prescribing another operation—would be impossible.

This is because, even in cases such as "the yellow-robed, four-armed, wise Brahmin," when a compound is employed with the intention of such a connection (anvaya), the resulting cognition is desired after considering factors such as the attainment [of the meaning]. By this, it is established that in a *karmadhāraya* compound like "wise-Brahmin" (*paṇḍitabrāhmaṇa*), just as in a sentence, the notion of a relationship between the subject and the predicate (*uddeśya-vidheyabhāva*) is excluded; therefore, "single-meaningness" (*ekārthībhāva*) is resorted to for the sake of a single unified presentation (*ekopasthiti*).

Otherwise, since the relationship of qualifier and qualified is possible between the two meanings presented by the individual powers of the word-parts, resorting to that [relationship] would be entirely redundant. For this very reason, in the case of the statement "The first draught belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer," it is simply an injunction of a different draught; the view that it is an injunction of priority with reference to a draught already obtained through the connection with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer by virtue of the name "the *hotṛ*’s cup" is thereby refuted.

Objection: If, according to the stated method, the comprehension of the relation between the qualificand (*uddeśya*) and the qualifier (*vidheya*) is accepted as occurring within the compound (*vṛtti*), then the postulation of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning) in a *karmadhāraya* is useless; for it cannot be established by the stated method.

Nor can it be argued that such a postulation is made to prevent the non-connection of one qualifier with another qualifier; for it has already been stated that this is not the result of that [postulation]. Response: This is not so—

Just as in the sentence "that which is blue and that which is a lotus," the word *ca* ("and") is not employed in the compound because a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is resorted to there; for this very reason, having raised the objection regarding a *dvandva* (copulative) compound here, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* that it does not apply because the *karmadhāraya* (descriptive determinative) compound takes precedence due to its lack of occasion. Therefore, the coexistence of either the two grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) or the two substrata (*dharmin*) appears. And thus, the cognition is either "the collection of 'blue-ness' and 'lotus-ness'" or "the lotus, which is non-different from that [blue] and is coreferential with blue"; the details of this are found elsewhere.

Regarding the phrase "the first consumption" (*prathamabhakṣa*), however, since direct statement (*vākya*) and direct audition (*śruti*) are stronger than conventional designation (*samākhyā*), it should be understood that by this [word] alone, the injunction for another consumption occurs first. [The notes] "and it is consistent" and "otherwise" mean: if one were to accept an additional power (*atiriktaśakti*) in a compound.

This is the point: in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, when the doubt arises as to whether the quality of redness (*aruṇa*), being separated from its syntactical context, enters into all substances within the ritual procedure (*prakaraṇa*), or whether it connects with the act of buying (*krīṇāti*) and thus belongs to that single one-year-old cow (*ekahāyinī*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was established as follows: "If it were connected with the act of buying, it would become an instrumental factor (*karaṇakāraka*) due to its connection with the third case ending. But since it is impossible for an incorporeal thing to be so [an instrument], it has no connection with the act of buying. Therefore, being separate and lacking any specific distinction, it enters into every substance mentioned in the context simply by virtue of being a word denoting a quality."

Nor should it be argued that, since the substance implied by that [word] can serve as the means for purchase, its connection should be with the verb *krīṇāti* (to buy) alone; otherwise, there would be no inclusion even within the context (*prakaraṇa*), because—due to its incorporeality—it cannot be connected with actions, and due to its being a factor (*kāraka*), it cannot be connected with substances.

Because, when the purchase is restricted to the *ekahāyanī* cow prescribed by the *śruti*, it is impossible for that [quality of redness] to be connected [to the purchase]. Furthermore, that prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is specifically appropriate regarding the aspect of redness; even if one does not accept a collective power (*samāsa-śakti*), since the words *piṅgākṣī* and *ekahāyanī*—like the word *aruṇā*—refer to the substance either through implication (*ākṣepa*) or through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), they lack the status of being directly stated by the *śruti*. Therefore, the prima facie position is also appropriate regarding that aspect.

"Direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is independent [of other means of knowledge]"—this is Āpadeva’s definition of the authority of *śruti* among the six means of proof. For that which is understood as dependent upon the cognition of the impossibility of connecting with other word-meanings is indeed indicative (*lākṣaṇika*); otherwise, even the substance indicated by the word *aruṇā* ("red") would have to be considered directly stated (*śrauta*).

Alternatively, since the *bahuvrīhi* compound is prescribed only when there is a relationship (*sambandha*) that serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the cognition produced by the other words, just like the word *aruṇā*, these two [words *piṅgākṣī* and *sāmnī*] also denote only a quality in the form of a relationship. Because these [qualities] are incorporeal, they cannot function as instruments (*karaṇatva*) in the act of buying; thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—which would have to split the sentence (*vākyabheda*) to apply redness alone—is impossible. Furthermore, the proponent of the prima facie view considers the feminine suffix (*ṭāp*) to be a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*), and he does not understand that words denoting qualities take on the gender of their substratum (*āśrayaliṅgagrāhitva*).

Furthermore, one does not perceive an identity between the relation and the related entity. Moreover, if an additional power (*śakti*) were admitted, the *bahuvrīhi* compound would denote a substance; since it would then be possible for that substance to be construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of buying, there would be no suspicion of those two [the relation and the related] being construed with the contextual substance through a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Thus, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established regarding that specific portion.

The conclusion that the word *aruṇā* (red) denotes the quality by way of identity with the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), and that the substance possessing the quality is proximate because it is heard in the sentence—namely, "only the one-year-old cow"—is consistent only through the acceptance of a qualified denotative power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*). Otherwise, since the substance possessing the quality is proximate as being heard in the sentence through the word *ekahāyanī* itself, the conclusion that "only the one-year-old cow" applies would likewise be untenable without accepting a qualified denotative power.

Otherwise, since the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) itself would be the denoter of the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), it would be impossible for it to denote the quality through identity (*tādātmya*). Furthermore, the reading "gavā" is not an authentic (archaic) one. By this, those who—claiming that if a qualified power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) is not admitted, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of this section would be inconsistent—conclude that the Vedic reading must be taken as including the word "gavā," are refuted. For this very reason, the author of the root-text stated, "there is no sublation of the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*," and not, "the prima facie view of the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*."

It is clearly stated elsewhere (Mīmāṃsādarśana 3.2.17) that the connection with the section on *aindrapīta* (the Indra-drunk cup) is established precisely because of the acceptance of a distinct power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*). As for the claim that in a compound such as "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*), there is no distinct power, but rather that the cognition of the qualified meaning arises merely through the recollection of that qualified object—which was previously experienced from a sentence having the same meaning as the compound—triggered by the hearing of the words in their derivative form (*vṛtti*) accompanied by the knowledge of the powers of the constituent parts (*avayavaśakti*); [this is incorrect].

Therefore, because there is a state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with qualifiers and the like. Since the *arthavat* sūtra (Pāṇini 1.2.45) includes the capacity to present a meaning through the cooperation of the knowledge of its own constituent parts, a compound (*sāmāsa*) possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In the case of "prāptodaka" and similar forms, even though the analysis (*vigraha*) is "this belongs to one who has obtained water," the understanding is that it is "related to one who has obtained water. And this relation consists in being the object of the attainment performed by that person, and so forth.

Alternatively, even in a compound (*samāsa*), there is a mutual connection only between those two elements that are presented as distinct, just as in a sentence (*vākya*). However, the distinction from a sentence is this: in a compound, the presentation of the words constituting the formation results in a mutual connection between them first in a single form, due to the very nature of the formation (*vṛtti*); therefore, in this case, there is no connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth. In a sentence, however, at the very moment the king is connected to the substantive (*viśeṣya*), prosperity (*ṛddhatva*) is simultaneously connected to the king; thus, because there is no cognition of [the king] being a mere part [of a larger complex], there is no connection in the manner of subject and predicate (*uddeśya-vidheya-bhāvena*), as implied by the phrase "in a single form."

Alternatively, there is the presentation of the qualified [referent], such as "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*), through *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Even if one does not accept a power (*śakti*) for the qualified [compound] itself, the status of being a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is established by the mere presentation of the qualified referent; thus, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the qualifier and so forth. (34) Refuting the Mīmāṃsaka position—which holds that the *karmadhāraya* is simpler because the *lakṣaṇā* in *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compounds and the like has a wider scope consisting of a relation (*sambandha*)—he says: "In cases such as *rājapuruṣa*... and so on. In that context, regarding the secondary derivative (*taddhita*): "...the reverse," and so on.

The meaning is that there is a reversal: although a *taddhita* suffix and the like are prescribed for meanings such as those expressed by verbal roots ending in *tiṅ* (finite verb endings) where the action (*bhāva*) is predominant, they nevertheless have substance (*satva*) as their predominance. He states this with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*), etc. The mention of *kṛt* suffixes is illustrative; it includes *taddhita* suffixes as well. Regarding the phrase "there is a subverting argument" (*bādhakam asti*): even if one assumes [the predominance of substance] in the aforementioned instances in order to maintain the identity of meaning between a compound (*vṛtti*) and its analytical sentence (*vākya*), this is not understood in cases where elision (*aluk*) does not occur, such as in "father's son" (*pituḥ putra*). [This is because] the rule "the *bahuvrīhi* is used in the sense of possession" (*matvarthe bahuvrīhiḥ*)—[as stated in] "when there are multiple words, it expresses another meaning" (*anekam anyapadārthe*, Pāṇini 2.2.24)—is intended to prevent the application of the *bahuvrīhi* when the meaning is already expressed by a single word. Thus, the *bahuvrīhi* is prescribed specifically to avoid redundancy when the meaning is not otherwise conveyed. Therefore, since the *bahuvrīhi* is not applied in cases like "father's son," it follows that in the case of "cow's horn" (*gośṛṅga*), the meaning is indeed understood through the single word "cow" (*go*), and thus the *bahuvrīhi* is not employed. Consequently, the *taddhita* suffix is not applied to express the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi*. Hence, the *taddhita* suffix is prescribed for meanings other than those of the *bahuvrīhi*. This is the subverting argument. Furthermore, in the case of "cow's horn," the relationship of inherence (*samavāya*) is understood from the single word "cow. If the *taddhita* were applied to express that same relationship, it would result in a tautology (*punarukti*). Therefore, the *taddhita* suffix is not applied to express the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi*. This is the subverting argument. Moreover, in the case of "father's son," the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is understood from the single word "father. Furthermore, [your position] contradicts the statements of the Sage (Pāṇini), such as: "The *bahuvrīhi* occurs when there is a sense other than that of the first case-ending" (*aprathamāvibhaktyarthe bahuvrīhiḥ*), "The *bahuvrīhi* is the remainder" (*śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ*, sūtra 2.2.23)—where "remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to [all case-endings] except the first three—and "The remainder is [everything] except the first three" (*trikataḥ śeṣaḥ*, Mahābhāṣya, Prauḍhamanoramā, p. 443). Nor can it be argued that while words ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) and so forth enter into the non-ordinary (*alaukika*) sentence, it is only words ending in the sixth case and so forth that enter into the ordinary (*laukika*) sentence, and thus there is no contradiction with those [rules].

For those who have entered the supramundane [system], once they have reached a definitive conclusion within an alternative view (*pakṣāntara*)—where no compound exists—it would be improper to abandon what is already present and instead postulate a mundane analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) composed of words not present in the original, even if such a usage were possible for the sake of communicating that meaning. Furthermore, the employment of that sentence is not solely for the purpose of conveying the meaning; it is also intended to demonstrate the optional nature (*vaikalpikatva*) of the compound. And according to the aforementioned method, that which demonstrates this is precisely "one whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya*) and so forth, but not your version.

For this very reason, the elders state: "An *avigraha* is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*). Otherwise, since the phrase "the maker of a jar" (*kumbhasya kartā*), which has the same meaning as "potter" (*kumbhakāra*), could theoretically exist, the status of that [latter] as a compulsory compound would be undermined. If it is argued that the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) is not a constituent of the compound, then by the same logic—since the application of the term "compound" occurs in the non-standard (*alaukika*) stage—the word "of the variegated ones" (*citrāṇām*) and so forth would likewise not be a constituent, and thus the undesired consequence (*āpatti*) would follow that these too are compulsory compounds. (ka-vṛtta = vṛttimat)

Nor should it be argued that the analysis *yasya citrā* (of whom there is a brindled cow) may also be accepted as an optional alternative, since even a dissolved form (*vigraha*) is used for the purpose of determining the meaning; for it is only when a sentence composed of the constituent words of a compound is impossible that a compound is considered "obligatory" (*nityasamāsa*), and thus the [dissolved form] cannot belong to the *bahuvrīhi*. This is because it would result in the simultaneous employment of two sentences for the sake of two distinct results.

Furthermore, in your statement—that the analysis (*vigraha*) is the antonym of the compound (*samāsa*) meaning "the state of being one," and that it implies the non-apprehension of the distinctness of the words constituting the compound—there is the impossibility of using such a construction as "this [is] of variegated cows" (*citrāṇāṃ gavām ayam*) in a sentence. Moreover, in the first alternative, for those who do not know such an analytical sentence, it is impossible to justify the specific presentation (*viśiṣṭopasthiti*) without postulating a primary expressive power (*śakti*).

Because it is impossible [to establish such a definition]. In the second case—regarding the statement that "the *vṛtti* is the cause of such a cognition"—the assumption of a *śakti* (potency) is more parsimonious than the assumption of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Furthermore, since the status of being a cause of cognition is untenable without a relation, a relation in the form of *śakti* is established. Moreover, since the state of being a *vṛtti* consists simply in being the locus of *vṛtti*, the status of compounds (*samāsa*) and so forth as *vṛtti*s would not be established [under the first two definitions]. In the third case—regarding cognition... (P. 02)

Because it is improper to speak of a qualified presentation through that [secondary signification] without a knowledge of the definition consisting in the relation between the word and its own denoted object; furthermore, since even words such as *paṅkaja* (lotus) would result in having secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) only with respect to the property of being a word, this would lead to the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*).

If it is argued that even in the case of a forest (*vana*), a secondary power (*lakṣaṇā*) is postulated there because of the recognition of sublation (*bādhādipratisandhāna*) and so forth, this applies equally to the compound (*vṛtti*) as well. Furthermore, since there is no cognition of anything other than the primary denotation (*śakya*) in a *karmadhāraya* compound, a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate; for in all cases, secondary signification is observed to consist in the cognition of a related meaning based on a connection with the primary denotation. If it is argued that the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣyaviśeṣaṇabhāva*) is likewise [the basis], then because that is already cognized in the sentence (*vākya*), it would follow that there is a single presentation (*ekopasthiti*) even in that case. This is the general direction of the argument.

Therefore, according to the method I have stated, even when there is a reversal of the qualifier and the qualified due to the force of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning), there is no loss of the identity of meaning between the compound (*vṛtti*) and the analytical sentence (*vākya*). Thus, the analysis (*vigraha*) for "rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ" (the king's man) and "citrā gāvo yasya" (he whose cows are brindled) is precisely as given. Furthermore, "identity of meaning" consists simply in having the same object (*viṣaya*); one need not insist on the stricter requirement that they must have both the same mode (*prakāra*) and the same qualificandum (*viśeṣya*).

In reality, however, even from a constructed sentence such as "citrā gāvo yasya" (he whose cows are variegated), which is intended merely to illustrate the meaning of the *vṛtti*, the understanding is precisely "one who has a connection with variegated cows," due to the transposition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*). It is for the sake of making this transposition known that the elders demonstrate it as "citragu. For this very reason, in the section on the technical name *sarvanāman* (pronoun), the *Mahābhāṣya* also states: "those of which 'sarva' is the first" (*sarvādīni sarvanāmāni*, sūtra 1.1.27; MaBh Pra-kha-pṛ).

203) This analysis (*vigraha*) has been demonstrated. However, because a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) generally refers to the predominant element, the teacher Kaiyaṭa maintains that in the expression "the owner of brindled cows" (*citraguḥ*), the predominance of the owner is shown by this [pronoun]. For this very reason, they demonstrate the analysis of "born after a month" (*māsajāta*) as "he who is born after a month" (*māsasya jātaḥ saḥ*).

Alternatively, in the sentence "he whose cows are brindled is the owner of brindled cows" (*citragavo yasya sa citraguḥ*), the word *citragu* refers to that which is to be understood by it; the cognition is that he who possesses a connection with brindled cows is the one denoted by the word *citragu*. Thus, the identity of meaning between the compound (*vṛtti*) and its analysis (*vigraha*) is quite evident.

A *vigraha* (analytic expansion) is a sentence directed toward three objectives: the meaning of the compound (*vṛttyartha*), the optional nature of its occurrence (*vṛttivaikalpikatva*), and the specific forms of the words constituting that occurrence (*vṛttighaṭakapadasvarūpa*). Consequently, in a detached sentence such as "he whose cows are brindled" (*citrā gāvo yasya*)—employed independently in common usage for the sake of conveying meaning—the relationship between qualifier and qualified remains exactly as it stands, because there arises the cognition: "the brindled cows belong to him. For this very reason, after beginning with the statement that in certain cases the status of objects as qualifiers is not intended [to be expressed], Hari [Bhartṛhari] says...

It has been stated: "Whatever indicates the meaning of a verb, a primary suffix (*kṛt*), or a secondary suffix (*taddhita*)—in that case, a reversal of the status of the subordinate and the principal is observed. (Vākyapadīya, Vākyakāṇḍa II, Kārikā 306). (The reading *taddhitakṛtoḥ* is found in current editions.)

The meaning is as follows: since secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) prescribed in senses such as "he plays" (*dīvyati*) have the means of action (*sādhana*) as their primary referent, it is observed that in the case of the verbal forms *dīvyati* etc. occurring in the sūtra and in the corresponding analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), the predominance of the abstract state (*bhāva*)—which is the reverse of the subordinate-predominant relationship seen in relation to the word *dāsīna-dīvyati*—is observed. Otherwise, the identity of meaning between the derivative formation (*vṛtti*) and its analysis (*vigraha*) would be lost. However, the interpretation stated in the root text—that a reversal is observed in the case of the secondary derivative—is not tenable, because it does not accord with the natural sense of the words.

This is because it is appropriate for the *tat* word to refer back to that very *pradhāna* (principal) which was previously referred to by the *yat* word; furthermore, because the meaning of the term "contrary" (*viparyaya*) consists precisely in the acceptance of another quality after abandoning a previously perceived quality within the same substratum; and because the author of the Bhāṣya did not count the reversal of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified as a result of the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). Moreover, in cases such as *prāptodaka*, if one were to postulate an additional reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship even in words like *prāpta*, it would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, there would be a violation of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—defined as the capacity to denote a single substratum—which is presupposed by a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Moreover, in cases such as *prāptabāryā*, since the preceding and following words lack the coreferentiality consisting in the generation of a cognition having a single qualificand, the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would erroneously apply. Therefore, in examples such as *prāptodaka*, the meaning of both the derivative formation (*vṛtti*) and its analytical expansion (*vigraha*) is precisely "the water which is the object [of the action] of reaching, [as qualified by] that which is non-different from the agent of reaching," and so forth.

However, due to the sublation (*bādha*) of the property of being the object (*karmatva*) in "water" (*udake*), the [denotative function] culminates in the qualifier "attainment" (*prāpti*), just as in the case of the expression "one who has perished while in heaven" (*svargīdhvasta*). On this view, there is no fault even if the state of having the same meaning consists in having the same qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) provided that there is the same mode of presentation (*prakāra*). Although the case-meaning (*vibhaktyartha*) is predominant, it should be understood that the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*) occurs through identity (*tādātmyena*). (8) (35) — 2 *Śakti* — 2. The meaning is: a specific power (*śakti*) which effects the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

"—2 Regarding the rule *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa-karmadhārayayoḥ*—2|| This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *bahuvrīhi*. It must be stated that the *bahuvrīhi* is *bahiraṅga* (extrinsic) because it brings about a cognition whose object is the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*), which lies outside the meanings of the constituent members (*vartipada*)."

And that [complex] is not possible here, because in the case of the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*), there exists a qualified denotative capacity (*viśiṣṭaśakyatva*) distinct from each individual component; thus, as in the case of words such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), it would simply be its own word-meaning. Therefore, he will say: "The *niṣāda-svāmika* [compound]"—this means the establishment of the final conclusion (*siddhāntasiddhi*) that, in this case, it is a *karmadhāraya* due to parsimony (*lāghava*). [Objection: "It would not [be so]. The sense is that since all three [members] are equally possessors of denotative power (*śaktimat*), there is no parsimony.

In the root [text]: *paryavaśyaditi* (Vai.Si.Kā. 36). That which is "paryavaśya" and is also "śabdabodha" (verbal cognition)—that is so [designated]. "From that not distant" (*tasmādavidūraḥ*) refers to the preceding moment, the moment immediately prior to the locus of cognition; "situated therein" (*tatrāsthite*) is a single word ending in the locative case, serving as a qualifier for the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*). —2 "At that time" (*tadānīntana*)—2.

And thus, the literal meaning is: "by taking recourse to the parsimony (lāghava) resulting from the presentation of word-meanings prior to verbal comprehension. The ellipsis is that this is inconsistent with the root text's consideration of "being extrinsic" (bahiraṅgatva). Regarding "in the assumption of that"—that is, in the assumption of intention (tātparya) elsewhere. The *sthapati* (chief/minister) is indeed the king, precisely because he is the first to be presented [to the mind]. In the sense of a *karmadhāraya* compound—namely, "a Niṣāda who is a *sthapati*"—there is a power (*śakti*) that generates rapid presentation; however, it does not apply to a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound and the like, because that would be extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

—2—that is the intended meaning (*tātparya*). This is the sense: compared to the apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) belonging to a *tatpuruṣa* compound—which has as its object only the meaning perceived in the sentence composed of the words constituting it—the apprehension of the expressive power belonging to a collection of words designated as a *bahuvrīhi* is "external" (*bahiraṅga*), because it has as its object a different meaning beyond the meaning perceived in the sentence composed of the words constituting it. (L.)

[Note: This is an additional reading. Likewise, the genitive *tatpuruṣa* is also "extrinsic" (*bahiraṅga*) compared to the *karmadhāraya*. This is because the apprehension of the word-meaning potentiality (*śaktigraha*) belonging to the collection of words termed a *tatpuruṣa*—which has as its object an additional element in the form of the meaning of the genitive case and so forth—is more complex than the apprehension of the potentiality belonging to the *karmadhāraya*, which has as its object only that meaning perceived in the sentence composed of the constituent words of the *karmadhāraya* itself. (The word "ādi" is not seen [in the manuscript].)

Therefore, because it is the lightest of all [options], the intended meaning (tātparya) is first postulated—according to the aforementioned logic—to reside in the *karmadhāraya* compound regarding the presented sense. This is because "when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, non-coreferentiality (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*) is improper. By this, the Mīmāṃsaka claim is refuted—that the intended meaning does not reside in the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* or the *bahuvrīhi* because they are inferior due to requiring the assumption of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the prior member, whereas in the *karmadhāraya* there is no such indication.

Furthermore, in your view, even under the theory of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), there is *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) in those cases; yet, according to the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*), even in *tatpuruṣa* compounds and the like, you yourself maintain that there is no *lakṣaṇā*. Moreover, even in *karmadhāraya* compounds, *lakṣaṇā* is necessary for you as well, in order to bring about a single unified presentation (*ekopasthiti*) and thereby prevent the connection between the subject and the predicate (*uddeśyavidheyabhāva*).

Now, an objection may be raised: since the word *niṣāda* denotes a caste (*jātiśabda*) and the word *sthapati* is a quality-word (*guṇaśabda*)—being a synonym for either "lord" (*svāmin*) or "chief" (*śreṣṭha*)—and because a quality-word is necessarily a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it would follow that if a *karmadhāraya* compound were accepted according to the stated method, the qualifier would have to be placed first. Furthermore, since the meaning of *sthapati* is always in need of a correlate, even the more cumbersome *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa* (genitive compound) would be more appropriate, as in the case of *narapati* and similar terms. This is not so.

The inversion [of the compound] is due to its inclusion in the *rājadantādi* group. Furthermore, the cessation of expectancy through syntactic connection is justified because, by implication, the relationship is obtained as belonging specifically to the Niṣādas. As for the statement "the *kūṭa* is the sacrificial fee," the determination that this is a *karmadhāraya* compound is made because the mark (*liṅga*) of the form *kūṭa* is seen to be connected with the Niṣādas; for the *kūṭa*—that is, the *sīraṅga* (a specific type of weapon)—is possible only among those of the Niṣāda caste.

Moreover, even in the case of a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, since sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is generally understood as residing in something of the same class as its own qualifier, there is no distinction from a *karmadhāraya* compound; thus, the *karmadhāraya* alone is preferred. For this very reason, from words such as *narapati*, the understanding of sovereignty and so forth arises through the word *nara* itself [i.e., the sovereignty of a man]. However, in the case of *mṛgapati* and the like, because the sovereignty of one belonging to the species of deer is not understood, the term "generally" (*utsargataḥ*) was stated. If it is objected: "But how can he perform sacrifices (*yājana*) when study (*adhyayana*) is impossible for him?"—we say no. This is because, in the absence of any other recourse, one may assume that he has studied what is necessary for the purpose. This is the direction of the argument. (9) (36) Thus ends the section.
