—0—0|| Śrīḥ || Regarding the verse from the *Vaiśeṣikasūtrakārikā* (37): "In the apprehension of power (*śakti*), [the relation] is internal," since power is present there and is the primary cause for determining the meaning, the author defines power. In the root text, this is done with the verse beginning: "Of the sense organs... (VS kā. 37). [This is also cited in] the *Vākyapadīya* (III, Sambandhasamuddeśa, kā. 29). In the phrase "in jars and so forth" (*ghaṭādiṣu*), the locative case indicates the object (*viṣaya*). "Cognizability" (*vijñeyatā*) consists of the nature of being produced [by cognition]. Furthermore, the term "jars and so forth" (*ghaṭādipada*) refers to the cognition whose object is the jar and so on.

And thus—the meaning is as follows: just as there is an eternal capacity for production residing in the sense organ, which is defined by the state of being produced (*janyatā*) residing in a cognition whose object is a jar or the like; so too, there is an eternal capacity for production residing in the word, which is defined by the state of being produced residing in a cognition whose object is the referent (*artha*). This is what is meant by "power" (*śakti*). He states this with the words "tadīyeti" (belonging to that). In reality, however, the meaning of this passage from the *Dharigrantha* is quite different, as is clear elsewhere. Furthermore, this "capacity to convey meaning" (*bodhakatva*) is indeed a distinct category (*padārthāntara*).

[Objection: Let that [causal capacity] be simply the will of God; there is no need to accept a separate category of entity. [Reply: No, because among the will, knowledge, and effort of God, there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) to establish any one of them as being that power. Otherwise, if one were to accept that [the power of] denotation exists even in those [three], there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), since the quality of being a denoter (*bodhakatā*) exists even in words used in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*). This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, "knowledge of the convention" (*saṃketajñāna*) means knowledge of the convention in its capacity as a convention.

"—*Agṛhītaśaktikāt*—" means from a word whose convention (*saṃketa*) has not been grasped. "—*Sāmānyataḥ*"—means precisely from a general property (*sāmānyadharma*). (V2: by way of delimitation through a general property). "—*Mīmāṃsakādīnām*"—refers to those who do not accept the existence of God (*anīśvaravādin*). By the phrase "the cognition of that object," both points are indicated: the necessity of the power (*śakti*) consisting in being a generator of cognition, and the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) [of the cause] in the view of those who maintain that the apprehension of that [power] is the cause. "—*Tat*"—means convention (*saṃketa*). (P.)

"This state is not perceived" [means] "only through the knowledge of the convention (*saṃketa*). Here, "convention" means "will" (*icchā*). Thus he says: "In that case also, this..."—[the phrase] "by way of immersion" means by way of embracing [the object] through dependence on will. The sense is that the knowledge of being a signifier (*bodhakatājñāna*) is the cause, whether by way of dependence or independence, in whatever manner it may be. He raises an objection with "If not..."—[the phrase] "because of the consequence of grasping that" [is used]. Regarding the first [of the two alternatives], it is quite clear that, by way of dependence on the meaning of the negative particle (*na*), there is the property of having the generation of a cognition qualified by the word as its object (*padaviśeṣyakabodhajanakatvaprakārakatvam*).

Regarding the second [definition], however, the point is that both types of cognition possess such a nature: namely, having as their qualifier the property of being a producer of a cognition whose qualificandum is restricted to the object, whose mode is restricted to the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*), and whose mode is restricted to a mode residing in the cognition itself, through the relation of possessing a generativity (*janakatā*) that is qualified by a generativity (*janyatva*) which is in turn qualified by that [first] mode. Regarding the first [definition], he says: "by non-sublation" (*abādhena*). This is to be connected with the phrase "due to impossibility" (*asaṃbhavāt*). Regarding the second, he says: "the apprehension of another" (*paragraham*).

"Otherwise"—that is, if a cognition possessing that [erroneous] mode were a cause even in the presence of a sublation (*bādha*). "Of one who knows the error" means: the consequence would follow that one who knows another's error—such as someone who themselves knows "this is not silver," yet knows another's error thinking "this is silver"—would himself be erroneous. In reality, the apprehension of a sublation is not an obstacle to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), because even at the time of having the cognition "the mountain is not possessed of fire," the verbal comprehension "the mountain is possessed of fire" can still arise.

Nor should it be argued that there would be no activity on the part of one seeking fire; for, due to the sublation-cognition from the previous moment, the verbal cognition arising immediately thereafter is apprehended as being invalid. It is only a cognition unassailed by the apprehension of invalidity that serves as the motivator for action.

Where there is a sublation-cognition (*bādhajñāna*) immediately following the verbal cognition, since the cause—consisting in the absence of a sublation-cognition—is present beforehand, you too must necessarily admit the postulation of non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*) in order to prevent activity toward that verbal cognition once it has arisen. In reality, however, a sublation-cognition is not an inhibitor of cognition in general, nor is its absence a cause [of activity], because [the prevention of activity] is sufficiently explained by the mere apprehension of non-validity.

The word "eva" (only) is not seen [in the text]. Thus, semantic competency (*yogyatā*) is not the cause of comprehension, nor is the ascertainment of its absence an obstacle to it; for comprehension arises even from an incompatible expression such as "he sprinkles with fire. However, it has been explained below that in such cases, the lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*) is apprehended in the comprehension due to the cognition of incompatibility. [The phrase] "from the knowledge of that" means from the knowledge of the convention established by the father and others. [The phrase] "because it is desired" means...

Even according to the primary view—that "superimposition of the delimitor of impossibility" (*aśakyatāvacchedakāropa*) constitutes *lakṣaṇā*—the bank (*tīra*) is sublated only in its form as a "flow" (*pravāhatva*). Furthermore, "flow-ness" (*pravāhatva*) is superimposed there [upon the bank]. For this very reason, because the word "Ganges" (*gaṅgā*) is well-known (*prasiddha*) in the sense of a flow, it possesses primacy (*mukhyatva*); whereas because it is not well-known in the sense of "bank-ness" (*tīratva*), it possesses secondary status (*gauṇatva*). (Note: In all manuscripts, the reading appears as "well-known in the sense of bank-ness" (*tīratvaprasiddha*); however, as that is inappropriate here, I have adopted "not well-known" [*aprasiddha*] based on the Prakrit manuscript.)

It is considered to be a scribal error; and such is the conventional usage. [The phrase] "due to commonality" means: for this very reason, the traditional maxim that "all words denote all meanings" is consistent. [The phrase] "deviation" means: because [the word] has a single delimited causal function in the form of being a verbal cognition (śābdabuddhi).

And it is not by way of the relation of "immediately following" (avyavahitottaratva)—this should also be understood as being by way of "co-referentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya). Thus, the meaning is: with respect to a verbal cognition qualified by a conceptual representation produced by [the word's] power, by way of both these relations—namely, co-referentiality with itself and immediately following itself. The inclusion of the first relation is for the purpose of preventing comprehension by taking into account a conceptual representation occurring at a different time within a single self; the second is for the purpose of preventing that same [undesired] comprehension by taking into account such a representation within a different self.

Regarding the case where the cause is not included within the delimitor of the effectness (or the effectness itself), he says: "Because of deviation" (*vyabhicāra*). Regarding the case where it is included therein, he says: "And because of complexity" (*gaurava*). "In the cognition of the capacity, [the relation of] cause and effect" means: the cognition of the capacity that "the word 'jar' and so forth is the signifier of that object" with respect to the cognition of an object qualified by jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*). "For the sake of exclusion, [the term] 'immediately preceding'" [is used].

The meaning is as follows: by way of the relation of *nirukta* (etymological derivation), a word such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) conveys its respective object; thus, in the cognition of an object qualified by the knowledge of such a power (*śakti*), the causality exists by virtue of being that very knowledge of power (*śaktijñānatvena*). Regarding the phrase "due to the delusion of power" (*śaktibhrāmāt*): this will be explained immediately hereafter. Consequently, since the causal relationship—composed of the knowledge of power regarding the respective delusions of words—exists for you as well in accordance with that [delusion], the point is that there is parity (*sāmya*). The term "by me" (*mayā*) refers to the proponent of *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

"Of either one" (*anyataratvasya*) means "of that which consists in being different from or non-different from that. "Because of complexity" (*gauravāt*) is the reason (*hetu*); "the state of being a cause" (*hetutā*) is the predicate. The ellipsis to be supplied is "with respect to the presentation of the word-meaning" (*padārthopasthitiṃ prati*). In this way, it should also be understood that in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the state of being a cause is precisely by virtue of being the presentation of the word-meaning produced by the knowledge of the expressive power (*śaktijñāna*). "Because of its inclusion" (*praveśāt*): the sense is that, since the knowledge of the expressive power is also necessarily required for a cognition produced by *lakṣaṇā* (which consists in a relation to the expressible), the state of being a cause is by that [knowledge of power] alone. "Of having the same object" (*samānaviṣayatvasya*): [this refers to the requirement that the two cognitions share a common objective domain].

The meaning is as follows: the cognition of the word "pot" (*ghaṭa-pada*) has the status of a cause with respect to the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) whose object is the referent of the word "pot," by virtue of its being a knowledge of the word "pot's" denotative power (*śakti*) regarding that referent. Otherwise—that is, if one does not accept that the relation of cause and effect must have the same object—one would [erroneously] conclude that there is a knowledge of the denotative power of the word "Ganges" (*gaṅgā-pada-śakti*) [with respect to the bank]. The phrase "in the current" (*pravāhe*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. And the phrase "and one remembers the elephant" implies that this is a case of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) where multiple items are presented as the objects of the cognition. Having thus explained the knowledge of denotative power with respect to a specific part [of the meaning], [the author proceeds].

"Leaving aside"—(the variant reading is "not from you," etc.)—he states the apprehension of the word-meaning in the same way: "from words such as 'jar' (*ghaṭa-pada*)," etc. "The elephant-driver" (*hastipaka*) means one who controls the elephant. "By being produced by the *vṛtti*"—this means "by being produced by the expressive power (*śakti*)" with respect to the [specific] part. What is the fault in that? To this he says: "And thus," etc.; "If it were so," etc.—this means "if one accepts, according to the stated method, that they have the same object (*samāna-viṣayatva*)."

And thus, because the knowledge of the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *gaṅgā* does not exist in the bank as the object (*viṣaya*) with respect to the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the bank-meaning as an object, and because the presentation produced by the knowledge of the denotative power of the word *gaṅgā* does not exist in the bank as the object with respect to the verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) whose object is the bank, the aforementioned defect does not arise. Consequently, you must accept two distinct causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for the knowledge of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the presentation, and the verbal cognition; therefore, your position is more cumbersome (*gaurava*). By this—namely, by the aforementioned defect—it is meant that it is impossible to state [a definition] that is not over-extensive (*anatiprasakta*). (37)

The Naiyāyika [responds] with the first half [of the verse]: "Having inferred" means having recollected. "Like writing" (lipivat): for by means of writing words are remembered, and through those remembered words there arises the cognition of meaning; such is the meaning. "Those [words] are the causes for the production of cognition in the case of correct words" (Vākyapadīya I.141). "In the case of correct words" means regarding the domain of correct linguistic items. "Those" refers to the correct words themselves. "By means of inference" means by means of recollection. "Causes for the production of cognition" means generators of understanding.

Some say that this is because the author of the treatise has explained them as being in the place of [correct] words (*lipisthānīyatva*). However, others maintain that according to the literal sense of the verse "asādhuranumānena" (Vai.Si.Kā. 38), what is obtained is that only incorrect words (*asādhu*) possess the capacity to convey meaning through a traditional lineage. Thus, they claim that the intention of the root-author—who states that these incorrect words [convey meaning] by means of inference regarding correct words (*sādhu*) through the mediation of the recollection of the correct word—is precisely this: that it is not direct [communication]. [The phrase] "as if having attained identity" (*tādātmyam upagamyeva*) [is used].

The meaning is that Apabhraṃśa words, having attained as it were non-difference from correct (*sādhu*) words, are revealers of word-meaning. Others say their identity consists in similarity. [Regarding the phrase] "not by the learned" (*na śiṣṭaiḥ*), because they are not followed by the learned in the traditional treatises (*smṛti-śāstra*) as synonyms are, nor are they taught as synonyms; therefore, the meaning is that they are "correct" (*sādhavaḥ*). Regarding the word "as it were" (*iva*): the learned do not follow incorrect (*asādhu*) words as they would synonyms.

The meaning is that since even the grammatical treatise (*smṛtiśāstra*) does not derive correct words [from them], they are therefore non-expressive (*avācaka*). He states their non-expressiveness directly by means of an illustration: when a child being taught to say "ambāmbā" speaks indistinctly as "bambaṃba," there arises a determination (*niścaya*) regarding the distinct [form] among those who know that—that is, among those who know the correct words. The meaning is that there arises a determination regarding the distinct object, namely "ambā."

"—*tena*"—by means of the corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*). "*Sādhuvyavahitaḥ*"—intervened by the correct word (*sādhuśabda*), [it functions] through the recollection of the correct word. "*Teṣu*"—in those corrupt forms. "*Teṣām*"—of the synonyms. "*Apabhraṃśe*"—in the domain of the corrupt form. "*Tathā*"—[there is] oneness in all regions (*sarvadeśeṣu ekatvam*). (P. *vakṛtve*) —"*Anyathā*" (not seen in P.)—if there were not oneness in all regions. "*Gaṇanāpatter iti*"—the sense is that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of having to enumerate [them individually], as in the case of lexicons (*kośa*) and so forth.

"And thus"—even if corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) are not directly expressive, "by that"—namely, from the correct forms (*sādhu*), for those common folk (*pāmara*). Having refuted the view of the logicians—that in the case of those who have acquired proficiency, understanding arises from the recollection of the correct form based on the corrupt forms—[the author] states their view regarding those who have not acquired proficiency: "Nor [is it] by power (*śakti*," etc.). Nor is there a misconception (*bhrama*) on the part of the common folk when the expressive power is not grasped; for a subsequent misconception is possible through a preceding misconception.

If it is asked, "How can that be so for the first [word]?"—it is improper to say, "[It is so] when the word *agargari* is uttered by one who is incapable," because the first [word] is already etymologically derived (*vyutpanna*).

If it is asked how this occurs: when the word *gagarī* is uttered due to incapacity, for a learned person who remembers the correct word (*ghaṭa*), there arises a cognition [of the object]. However, for a common person (*pāmara*) observing that [process], there is an illusion—due to the insertion and deletion [of phonemes]—that the word *gagarī* itself is the signifier. And that illusion produces cognition precisely because it remains unrecognized as an illusion; for only the apprehension of a word’s expressive power (*śakti*), which is not undermined by a cognition of its invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-jñāna*), generates understanding.

For this very reason, at the time of grasping the word-potency (*śakti*) for the word *Bhīmasena* as referring to the object Bhīmasena, since speakers do not employ the word *sena* separately from the word *bhīma*—which is a constituent of that [compound] *Bhīmasena*—there is no cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) from the word *sena*, because non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*) is postulated regarding that portion. Regarding the phrase "because it is not erroneous" (*abhrāntatvāt*): the point is that since being a cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is present in what lacks that [qualifier] constitutes error (*bhrāntatva*), and since there is an absence of the state of being a cognizer of the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛtabodhakatva*), there is no error.

"—and because it arises from error. The meaning is that, since the words *ghaṭa* and *gagara* have different sequences of phonemes, there is no sublation [of the cognition] due to the perception of a common property—which is the cause of error—such as the glittering appearance seen in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver. Consequently, since comprehension occurs even from corrupt forms (*asādhu*), it is established that corrupt forms also possess the capacity (*śakti*) characterized by being expressive. Regarding this point, he also cites the consensus of Hari: "And it has been said... [referring to the verse beginning with] "...by way of tradition" (*pāraṃparyāt*). (Vākyapadīya 1.45)

143) — Among those who are devoid of merit, lacking in qualities, base, and prone to corruption—among such speakers and users—it is for this reason that words employed by women, Śūdras, children, and other base persons have attained the status of *apabhraṃśa* (corrupted forms), and it is with these very forms that common usage (*vyavahāra*) is well-established. Even when correct words (*sādhuśabda*) are available, the determination of meaning for those base persons is made solely through the *apabhraṃśas*, which serve as their explanatory guides; therefore, for them, only the incorrect form is expressive. [Direct perception] (P. 01-0).

The meaning is as follows: a word that is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) is not "correct" (*sādhu*) if it is suggested by a grammatical analysis (*vyākaraṇa-vyaṅgya*). A word is "correct" (*sādhu*) [only] when it is not suggested by a discordant grammatical analysis (*asādhu-vyadhikaraṇa-vyaṅgya*). However, it is in the domain of those who are proficient in grammar (*vyutpanna*) that one establishes what is correct. Regarding the verse from the *Vākyapadīya* (I.144), "divine" (*daivī*) means "Sanskrit. "Interspersed" (*vyavakīrṇā*) means mixed with corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). In a former aeon (*pūrva-kalpa*), the divine speech was unmixed.

At that time, only the correct forms (*sādhavaḥ*) have attained established usage, just like the distinction between those who may be approached and those who may not (*gamyāgamyavyavasthāvat*). They are seen and remembered by those distinguished by the specific distinction between correct and incorrect forms, constantly and without interruption. Some say that this refers to those who perceive [the forms] eternally and accept them as the cause of dharma for the virtuous (*sādhūnām*), whereas it refers to those who perceive [them] non-eternally—the unvirtuous (*asādhavaḥ*), meaning those who maintain the non-eternity of words. These very ones are indeed the virtuous (*sādhavaḥ*).

[The opponent objects: "Because there is a difference in the sequence that delimits the expressive power (*śakti*). [The author] replies: "In corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), just as in synonymous forms (*paryāya*), the expressive power is established"—thus he says, "Furthermore, regarding the sequence... Since they possess expressive power, they have meaning; therefore, by virtue of being nominal stems (*prātipadika*), the derivation of case-endings (*sub*) follows, though this must be understood through the principle of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*). [Objection: "But if they possess expressive power, would it not follow that..."—the intention is that correctness (*sādhutva*) consists in being a denoter (*vācakatva*). [Reply: "Regarding the restriction (*niyama*): [Objection: Since the horse-word (*go*) possesses such a genus (*jāti*) manifested by grammar and so forth, it would follow that the word *go* is correct when applied to a horse.

Therefore, he says "evameva ca" in order to define correctness (*sādhutva*) by including it within a specific meaning. [Objection: But how can there be correctness in the case of modern names such as Devadatta, given the absence of grammar and other means that manifest the *jāti* which delimits the production of merit? To this, he says "ādhunikadevadatte. Regarding "gauṇānām" (of secondary meanings), such as "gopī" and so on—because they are derived from [the word for] a cowherd's wife (*gopastrī*) through their qualities (*guṇaiḥ*), according to the rule of the treatise: "In the case of a name [derived] from connection with a male" (*puṃyogādākhyāyām*, Pāṇini 4.1.48).

"—it is indeed desired"—because there is an absence of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) indicated by grammar. On the contrary, he states that which is opposed to it: "—for this very reason"—meaning, because of a power distinct [from the word], namely a power consisting in the capacity to convey a meaning distinct from the power established in the Nyāya school's tenets. (38) II.2.38)

Here, in the term *sambandha*, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *arśa-ādibhyo'c*. The meaning of the locative case is "constituent of. Thus, the meaning is: "in the word *sambandha*, which constitutes the word *sambandhi*, [it denotes] that which is fit for relation (*sambandhayogya*). Alternatively, this is exactly as it is heard [in the text]; the meaning of the locative case is "denotability" (*vācyatva*). Accordingly, the meaning is: "that which is denoted by the word *sambandha* is precisely the fitness for relation (*sambandhayogyataiva*)."

How is this to be understood? To that he says: "The accusative case [is used] in the sense of 'fitness' (*yogyatā*). The meaning is that fitness is known precisely from the determination of the definition. The intention is that, because of the linguistic usage "this word is fit for this meaning," fitness itself is the relationship between word and meaning. However, the author of the treatise explains it otherwise: "For instance—the relationship is the object."

In the word "relation" (*sambandha*), the relation that constitutes its object—that is, by means of which one employs the word with the thought, "this word possesses a relation to this meaning"—is what is intended. Now, if fitness (*yogyatā*) alone constitutes the relation, what is the utility of convention (*saṃketa*)? To this he says: "from convention" (*samayāt*). Fitness is determined through convention, which is synonymous with the continuous tradition of the usage of elders. For even the relationship between producer and produced—such as "this is the mother of this son"—is not merely conventional; rather, it is the communication of that which is already established in reality. This is the essential point here.

It is clearly stated elsewhere that the relationship between word and meaning is specifically that of the denoter and the denoted (*vācyavācakabhāva*), because the capacity of a word to convey meaning would otherwise be inexplicable; it is not merely the capacity to convey meaning itself. According to common usage, this capacity alone is said to be the relationship. However, according to the final doctrine (*paramasiddhānta*), the sentence-sphoṭa—which is partless and unitary—is the sentence-meaning, and its manifestation (*pratibhā*) is the cognition thereof. Furthermore, the relationship between word and meaning is the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*) in the form "this is that," as is clear in the *Mañjūṣā* (Laghumañjūṣā).

(p. 54) However, this must be understood: in order to exclude the cognition of "space" (*ākāśa*) from words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*), it is held that the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārtha*) through a linguistic function (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, in cases such as "enter," there is a syntactic ellipsis (*śabdādhyāhāra*) of a word. In this context, the term "word" (*pada*) refers to any expressive unit whatsoever, since verbal cognition arises even from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). In reality, however, in accordance with the requirement for the ellipsis of meaning (*arthādhyāhāra*), the property of being "generated by a word" (*padajanyatva*) should also be included [in the definition].

However, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) must be avoided by establishing a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) based on the fact that the cognition of word-potency (*śaktijñāna*), the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*), and verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) possess identical modes (*samānaprakāraka*). Furthermore, the presentation of the word-meaning is not of the nature of memory (*smṛti*), but is indeed of the nature of verbal cognition itself. By this, the view that another relation must be postulated—on the grounds that the presentation of the word-meaning follows the recollection of the word and occurs through the principle of "the cognition of one related thing" (*ekasambandhijñāna*)—is refuted, because the presentation of the word-meaning lacks the nature of memory.

The relationship between word and meaning is solely a conventional one (*saṃketalakṣaṇa*); that itself is the *śakti*. For the logicians (*tārkika*) who maintain that "a word is that which possesses the capacity" (*śaktaṃ padam*), the conventional usage that the word *gaṅgā* is "indicative" (*lākṣaṇika*) with respect to the bank is mutually contradictory. However, it should be understood that for us, there is no contradiction, because the term "word" (*pada*) refers here to a nominal stem (*subanta*) that conveys meaning.

[Objection: But surely, even if words such as *gagara* used by common folk (*pāmara*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) according to the method stated above, they would lack the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*). Consequently, the cognition produced by them would also lack validity (*pramātva*), because only a word spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*) is a means of valid cognition. This is because "being a reliable person"—defined as possessing knowledge that accords with reality and being free from delusion (*bhrama*), negligence (*pramāda*), and the desire to deceive (*vipralipsā*)—is impossible [in the case of common folk], and thus reliability (*āptatva*) is absent. [Response: If this is argued, it is not so.

For just as even common folk dwelling in the forest are considered authoritative (*āpta*) regarding the instruction of a path, so too are those who employ expressions such as "the sound of a kettle-drum in a jar" authoritative even with respect to that particular aspect [of their statement]. Indeed, truthfulness is not intended in every respect; otherwise, even contemporary scholars would fail to be authoritative, since the cognition produced by such [statements] is indeed valid, as is experienced from that very source. The only distinction is that these [latter statements] lack utility for scriptural purposes.

In reality, every word is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the cognition produced by a word, it is not the knowledge that the speaker is one who has realized the truth (*āptotattvajñāna*)—which takes the word as its subject—that is the apprehender of validity (*prāmāṇyagrāhaka*). Rather, it is solely the knowledge that the speaker is one who has not realized the truth (*anāptotattvajñāna*) that is the apprehender of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyagrāhaka*) in the cognition produced by that [word]. Thus, since the speaker in the present context is characterized by the aforementioned definition of being an *āpta*, there is no invalidity in the understanding produced by him; this suffices. — The Determination of the Meaning of Negations—
Salutation to Śrī.

Following the examination of the expressive power (*śakti*) of compounds, and having—by way of occasion (*avasara*) and relevance (*prasaṅga*)—defined the category of *śakti*, [the author] states, beginning with "In a compound with *nañ*" (*nañ-samāse*, Vaiśeṣika Sūtra Kārikā 40), in order to define the expressive power of the negative particle (*nañ*) both in its compounded and uncompounded forms: "[Because of the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member]" (*uttarapadārthasya prādhānyāt*). The conventional designation of the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member occurs precisely by taking the meaning indicated (*dyotya*) by the preceding member, *nañ*. And this very [point is established by] the rule "The negative particle [*nañ*]" (*nañ*, Pāṇini Sūtra 2.2.6).

This is because the entire word (*sarvapada*) possesses a secondary meaning (*gauṇatva*), consisting in its presenting an object that serves as a qualifier for the meaning of the subsequent member of the compound. In my view, however, there is no fault, because "superimposedness" (*āropitatva*) is a meaning manifested by the particle (*dyotya*) and thus functions as a qualifier.

Nor should it be argued that superimposedness alone is the denotation of the negative particle (*nañ*) while also serving as a qualifier; for it is impossible for the superimposedness denoted by *nañ* to have a relation with the referent of the word *brāhmaṇa*, which is capable of signifying a primary Brāhmaṇahood that is not superimposed.

Granted that even when the negative particle (*nañ*) has the meaning of non-existence (*abhāva*), in cases such as "not all" (*asarva*), it functions solely as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); therefore, following the principle to be stated later—that "it is non-existence"—one should accept the non-existence as being implied (*ārthika*), or according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). He states this with an example: "In cases such as 'the jar does not exist' (*ghaṭo nāsti*)," etc. [The portion from *tasya*—meaning "of that"—referring to the object of the negative particle, up to *ucitatvāt* on page 12, is not found].

It appears that [the word] has been abandoned. It is more appropriate to say "the cloth does not exist" (*paṭo na asti*) and so forth, because in the case of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*), such as "not all" (*asarva*), the negative particle (*nañ*) signifies difference (*bheda*) due to its having the same case-ending (*samānavibhaktikatva*), which consists in the absence of contradictory case-endings. However, in cases such as "there is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭo nāsti*), there is indeed the cognition of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the action when it is co-uttered with another action; for in that instance, the locative case following the word denoting the locus (*anuyogin*) is the governing factor (*tantratva*).

For this very reason, the analysis of compounds such as "you are not" (*atvaṃ bhavasi*) as "one whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is 'you'" and so forth—which will be explained later—is consistent.

If it is objected: "In both cases—such as 'the pot is not a cloth' and 'the pot does not exist'—according to the established doctrine, the word *nañ* directly conveys only superimposedness (*āropitatva*). Since both absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) are equally implied (*ārthika*), this [distinction] is not tenable," we reply: No. Even though they are equal in being implied, in the first usage (*prayoga*)—namely, "the pot is not a cloth"—because there is a superimposition of identity (*tādātmya-āropa*), it is precisely the superimposedness residing in the meaning of the noun that is conveyed.

The word "gata" (gone/attained)—[it is] not [the case that] because difference is required by the cognition (*bodha*), the example in the illustrative instance (*dārṣṭāntika*) such as "not all," etc., is appropriate only for a difference that is implied (*ārthika*); rather, the intended meaning is that it is not [appropriate] for one who possesses an absolute absence of implied activity. This [cognition] has non-existence as its object. The phrase "mental cognition" (*mānasa*) is the implied sense [of the term] "cognition" (*bodha*). The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is to be supplied [as the locus].

The point is this: when the status of a Brāhmaṇa is superimposed upon a Kṣatriya or the like, since the absence of primary Brāhmaṇahood and so forth serves as the basis for that [superimposition], the cognition of that absence—which constitutes the basis—is understood immediately after the verbal cognition of the superimposition itself. Thus, in this view, regarding expressions such as "He is a Brāhmaṇa" or "He is not [a Brāhmaṇa]," the cognition is that the Brāhmaṇa who is the object of the superimposition is the locus of the superimposition (the substratum), and the Kṣatriya is the object [of the negation].

—(04-0) "There is no color in air"; (L. Nor is it the case that color does not exist in a qualified cognition; for in cases such as "the yellow conch does not exist," the understanding [of the sentence] would be incorrect and a corrupt reading if it were to take the form: "the superimposed existence residing in color is superimposed upon the air," or "the existence of the yellow conch superimposed [upon the air]," etc. In "the yellow conch does not exist," etc., the understanding is not according to the pattern where the existence residing in color and superimposed [upon it] is superimposed upon the air as the existence of the yellow conch. Nor is the qualified [object] unestablished, because the qualified is not distinct from its individual components).

And because each [element] is well-established individually; even in cases such as "the jar does not exist," the cognition is that there is a superimposed non-existence residing in the jar. It has been stated that the cognition of absence (*abhāva*), however, is implicit (*ārthika*). Some, however, maintain that although the cognition of absence is implicit—since the state of being superimposed is expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*) in a compound—in instances where there is a common case-ending (*samānavibhaktika*), such as "the jar is not a cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*), the negative particle expresses only difference (*bheda*). (Note: *L.* refers to the location in the source text.)

In cases such as "there is no jar" (*ghaṭo nāsti*), when [the word *na*] is co-uttered with a verb, it denotes only an absolute absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the action; it does not denote the fact of being superimposed (*āropitatva*), because that alone is what is understood. Thus, since there would be the consequence of [the word *sarva*] failing to establish its meaning as an absence functioning as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the intended sense is that the word *sarva*—as a qualifier of the absence—is secondary (*gauṇa*) in the manner previously described.
Out of parsimony, he states another alternative: "mere superimposition" (āropamātra); this means "the final conclusion" (niṣkarṣa) according to the moderns (navyāḥ).

[Objection: "Let it be that even when [the word *sarva*] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatva*), the grammatical operation (*kārya*) pertaining to a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) still applies. To this, the author states in the root-text: "For not this... (Vai.Si.Kā. 40). The intention is that if that were the case, the grammatical operation of a pronoun would apply even to the word *atisarva*. However, it will be stated later that this [position] must be reconsidered from the perspective of ultimate reality (*vastutaḥ*).

The indicative nature (*dyotakatva*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) as a constituent of a compound consists precisely in its abandoning the well-known meaning of the word with which it is co-uttered and adopting an unknown meaning; it is not, however, the [meaning] pertaining to prefixes (*prādi*), which will be explained later. By this much alone, the technical usage of "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) is established, just like the usage [of the term] "predominant in the meaning of the second member" (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*). Regarding the cessation [of the objection]: he states "yat tu" in order to refute the view of Kiyata. "Dārtha" refers to the primary meaning of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth, which resides in a Kṣatriya or similar person. "Anyathā" means if that [primary meaning] were the denoted object. "Sādṛśyāder api" (even of similarity, etc.)—the sense is that this is because it is rooted in superimposition (āropa). In that regard, in expressions such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), after there arises a cognition of the superimposed Brahminhood—rooted in a similarity defined by the Brahmin—with respect to a Kṣatriya or other [caste] who is distinct from a Brahmin, there subsequently arises a cognition of the similarity that serves as its basis. This is similar to how, in expressions such as "the boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*), the negative particle (*nañ*) functions to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) for the word "boy" (*māṇavaka*) and so forth to convey a meaning characterized by the superimposed nature of a lion (*siṃhatva*).

This is because [the negative particle] functions as an indicator of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) that the words co-uttered with it, such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so on, have superimposed (*āropita*) Brāhmaṇahood and the like as their grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Furthermore, in cases such as "sinless" (*apāpa*), after there arises a cognition of superimposition based on a relationship rooted in similarity or difference, there is a cognition of the absence of that very relationship, since that relationship is indeed absent. Similarly, in cases such as "non-horse" (*anaśva*) or "non-bird" (*advija*), there is a superimposed horsehood or birdhood based on the difference [from the referent]; after the cognition of that [superimposition], there follows the cognition of the difference which is its basis.

In cases such as "the girl with no belly" (*anudarā kanyā*), the absence of a belly is superimposed by means of its smallness; then, through the co-occurrence of the negative particle (*nañ*), there arises a cognition of a superimposed belly as a qualifier, and the ultimate resting point lies in that smallness which is the basis for that [superimposition]. In cases such as "not-cattle" (*apaśavaḥ*), the absence of cowness is superimposed upon animals other than cows by means of their lack of excellence; then, through the cognition of those possessing superimposed cowness, there arises the cognition of the lack of excellence which is the root of that [superimposition]. (Note: *paśutva*—superimposed—is not seen.)

In expressions such as "adharma," the cognition of the absence of dharma (dharmābhāva) arises based on opposition; this superimposed cognition of being a property (dharma) gives rise to the cognition of its opposite, which is its root. Thus, the meaning is that similarity and other factors are implied (ārthika). Regarding the phrase "pratiyoginī" (as the counter-correlative): likewise, in cases such as "there is no jar" (aghaṭo'sti), the understanding is that existence (sattā) has as its locus the jar, which is the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) of the difference (bheda). Regarding the phrase "tathā ca": this connects with the word "upapadyate" (is established/justified). The meaning is: "and in the case of [the term] being a qualifier."

Otherwise—[if there were] no connection of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the referent of *yuṣmad* as a qualifier—[there would be no problem]. But [if there were] a connection as a qualifier, then in our view it would be auspicious. For in reality, this being the case, when one says "bring the non-pot" (*aghaṭam ānaya*), it would follow that one must bring a pot that is either the counter-correlate of some difference residing in something, or that possesses a difference whose counter-correlate is something [else]. (L.)

[Nayana: [The opponent] objects: "Precisely for this reason, under the view that a negative *tatpuruṣa* compound is dominated by the meaning of its final member (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*), when it is said, 'Bring the non-Brahmin' (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), it follows that the bringing of any Brahmin whatsoever would result. Anticipating this objection (*āśaṅkā*), he states that upon the use of the negative particle (*nañ*), there will be the bringing of one qualified by the meaning of the negative. Then, in response to the question, "But who is this one qualified by the meaning of the negative? the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Nañ-sūtra* (Pāṇini 2.2.6, Prauḍhamanoramā edition, page [number]) states: "One whose word-meaning has ceased" (*nivṛttapadārthaka*).

425) It has been stated: "The word-meaning that is excluded (*nivṛtta*)—that is, the primary status of being a Brāhmaṇa—is what [the negative particle denotes] in the case of a Kṣatriya or other such person. Regarding this, Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa holds that through similarity (*sādṛśya*) and so forth, the status of being a Brāhmaṇa is superimposed (*adhyāropita*), and thus the object denoted by the negative particle remains in that state. Furthermore, according to the technical dictum that "the counter-positive and its absence share the same status" (*pratiyogyabhāvau tulyayogakṣemau*), it is not logical for the difference expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*) to function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). This is because it must be accepted that wherever the counter-positive has the status of a qualifier (*prakāratā*), there the absence of that counter-positive likewise has that status; and wherever the counter-positive has the status of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*), there the absence of that counter-positive likewise has that status. By this very principle, it should be understood that the locus of the absence is indeed the locus of the counter-positive. (It should be understood.)

Now, [one might object]: in order to exclude the cognition "there is no jar here" in a place containing a yellow jar, it is established by the force of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that when a negative particle (*nañ*) and so forth are used in proximity, the relation [of absence] has as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) that which is delimited by the delimitor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka*). For this very reason, from the cognition "there is no color in the air," the non-existence of color in general (*rūpasāmānyābhāva*) is established; for it is impossible to derive from that [cognition] a collection (*kūṭa*) of absences of specific [colors]. Here, by the term "delimitor of the correlate," a qualifier that is correlated with the meaning of the negative particle is meant.

For example, in the case of "yellow pot" (*pīto ghaṭaḥ*), the yellow color is the [qualifier], while the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) there is also just "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), because only a property residing in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of a qualified cognition can be the delimitor of counter-correlativity. Furthermore, the counter-correlativity delimited by that [pot-ness] resides specifically in the individual yellow pot, due to the force of the qualifier "yellow" and so forth. And the qualified entity is not entirely distinct from the primary [constituents].

Thus, the negation is construed as delimited by the delimitor of the locus (*ādhāratāvacchedaka*). This is because of the conventional usage: "In the jar, there is an absence of being a yellow jar. Similarly, in the case of the statement "A blue jar is not a jar," since being a yellow jar exists [in that context], there is an absence of the superimposed jarhood (*āropitaghaṭatva*) therein.

If it is argued that there is indeed a distinction between the two cognitions—one apprehending the relation of pure counter-positiveness (*śuddha-pratiyogitā*) in "you do not exist" (*atvaṃ bhavasi*) and so forth, and the other in "there is an absence of you" (*tvad-abhāvo'sti*) and so forth—what follows from this? For even with that much, the systematic arrangement of the person of the utterance (*vacana-puruṣa-vyavasthā*) remains unestablished. Regarding the phrase "by the indicator" (*jñāpakāt*): the meaning is that in the rule *hali* (Pāṇini 6.1.111), the word *asamāse* ("in a non-compound") serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Specifically, in the rule *etattadoḥ sulopo'koranañsamāse hali* (6.1.132), the mention of *asamāse* indicates [that the elision of *su* occurs even when the pronoun is part of a compound]. Thus, the sense is that it is by virtue of this indicator that [the required distinction is understood].

Thus he says: "—2asa-2 iti" || "—2gauṇatvāt iti—" || "—2akor iti—" || This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication). [The point is: when the word *asoḥ* (of *as*) in the rule "etattadoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.132) functions as a qualifier of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) by way of its meaning, the intended sense is that there is elision of *su* which expresses the number residing in the meaning of *etad* or *tad*. Since this would result in the non-application of elision in cases such as *asaḥ*, [the mention of *asu*] being otherwise redundant serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) for this very point. "—2jātyabhiprāyam—" means having in view the genus (*jāti*) consisting of the nature of being an absence (*abhāvatva*). This is because *abhāvatva* is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) and is therefore on the same footing as a *jāti*.

In reality, there is no fault, because it will be stated later that even "non-existence-ness" (*abhāvatva*) and other such properties possess the status of a universal (*jāti*). —2 Autogenous (general rule)—2: In rules such as "dvi-eka-yoḥ" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.22), it is clear from the division of the *yoga* (the rule) that the meaning is the general absence of number; this is evident elsewhere as well. —2 Each one—2: With respect to the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). —2 For this very reason—2: Precisely because the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). If it were the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), its inconsistency would be quite obvious. —2 With the referent of "you" (*yuṣmadartha*)—2: That is, with the metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) meaning.

The intended meaning is that the coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the referent of the second person pronoun (*yuṣmad*) alone is the cause for that [the application of the suffix *tvam*]. In reality, although in a non-compound expression such as "the cloth is not a jar" (*aghaṭaḥ paṭaḥ*), one might accept difference (*bheda*) as the qualificand (viśeṣya) because of the potential occurrence of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so on, in a compound, by virtue of the force of unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), the genitive and other cases based on difference do not apply; thus, if one were to accept difference as the qualificand, there would be the undesirable consequence that in the usage "it exists as distinct from those two" (*ābhyāṃ bhinno'sti*), the dual number would not occur and the singular number would instead result in the form *ataustaḥ*.

Furthermore, by force of the requirement of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), there would be the undesirable consequence of using the singular number even in cases such as "the non-rainy season is *hemanta*" (*avarṣāḥ hemantaḥ*), just as in the rule "many [are expressed] by one" (*anekaṃ syāt* [Pāṇini 1.2.64]). Moreover, there is no grammatical injunction (*anuśāsana*) stating that when a number inherent to the [qualifier] or another [number] exists, the expression must follow the number inherent to the qualified object. Therefore, expressions such as "many fall" (*patanty aneke*) are simply ungrammatical (*asādhu*). As for the claim that the usage "many" (*aneke*) arises from the rule of "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*), that is not correct.

Since the comprehension of all objects can occur through a single word alone, there would be no occasion for the employment of multiple words; thus, instead of using many words, one would simply say "an elephant and a horse in the chariot. Furthermore, if the qualifying words such as "chariot" were to have separate case-endings, then—given that the connection occurs through the repetition of only a single word—one would find no utility in the *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of only one of several identical words), because even when they are expressed as a *dvandva* compound, the connection could still occur with only a single collective term. Thus, in either case, the *ekaśeṣa* rule would be useless.

For this very reason, in the commentary on the *nañ* sūtra (Pāṇini 2.2.6), the Mahābhāṣya (Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 428) states: "Furthermore, this [rule] is indeed included when the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is predominant. What is included here? The singular number. It has been stated that because there is a cognition of many things as possessing a superimposed singleness, the word *aneka* (many) remains [in the singular]; for no qualifier is seen in the Bhāṣya. Moreover, the form ‘aneko jana āgataḥ’ (many people have come) would result in being grammatically correct [if the rule applied]. Furthermore, there would be the difficulty of having to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in cases such as ‘atvaṃ bhavasi’ (you are not you)."

Nor should it be argued that in expressions such as "non-pot" (*aghaṭa*), where the negative particle (*nañ*) is used in co-occurrence, the meaning of the word "pot" itself is "that which is different from a pot," because the negative particle would then merely be an indicator (*dyotaka*) and the difference (*bheda*) would consequently fall into the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). If it is argued: "In the rule regarding non-negative compounds (*anañ-samāsa*), the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) [contained in the phrase] 'of that which indicates the agent' (*kartṛ-jñāpakasya*) is intended in a general sense; therefore, even when the meaning of the prior member is predominant, this *jñāpaka* indicates an operation conditioned by the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member. Thus, the correct application of gender (*puruṣa-vyavasthā*) is established in the cited example"—this is not so.

In order to avoid contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*, it is appropriate to indicate—by means of the technical indicator (*jñāpaka*) "in a non-negative compound" (*anañ-samāse*)—that in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the predominance belongs exclusively to the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha-prādhānya*). (Note: The portion beginning from "aghaṭa" on the second page of manuscript T up to this point is not observed. Having thus established the case of the compounded negative, he states the distinction regarding the uncompounded negative: "Thus, not so. Herein lies the truth: in all instances, whether in an analytical expression (*vyāsa*) or a compound (*samāsa*), it is precisely the superimposed [negation] that is manifested by the negative particle (*nañ*).

The meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is superimposition (*āropitatva*) only in a compound, whereas it is non-existence (*abhāva*) in a non-compound; there is no reason for such a distinction. Furthermore, in expressions such as "the pot is not a cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*), if the negative particle were to signify difference (*bhedārthaka*), then a genitive case-ending would result after the word denoting the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), just as in cases like "highly" (*uccaiḥ*).

If it is argued that there is a valid interpretation by assuming that the word *paṭa* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "that which has cloth as its counter-correlative" (*paṭapratiyogika*), such that it connects with [the verb] through the relation of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*), while the difference (*bheda*) connects with its own substratum (*anuyogin*) by way of implication (*ākṣepa*)—this is not so, because it would violate the established linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) regarding the connection of non-difference. Furthermore, there would be the difficulty of having to assume that this [non-difference] applies to something other than a particle (*nipāta*). Moreover, it would result in a violation of the rule requiring identical case endings for the locus of difference (*bheda-āśraya*) and the counter-correlative of difference (*bheda-pratiyogin*).

And because difference (*bheda*) cannot be defined [in this context], therefore, here the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is precisely superimposition (*āropitatva*). The cognition is simply that "the jar is one whose identity with a jar is superimposed," or "the jar possesses superimposed jar-ness. However, the actual referent (*artha*) is the cognition of difference. For this very reason, according to the maxim "when *nañ* is present," there is the cognition of something other than what is similar to that [superimposed object].

Thus, even in cases involving absolute non-existence, such as "there is no jar" (*ghaṭo nāsti*) and the like, the cognition is precisely this: "the superimposed existence having the jar as its agent," [which is to say] "having as its locus this particular place" (*etad-deśādhikaraṇikā*). For this very reason, regarding the statement "not one beloved" (*na na ekaṃ priyam*), it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* that in the verbal cognition—"one beloved belonging to us (*naḥ*, i.e., *asmākam*) has a superimposed state of being beloved"—there arises, by implication (*ārtha*), the perception of multiple beloveds upon the negation of the single beloved with whom one is connected. This should be understood as an illustration of a quality (*guṇa*).

If this is so, one might object: "In the case of a non-compound (*asamāsa*), how could there be a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) as to where there is connection with a substance (*dravya*) and where there is connection with an action (*kriyā*), since there would be no regulating factor? For me, however, such a rule is possible—namely, that when [the particle] has the sense of difference (*bheda*), there is connection with a substance, and when it has the sense of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), there is connection with an action. To this we reply: No.

Since it is possible to establish a distinction such that "superimposedness" resides in the meaning of the noun where there is a superimposition of identity (*tādātmyāropa*), whereas "superimposedness" resides in the action where there is a superimposition of relation (*saṃsargāropa*), [the following holds]. (The reading *abhedena bodha* is an interpolation. Furthermore, in cases such as "One should not eat *kalañja*," the cognition is simply that the eating of *kalañja*—which is superimposed—is the object of the instigation (*preraṇā*). Consequently, there would be no violation of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that [a suffix] conveys its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*).

The claim that the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys "being a means to an undesirable end" has already been refuted in the investigation of the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*). The cognition of non-existence, however, is merely implied (*ārthika*); even the capacity of a subverting cognition to act as an obstacle must be explained by resorting to this implied cognition of non-existence. Alternatively, let it be granted that the cognition of being superimposed (*āropitatva-jñāna*) acts as an independent obstacle to the cognition of a thing possessing a property; yet, it is not by virtue of apprehending its absence (*tadabhāvāvagāhitayā*). For in this view, apart from the state of being superimposed, there is no instance anywhere where a cognition of non-existence occurs upon the co-occurrence of the negative particle (*nañ*).

If it is argued that there is the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) because, if the negative particle functions as an independent inhibitor, one would have to postulate an additional relationship between the inhibited and the inhibitor, we reply: no, for such complexity is authentic (*prāmāṇika*) and not excessive. Furthermore, since it is precisely the state of being superimposed (*āropitatva*) that is expressed by the negative particle in all cases, this accounts for the inclusion of "difference" (*bheda*) and "non-existence" (*abhāva*) among the meanings enumerated by the learned authorities in the verse beginning with "similarity to that, non-existence, etc. (T. 01-0).

Therefore, it has been calculated that "the state of being superimposed" (*āropitatvam*) alone is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) everywhere; thus, the first position stated in the root text is indeed logical. This is the general direction. In cases such as "one should not look" (*nekṣeta*), the specific meanings of the negative particle should be understood according to the context (otherwise they would be different). They are not written here for fear of making the book too voluminous. Regarding the phrase "as long as there is absolute [non-existence]," etc., by the words "in the form of *tvādi*," etc., the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) are included.

The meaning is this: non-existence (*abhāva*) is fourfold—namely, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). The definitions of these are well-known in the treatises of the logicians (*tārkika*), and their mutual distinction is understood precisely by way of those [definitions]. In reality, however, non-existence is twofold: absolute non-existence and mutual non-existence. The first is the absence of a relation other than identity (*tādātmya*); the latter is the absence of identity itself.

And identity (*tādātmya*) consists either in the nature of a unique property residing in that [substratum] or as something distinct. Of these, the former applies in the case of the connection with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) which is the meaning of a finite verb; the latter—

—04— Because in a cognition where the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) whose meaning is not compounded with *nañ*, the semantic presence (*upastiti*) produced by the verbal root is the cause [of that cognition]. —05— In cases of co-extensive non-existences (*samaniyatābhāva*), just as one [non-existence] can have multiple counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), both of these [the absence of existence and the absence of a jar] have existence residing in a jar, etc., as their counter-correlate. Furthermore, having a jar, etc., as the counter-correlate is the relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*) of the existence of a jar; this is because there is co-extensiveness (*samanaiyatyāt*) between the absence of existence and the absence of a jar. (T.)

Because there is a co-extensiveness (*samanaiyatyam*) between the absence of identity with a jar and the absence of the jar itself; and because, through the very cognition of that [absence], as established by such cognitions as "the jar was" and so forth, there is no doubt regarding the jar, precisely due to the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and the destructive absence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). By this, those who have proposed other definitions are refuted on account of their prolixity (*gaurava*). Since the prior absence and the destructive absence are established by such cognitions as "the jar will be" and "the jar was," they are not [ontologically] distinct entities.

Because [the action] is not established as something other than the time that serves as the locus for the production and so forth of a jar and the like. And thus, what is to be included by the word "etc. (*ādi*) is indeed to be considered [as such]; and this has been explained in the *Lakārārthavāda*.
Thus ends the *Laghubhūṣaṇakānti*.

[Response: This is not so.

This is because the author of the Kaustubha himself has provided the following resolution: taking as the delimiting condition of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) either "the state of being a particle" (nipātatva)—which is an indivisible [property] consisting in the possession of the form of a particle-word through a relation of power (śakti)—or simply "non-particle-ness" (anipātatva) as the reason, it is proper to prove the absence of denotative capacity (vācakatvābhāva) in accordance with those particles that possess meaning; for "proofs tend toward the general."

In reality, since "being a particle" (*nipātatva*) is more pervasive than "being a preposition" (*upasargatva*), if one were to establish its denotative function (*dyotakatā*) by delimiting it as being a particle, then because that [status of being a particle] is even more pervasive than that, it would follow that the function is established merely by delimiting it as having the property of being an indeclinable (*avyayatva*). However, if such an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) were accepted, then even for words like *svar* and others, there would be the unwanted consequence of their not being used independently in expressions such as *svaḥ paśyet*. This is because it will be demonstrated later that there is a rule stating that the meaning indicated by a particle must necessarily be a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Regarding the rule *svarādinipātamavyayam* (Pāṇini 1.1.37), since the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) would already be established by the fact that it is merely an indicator (*dyotaka*), the inclusion of the terms *svarādi* and *nipāta* would otherwise result in redundancy. Furthermore, it should be understood that because the designation *avyaya* is both conventional (*laukika*) and etymological (*anvartha*), its establishment is not dependent on its being preceded [by another term]; thus, there is no circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*). As for the phrase *tenaiva*, he supplies the word *tat* (that) because of the necessary connection between *yat* (which) and *tat*, and joins it accordingly. Regarding the expression *vyutpatteḥ*: [The text ends here.]

The phrase "lest it result in [the root] being non-verbal" (*akarmatvāpatti*) is also to be understood. The phrase "and lest it result in [the suffix] *pratyaya*" means that the suffix *anu* would have the sense of "experience" (*anubhava*). The phrase "due to prolixity" (*gauravāt*) means that, according to the principle that "when a parsimonious [denotative power] is possible, there is no recourse to a prolix one," the status of being the delimitor of denotative capacity (*śaktatāvacchedakatayā*) is not accepted for a prolix [expression]. Furthermore, if the qualified [form] were considered a verbal root (*dhātu*), it would result in the occurrence of the *laṭ* suffix and other such markers. The phrase "it is indicative" (*dyotakatvamiti*) implies that the Naiyāyikas are the intended subject.

He states the refutation: "And that... and so forth. The author himself [states] "svārtha" (its own meaning) to show the fruitfulness of the qualification; he says "of the verbal root" and "it would not be so. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). If "worship" (*upāsanā*) were not the meaning of the root, then in cases such as "upakaroti" (he assists), there would be the consequence of perceiving worship [instead], and because it would not be the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*), there would be the consequence of its non-connection with the meaning of the suffix. He says "due to prolixity": even if it were expressive of an action, since the specific form is not recited in the list of verbal roots (*gaṇapāṭha*), it would not obtain the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*), and thus the formation of the *l*-suffixes would be untenable.
If it is argued that "this illustration is abundant," then one must consider that the augment *ā* and so forth would also apply to prefixes (*upasarga*) following a dual ending.

(1) [42] —2 otherwise—2 [i.e.,] when different from *pra* and the others; —2 in those respective senses—2 [i.e.,] in the sense of an activity conducive to direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) and so forth. By this, [it is shown that] in the case of the root *kṛ* having the meaning of an activity conducive to production... (L.)

Even if there is an activity (*vyāpāra*), it is indicated that there is no escape even from the state of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*). He will say this very thing [in the passage beginning with] "even though" (*yadyapi*)—referring to these [words] such as *sākṣāt* and so on. Regarding the fact that the root *kṛ* has the sense of production (*utpatti*): "in these"—that is, in cases such as *sākṣātkāra*. "Otherwise"—that is, if one were to accept the grammatical operation (*kārya*) triggered by transitivity merely because of the presence of an object, even when there is a different meaning. "It would be so"—the meaning is that the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) would occur in the sense of the object (*karman*).

"—because of the natural sense of the two *kośas*. It should also be understood that this is because the word *namaḥ* alone, as in "namo haraye" (*salutation to Hari*), is seen to express the act of salutation. He says "svasva... because the definition of transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) as stated [in the previous verse] suffers from the fault of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) due to the fact that the fruit (*phala*) does not have its own self as its object (*svārthatvābhāva*). The meaning is: "sva" refers to the verbal root (*dhātu*) and "sva" refers to the particle (*nipāta*) joined with it; thus, it is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the meaning of either one of these. He says "suvacam" (it is easy to state).

In this view, even the status of being an object (*karmatva*) consists simply in possessing a result that is the meaning of either the verb itself or the particle associated with it; thus, there is no failure to establish the *lādi* suffixes in the sense of the object. [The phrase] "by way of non-difference" means [the relation of] "favorability" (*anukūlatā*). [The phrase] "because of the impossibility of syntactic connection" means that the intention is as follows: one accepts that the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by a suffix is the cause for a cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of a noun (*nāmārtha*) through a relation other than identity (*abheda*). Otherwise—that is, if such a grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) were not accepted—one would have the sentence: "The rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*).

In this context, the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not apply because *karmatva* (the state of being an object), being a relation (*saṃsarga*), is not the meaning of the case suffix; furthermore, in rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), it is difficult to obtain a cognition from a transitive verbal form (*sakarmaka-pada*) in the form of "that which is connected to its own [action]," etc. Moreover, the nature of "being one or the other" (*anyataratva*)—which consists of a difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by two differences—is excessively complex. Finally, it is difficult to ascertain for those who have not mastered the system (*tāntrika*), due to the ignorance regarding the world.

Even in the refined definition—that "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) consists in having a meaning connected with an object designated as *karman* according to the respective technical treatises—there is a further difficulty: since it is more appropriate for that which is designated as *karman* by virtue of being the locus of the result to be construed with the very result that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root, this cannot be established without [the suffix] being expressive (*dyotaka*). He states another refutation by means of a counter-objection: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). "No connection with that" (*na tadanvayaḥ*) means no connection with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). "Therein" (*tatra*) refers to the beginning [of the argument].

"—2 'Thus, there is another means of accomplishment'—2|| This also means that in words such as *ca* ('and') and so forth, there is another factor of accomplishment (*sādhakatā*). —04-0-2 'Because the consequence is equal'—2|| (L. Regarding 'consequence'—of whom is it not seen? In my view, however, since particles such as *ca* also serve to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*), they are not meaningless, and thus there is no fault."

"—the impossibility of syntactic connection (anvayāsambhava)—" means that the understanding of a syntactic connection between two nominal stem meanings through a distinction [from one another] requires the presentation (upasthiti) produced by an inflectional suffix (vibhakti). This is the underlying intention. "—Otherwise—" means "without [the intervention of] the meaning of an inflectional suffix between the two nominal stem meanings. "—The consequence of a distinct syntactic connection"—means that it would follow [unintendedly], as in the case of *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), that there would be a distinct syntactic connection [between the particles and their own meanings]. In reality, however, due to the inherent nature of word-potency (*śabdaśakti*), particles are always dependent; thus, there is no possibility of their own meaning being connected as a qualifier of another, and the application of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur.

Furthermore, in expressions such as "see the jar and the cloth" (*ghaṭaṃ paṭaṃ ca paśya*), the accusative case in *ghaṭam* indicates that its syntactic connection (*śābdānvaya*) is with the action itself, namely seeing. The cognition is: "see the cloth which possesses a conjunction with the jar. This being the case, when there is an expectancy for the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) of the conjunction, the jar—being proximate—is the counter-correlate, whereas the cloth is connected to the conjunction through difference (*bheda*); it is not the case that the cloth is connected to the conjunction [as its own correlate]. ||2|| (43)

Furthermore, since the genitive case prescribed for expressing difference (*bheda*) is enjoined only after a word denoting the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), there is no occasion for the genitive [to apply here]. Moreover, according to the maxim "a word-meaning [is construed] with a word-meaning," there would be no connection with the qualifier; thus, to prevent deviation from the established rule that difference is construed [with its correlate], one must state the qualification "being other than a particle" (*nipātātiriktatvam*) within that [rule] regarding the linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) for the construction of difference. (L. 'ṣa' - na) Having stated that qualification, (L. 02-0) [the argument continues:]...

The particle ‘ṣa’ (na)—in order to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) for non-difference relations (*abhedānvaya*), he provides the qualification "other than a particle" (*nipātātiriktatva*) even there, by means of the phrase beginning with "the meaning of a word" (*padārtha*). Regarding the phrase "of the linguistic competency for non-difference relations": [it refers to] the cognition of a verbal object (*śābdabuddhi*) which has the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) as its qualifier (*prakāraka*), [arising] through the relation of non-difference.

Since no [such] distinct case-ending (*vibhakta*) is observed, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—namely, that "the cause is the apprehension (*upasthiti*) produced by either a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or a verbal root (*dhātu*) whose meaning is not obstructed by a conflicting case-ending"—which is necessary to prevent the cognition of identity (*abhedabodha*) in the case of "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), given that it applies to instances such as "blue jar" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*) and "he cooks slightly" (*stokaṃ pacati*), [is established]. (L. 04-0ab)

The sense is that [if one were to add] the qualification "being other than a particle" (*nipātātiriktatva*) to avoid over-extension (*atiprasakti*) in cases such as "the pot also exists" (*ghaṭaś ca*) or "he conquers" (*prajayati*), it would result in the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). In reality, however, since the rule for the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of difference has as its domain things other than particles, this well-attested (*prāmāṇika*) complexity is not a defect; thus, even if they possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), there is no room for the syntactic connection of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*). Furthermore, according to the view that they possess denotative power, the primary expressive capacity (*śakti*) of *ca* and so on does not reside in conjunction (*samuccaya*) itself, but rather in that which is conjoined.

As it has been said: "But when there is a simultaneous non-sublation [of both], there is no negative concomitance" (Vākyapadīya, Kāṇḍa II, verse 195). And thus, since even in the two-fold derivation the application of the genitive case does not arise at all, the condition of being "other than a particle" need not be included [in the definition of a kāraka]. It should be understood that the complexity resulting from the postulation of a denotative power (*śakti*) regarding the substratum (*dharmin*) is not a defect, as it is supported by authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇika*). For this very reason—namely, because they are merely indicators (*dyotaka*)—[the absence] is that which has a jar as its counter-correlate (*tat-pratiyogika*), i.e., an absence whose counter-correlate is a jar.

The sense is that otherwise, since the connection of the jar with the meaning of the negative particle—namely, non-existence—as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) would be possible even without resorting to *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication), their acceptance of it would be in vain. By this, it is also indicated that you contradict the view of the Naiyāyikas as well. ||3|| (44)

He states another objection regarding its being a denoter (*vācaka*): "—2api ca—" etc. "—2sādhya—" etc.: the word "in the case of being an indicator" (*dyotakatve*) is to be supplied as the remainder. "—2paratve—" : the sense is that it would be through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). "—2anyathā—" : if one were to accept that the particle *iva* is a denoter. "—2tasya—" : of that which has the meaning of similarity (*sādṛśya*) as its object. "—2anena—" : by the suffix following the word *usra*. "—2asambhavāditi—" : because of the established rule (siddhānta) that, based on the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "avyayādāpsupaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.82), even when the case-endings (*sup*) are produced after an indeclinable, only the nominative singular ending is produced.
And thus, the idea that even a similar [entity] could possess the status of an instrument is cast far away; this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: "Surely, by accepting that the word *iva* denotes a property (*dharma*) consisting of similarity, and by means of either the rule [Pāṇini 5.3.66] which indicates the production of the neuter singular ending for all case-endings, or the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.82] *avyayād āpsupa* which indicates the production of the singular number for all case-endings after an indeclinable, there will be the production of the instrumental case; and since the base-meaning—namely, that which is similar—is the instrument (*karaṇa*), there will be a non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) between that [instrument] and the similarity. To this, he says: "Or, if it is possible" (*saṃbhave vā*). The word *vā* expresses a lack of commitment (*anāsthā*).
Even if the instrumental case were produced—[the rest of the argument follows regarding the nature of the instrument].
It is not perceived; and even if it is not heard due to its elision (*luk*), it does not possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) because it would be purposeless.

[Objection: But even if [the words] have the substratum as their meaning, since there is no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the gender-markers (*liṅga*) and so forth, and because they are classified as indeclinables (*avyaya*) due to being listed in the *svarādi* group, the third case ending would not be heard due to the non-arising of elision (*luk*); therefore, he says: "The word *usra* follows" and "there is no syntactic connection. The point is this: if the word *usratva* and the others have meanings similar to those [of *usra*, etc.], then the status of being the object of the act of speaking (*vadikarmatva*) and so forth is well-established for the two words *vāk* (speech) and *artha* (meaning), which refer respectively to Pārvatī and Parameśvara who resemble those meanings. However, the state of being conjoined (*saṃpṛktatva*) is a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), which is another matter.

In examples such as *kaṭam api bhīṣmam api*, since the action (*kriyā*) connects only with the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not apply to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) due to its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [substantive]. With this view in mind, he says: “because it is distinct” (*bhedārthatvāt*).
