He says “not alone” (*na kevalā*) in accordance with the principle: “A base (*prakṛti*) should not be used alone, nor should a suffix (*pratyaya*) be used alone” (cf. *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau*, Pāṇini 1.2.64; Mahābhāṣya, Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 75). He says “for the sake of grammatical correctness” (*sādhutvāya*). He says “not similar to a tear” (*asrasadṛśa*).

The meaning is that, in reality, they are a refuge for those who resemble rays of light (*usra*). Regarding the phrase "by way of non-difference" (*bhedena*): the ellipsis is "together with the referent of the word *usra*. The intention is that, according to the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that two words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) must have their meanings connected only through non-difference, [the connection is established]. The intention is that if the word *usra* signifies "one who resembles a ray of light," then non-difference is achieved.

Now, even if particles such as *iva* are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), since it will be demonstrated later that the meaning indicated by an indicator must necessarily function as a qualifier, how can the identity relation between *usraih* and *śaraiḥ* be established, given that *usraih* does not mean "those similar to rays"? Furthermore, in cases such as *ghanaśyāma*, if the word *ghana*—according to your own theory—refers to something similar to a cloud in both the analytical statement (*vigraha*) and the compound (*samāsa*), [then...]

In that case, there would be no compound by the rule *upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.55), which means that words expressing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) are compounded with words denoting the object of comparison (*upameya*) when they are in grammatical apposition and qualified by a common attribute. This is because the word *ghaṭa* (pot), in its sense as the object of comparison (*upameya*), lacks the status of being a word denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Nor can the status of being a word denoting the standard of comparison be attributed to it by way of its former state (*bhūtapūrvagati*), as in the case of the popular analytical sentence (*laukikavigrahavākya*); for even there, the aforementioned condition is absent.

In the expression ‘dhanena tulya’ (equal to wealth), although the word *dhana* denotes a pure standard of comparison (*upamāna*), because it lacks coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*), it is appropriate to accept its status as denoting a standard of comparison in both instances—namely, in the repetition [of the compound] and in its analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*)—due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Furthermore, if one accepts the formation of a compound by treating even a non-coreferential colloquial sentence as an analytical sentence (*vigraha*), then in cases such as ‘mṛgacapalā’ (fickle as a deer), there would be a connection with the deer (*mṛgī*) according to the stated method; and [if] ‘capalā’ were also [taken as] an analytical sentence...

Because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the cause [of the compound] and [the word], the application of the masculine form (*puṃvatva*) does not occur. (The phrase *puṃvatva* has been omitted up to this point. This is because the application of the masculine form occurs only when there is coreferentiality in both the derivative formation (*vṛtti*) and the analytical statement (*vigraha*) through immediate proximity. Furthermore, if the word *mṛgī* were construed with the referent of the word *capalā* by way of a relationship of similarity, then, due to the even greater impossibility of coreferentiality, the masculine form of the compound would likewise be untenable.

Furthermore, since the word *ghana* in the compound *ghanābha* is intended to refer to the object of comparison (*upameya*), it cannot be construed with the quality [of being dense] within the compound; consequently, because *ghana* would lack the specific property that characterizes it as the subject of comparison (*upamāna*)—which, as will be explained later, consists in its capacity to distinguish the other—it would not form a compound. This point is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *upamānāni* (Pāṇini 2.1.55). If this is so, then let the view that the word *iva* functions as an indicator of similarity (*sadṛśadyotaka*) be abandoned. If one asks, "How then is the difficulty resolved?"—on this point, our supreme teachers [state as follows]:

(Laghumañjūṣā – On the Meaning of Particles, p. 618): "In words such as *iva*, there is the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamānatā*) with respect to that which is co-uttered with them, because [the object] is perceived as a standard of comparison. Furthermore, since it would otherwise be untenable without the cognition of the object of comparison (*upameya*) as qualified by a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), these particles also function to grasp the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) regarding the cognition of the connection with the common property in both cases. Moreover, the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamānatva*) consists in being the delimiter of the other [the object of comparison] by way of being qualified by the common property; and the status of being an object of comparison (*upameyatva*) consists in being that which is delimited as possessing that [common] property."

However, that which was stated by the Alaṅkārikas—that [the rule] is authoritative—is not so, as this has been indicated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "upamānāni" (Pāṇini 2.1.55) (*Mahābhāṣya*, Prauḍhamanoramā-khaṇḍa, pp.

396–397). Furthermore, the connection with the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) occurs in both cases. Thus, in examples such as "The face is like the moon, [both being] delightful," the cognition arises in the manner: "The delightful face is non-different from the delightful moon, which serves as the standard of comparison. Consequently, because of the requirement for the connection of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), the restriction that they must possess identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktikatva-niyama*) is difficult to maintain. (L.)

Furthermore, the connection with a common property occurs sometimes as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), as in [the examples] mentioned above; and sometimes it occurs even as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), as in "The face gladdens like the moon," and so forth. For in this case, the understanding is that the gladdening performed by the face is non-different from the gladdening performed by the moon, which serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

Regarding this, for those rhetoricians who state that the ground for the similarity to the moon is "the delight caused by the face as its agent," there is the restriction of identical case endings (*samānavibhaktikatva*) between the two; however, this is an addition [to the rule], as no such statement is found in grammar regarding the identical case endings of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). In the first example cited, although there is a distinction between the moon and the face by virtue of their respective natures as "moon-ness" and "face-ness," there is nonetheless non-difference through the metaphorical treatment of non-distinction based on the common attribute perceived as a qualifier.

For this very reason, the elders maintain that the primary [type of] simile involves both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*). However, the cognition of similarity between the moon and the face is purely implied (*ārthī*). Likewise, in the case of *vṛtti* (compound) expressions such as "dark as a cloud" (*ghanaśyāma*) or "dark like a sword-blade" (*śastrīśyāmā*), there is the understanding: "Devadatta is non-different from the dark one who is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)" (*śyāmo devadattaḥ*), and "The dark Devadatta is non-different from the sword-blade which is the standard of comparison" (*śyāmā devadattā*). If it is asked how the connection with the quality of darkness (*śyāmatva*) can be verbal (*śrauta*) in both instances, listen: [The answer follows:]... [the text continues with the technical grammatical analysis].

In that case, both [the quality and the possessor] are present; this is because, according to the authority of the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "upamānāni" (Pāṇini 2.1.55), the word *upamāna* (standard of comparison)—such as "dark-complexioned" (*śyāma*)—also applies to the object of comparison (*upameya*) through the determination of a difference based on similarity. Consequently, for the sake of establishing that similarity, it must necessarily be stated that this very quality of darkness (*śyāmatva*), which serves as an attribute of the object of comparison, is connected to the standard of comparison as well, by means of *tantra* (simultaneous application) and other methods. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa (in his *Pradīpa* on the *Mahābhāṣya*, Prākṣiptakhaṇḍa, p.
396) states: "When [the word 'dark'] refers to Devadatta, who is the referent of the word 'dark'..."

The status of being the object of comparison (*śastritva*) is superimposed [upon the moon]. Anticipating the objection—"If it is due to similarity, then based on what quality is there a similarity between those two?"—it is resolved as follows: "In cases such as *candramukhī* ('moon-faced'), although many qualities exist in the moon, it is by virtue of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) that 'loveliness to behold' (*priyadarśanatva*) is superimposed. Even though this quality is not explicitly mentioned here, it is understood from the usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) to be the cause of the simile. Since the quality of 'darkness' (*iyāmatva*) and so forth is heard directly in the word denoting the subject of comparison (*upameya*) in the present context, how could it not touch upon the object of comparison (*upamāna*) through proximity? Thus it is settled.

For this very reason, in the sūtra *upamānāni* (Pāṇini 2.1.77), although the term "by means of generalities" (*sāmānyaiḥ*) alone would have sufficed, the expression "by means of words denoting generalities" (*sāmānyavacaiḥ*) was stated. This is intended to indicate, through the method of *tantra* (simultaneous application), that the word conveys the property residing in both [the standard of comparison and the object of comparison] by virtue of being connected to both. Therefore, it is established that the verbal connection of the common property with both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison occurs whether they are expressed separately (*vyāsa*) or together in a compound (*samāsa*).

—0kha—0 [Objection: But if this is so, then even in the case of "The man is brave like a tiger" (*puruṣo vyāghra iva śūraḥ*), since there is a connection in both instances, the qualifier would also be accompanied by its own qualifier. Consequently, because the rule "there is no composition of those accompanied by qualifiers" (*saviseṣaṇānāṃ vṛttir na*) would apply, the compound would not be obtained; thus, the meaning is that the rule "when the general term is not employed" (*sāmānyāprayoge*) would be rendered purposeless. [Response: It is not so—the phrase "when the general term is not employed" is not redundant.

There is no fault here because the tiger, which serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), is necessarily dependent upon the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) for its function of conveying meaning. It was stated previously that being a determiner by virtue of possessing a common attribute is what constitutes the state of being a standard of comparison (*upamānatva*). This is clearly explained elsewhere in works such as the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, where it is shown that the natural sense is likewise the same. Thus, when words such as *iva* are employed, the cognition of similarity—which consists of the relation between the common attribute and the standard—is verbal (*śābdī*), whereas the actual simile (*upamā*) itself is extrinsic (*ārthī*). When words such as *sadṛśa* (resembling) are employed, the cognition of similarity is verbal, while the simile itself is extrinsic.

And similarity (*sādṛśya*) is an indivisible, distinct category (*padārtha*), established as the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) of words such as "similar" (*sadṛśa*), which is brought about by the relation to a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*). It is not, however, the nature of the common property itself, as defined by the phrase "being different from that" (*tadbhinnatve sati*) and so forth. For this very reason, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *akartari ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.19), it is stated: "When [a word] is joined with the negative particle (*nañ*) or with the word 'like' (*iva*), the operation is understood to apply to something else that is similar to it; for in this way the meaning is comprehended. (Mahābhāṣya, Vol. II, p. [page number]).

225) According to the maxim *nañivayukte* (when *nañ* or *iva* are joined), the word *anya* in the compound *anyasadṛśa* is meaningful. Since similarity to another (*anyasādṛśya*) is constituted by difference (*bheda*), that [difference] would be obtained by the word *sadṛśa* alone; thus, the word *anya* would be redundant. For this very reason, when it is said "this is similar to that," the inquiry arises as to "by what property is there similarity between these two? rather than "which property is the similarity between these two?"

(The reading is incoherent: "[And it is distinct due to the difference between the suggester (*vyañjaka*) and so forth—]" for even from the Bhāṣya statement, "for by that there is the comprehension of the meaning," in the case of a connection with *iva* and the like, there is merely the apprehension of similarity; however, its status as being either suggested (*dyotya*) or denoted (*vācya*) is not perceived. From this also, it is obtained that in a connection with *iva* and the like, the cognition of similarity is semantic (*ārthī*). As for the example in the rule "nañivayukte... (Pāṇini 2.2.6), it is "śākhya" and so forth, derived under the governing rule "ive pratikṛtau" (Pāṇini 5.3.96) by the rule "śākhādibhyo yaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.103).

In that regard, it is understood that *somabhadra* is similar to Soma. Nor should it be argued that even if similarity is admitted despite non-difference, how can there be a similarity produced by that [non-difference], since a property residing in multiple instances (*anekavṛttidharma*) alone constitutes an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), and such a property is absent here.

For through methods such as *tantra* (simultaneous application) or *āvṛtti* (repetition), even a single entity can function as many; this is clear from the commentary on the *Śivasūtra* "aiuṇ" and other sources, which maintain the position that the individual phoneme (*akāravyakti*) is one.

Nor should it be argued that even in the case of non-difference (*abheda*), if one were to accept [the figure of] *upamā* by taking recourse to a difference created by concealment (*āvṛti*) and so forth, and thereby establishing the presence of a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), then in instances such as "not a face" (*amukha*), one could likewise take recourse to a difference created by time (*kāla*) and so forth and treat it as *upamā*; this would result in the undesirable consequence (*apatti*) of the total disappearance of the poetic figure *ananvaya*.

"Because that distinction is not touched upon by the word. All of this is clear in the *Laghumañjūṣā* (*Nipātartha*, pp. 618–22), so enough [of citing it here]. In the phrase *śarairusraih* ("by arrows that are rays"), according to this view—just as in the case of *candramukhī* ("moon-faced") and similar expressions—the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is understood through established usage to be "sharpness"; thus, the cognition is: "by sharp arrows that are non-different from the sharp rays, which serve as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). (4) (45)

He raises an objection: "Not so"—this refers to the phrase "of the prefix" (*upasargasya*). This is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the particle (*nipāta*) in general. "Due to the absence of meaningfulness" (*arthavattvābhāvena*): the sense is that, according to his view, there is no function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vṛtti*) distinct from direct denotation (*śakti*) and indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*). "It would not occur": consequently, because of the prohibition "one should not employ what is not a word," its usage would not take place; and the sense is that [the particle] would lack those grammatical operations which are dependent upon being a word (*padatva*), and so forth. "That very thing" means "that which is manifested."

The intention is that even *dyotanā* (manifestation), which is a synonym for *vyañjanā*, is accepted as being a function (*vṛtti*). [Regarding the phrase] "the status of being a nominal stem" (*prātipadikatvam*): the intention is that from that [status], the derivation of case-endings (*sup*) occurs.

[Objection: But surely, since the term *arthavat* (Sūtra 1.2.45) is understood to mean "that which generates the cognition of meaning solely through a relationship consisting of either direct denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*"), how can there be the status of a nominal stem (*pratipadikatva*)? Therefore, he says "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) to address the objection that the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is not accepted. [Furthermore,] because resorting to an interpretative indicator (*jñāpaka*) involves excessive difficulty, he says "of a particle" (*nipātasya*) [referring to Sūtra 1.1.14]. And since that [rule] is also refuted by the indicator in the rule "adhi-pari" (Sūtra 1.4.93), he says "kṛt-taddhita-" (Sūtra 1.2.46).

In reality, since the necessity of *vyañjanā* for grammarians has been established elsewhere, it should be understood that in the context of the *sūtra* "arthavat" (Pāṇini 1.2.45) and others, the term "meaning-bearing" (*arthavat*) refers precisely to the capacity to produce cognition through any one of the relations—namely, denotation (*śakti*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), or suggestion (*vyañjanā*). Thus, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is secured by that very *sūtra*. This has already been demonstrated below in the section on Denotation (*śaktivāda*).

He concludes: "Therefore... In this regard, he cites the consensus: "And it has been said... Regarding the fourfold [classification]—namely, nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*)—of the two types, namely those consisting of nouns and verbs, there is no function (*vyāpāra*), that is, no operation (*vṛtti*), in the form of either *śakti* (denotation) or *lakṣaṇā* (indication). The sense is that, according to this view, the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vṛtti*) is simply not admitted.

—2 otherwise—than its own meaning, as in the case of the word *brāhmaṇa* and others. Although in common usage there is no cognition of a qualified entity [separate from its parts], it is precisely the qualified entity that expresses the action. The separate conceptualization of the root and the prefix occurs only for the sake of establishing the application of the augment *aṭ* and so forth. As it has been said:
"The separate conceptualization [of the root and prefix] is for the sake of establishing the application of the augment *aṭ* and the rest."

"In the grammatical treatise, [the distinction] belongs to the root alone, even when there is a prefix. Thus, [it is said]: "Specific actions are initiated by means of combinations [of roots and prefixes]; such is the case. Considering the internal sequence of operations, the root and the prefix enter into a relationship with the grammatical factors (*sādhana*), and that action is of such a nature. Nevertheless, [this is stated] in accordance with the rules: "The *suṭ* augment precedes the root" (Pāṇini 6.1.135), and "A motion-word (*gati*) [is compounded] with a word denoting a motion" (Pāṇini 2.2.18).

On account of the authority of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra beginning with *8-1-70*, since an action (*kriyā*) is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it cannot exist without connection to a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); thus, its status as an action remains unimpaired. Furthermore, because it is impossible for a word designated as a prefix (*upasarga*)—which is based on such a connection—to occur without that connection, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is first joined with the means of accomplishment, not by interposing the meaning of the prefix.

Therefore, it is established that when the status of being an action (*kriyātva*) has not yet been accomplished, there is a connection with words designated as *upasargas* for the sake of bringing about the cognition of the agent (*kartṛ*). As it has been said [in the Vākyapadīya, II.218–219]: "Just as, due to the impending connection with a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), there is a loss of the status of being a verbal root (*adhātutva*) and the emergence of the state of being an object (*karmabhāva*), so too should other cases be observed."

"The distinction between a root and a prefix, though internalized even from the closest connection, becomes manifest at the time of word-formation (*padakāla*)"—this previously cited statement by Hari is unacceptable because it is not supported by the *Bhāṣya*. Thus, as is clear elsewhere (e.g., in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*, under the *Antaraṅga-paribhāṣā*, verse 50), these two rules—"first [the suffix] with the root's *sādhana*" and "first [the suffix] with the prefix"—constitute a single syntactical unit.

And thus, from this as well, the status of being a *dyotaka* (indicator) is obtained. Furthermore, from the commentary on the rule "upapadaṃ tiṅ" (Pāṇini 2.2.19)—specifically from the Mahābhāṣya (Pra-kha-pṛ. 440, Bhā-pṛ. "First the verbal root is joined with its *sādhana*, afterwards with the prefix")—the status of being a *dyotaka* is established. Having raised the objection that there might be a compound (*samāsa*) of two prefixes, [the author] states: "First the verbal root is joined with its *sādhana*; therefore, first there would be semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) only with that which is qualified by a *tiṅ*."

In this regard, it has been resolved that because of the prohibition "not a verbal root" (*atiṅ*), there is no *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning) with what is not a verbal root. If the connection with a word bearing the designation *upasarga* occurred prior to the connection with the verbal root, and that [word] were expressive of the verbal root itself, then compounding would indeed be unavoidable. Furthermore, the connection of the verbal root with its *sādhana* (grammatical factor) occurs prior to the connection with the *upasarga*, precisely by internalizing the meaning of the *upasarga* according to the method already stated; otherwise, in examples such as *upāsyate guruḥ*, the suffix *la* etc. would not arise in the sense of the object (*karman*).

There is no fault [in our position] because even in the case of *nerviśa* (Sūtra 1.3.17), the meaning is that it is due to its connection with the suffix *ni*. For this very reason, the formation of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in other instances such as *viśate* is established. Enough of this. (46)

"—2coktarītyeti—2||" means "according to the manner stated [previously]. In examples such as *prajayati*, it is said that, through co-occurrence with the prefix *pra* (as indicated by the ellipsis *pra*... *avayava*... *dṛśyate*), the verbal root itself possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for victory qualified by excellence and so forth; this is the meaning. "—2tiṅādeḥ syāditi—2||" means: "In that case, there would be [the consequence] for the *tiṅ*-suffixes and so on. The implication is that, consequently, the individual power (*avayavaśakti*) [of the components] would be difficult to ascertain (*durjñeyatā*) in all instances.

In reality, as was established below, since "the meaning of the verbal root consists of five [factors]," it is actually accepted that suffixes such as *tiṅ* are merely *dyotaka* (indicative). The phrase "it is not established" means that this entity consists of the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) regarding the relation of difference (*bhedānvaya*). The phrase "also this" means that this consists of the grammatical rule regarding the relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*). The phrase "likewise" means that it concerns objects other than particles (*nipāta*). Thus, the sense is that both types of grammatical rules concern objects other than particles. The phrase "having reached" [refers to the fact that]...

In the theory that [prefixes] are indicators (*dyotaka*), regarding forms such as *prajayati* ("he conquers excellently"), there is the view that either the verbal root has the power (*śakti*) or the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for victory qualified by excellence, or else the prefix *pra-* possesses the indicatorship for that respective meaning. The point is that since postulating two such functions (either *śakti* or *lakṣaṇā* for the root, or indicatorship for the prefix) involves greater complexity (*gaurava*), the complexity resulting from providing the qualification "being distinct from a particle" (*nipātātiriktatva*) when assuming two powers is not a fault. In fact, even under the theory of denotation (*vācakatva*), since particles like *ca* denote conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth, and since conjunction is a part of the meaning of the particle itself, it does not follow [that the root denotes it] according to the maxim "the meaning of a word [is connected with] the meaning of a word."

Nor is there a connection with qualifiers such as "beautiful" (śobhana), nor is there a genitive case. Thus, in cases such as "the pot and [so on]" (*ghaṭaśca*), since there is no obstacle to the non-difference (*abheda*) of the pot and so forth being construed with the meaning of *ca* as a conjunctive particle, it was stated previously that the qualification "being other than a particle" (*nipātātiriktatva*) need not be included in either of the two grammatical rules (*vyutpatti*).

"—The futility of the rule (vidhi-vaiyyarthyam)"—the meaning is that there is simply no such thing as a meaningless particle (anarthaka-nipāta). "Of the meaningless one" (anarthakasya)—the sense is that since a meaningful particle does not exist [in this context], there is nothing to be excluded [by the rule], and thus it would be useless (vyartham). "It must be accepted" (abhyupeyam)—the sense is that in that case, the meaningfulness of both [the particle and the suffix] is clearly established. "For thus" (evam hi)—that is, in order to ward off the suspicion of the futility of the Vārttika; for even though all [particles] are indicators (dyotya), he states the meaningfulness of the Vārttika with the words "of all meanings" (sarvārtha).

Regarding the words *upāttānām*, *tu*, *hi*, *ca*, *vai*, and so forth; and regarding that *vārttika*: [the phrase] "and because it has been rejected" refers to the rule "The prefixes *adhi* and *pari* are meaningless" (Pāṇini 1.4.93). The intention is that this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) with respect to general cases (i.e., it indicates that such particles are not indicators of meaning in general). He refutes the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, who maintain that particles possess denotative power (*vācakatā*), by stating: "The plural number," and "by positive and negative concomitance he says: 'only,' and 'only the word *ca*. Thus, it is the particle itself [that is being discussed].

The exclusion of words such as "tree" (vṛkṣa) mentioned together with [the particle] is by way of indicating the intended meaning (*tātparya*), that is, by way of indicating its suggestiveness (*dyotakatā*). The phrase "are useful" means they are useful not by way of indicating the primary denotative power (*śakti*), but rather by way of indicating the intended meaning. As for the statement "the definition applies to the combined [particle and word]," this is because it will be demonstrated immediately hereafter that the suggested meaning appears only as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). The term "necessary" (*āvaśyaka*) [is used].

The meaning is that, with respect to the cognition of the object "cloth" as a composite form dependent upon the word "paṭa," the mental presence (upasthiti) produced by secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) is the cause; thus, "power" (śakti) [is defined]. With respect to the aforementioned cognition, the mental presence produced by the power residing in the word "paṭa" is the cause. This is the sense.

"—In both positions" means: in the positions of being indicative (*dyotakatā*) and being expressive (*vācakatā*). "Precisely for this reason" means: precisely because both positions are accepted. "Because of the possibility of specific [meanings]" means: in cases such as *prapacati*, the prefixes indicate excellence (*prakarṣa*) and so forth; however, in the case of *pratiṣṭhate*, there is the cognition of the commencement of the cessation of motion (*gatinivṛtti*).

The meaning is that prefixes (*prādi*) possess only a *dyotakatva* (indicative function); however, when there is the cognition of motion (*gati*), they also possess *vācakatva* (denotative function). Although, according to the view that prefixes are indicative and verbal roots (*dhātu*) are denotative, there is no parsimony (*lāghava*)—[as it would require positing] [the capacity for all] *syādi* suffixes [to denote]; nevertheless, because a single prefix has different meanings according to the difference in the root, and because it is sometimes meaningless, as well as due to the contradiction with the *Nirukta-bhāṣya*, they possess only *dyotakatva*. For this very reason, it was stated by Hari: "Where motion and so forth are not understood by the *syādi* suffixes alone..."

"In that regard, based on the two kinds of inference, its properties such as 'forward motion' (*prāc*) and so forth are stated" (Vākya-padīya, Kāṇḍa II, verse 189). [The reading found in the available manuscript is: "But by means of [the suffixes] *sthā* and the others alone, movement (*gamana*) and so forth are understood.
In some places, the possible distinctions have been shown by means of [the suffixes] alone.

"By means of a prefix (*upasarga*), such as *pra* and others, [the meaning] is manifested" (Vākyapadīya, Kāṇḍa II, verse 190). Thus, in the case of the word *pratiṣṭhate*, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the meaning "going forth" (*gati*) belongs to the root alone. The prefix *pra*, however, is merely an indicator (*dyotaka*) because it is a prefix; this is inferred from its being an indicator in words such as *prapacati*, by means of a valid inference (*anyathānupapatti*). It is of two kinds: positive (*anvayin*) and negative (*vyatirekin*). Its properties (*taddharmāḥ*) are the properties of being an indicator; such is the meaning of that [verse].

—2 Upādhiḥ—2: An indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhiḥ*). —2 In the general category (*sāmānye*)—2: That is, in a pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*). [This refers to] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), i.e., the instruments of knowledge such as inference (*anumāna*) and so forth, and the apprehension of the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatāgraha*). (6) (47) —2 "Precisely by that delimitation"—2. —2 "These are indicators (*dyotaka*) or denoters (*vācaka*)"—2. The sense is that between being an indicator and being a denoter, since the general property of being a particle (*nipātatva*) is accepted as the delimiting factor in the apprehension [of the meaning], it is not [the specific properties] such as being a prefix (*upasargatva*) and so forth.

In reality, it should be understood that since the quality of being a *dyotaka* (indicator) as determined by that [meaning] resides in that particle (*nipāta*), the specific property of its function (*vṛtti*) must necessarily be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). There is no evidence for a general property to serve as the delimiting factor, and furthermore, cognition occurs even in one who does not know [the category of] "particle-hood" (*nipātatva*). In this regard, the following should be noted: particles (*nipātas*) that convey specific features pertaining to an action possess the status of being *dyotakas*; moreover, this is strictly regulated. Among these, the first case is, for example, the denotative power (*vācakatva*) of the uncompounded negative particle (*nañ*).

For this very reason, the cognition of non-existence arises from the word *na*, and a desire to know "of what? is observed, just as it is with the word *abhāva*. Furthermore, in expressions such as *parvatādau* ("on the mountain, etc."), the understanding of the meaning "prior to the mountain" is observed. For if [the direction] were merely indicated (*dyotya*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) would not occur; that is, because the indicated object functions as a qualifier, and the ablative suffix denotes the qualifier of the indicated meaning. (L. *viśeṣatvāt*) For this very reason, [it is stated in] "striyām" (Pāṇini Sūtra...).

In the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra *striyām* (4-1-3), having raised the objection that if femininity (*strītva*) were denoted by the suffixes *ṅīp* and so forth, it would be the primary meaning of the affix and thus the number [of the base] would be inapplicable, it was resolved by treating it as merely indicative (*dyotaka*). (MaBh II, p. 300). For this very reason, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra *hetumati ca* (3-1-26), having raised the objection that if the *ṇic* suffix were indicative of the causal operation (*prayojakatvavyāpāra*), it would result in that operation becoming a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), it was resolved by treating it as expressive (*vācaka*). (MaBh II, p. 59).

Now, one might object: "In the rule *svarita* (Pāṇini 1.3.72), according to the view of Kaikyaṭa regarding 'arrangement' (*saṃvidhāna*) as stated in the Mahābhāṣya (Prakriyā-khaṇḍa, p. 284), there is a lack of pervasion (*vyabhicāra*), because the 'arrangement'—in the form of the instigating activity indicated by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)—is not the qualificand. If this is raised, we say no.

Even in that case, there is no fault, because the status of being expressed by the middle-voice (ātmanepada) suffix is accepted. For this very reason, the statement by Hari—that "the middle-voice occurs optionally with the causative suffix (ṇiC) when the agent's own interest is involved"—is consistent. Alternatively, it should be understood that the meaning of *apacate* is simply the act of cooking (*pacikriyā*) performed by the instigated agent (*prayojyakartṛ*), which has as its object the operation of the instigator (*prayojakavyāpāra*); thus, there is no deviation regarding its being indicated (*dyotyatva*).

In some cases, [the particle *iva*] functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*), as in "like rays with arrows" (*śarairusrairiva*) and so forth; this has already been clarified previously in the root-text itself. In other cases, it also functions as a denoter (*vācaka*), as in "O King, eat the myrobalan fruit (*harītakī*), which is beneficial like a mother. Here, the mother is construed as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) with respect to the similarity that is the meaning of the word *iva*; thus, the nominative case (*prathamā*) occurs solely because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) alone is intended.
Nor should it be argued that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would result by taking the relation of difference (*bheda*) in the form of counter-correlativity as the governing factor.

The ancient scholars (*prāñcaḥ*) maintain that because the word *iva* has, by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), as its referent a similarity qualified by the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), there is no occurrence of the genitive case; for [the genitive] would not apply since there is a coreferential relation (*abhedānvaya*) with the counter-correlate, which is a single part (*ekadeśa*) of that [similarity]. However, in reality, this is incorrect—since the nominative case is grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) only when it is coreferential with a verb. For this very reason, rules such as "the nominative occurs in coreferentiality with a finite verb ending (*tiṅ*)" are consistent. Furthermore, in this instance as well, if *iva* were merely indicative (*dyotaka*)—as in the case of *usraih*—then those two [words] would result in having identical case-endings; therefore, it must indeed be expressive (*vācaka*).

Nor should it be argued that there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of [the particle] *ca* being used in the sense of "like" (*iva*), as in the case of *na ca māteva*, because similarity exists when it denotes the meaning of the word *iṣu*;

for such usage is not attested among the learned (*śiṣṭa*), and their grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is accepted only when they are employed in conjunction with words such as *upamāna*. As it has been said:
"Some particles are indicators (*dyotaka*), while others express distinct meanings."

"Some may be like scriptures (*āgama*), expressing a meaning through their combination" (Vākyapadīya II.192). The word "some" (*kecit*) connects with both [the preceding and following clauses]. By the phrase "like scriptures," he asserts that certain suffixes, such as *tv-* and others, are devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*); that is, suffixes such as *-tva* (*thāL*) and so on are purely *svārthika* (meaning those which do not alter the original sense), and are indeed meaningless, rather than being indicators of the occurrence of a mode (*prakāra*). This is because in examples such as "He who is Hari is Hara," the meaning is understood from the base (*prakṛti*) alone even without that suffix. By this, the claim that there is indeed a state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) for the indicated meaning (*dyotyārtha*) in that case is refuted.

In cases such as *brāhmaṇajātīya* and the like (*jāti-patyādau*), however, by the rule *jātyantāccha* (Pāṇini 5.4.9), the suffix *cha* denotes only a relative who is the locus of the genus (*āśrayarūpabandhu*). Therefore, even though this [genus] functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is no deficiency. Thus ends the *Laghubhūṣaṇakānti*.
— The Determination of the Indicative Function (*dyotakatā*) and the Denotative Function (*vācakatā*) of Particles (*nipāta*)—
Salutation to Śrī.

—0— Determination of the Meaning of Suffixes Denoting Absence —0— Following the description of *vṛtti* (and with the additional reading "in compounds"), having analyzed the negative (*nañ*) compound in connection with the topic of compound *vṛtti*, and having also examined the meaning of particles (*nipāta*) in connection with that [negative] because the negative functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*), and once the curiosity of the students—who were previously hindered—has been removed, then by way of the "opportunity" (*avasara-saṅgati*) consisting in the necessity of what must necessarily be stated, something that ought to be explained according to the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim is now to be described among the *taddhita* suffixal operations. —0—4—0— In the *taddhita* *vṛttis*... (T.)

The word "gata" is an additional reading. The root text explains the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) as follows: "In the rule *kṛttaddhite* (Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudī, Kārikā 49), [the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita*] is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication)," because this conforms to the statement of Harivṛṣabha regarding the abstract suffix. He states that this is not something new by saying "this meaning," etc. Thus it has been stated in the *Samāsavāda*.

[It] is not possible in the view of non-difference (abhedapakṣa). The meaning is that, in the view of non-difference (or according to the variant reading *tatpakṣe*), difference itself serves as the qualifier. However, in the second and third views, since the relation denoted by the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha-sambandha*) is included within the compound (*vṛtti*), and since the knowledge of that [relation] is the cause for the application of the word, suffixes such as *tvā* occur precisely there [in those cases], as in *rājapuruṣa*, *aupagava*, and so forth.

In words such as ‘pācaka’ (cook), because the distinction between the agent and the action is invariably perceived even when the kṛt-affix is used—and thus there is no deviation—since the word applies to the substance only through the cognition of its connection with an action, the suffixes *tvā* and so forth apply to that [action] alone. He states this very point: “And thus... the relation”—the meaning is that it possesses a relational object (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*).

As for the claim that a relation appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) because it is denoted by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), that is not tenable; for the term "relation" is applied precisely to that which appears as a relational object (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*). Moreover, it is universally accepted that even a relation denoted by the genitive case and others appears as a relation (*saṃsarga*). By this, the view that a word-meaning is necessarily a qualifier alone is also refuted.

"—But [in the case] of an invariable relation... This means that in the view where the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is "Upagu himself," because the relation between offspring and progenitor is invariable for the offspring named Upagu, [the suffix denotes the base itself]. However, this must be considered further, as there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇābhāvāt*). An example [of such a case] is "ākṣika" and so forth.

He states that this too is generally the case: "—2dāmoda etc.—2. By the word "etcetera," [the examples] *sattā* (existence) and *śuklatva* (whiteness) are included. It should also be understood that [this applies to] a particular genus (*jāti*) as well as a particular quality (*guṇa*). This was stated [in the context of examples] such as "—2dāmodaratvam etc.—2" because of the cognition of non-difference (*abhedapratyaya*), [showing that] it belongs to the quality itself. The non-difference in "This is that" is based on recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), whereas the non-difference in "The jar is white" is due to the cognition [of identity]. (T.)

Because the relationship based on the distinction between the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) is obscured by the substance (*dravya*), and because that relationship lacks the status of being the ground for the application of a word, the meaning is that the quality itself is the reality. Now, one might object: "If the cognition of non-difference in the expression 'the white of the jar' is thus accounted for, then the rule prescribing the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup-luk*) is useless. This is not so—

Because the distinct usage "the whiteness of the jar" (*ghaṭasya śukla*) also exists, [the suffix] is introduced in order to exclude the usage "one who has attained whiteness" (*prāptaśuklavān*). And thus, since this [suffix] is etymologically derived (*yaugika*) from the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), it takes the gender of the substantive (*viśeṣyaliṅgatā*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Amarakośa* (First Book, Section on Words, Verse 17): "Words such as *śukla* [denoting a quality] are masculine when [used for] the quality, but they take the gender of the possessor when [used for] that which possesses it. Their application to that which possesses it occurs through non-difference (*abhedena*) by means of elision (*luk*).

Or it should be understood through differentiation (*bhedena*). And this suffix *buk* occurs only when there is the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of a word denoting a substance that is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with it, or when that [coreferentiality] is understood through context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth. If, however, it is argued that because of non-denotation (*anabhidhāna*), the suffixes *matup* and others do not arise from it, and that its possession of all genders also follows simply from the inherent nature of denotation (*abhidhānasvabhāva*), then the rule for elision (*lugvacana*) would be redundant. In the third [case], regarding "invariable relation" (*avyabhicaritasambandha*): "The state of being existent is 'existence' (*sattā*). Because the relation between "existent" (*sat*) and "existence" (*sattā*) is invariable, it is only the universal (*jāti*) [that is denoted]. (L.T.)

The suffix expressing *bhāva* (abstract state) denotes the meaning of the relation (*sambandha*). However, in the case of [compounds] such as "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*), because the relation is subject to deviation [from its terms], the relation is expressed by means of a *bhāva*-suffix. Thus ends the direction [of the argument]. The meaning of this is that the expression of the relation occurs not only in cases such as "king's man" or "possessor of variegated cows" (*citragu*), but because it indicates the sense that the mere meaning of the case-ending appears as a relation, just like the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*).

Now, one might object: "In expressions such as *nīlaghaṭatvam* ('the state of being a blue pot'), what is the meaning of the suffix? It cannot be said that the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is the relation between the blue and the pot; for, according to the reasoning already stated, since those two are identical in form, there exists no relation between the meanings of the preceding and following words other than that of qualifier and qualified. If this is argued, we reply: No—the meaning of the suffix is simply the property residing in the blue pot and so forth, namely *ghaṭatva* ('potness') and the like. And that very [property] is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *nīlaghaṭa* ('blue pot').

Nor should it be argued that, if "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) alone were the basis for the application of the term, then since that [pot-ness] exists even in yellow pots and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that individual instances such as yellow pots would also appear when the word "blue pot" is uttered.

By virtue of qualifiers such as "blue" and so forth, it is precisely the individuals that are blue which appear under the form of "pot-ness"; thus, it is "pot-ness" as co-referential with "blue" that appears as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Since a difference in pot-ness and the like is admitted due to the difference in their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), this refutes the view that in expressions such as "blue-pot-ness," the co-reference of the quality and the universal—which serve as the grounds for application—is the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

However, there is no evidence for its being denoted by the suffix *bhāva*, because it does not appear as the base (*prakṛti*) of that suffix. Even if its appearance were granted according to the method stated in the *Samāsavyākhyā*, since it resides in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it lacks the status of being the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*); thus, there is no evidence for its being expressed by the *bhāva*-suffix. (1) (49)

Some, however, say that the collection (*samudāya*) of "blue-ness" and "jar-ness" is the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*). In cases such as *dhava-ravira-tvam*, according to the author of the *Mūla* [the Mahābhāṣya], since the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) is the qualifier in an *itaretara-yoga* (copulative compound), the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is precisely that relationship consisting of that form. In the view where the collective aggregate is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—or rather, the qualifier—in both types of compounds, the denotation in both cases is a collection of universals (*jāti-samudāya*). Since its constituent parts are not manifested (*anudbhūtāvayavatva*) in both instances, the singular number is employed.

If the parts were manifested [as a whole], there would even be a dual number, as in "the dhava and khadira trees. He restates the Mīmāṃsaka position, which maintains that words have mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), in order to refute it—namely, the view that in cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), the referent is merely the substance (*dravyamātra*). By the word "merely" (*mātra*), the exclusion of a relation (*sambandha*) is intended. The cognition of that [relation] occurs, however, by way of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*); likewise, in his view, even in the case of "cook" (*pācaka*), the relation is not the meaning. As it is said: "The root *pac* itself expresses the act of cooking, while the suffix *aka* expresses the agent."

For it has been stated: "Furthermore, an agent endowed with the act of cooking cannot be denoted by any single [word]. Thus, even the apprehension of word-meaning (*śaktigraha*) is possible regarding infinite substances, by taking a staff or similar object—which is subsumed under the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—as a mere indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). [The phrase] "of that which belongs to it" (*tadgatasya*) refers to [the agent]. [The phrase] "by not being expressive" (*anabhidhāyakatvena*) means by the observation of its non-expressiveness. [This refers to] the Mīmāṃsakas.

For those who maintain that there is a cognition whose qualifier is the mere staff (*daṇḍa*) without [the relation] being its qualifier, the expression "denoting that" means "denoting the relation. A "qualifier" (*prakāra*) is that which is the locus of a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) determined by a primary subjecthood (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*). Otherwise, in cases such as "having a mountain possessing fire" (*vahnimat-parvatavattvam*), it would follow that the suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) denotes the relation between fire and the mountain.

A certain [scholar] maintains that even by way of a traditional method, that is the meaning; as it has been stated in the case of "the nature of dhava and khadira" (*dhavakhadiratva*) and so forth, that it is a collection of universals (*jātisamudāya*). Otherwise, if the first and second [universals] were not presented in their respective order—[as in the phrase] "of substanceness, etc. (*dravyatvādeḥ*)—because that [substanceness] inheres in the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*); and [as in the phrase] "of the staff, etc. (*daṇḍādeḥ*), because in your view that [staff] is the mode (*prakāra*) of the cognition produced by the base. Thus he says:

"—2na ceti—" means "no. The point is that if the relation (*sambandha*) were the meaning of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*), then because both [the possessor and the relation] would be present, the relation would be denoted by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). Even though in cases such as *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer") the secondary suffix does not have the relation as its meaning, it is nonetheless denoted by it out of necessity (*agatyā*).

He refutes the statement of that commentator: “—*yat tu*—” and “—*vācya āśrita*—,” which means [the fault] of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). The sense is: as in the case of “the king’s man” (*rājapuruṣa*) and so forth. This is the disparity; the meaning is: in “pot-ness” (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, there is a universal (*jāti*) and so on, whereas in “king-man-ness” (*rājapuruṣatva*) and so forth, there is a relation; this is the disparity. (50)

In the root text—“...-0ka-0’-2prakāratāmi-2... (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra Kārikā 50)—the word “cognition” (*buddhi*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Thus he says: “by way of being a qualifier (-2prakāratayeti-)”—the remainder is “because it is the state of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) of ‘pot-ness’ (*ghaṭatva*)”. “By the subsequent suffix (-2taduttarapratyayena-)”—that is, by the suffix following the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). “But here there is no brevity (-2natvatra laghu iti-)”: the meaning of the suffix is simply the form consisting of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth; there is no evidence for [the meaning] being “pot-ness-ness” (*ghaṭatvatva*), which consists in residing in all pots while not residing in anything other than pots.

"—'Due to the difference in the relata, etc.'—this is the intended meaning: the very universal (*jāti*) called Great Being (*mahāsattā*), which is the nature of the Supreme Brahman, appears as if divided through the differences of individual entities such as cows that are its relata; thus it is called the 'cowness' (*gotva*) universal and so forth, being [in reality] devoid of difference but designated as such through metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*). All words are established as denotators of that very Being of Brahman. Since both [the word and the object] possess fourfold aspects, the state of being indefinable (*nirupākhya*) is what is expressed by suffixes such as *tva* and *tal*. That alone is the essential nature of the Being of Brahman. —01— Therefore (T.)*.

Existence (*sattā*) itself is called the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), and it is termed "existence. Likewise, even among actions, it is Great Existence (*mahāsattā*) itself—distinguished by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) according to its own nature—that is expressed by verbal roots; and that is a universal (*jāti*). Furthermore, it is distinguished by the limiting adjuncts of the states of being accomplished (*siddhatva*) and being to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*). It alone is called the "Great Self" (*mahān ātmā*) and "eternal," since this entire world-appearance is its illusory manifestation (*vivarta*).

In reality, in expressions such as ‘ghaṭatvatvam’ (the-ness of pot-ness), the understanding is simply that there is a property related to pot-ness; and that [property] is a specific property in the form of a qualifier (or, according to an alternative reading, an additional one). Alternatively, according to the method to be described regarding the cognition produced by the base (prakṛti), the individual (vyakti) alone is the qualifier; thus, it is that very [individual] which is the meaning of the suffix *tva* in ‘ghaṭatvatvam’. However, a ‘pot-ness-ness’ of the aforementioned form is not tenable, because it would involve an excessive complexity (*gaurava*) due to being composed of multiple word-meanings.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because that [property] consists of the existence (*sattā*) of Brahman; for, rather than postulating that a property which is more cumbersome (*guru*) consists of the existence of Brahman, it is more appropriate to postulate that a property which is simpler (*laghu*) itself consists of that [existence]. This applies elsewhere as well. To illustrate: in the case of absences (*abhāva*), one does not postulate that the "nameless-ness" (*anirūpyatva*) and so forth—which are inherent in them and possess parts (*sakhaṇḍa*)—consists of that [existence]; rather, having accepted the generality (*sāmānya*) of "absence-ness" (*abhāvatva*), one postulates that this alone consists of that [existence].

For grammarians accept [the term] everywhere according to the method of the Naiyāyikas, provided there is no subverting evidence; thus, in cases such as *akṣāḥ* (T.L. *akṣya*), even though they belong to different classes (*jāti*), because that very [quality] is accepted as a class (*jāti*)—(T. the reading "due to the acceptance of another class" is inappropriate)—it is precisely that which is expressed by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). (L. in the suffix)

For this very reason, the rejection of the *ekaśeṣa* rule is consistent. Likewise, it was stated previously that even "ḍitthatva" is simply a universal (*jāti*). Alternatively, among many instances of the word "akṣa," there is a universal distinct from [the individual] words called "wordness" (*śabdatva*), which serves as the cause for the cognition and denotation [of those words]. In that regard, due to the identification through the judgment of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*)—namely, "this is that"—[the universal] resides in the designata (*saṃjñin*) which possess the word "akṣa. That very same [universal] is what is expressed by terms such as "akṣatva."

In this way, "generality-ness" (sāmānyatva) is also simply a genus (jāti); for this very reason, there is the conventional usage that "cowness and horseness are generalities. By this, it should be understood that the Naiyāyika statement, "generalities are themselves devoid of further generalities," is made according to that very same system. Likewise, "ether-ness" (ākāśatva) is also simply a genus; the details of this are explained elsewhere.

If it is asked, "How then is there the linguistic usage [of terms] such as 'quality-word' (*guṇaśabda*) in the case of words like *śukla* ('white')?"—the answer is no. For, whether one follows the position of the fourfold classification (*catuṣṭayīpakṣa*) or the position of the threefold classification (*trayīpakṣa*), the explanation is established in all cases exactly according to the method stated for the position that it is "only the universal" (*jāti*). This has been demonstrated in the *Nāmārthanirṇaya*.

Regarding the phrase "of which quality" (*yasya guṇasya*), in this *Vārttika*—as stated in the *Mahābhāṣya-pradīpa* (Vol. II, p. 538)—the word "quality" (*guṇa*) denotes any differentiating factor that depends on another, such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, having the nature of a basis for linguistic application (*pravṛttinimitta*). If it is asked how genus and the like are conventionally treated as "qualities," the answer is that in common usage the word "quality" refers to that which is dependent on another; since genus and the like are also dependent, they are designated as "qualities" by way of being the meaning of the suffixes of speech.

For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "For heroism is one quality, while manhood is another. The underlying meaning is as follows: according to the view of the Bhāṣya—that a substance (*dravya*) is a collection of qualities (*guṇa-samudāya*)—due to the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabda-śakti*), in some cases a collection distinct from the genus (*jāti*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the genus is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); likewise, in words such as "cow" (*go*), in certain instances a quality distinct from the genus is the qualificand and the genus is the qualifier, and that very [quality] is the ground for the application of the term (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), just as it is in the case of words like "white" (*śukla*). This applies elsewhere as well.

And therefore, whatever particularity such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, being a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*), is placed forward as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word in order to convey an object—that property (*dharma*) is the meaning of suffixes such as *tva* and *tal*. And the state of being the ground for the application of a word is the fact that from the knowledge of which the word is applied to the object. [This applies] "from words such as *rūpa*" and so forth.

In the case of words such as *rūpa* ("color/form") and others, because they function solely to denote a quality (*guṇa*), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) denotes the genus (*jāti*) residing therein. Regarding the rule "in the case of a quality" (*guṇe*): since those [words] refer to the substratum of the quality (*guṇin*) with the quality as a subordinate element, when a word such as *śukla* ("white") refers to a quality, the abstract suffix likewise denotes the genus. However, in the case of words such as *aṇu* ("atom/small"), because they necessarily refer to the substratum of the quality, [the suffix] denotes the quality itself.

Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is fourfold: minute (*aṇu*), large (*mahat*), long (*dīrgha*), and short (*hrasva*). However, the usage of logicians (*tārkika*) regarding dimension as residing in the minute and so forth is to be understood as meaning that it subsists in [substances] such as the minute. Regarding the term *sūpapāda* ("easily established"): Now, although [the denotation of] universals and qualities is established by the aforementioned method, since it is possible to grasp the expressive power (*śakti*) with respect to the pure individual alone—taking [properties] such as "k-ness" (*katva*) as mere secondary indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), just as in the case of [words like] "it" (*saḥ*) and so forth—it follows that the individual instance of "k-ness" and so on itself... [is the denotatum]. (Note: The text fragment provided ends abruptly; the translation reflects the logical flow of the argument concerning the denotation of words.)

If it is argued that, because words such as *kakādi* have the defective sound (*kuśabda*) as their denotable object, there is no meaning of an affix distinct from the meaning of the base, and the same applies to words such as *ḍittha*, we say: no.

This is because it is accepted that the individual (*vyakti*) alone appears through two types of objecthood (*viṣayatā*). In that case, the individual as delimited by the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), while that same individual as delimited by the state of being the qualifier (*prakāratva*) is the meaning of the suffixes such as *tva*. Alternatively, since there is no fault in the suffix denoting the abstract state (*bhāva*) in the form of the meaning itself—rather than the word itself—following words like *śabdatva*, the words *kukutva* and *ḍittha* (or *ḍitthatva*) are synonyms. For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *tasya bhāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.119), [it is stated... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

Having raised the objection that there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the Sūtra with respect to intention (*abhiprāya*) and so forth, [the author] stated the rule "because of the existence of which quality... (*yasya guṇasya bhāvāt...*). Yet, even that is under-extended (*avyāpti*) to names such as *ḍittha*; therefore, having raised the objection that it is because of the existence of a property distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), he provided one solution: that the individual itself appears through two types of objecthood (*viṣayatā*). Then, he stated another solution with the words: "Or rather, all words exist by means of their own referent; that is their referent, and the suffixes *-tva* and *-tal* are used to denote that."

The meaning of this is as follows: A word has two kinds of meanings—the denoted object (*vācya*) and that which serves as the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). (It should be understood that "the individual" [*vyakti*] is intended. When either of these is denoted, there is a corresponding cognition. In cases such as *ghaṭatvam* ("pot-ness"), the latter [the ground for application] is denoted. However, the base (*prakṛti*) is directed toward the meaning itself. In cases such as *kutvam* ("the state of being Ku") or *ḍitthatvam* ("the state of being Ḍittha"), the former [the individual] is denoted. In those instances, because the connection with the meaning of the suffix would otherwise be untenable, the base is directed toward the word itself; and the relation [between the base and the suffix] is the status of being the mode of the cognition produced.

Therefore, on the strength of this Bhāṣya and Vārttika, it must be assumed that in the case of technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*), the base (*prakṛti*) refers to the word itself. Some, however, maintain that in the case of a technical term, the denotable object (*śakya*) is indeed a substance (*dravya*); and since, in such cases, the meaning of the suffix (i.e., the meaning of the base-suffix complex) consisting of the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is difficult to specify, it is necessary that the base there refers to the word itself.

The reading "bhāva" is an interpolation. Due to the impropriety of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) principle, every base of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*)—by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—is primarily denotative of the word itself (*śabdapara*). Its primary meaning is the "mode" (*prakāra*), which is precisely the ground for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*). This [mode] is related [to the word] either as being the mode of the cognition produced by it, or as being the object of that produced cognition, according to the specific case. In expressions such as "cowness" (*gotvam*), the cognition is: "Cowness is the mode of the cognition produced by the word 'cow'. In expressions such as "king's-man-ness" (*rājapuruṣatvam*)...

The cognition is: "The relation that is the object of the cognition produced by the word *rājapuruṣa*. Even according to the view that the word itself appears in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the word does not serve as the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Therefore, from expressions such as *gotvam*, the cognition is not "the word *go*. It has been stated that the status of being a basis for application consists in that by knowing which a word is applied to its referent. And in the case of jars and the like, this is the universal (*jāti*). In the case of words like *śukla* ("white") when they refer to a quality-possessor (*guṇin*), [it is the quality]. (T. 03-0) In the case of those referring to a quality... (T.)

[The reading "guṇo guṇe pareṣu teṣu" is an additional one. In words such as *pācaka* ("cook"), it is the genus (*jāti*) residing in that [action] which is the basis; in verbal action-words (*kriyāśabda*), it is the action itself. Through connection with that [genus or action], in cases such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man") and *aupagava* ("son of Upagu"), it is the relation [that is denoted]. In words such as *ḍittha*, it is the substance itself, because it appears through two objects of cognition (*viṣayatā*). Thus, the substance alone is the ground for the application of the word (*pravṛttinimitta*); and since it is precisely that [substance] which appears as qualified by the mode (*prakāratā*), it constitutes the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). Therefore, the distinction between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is easily stated.

Because the base [of the suffix] refers to the word (*śabda*), there is no inconsistency regarding the aforementioned relationship; thus, they say that the cognition consists in the understanding that "this individual is the very mode of the cognition produced by the word *ḍittha*. That is incorrect—for there is no evidence for assuming that the base of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) everywhere refers to the word, nor is there any evidence for such a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). [As stated in the rule: "The abstract state of that... (*tasya bhāvaḥ*, Pāṇini 5.1.119).

In the rule *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.124), the word *tat* refers merely to the word-form itself; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the word] falling under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "word" (*śabda*). Furthermore, throughout the section on secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), in rules such as *tasyāpatyam* (Pāṇini 4.1.92), we observe that *tat* refers exclusively to the meaning. Moreover, the aforementioned Bhāṣya and Vārttika apply only to the domain of technical names (*saṃjñā*). Regarding the phrase "of those denoting a genus" (*tatra jātīvacakānām*): the meaning is "of those ending in suffixes whose base is a word denoting a genus, such as 'jar' (*ghaṭa*) and so forth."

The meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is [the property] related to all its own instances by the relation of "subsisting in all those that do not exclude others" (*itarāvṛttitvāvacchinna-nikhila-svavṛttitva*). Since the individuals denoted by the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) function as qualifiers (*prakāratva*) for the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), he says: "And thus... and "uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). By this, it is stated that the property is denoted in its respective specific form (*tattadrūpeṇa*), and not merely as "property-ness" (*dharmatvena*). Thus, from expressions such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvam*), the cognition is: "the property in the form of pot-ness, qualified by the individual denoted by the base, through the aforementioned relation.
However, including the relation within the scope of the cognition, the understanding described in the root text is "subsisting in the pot" (*ghaṭavṛtti*), and so forth.

In reality, the capacity for the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) to denote a thing lies solely in its nature as *dharmatva* (the state of being a property), and not in each specific form [of that property], because that would result in an infinite number of capacities (*śakti*) and because it would entail that suffixes such as *-tva* have multiple meanings. For instance, according to the rule "tasyāpatyam" (Pāṇini 4.1.92) and others, words such as *aupagava* convey their meaning solely as "the offspring of Upagu," and not by means of properties such as *caitratva* (the state of being Caitra) which reside in the offspring of Upagu. Similarly, regarding the rule "tasya bhāvaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.1.119)...
This is because, in the sūtra (Pāṇini 5.1.119), the word *tasya* is heard as signifying [the relation] in its capacity as a relation (*sambandhatvena*).
Nor should it be argued that the manifestation of "being a function" (*vṛttitva*) occurs because it is a relation defined by the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*).

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) arises only from that which is semantically capable (*samarthāt*), because it is appropriate for the relation itself to be manifested through the prescription of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*); otherwise, expressions such as "the potness of the pot" (*ghaṭasya ghaṭatvam*) would not be possible. Therefore, in reality, the meaning of the suffix *tva* and so on is the property—such as "potness"—which serves as the ground for the application of the word and constitutes the mode (*prakāra*) of the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, the individual denoted by the base is the mode in that [property] by way of the relation consisting in "being related to everything except itself," as delimited by "not being related to anything other than itself."

And thus, through the aforementioned relation, there is the cognition "the property qualified by the jar," which amounts to "the property related to the jar. [If—] in cases such as "gravity" (*gurutva*), the cognition [of it] as "gravity-ness" (*gurutvatva*) and so on is established by experience (though this cognition of gravity-ness etc. is not observed), then, just as the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is conveyed even though it is not the primary denotation (*aśakya*) of the word "cow" (*dhenu*), so too gravity and the like should be understood by relying on a contextual condition (*prayogopādhi*). This should be understood similarly for words such as "quality" (*guṇa*); the details are found elsewhere.

With the intention that this alternative view mentioned in the Bhāṣya regarding the word *saṃkhyā* also pertains to words such as *jāti* (genus), etc., he introduces the root text [of the Vārttika] with the words: "He states another alternative view. Alternatively, the word "or" (*yadvā*) is present in the root text. The phrase "for the purpose of indicating that" means it serves the purpose of indicating the Vārttika; or rather, the sense is that the Vārttika is composed of the word "or. The word "also" (*api*) indicates that this is yet another alternative view. Thus is the sense.

The meaning is "words. According to the view that even a word is the referent of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), he explains [the sūtra] as "by its own form, by the object"—that is, by the very nature of the word—as being the domain for the employment of all words denoting universals (*jāti*) and so forth. The meaning is "by the object in the form of the word itself," because a word is employed for the purpose of conveying an object. Since the object is the cause for the occurrence—that is, the employment—of the word, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used. However, some [commentators] hold that after the word *bhāvāḥ*, the word *yasmāt* ("because") is to be supplied; thus, the ablative case is used in the sense of the elision of a gerund suffix (*lyablope*).

And thus, that which serves as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) by relying upon which words come into being for the purpose of conveying meaning and function as denoters—that is the ground for application of those [words]. He explained that the word "bhāva" here also takes the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) according to the rule *hetau* (Pāṇini 2.3.23), because in this usage of the word, it is the cause of the meaning. Another explanation is also clear in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*. He establishes this with the words: "This is the sense"—[namely] "possessing meaning" (*arthavat*), meaning possessing such meanings as genus (*jāti*) and so forth.

—In the case of a substance (dravya) and an individual (vyakti). Here he states the reason: "Hari-Hara"—meaning that which is denoted by them—that is, that which is denoted by words such as "Hari" and so forth. Otherwise, if one were to accept that only the universal (jāti) and so on function as qualifiers (prakāra) with respect to the substance, while the word itself does not function as a qualifier therein.

"—Regarding 'toward city-dwellers'—it is for the sake of instructing the villagers, who lack knowledge of that [object], by means of those city-dwellers. Regarding 'on account of the transgression'—the sense is that city-dwellers do not grasp the denotation with respect to things such as forests and medicinal herbs when they are delimited by a genus (*jāti*). 'In this very way' means precisely through the word as the qualifier (*śabda-prakāraka*). Regarding 'words whose referents are unestablished'—this refers to technical names (*saṃjñā-śabda*). Both [the qualifier and the qualificand] consist of the genus and so forth, and the word..."

Regarding the example "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*), he says "of this" (*asya*) in accordance with the linguistic analysis of the word *puruṣa*. Likewise, it is to be understood that for one who has acquired the knowledge of the word-meaning (*śaktigraha*) through a qualifier such as a universal (*jāti*) and so forth, there is a presentation [of the object] by way of its own form (*svarūpeṇa*). "Specifically" (*viśiṣya*) means specifically by way of the nature of the word "pot" (*ghaṭapadatva*) and so forth—that is, by way of a universal and so forth—[as opposed to] from proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*) and the like. "In that very same way" (*tathaiva*) means precisely as a qualifier of the word (*padaprakāraka*). By this, it is indicated that such a conceptualization occurs only in the case of proper names.

If this were accepted everywhere, there would be the undesirable consequence that even in cases such as *gautvam* (the state of being a cow), the cognition "the word 'cow'" would arise. However, in the case of words like *go* (cow) which primarily denote a pure universal (*jāti*), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) refers to the form of the word itself; for, due to the superimposition of non-difference between the word and its meaning, that very form serves as the occasioning ground (*pravṛttinimitta*) for the application of the suffix.

If it is objected that, [if the word denoted] were merely the pure universal (*jāti*), then the expression "the cow is a *sābaleya*" (a brindled cow) would also be possible—this is not so; for such usage does not occur, and thus in such an application, there is no intention to refer to the universal alone. However, the expression "the cow is eternal" (*gaurnitya*) is indeed accepted. In cases such as "the state of being *ṣ*," "the state of being *ṇ*," and so forth, since there exists either a real or a conditional difference among the phonemes (*varṇa*), it is precisely non-universality (*ajāti*) that is the meaning of the suffix. Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that this [suffix] has the form of a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

In reality, when an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) denotes [a property] derived from words such as *jāti* (genus) or *para* (other), then according to the aforementioned method, it is the individual (*vyakti*) itself that is the denotation of the suffix—as in the case of *gotvam*. Similarly, in expressions such as *ṣatvam*, the abstract suffix likewise refers to the meaning itself, just as in the word *kutva*. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, in cases such as *nānātva* (manifoldness) and *yaugapadya* (simultaneity), the suffix denotes the mode (*prakāra*) of the cognition produced by words like *nānā*, namely, the state of being non-concurrent (*asahabhāva*).

Coexistence (*sahabhāva*) and simultaneous existence (*yugapadbhāva*) constitute the meaning of the suffix; this is sufficient. Thus ends the determination of the meaning of abstract nominal suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the *Laghubhūṣaṇakānti*.
—0— Homage to Śrī.
—The Determination of the Meaning of the Case-suffixes for Deities. Homage to Śrī.

In connection with the discussion on *taddhita* formations, [the author], for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of *devatā-taddhita* suffixes according to different opinions, introduces the root text beginning with “*pratyayārthasya*” (*Vaiśeṣikasūtrakaumudī*, verse 52) by stating: “*sāsya devatā* here. This means: in the examples of the rule “*sāsya devatā*” (Pāṇini 4.2.24). Regarding the phrase “*pradeyam*”: that [deity] can only be understood as being related [to the offering], not as something that is itself to be offered.

The phrase "that which is to be given" (*pradeyam*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the mantra. By this, the inclusion of the statement "the mantra belongs to Indra" (*aindro mantraḥ*) is also achieved. For this very reason, in the case of the passage "That *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas" (*sā vaiśvadevyāmikṣā*), the words *āmikṣā* and so forth merely provide the substantive (*viśeṣya*) for that which has already been cognized as being related [to the deity] by virtue of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). As he will state: "For this very reason, [he says] 'the *āmikṣā*'. (11.2) (53)

[Objection: But surely, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), let this very [word] be the meaning of the suffix; since the deity can be obtained by the word "Indra" and so forth itself, he says: "The deity of Indra and others. The sense is that even though the word "Indra" and so forth—which brings to mind the status of being Indra (*indratva*) and so on—is present, there is no other word [to express the deity]. "In that form" means in the form of being a deity. "The *āmikṣā* is connected with the deity"—this refers to Mīmāṃsādarśana 2.2.23, Adhikaraṇa 9.

In the *Tantravārtika*, the sixth verse states: "By the phrase 'āmikṣā as a related entity' and 'connected with it as a deity,' the qualified position (*viśiṣṭapakṣa*) is stated; thus, there is a connection through the support of the subject under discussion.
