In reality, however, by the word "phoneme," both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) are intended. —2 "Meaningless" (*anarthaka*) means purposeless. —2 "Having a bad meaning" (*durarthaka*) means having a defective meaning, because [in such a view] only the parts [of words] would have their meanings established, and there would be an absence of the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*). —2 "Of others as well" refers to the proponents of the *varṇasphoṭa* theory.

The word "api" (also/even) signifies that the aforementioned other established doctrines are also included. "Thus there is a disagreement"—this means that such is the very nature of the disagreement. There is no disagreement as to whether the expressive elements contained within correct words (*sādhuśabda*) are denotative or not; for in the opinion of all [schools], the elements such as *Upagu* contained within correct words like "Aupagava" are indeed denotative. (61)

"—And because of non-deviation. This means that the cognition of the suffix *la* is the cause for the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, and the presentation produced by the word-element *la* is the cause for a cognition having the agent and so forth as its qualificand (*viśeṣyaka*), both by virtue of being the suffix *la*. He states the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) according to the opponent's view: "—of the substitutes (*ādeśānām*)."

"—2na ceti—2" means that its necessity exists in cases of corrupt forms (apabhraṃśa); this is the intended sense. "—2mānābhāvāditi—2" means: it should not be argued that the very postulation [of the universal] is the proof, because the sequence of many [phonemes] serves as the delimitor of the expressive power (śaktatāvacchedaka).

For you as well, according to the sequence previously stated, because the instructor is manifold, there is an equal degree of complexity resulting from the infinity of the delimiters of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). [Regarding the phrase] "of various distinct [things]"—the meaning is: in the manner of some saying "sim," some saying "suṃ," and some saying "rum," and so forth. [Regarding the phrase] "by the principle of 'that cause'": the meaning is by the maxim, "Let that very cause suffice; what is the use of that? (The formal nature of the maxim is: "If it exists in the very cause of that, what is the use of that?"). Thus is the meaning.

[Objection: Even if such a co-occurrence of phonemes (*varṇa*) is the cause [of meaning-comprehension], the status of the phonemes as denoters (*vācakatva*) is not yet established. To this, he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). In reality, this point is to be reflected upon, as is clear elsewhere. However, some hold the view that "the original (*ādeśin*) is reminded by the substitute (*ādeśa*), and by that [remembrance] the meaning is understood. According to this view, those things which are the delimiters of denotative capacity (*vācakatāvacchedaka*) in our own system must be stated as the delimiters of the capacity to remind (*smārakatāvacchedaka*) in their system. And thus, by the maxim *taddhetoh* (that which is the cause of that), it follows that those very same things are the delimiters of denotative capacity; this is the intended sense.

Nor should it be said that [the suffix] functions as a reminder (*smāraka*) in any form whatsoever, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), so they say. And this is correct, because of the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word *taddhetu* (the cause of that). [The phrase] "it would not be" [is used] because there is no reason for a discrepancy when the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is identical; this is the sense. [The phrase] "due to its non-application" should also be understood as follows: since the governing topic (*adhikāra*) concerns meaning, even in the rule *kartari* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), the word *kartṛ* would have to refer to the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*). Consequently, the meaning you have proposed would not be applicable. || 21/2 || (621/2)
"—*asyāditi*—" means: the sense is that this would follow for you, who maintain that the *tiṅ*-suffix expresses the *bhāvanā*. —"*āpatteḥ*"—means: because of the consequence [of such an error].
Nor should it be said that the determination of the meaning of the suffix *śānac* occurs elsewhere through its expressive power (*śakti*).

Because it is impossible to determine that [meaning] in a practical usage such as "śuddhapacamānaḥ" (one who cooks purely), as stated in the discussion on the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvarthavāda*). Thus ends the determination of the *sphoṭa* of phonemes (*varṇasphoṭa*). Now, the *sphoṭa* of words (*padasphoṭa*).

[Objection: "But surely, the recollection of the meaning is produced by each individual phoneme (*varṇa*), and it is produced clearly again by the final one; thus, there is no undesirable consequence of the meaning being understood from each phoneme individually. Therefore, the *varṇasphoṭa* is faultless. To this, he says: "With respect to each phoneme" (*prativarṇam*). And thus, the statement that the word (*pada*)—in the form of a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*)—is the expressive [unit] is also [established]. The phrase "of other theorists" (*vādinām matāntarasya*) means: "that which belongs to other theorists" (*yad etad vādinām matāntaram*). This is the sense.
He states that very same refutation: "Rāma exists"—this [statement] is not established if [the word] does not denote a name; therefore, its denotative capacity must be accepted. (64)

Having stated that a word (*pada*)—defined as a collection of phonemes—is the expressive unit by the rule "A word ends in a suffix" (Pāṇini 1.4.14), and so forth; he says "of the division" (*vibhāgasya*) even when there is some kind of knowledge of the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). This [statement] refers to an impossibility. He also states the absence of knowledge of those two by saying "of the division. This too refers to an impossibility. He further states the absence of knowledge of those two by saying "all" (*sarve*). "Easy to understand" (*sujñeya*): the meaning is that this is due to the force of rules such as "ṭāṅasiṅasāminātsyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.12). || 5 || (65)

—2 He says this—2—to state that [the word] is expressive. He establishes the distinction between the *sphoṭa* of a word and a sentence as having parts by means of the passage beginning with "O Hari" (hare've) etc.—2. By "acquisition of proficiency" (vyutpattyā)—2—that is, by the knowledge of the [word's] power (*śakti*). Indicating the seed of the sentence's power, he states a specific point: "In reality" (vastutaḥ)—2. "Otherwise" (anyathā)—2—that is, if one were to accept that a word already proficient in its own meaning brings about the presentation of the sentence-meaning. "Of one devoid of such proficiency"—2: of one who lacks proficiency regarding such a sentence-meaning within such a sentence.

The meaning is as follows: in cases such as "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*), since the presentation of the sentence-meaning is possible—just like the presentation of word-meanings through the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "pot" found in sentences like "bring the pot"—it would follow that there is a comprehension of the sentence-meaning even without the linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) pertaining to the sentence. Nor should it be argued that, in the same way, one could maintain the presentation of word-meanings by taking the power residing in the phonemes (*varṇa*) within the phoneme-sphoṭa (*varṇasphoṭa*), and that the comprehension of word-meanings arises from that alone, so that a distinct word-sphoṭa (*padasphoṭa*) need not be postulated.

Because even Brahmā could not possibly state the division between base and suffix in words such as *vasna-sā* (the act of selling), and because no such usage is observed among the elders (*vṛddha*) regarding that portion; furthermore, there is a contradiction with experience if each individual phoneme were a signifier (*vācaka*). [The author] raises an objection—“in that very case”—to prevent the unwanted consequence of cognition in instances such as *ghaṭaḥ karmatvam* (the pot is the object). The phrase “in that very case” means “in the very sentence ‘bring the pot’”; or else, it is an adjective qualifying the cognition itself.

And likewise, because there is an absence of knowledge regarding such co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), there is no such cognition in cases like "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*). [Regarding the phrase] "of the word-meaning such as 'pot'": in cases like "bring the pot" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the knowledge of the power (*śakti*)—in the form of denotative capacity (*bodhakatā*)—is the cause for the cognition of the word-meaning such as "pot. However, for the cognition that "the bringing has the pot as its object," both [the knowledge of power and the knowledge of co-utterance] are causes; since this would involve complexity (*gaurava*) in having two causes, it serves as an illustration according to the principle of being a cause for that [cognition]. [Regarding the phrase] "of the causality of the knowledge of the linguistic function (*śabdavṛtti*)."

The meaning is: "of that which is the function of the word, namely its being the cause of the cognition of the object. He says "and this is appropriate" by means of the very logic of [the term] "cause" (taddhetu). "Mātram" means "in its entirety" (kārtsyena). By that...

This is a summary of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) concerning both the meaning of individual words (*padārtha*) and the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). Regarding the aspect of syntactic relation (*anvayāṃśa*): even in the previously raised position that the function (*vṛtti*) residing in the word which is conducive to the cognition of the sentence-meaning [is the same as that for the word-meaning], this is the underlying intention: for those who hold that the sentence-meaning is indicated (*lakṣya*) by the word, or for those who hold that the power (*śakti*) of the words resides in the related (*anvita*), how can there be a resolution? For, since the sentence-meaning is not present beforehand, it is impossible to grasp the function [of the word with respect to that meaning]. Now, once the word-meanings have been presented by the words, through the assistance of the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣājñāna*)— [The text continues: ...[the sentence-meaning is understood]. Therefore, the view that the sentence-meaning is indicated by the word is untenable. Nor is it possible to assume a distinct function for the sentence-meaning, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, the sentence-meaning must be understood through the power of the words themselves, and thus the theory that the power of words resides in the related (*anvitābhidhānavāda*) is established. This is the sense of the verse. Regarding the term "verbal cognition" (*śābdabodha*): it is called "verbal" (*śābda*) because it arises from words (*śabda*), and it is called "cognition" (*bodha*) because it is a form of knowledge (*jñāna*). It is not a mere recollection (*smṛti*), because it possesses the unique characteristic of being produced by the knowledge of the relation between a word and its object (*padapadārthasaṃbandhajñānajanya*). Furthermore, it is not a case of inference (*anumāna*), because it does not depend on the knowledge of a logical mark (*liṅga*). Nor is it a case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it lacks the contact of the senses (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*). Thus, it is a distinct category of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As for the phrase "regarding the aspect of syntactic relation": this refers to the fact that the cognition of the sentence-meaning is not merely the cognition of isolated word-meanings, but rather the cognition of the mutual connection (*samanvaya*) between them. This is what is meant by the expression "in the aspect of syntactic relation. Finally, regarding the statement "even in the previously raised position": this refers to the objection that if the function of the word is restricted to its own meaning, then the sentence-meaning—which is not the direct object of that function—could never be cognized. The response is that although the word-meaning is primary, the sentence-meaning is understood through the process of *tātparya* (intentional import), where the meanings of the words, when combined and supported by expectancy, proximity, and compatibility, lead to the comprehension of the unified sentence-meaning. Thus, the theory of the power of words residing in the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) remains the most consistent explanation.

Even if the meaning of the sentence is thus presented, that cognition is not verbal because it is not presented through a *vṛtti* (direct denotation or indication); therefore, the apprehension of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) occurs in the interim. If it is argued that this is like the case where a person who previously did not know the specific river named Haridrā hears the sentence "There is a hamlet on the Haridrā river," and at that very moment, through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "river," he apprehends the primary power (*śakti*) of the word "Haridrā" as referring to that specific river, and consequently understands the bank as being connected to it by means of the gender/signifier (*liṅga*) of the word "river"—then this is exactly the same for us as well.

He speaks according to the view of the Anvitābhidhānavādins, beginning with "yadi" (if) and "ajñātā eva" (unknown indeed). The ellipsis is "the word-potency is known indeed. [Now, one might object—] he says "nanu" (but surely) in order to provide a resolution through an alternative position regarding the doubt that the sentence-meaning is something previously unknown. "By the mind" means by the mind accompanied by the linguistic usage of elders. "Like the word-meaning" means like the apprehension of potency with respect to the word-meaning. "Its apprehension" means the apprehension of potency.

This is the intended meaning: Just as the determination of the primary denotative power (*śakti*) occurs through the usage of elders by means of the mind, so too here, when the presentation of word-meanings has occurred through words, their presentation by the mind is not untenable; however, since mental cognition would otherwise be unavoidable in the form of doubt, there is a preference for verbal [cognition]. But in the case of the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*), because there exists a determinative factor such as an inferential mark (*liṅga*), no doubt arises. 61/2 (661/2)

He states another alternative in the manner beginning with "from the standpoint of the actual entity" (*vastutaḥ*) and so forth: "—2 *vastutastu* —2. "—2 *prathamam* —2" means not after the cognition of the word-meaning through the power of the word (*padaśakti*). "—2 *pratyekam* —2" means for each individual word-meaning. "—2 *iyameva* —2" means that when the presentation of the word-meaning has occurred through the words, and the presentation of the sentence-meaning occurs by means of the mind, there is the apprehension of *lakṣaṇā* (indication); such is the meaning of "this very [process]. The reading is "two alternatives" (*pakṣadvayam*). Its meaning is that it consists of the forms of *padasphoṭa* (word-sphoṭa) and *vākyasphoṭa* (sentence-sphoṭa).

In the alternative reading *padapratyakṣam*, the meaning is quite clear. Regarding the phrase "from the arising" (*utpatteḥ*), the word "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "At once" (*ekadā*) means simultaneously. Because it is indeed divisible (*sakhaṇḍatvāt*), he says "collection of phonemes" (*varṇasamūha*). "Collection of those" (*tatsamūha*) means a collection of words (*padasamūha*). "In that" (*tasmin*) refers to the subsequent phoneme. "Perception of what follows that" (*taduttarapratyaya*) means the perception of the phoneme following that. "Possessing that specific phoneme" (*viśiṣṭatadvarṇavattvam*) means the state of possessing a subsequent phoneme qualified by the preceding phonemes. (Now, the indivisible *sphoṭa*.)

"—'An undivided part' (akhaṇḍapakṣa) means that [the sentence] is indivisible externally through the distinction of phonemes, words, and sentences. —'The meaning is that [it] does not exist' means that words do not appear within the sentence."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the very cognition—"I hear the letter *ka*" or "the letter *va* has been recited"—is the proof [for the existence of letters]? To this, he says: "In each of those letters... [etc.]. [Objection: But even so, [this is not correct], because the perception [of pitch, etc. is explained simply through the superimposition of a specific universal (*vaijātya*) residing in the conjunctions with air (*vāyusaṃyoga*), which is what is actually manifested by the pitch (*tāratva*) and so forth. [Response: It would not be so; for the principle is that "the effect follows its cause" (*taddhetor*). This is the intended meaning. Thus, it is established that [the word] is partless (*akhaṇḍa*). Furthermore, it is stated in the *Kaustubha* and other works that even the letters themselves are not necessary under these two views.
—2By accepting the sphoṭa consisting of phonemes (varṇasphoṭa)—2; —2of those—2phonemes—2—2it is common—2.

If it is argued that there is no unity in the cognition "saro rasa" and so forth because the formation of a collective representation (samūhālambana) occurs in the very same sequence as the impressions produced by the individual experiences, we say: no.

Because there is no evidence for a rule that knowledge produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) must occur sequentially. "Manifested by sound" (*nādābhivyaṅgya*) means manifested by the phonemes (*varṇa*) which are themselves manifested by sound. For this very reason he says, "of the phonemes. For this very reason [he says], "because they are manifested in various ways," such as through the universal of phonetic quality (*gatva*) and so forth. "Non-acceptance of its excess" means non-acceptance of a distinction within the *sphoṭa*. And thus, "in each being a manifester" means in each [phoneme] being a manifester. "In the locus of its own cognition" [is the meaning].

Just as in the case of the word "ghaṭa," the letter *ṭ* has as its object that cognition of *ṭ* which arises in the moment that serves as the locus for the cognition of *gha*; thus, there is no fault such as the impossibility of word-cognition. [The phrase] "because it is appropriate" implies "in your own view. Furthermore, he states the parsimony [of this view]: "that being so... and so forth.

The meaning is this: having accepted the *sphoṭa*, one might argue that its status as a cause depends on its being the grasper of the capacities residing in various synonyms (*paryāya*). However, there is greater parsimony (*lāghava*) in accepting its status as a cause simply by virtue of being the grasper of capacity. Therefore, the cumbersome *sphoṭa* should not be accepted. [Note: *tattve* = "in its being"; *hetutve* = "in its being a cause"; *gauravāt* = "due to complexity," i.e., due to the complexity of the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*); *padārthānām* = "of the word-meanings," i.e., those whose nature is *sphoṭa*; the meaning of "by this" (*etena*) is stated as "in the synonyms" (*paryāyeṣu*); the proof for that is stated as "not from sound" (*na āditi*): The meaning of "by this" (*etena*) is stated as "in the synonyms" (*paryāyeṣu*). He states the proof for that as "not from sound" (*na āditi*).

And thus, there is a difference in power (*śakti*) due to the difference in delimiters (*avacchedaka*). [This occurs] in the *Varṇamālā*—that is, in the collection of phonemes (*varṇa-samudāya*). Otherwise—that is, if, according to the aforementioned method, every *sphoṭa* were real as a phoneme—it would follow that [the phonemes are merely] for the sake of attaining the goal (*upeya-pratipatty-artha*). [This is stated in] the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-kārikā* (verse 69). This is a qualification of the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Thus he says: "for the sake of attaining the goal. [This is explained] in the *Ānandavallī*.

In the *Bhṛguvallī* (the third chapter of the *Taittirīyopaniṣad*), following the questions posed by Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, after his father Varuṇa had stated that "Brahman consists of food," "Brahman consists of vital breath," and so forth, it is heard [in the scripture]: "Brahman is the tail, the support. Herein is the meaning: because it is a transformation of the essence of food (*annarasa*), the body is denoted by the word "food" (*anna*). By this, the delusion regarding the selfhood of things other than the body—such as sons, wives, and the like—is dispelled.

Having observed its origination and so forth, when the question was asked again and it was stated that Brahman consists of breath (*prāṇamaya*), the non-selfhood of the external [body] was established by teaching the Self as qualified by breath and the rest; having further observed that even for that [body], such a state of being an object of experience does not belong to the breath but rather to the mind alone, when the question was asked again and it was stated that [Brahman] consists of mind (*manomaya*), the very same result as previously mentioned was established.

It was prepared. Of that too, when it was consecrated with the *āśis* mantra, the food became threefold: that which was coarse became feces; that which was middling became flesh; and that which was subtle (*aṇīyaḥ*) became the mind.

Thus, because the scripture mentions "origination" (*utpatti*), when asked again, it says "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). Here, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) means that by which one knows; it is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Therefore, the Self as qualified by the internal organ—which possesses the modification (*vṛtti*) called intellect (*buddhi*)—is taught to be "consisting of consciousness. Since that [Self] also exists as such only by being conditioned by its modification, when asked again, it says "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*). Thereupon, the Self as qualified by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that manifests bliss is taught to be "consisting of bliss."

Since that [bliss] as well is indeed qualified by limiting adjuncts (sopādhika), it is said: "The tail, the foundation, is Brahman. And their status as sheaths (kośatva) is due to their similarity to the sheath of a sword, in that they externally cover the Self situated within. That which is designated as the "tail"—the Truth, Knowledge, Infinite Brahman, which serves as the support for the Ānandamaya—is the primary foundation and locus of the "Brahman."

If it is asked: "How can it be that in the Vyāsa-sūtra (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.13), 'The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of the repetition,' etc., the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is presented as the primary subject?"—the answer is that this is clear from the commentary on that [sūtra], which states: "Because the word *ānandamaya* has its purport (*tātparya*) upon the word *brahman* heard in the remainder of that same passage" (Brahma-sūtra Śāṅkara-bhāṣya, Adhikaraṇa on the One Consisting of Bliss, p. 190). [Regarding the phrase] "because of being a refuter": for this very reason, some propose the suffixes *sum*, *it*, *iyar*, *siman*, and *yu*.

Therefore it has been said: "The means [of knowledge] are for those who are being instructed" (Vākyapadīya, Kāṇḍa II, verse 238). And likewise: regarding grammar as a means—specifically, regarding the knowledge of the produced [sphoṭa]. Regarding that knowledge: the meaning is "of that knowledge," namely, of the knowledge of the sphoṭa which is the goal, and which arises from the knowledge of the division between base and suffix produced by the study of grammar. Such knowledge of the sphoṭa is the direct means to [attaining] heaven and so forth; or, indirectly, it is a means to those [ends] by way of the purification of the body.

By the phrase "tadvārami" (Vākyapadīya, Brahmakāṇḍa, verse 16), that [meaning] is indicated through a traditional succession. Regarding the term "kevalām": regarding the example "the line-drawn gavaya"—just as someone instructs another by means of a drawing, saying, "This is a gavaya," and that intelligent person, while mentally grasping that "this is not a gavaya," realizes that this must surely be something possessing hands, feet, a tail, and so forth, similar to the lines [of the drawing], and concludes that some sentient being is a gavaya.

Similarly, when one perceives—according to the aforementioned method—that there is no denotable meaning in the stems (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) as analyzed by grammar, one grasps that the *sphoṭa*, which is distinct [from them], possesses the denotable meaning, just like words similar to it. This is the meaning of the maxim (one should accept "pādārtha" or "padyārtha" in place of "nyāyārtha"). 91/2 (691/2).

Now, regarding the dilemma as to whether the property of being a *sphoṭa* resides in the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves, such as the letter *ka*, or rather in the conjunctions of air (*vāyu-saṃyoga*) that manifest them—the author states the refutation of the first alternative with the words "the letter *ka*" (*kakāra iti*), and of the second with the words "the *ka*-series" (*kādīti*). In the root text, the phrase "of the imagined" (*kalpitānām*) refers to the conjunctions of air. The term "of another" (*anyasya*) expresses the sense of the genitive case; the meaning is that [the *sphoṭa*] resides in the conjunctions of air (*vāyu-saṃyoga-niṣṭha*).

"—Because of oneness."—The sense is that, likewise, in a single substratum (*dharmin*), the conventional usage of contradictory distinctions such as "acute" (*udātta*) and "grave" (*anudātta*), as well as the conventional usage of "origination" and so forth, would not be possible [if it were eternal]. "And that"—meaning eternality. This is because of the maxim: "Who could destroy later that which is stable and one for such a long time? Its object is the object of non-differentiating recognition (*abhedapratyabhijñā*); it is not, however, the absence of difference relative to some *ga*-sound residing in the universal *gatva*.

Even if one resolves [the objection] by asserting that the genus (*gati*) and so forth are not distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), he states the resolution regarding the fact that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has as its object an individual distinct [from the genus]: "Even in the case of the individual-part" (*vyaktyaṃśe 'pi*)—meaning "of that which has the nature of being existent while previously being non-existent. If the qualifier were not employed, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying the conventional usage of "origination" even to eternal things such as the Self (*ātman*). If the qualificand were not employed, there would be the undesirable consequence of applying that usage to a jar or the like—which was previously non-existent—even if it were still non-existent now. Therefore, both are employed. Furthermore, since phonemes (*varṇa*) lack prior non-existence, they do not possess the quality of having been produced (*utpannatva*).

[Objection: But is not utterance (*uccāraṇa*) also just a production (*nirvartana*) by means of the operation of the palate, lips, and so forth? To this he says: "The state of being uttered" (*uccāritatva*). [He explains: "Sound" (*dhvani*) means sound in the form of the conjunction with the primary air (*prākṛtavāyu*). [The phrase] "by way of succession" (*paramparayā*) means through the relation of being manifested by its own substratum (*svāśrayavyaṅgyatva*). He speaks of [production] and so forth as if they were direct, by means of superimposition; thus he says: "directly" (*sākṣāt*). [The phrase] "that too" (*tad api*) means "like the state of being an error" (*bhramatvavat*).

The meaning is as follows: just as you accept the erroneous nature of the non-difference between the individual [phoneme] and the cognition "this is the letter *ka*," I likewise accept the erroneous nature of [the notions of] production and so forth regarding the aspect of direct relation. Regarding the phrase "lack of evidence" (*mānābhāva*): in the case of sound consisting of substance (*dravyātmaka-śabda*), there is an acceptance of *dhvani* (articulatory sound) because there is the mental apprehension of its producer, such as the effort of the vocal organs. Regarding the phrase "the postulation of the relationship between the preventer and the prevented" (*pratibandhyapratibandhakabhāvakalpanā*): he concludes the illustration with the word "thus" (*evam*).

He states the position of other logicians (*tārkika*)—namely, "And thus"—as follows: "In this way, there are five types of *vyakti-sphoṭa*s. (101/2) (701/2) [Note: This refers to the *jāti-sphoṭa*]. Now, one might object: according to the aforementioned method, since one must accept numerous *vyakti-sphoṭa*s for every instance of a jar or the like due to the distinction between various individual phonemes, words, and sentences, such an approach is cumbersome (*gaurava*). Therefore, rather than that, and out of parsimony (*lāghava*), one should instead maintain that it is the universals (*jāti*) residing within those phonemes, words, and sentences that possess the expressive power (*vācakatva*). To address this, following the method stated by Vopadeva, he says in the root-text: "If [the universal] were the denotable object (*śakyatva*)," etc. (Vai.Si.Kā.)

71) Just as there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in [accepting] the universal (*jāti*) as the denotable (*śakya*) or the expressed (*vācya*), let parsimony be observed—that is, seen—in [accepting] the universal as the expressive (*sakta*) or the signifier (*vācaka*). This is according to the aforementioned method; that is, by not accepting individual phonemes (*varṇa*) and instead resorting to the view that universals such as "g-ness" (*gatva*) reside in the *sphoṭa*. Thus it is said: "This is that."

The point is this: just as the Bhaṭṭas and you yourself accept the oneness and eternality of the phoneme (*varṇa*) by the force of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of its non-difference, so too, through the oneness of the *sphoṭa*, there would arise an appearance of non-difference between the *ga* and *ha* sounds, since they are of the nature of that [single *sphoṭa*]. [Notes: - "By those who maintain the eternality of phonemes" refers to the Bhaṭṭas. - "Having superimposed" means upon the *sphoṭa*. - "Because it is possible as a property" means because it is established as such. - "By cognition" means for the sake of a uniform cognition. - "By delimitation" means by way of exclusion.

The specification of the delimitor of the objecthood (*karmatāvacchedaka-nirdeśa*). —2 By way of being its delimitor—2 means by way of entering the scope of the delimitor of the causal status (*hetutāvacchedaka-kukṣi-praviṣṭatayā*). The meaning is: "by the delimitor of the delimiting property" (*avacchedakatāvacchedakena*). —2 Regarding "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhi*)—2: the sense is that, in that case, even by way of being the delimitor of the effect-status of a staff (*daṇḍa-kāryatāvacchedakatva*), the establishment of a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth would not occur. —2 Regarding "its delimitor" (*tadavacchedikā*)—2: the meaning is that it alone is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*vācakatāvacchedaka*). —2 Regarding "manifestor" (*abhivyañjikā*)—2.

Just as a specific form [such as roundness] manifests a particular universal such as "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), so too it is specifically the particularity of the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) that manifests a particular universal. Thus, from the difference in sequence arises the difference in universals; from that difference arises the difference in the cognitions that serve as the cause; and from that difference arises the difference in verbal cognition—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*): although the universal of the phoneme is in fact one, the intended meaning is that there is a difference in universals due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as being a *tāra-mantra* and so forth. 111/2 (711/2)

"—lest there be [the fault of] non-restriction. And thus, since the contingency [of the fault] is equal, the intent of the objection is: "Why should not the individual phonemes themselves be the denoters? "—by way of being the meaning of the etymological derivation (*yogārthatayā*). This is because of the etymological analysis: "that by which the object is clearly manifested" (*sphuṭayate 'rtho 'nayā*). [This refers to] the acceptance that multiple phonemes possess the capacity to manifest [the word-meaning]. "—established by the means of cognition that apprehends the substratum (*dharmigrāhakamānasiddha*). The meaning is: because it is established as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the causality of the aforementioned conforming cognition. "—it must be accepted."*

In their view, it should be understood that only the *dhvanis* possess the power of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*). He provides the authoritative support for adopting the position that individual phonemes (*varṇavyakti*) are themselves *dhvanis* with the words "For it has been said" (*uktam hi*), [referring to] the first chapter (*ullāsa*), verse 121/2 (721/2).

"—Brahman alone is the universal class (*jāti*). And this has also been stated by Hari [Bhartṛhari] in the *Vākyapadīya* (III. Jāti-saṃdeha-kārikā 33): "It is existence itself (*sattā*) [that appears as various classes], due to the difference of the relata," and so forth. Here, this should be understood: because linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) has no beginning, the beginninglessness of the stream [of words] must be accepted by others [the opponents] for the word, just like the sky and such. In that regard, there is economy (*lāghava*) in accepting a single eternal word rather than postulating an infinite number of words. For just as gold remains the reality even when modifications such as earrings and the like arise.

Thus, the word-sphoṭa alone, which pervades all particular instances, is the reality. Thus, the word-sphoṭa alone, which pervades all particular instances, is the reality. In this context, the term *sphoṭa* is well-known in the Vedas (*śruti*) as referring to Brahman. That Brahman has the nature of sound is well-established in the Vedas. [The phrase] "the real part is the genus (*jāti*)" is used because that [genus] is eternal. [The phrase] "the unreal" is used because those [particulars] are non-eternal. [The phrase] "qualified by the unreal" means that the individual (*vyakti*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the unreal; [the word-sphoṭa] is delimited by it—meaning, it is conditioned (*upahita*) by it.

—2 *Brahmatattvam* —2. Brahman itself is the reality (*tattva*), that which constitutes the ultimate truth (*paramārthabhūta*). The mention of the word "substance" (*dravya*) is an illustration intended to include other categories as well. —2 "How then? —2. This is to be construed with the word "Kaiyaṭa. —2 *Brahmadarśane* —2. In the philosophical system (*darśana*) that propounds Brahman, that is, in the doctrine (*mata*)—meaning, in the Vedānta doctrine. —2 "It is based on ignorance (*āvidyaka*)" —2. And in this view, it is entirely logical that the universal (*jāti*) such as "cowness" (*gotva*), being constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*), is unreal. 131/2 (731/2)
In the root [text]: "The reality of sound (*śabdatattva*). (Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-kārikā 74). The word *tat* denotes the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-vastu*). As stated by Hari:

"Self (*ātman*), thing (*vastu*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), body (*śarīra*), and thatness (*tattva*)—these are synonyms for this [reality]. It is traditionally held that *tattva* is thus [defined as] 'that' (*tat*) and 'eternal' (*nitya*). (Vākyapadīya III, Dravyasamuddeśa, verse 1).

The inner, partless essence of consciousness, consisting of both word and meaning, undivided, is the *śabdatattva* (the reality of sound); that alone is called *parāvāk* (the supreme speech) and *śabdabrahman* (the Brahman of sound). It is indeed Brahman; it is like Brahman. To the one whose nature is full, to the one whose will is unimpeded, I shall unfold [this grammar]—the word "I" is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. This is a statement from the Upanishads. That very same [reality], when it pertains to the portion of its formal manifestation (*prakriyā*), is called *avidyā* (ignorance). As it was said by Bhartṛhari: "Because the system of the meaning of the treatise exists for the sake of ultimate worldly usage."

The systems of exposition in the scriptures are intended solely for the instruction of the ignorant; therefore, their purpose is such that they are unable to express the state of being endowed with the scripture directly. Consequently, he says, "In the scriptures... (Vākyapadīya, Kāṇḍa II, verse 233), meaning that it is ignorance itself that is described in the scriptures through the various distinctions of its systems of exposition.

If it is argued that, in this case, recourse to the methodological framework (*prakriyā*) of the scriptures—which present ignorance (*avidyā*)—would be something to be disregarded by discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*), [we reply: it has been stated by Hari: "But ignorance, devoid of scriptural conceptualization, manifests itself" (Vākyapadīya 2.233). By the destruction of ignorance, the manifestation of ignorance—which is free from the conceptualization of scripture and devoid of the elaboration (*prapañca*) of scriptural methodology—becomes manifest. And thus, the meaning is that ignorance itself is the means (*upāya*) to knowledge (*vidyā*).

Just as an effect, which exists in a subtle form within its cause, becomes manifest when its own causal complex (*sāmagrī*) comes together, so too does knowledge (*vidyā*) become manifest upon the dissolution of ignorance (*avidyā*); such is the intended meaning. —2 Commencement —2 —Origination— Of the yogic [subject], namely, the object which is the nature of Brahman. For the sake of unimpeded accumulation—that is, for the sake of unimpeded movement. 14.
